<meta>This entry describes the physical exterior binding of the manuscript, which serves as the protective housing for the handwritten pages within.</meta>

The exterior of this volume features a <term>binding</term><note>The protective cover of a book, consisting of the boards and the spine.</note> crafted from dark brown leather along the spine and decorative paper on the front and back covers. The <term>leather spine</term> is reinforced with raised horizontal bands, which were traditionally used to cover the cords where the pages are sewn together. A small, red leather title label is affixed to the spine, bordered with intricate <term>gold-tooled decoration</term><note>A process where gold leaf is pressed into the leather using heated brass stamps.</note> in a zig-zag pattern. 

The gilt-stamped text on the label has faded significantly over time, leaving only a few fragments of what was likely a formal title in Latin:

The front cover is finished with <term>marbled paper</term><note>Paper decorated with multicolored, swirling patterns that resemble marble stone.</note> in a "snail" or "curl" pattern. This design displays vibrant swirls of light blue, ochre yellow, and terracotta red-brown. Such decorative papers were a popular and elegant choice for high-quality bookbindings in the 18th and 19th centuries.

To you, MOST SERENE PRINCE, I offer this book, which—to confess frankly—I had decided to dedicate openly to no mortal, but silently to Him alone <note>original: "Soli Illi"; a reference to God</note> to whom all people owe everything. For throughout the entire time I spent composing it, and even beyond that, I very truly intended in my mind to keep my name hidden. This is even evident from the writing style itself: since it is expressed in the first person as if [the soul] were speaking about itself (in the manner of those in meditation <note>The author refers to a tradition of philosophical or spiritual "meditations," where the "I" represents a universal human soul rather than a specific individual.</note>), it does not seem to allow the reader to modestly form an idea of a specific person identifying themselves by name. But when those among my friends whom I know to be most accomplished later urged me with various reasons to declare my name—even though there was no longer time or space in the discourse to change the style—I consented, because the process has been an honest one, without any effort to either please or displease anyone. However, just as the reasoning of others pushed <note>original: "impule-"; continued on the next page as "impulerunt"</note> me to this point—

To you, MOST SERENE PRINCE, I offer this book, which—to confess frankly—I had decided to dedicate openly to no mortal, but silently to Him alone <note>original: "Soli Illi"; a reference to God</note> to whom all people owe everything. For throughout the entire time I spent composing it, and even beyond that, I very truly intended in my mind to keep my name hidden. This is even evident from the writing style itself: since it is expressed in the first person as if [the soul] were speaking about itself (in the manner of those in meditation <note>The author refers to a tradition of philosophical or spiritual "meditations," where the "I" represents a universal human soul rather than a specific individual, much like the style of Descartes.</note>), it does not seem to allow the reader to modestly form an idea of a specific person identifying themselves by name. But when those among my friends whom I know to be most accomplished later urged me with various reasons to declare my name—even though there was no longer time or space in the discourse to change the style—I consented, because the process has been an honest one, without any effort to either please or displease anyone. However, just as the reasoning of others pushed <note>original: "impule-"; continued on the next page as "impulerunt" (driven/pushed)</note> me to this point—

This is even evident from the style itself, which, being expressed in the first person as if the mind were speaking about itself (after the manner of those in meditation <note>This refers to the "meditative" style of philosophy made famous by René Descartes, where the author writes from the perspective of their own internal thought process.</note>), does not seem to allow for modestly presenting to the reader the identity of a person designating himself by his own name. # EPISTLE

me; so my own reasoning led me, being willing, to entrust this work to the patronage of **Your Name, Prince**, since you have deigned to embrace me and my affairs with your favor, and under whose rule and protection these writings had their origin. And although I know that you chiefly desire solid **Truth** and **Piety**, which are drawn from the **Sacred** oracles <note>A common scholarly way of referring to the Bible.</note>, and it might not seem particularly appropriate to propose **Philosophical Speculations** at a time when, after the loss of the **most illustrious** family members who were so dear, military fury has devastated **Your Duchy of Zweibrücken** <note>original: "Ducatum Tuum Bipontinum." Bipontum is the Latin name for Zweibrücken, a state within the Holy Roman Empire.</note>; nevertheless, even **Divine** revelation itself calls us, even in the midst of calamities, to natural considerations—indeed, to the governance of the stork, the oxen, and other animals and elements—by which, being recalled to God, we may find Him merciful. 

How much less, therefore, should a serious return to our own Mind (which the sacred pages also emphasize) be judged out of place? For in the Mind, the **Divine Mind** has not left itself **without witness** <note>original: "ἀμάρτυρον" (amartyron). This is a direct reference to the Book of Acts 14:17, suggesting that God's presence is evident in the structure of human thought.</note>; there, more solid and eternally lasting goods are shown, compared to which all other things so vanish that when we are deprived of them, they affect us less. There also the origin of true evils lies hidden, and can be so uncovered that it becomes clear that external calamities should not be counted among the primary ones; but rather those evils by which minds are confused and scattered by the tumult of objects and passions. This evil must be remedied without delay if...

<meta>catchword: soluto [dissolved/released]</meta>

# D E D I C A T O R Y.

...be judged as less significant; rather, once the physical body has dissolved, let us aspire toward lasting comforts through the **Eternal Mind** <note>original: "Æterna Mente." This refers to the divine aspect of the intellect that the author believes survives physical death.</note>. God has laid these things open in the very nature of our Mind. Would that Christians had paid attention to them! For they have now bid farewell to the dictates of both **Nature** and **Scripture**—an observation you yourself are accustomed to make and grieve over—being instead consumed by a single concern for the "thick mass" of material things that is bound to collapse <note>The author uses the phrase "crassæ molis" (thick mass) to describe the heavy, temporary nature of the material world compared to the lightness of the spirit.</note>. 

Perhaps they would have drawn more solid lessons for their own instruction from these natural truths than from those things which most **Guides of Souls** <note>original: "Animarum Ductores." A critical reference to the clergy or religious leaders of the time.</note> poorly tear from the **Divine Codex of Scripture**, interpret even worse, and most wretchedly adapt and force upon the people. The intellect and conscience of these men are not illuminated even by **natural light** <note>original: "lumine... naturali." In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to basic human reason and moral intuition that God provides to all people.</note> or righteousness. For although these men—along with others who pursue studies in the customary manner—are said to have acquired in the schools *a knowledge of divine and human things insofar as it can be obtained through the light of nature* (which is how they define their **Philosophy**), they actually gather nothing there but the sterile trifles of sophisticated hair-splitting.

As a result, they are rendered more capable of corrupting everything else—or of fostering what is already corrupted for the future—than they would have been otherwise. There are few who emerge from such schooling with their reason intact, even if they had brought a great deal of it with them. Those who do escape and manage to obtain more certain principles of **Nature** and reason usually end up striking other rocks; specifically, they descend into trivialities <note>original: "minuta objecta."</note> that would have been better left alone, and there they spend the whole of their lives...

# D E D I C A T O R Y  E P I S T L E.

...they spend their time, or even the chief part of it, in the speculation of these things, while that which is greatest and most necessary is handed over to neglect and ruinous oblivion. When Divine grace began to free me, in whatever way, from this sea of a thousand rocks, I hung up this **votive tablet** <note>original: "Tabellam." A reference to the ancient custom where sailors who survived a shipwreck would hang a "tabula votiva" (votive plaque) in a temple to thank the deity who saved them. Poiret uses his book as this symbolic tablet.</note>—saved from the shipwreck, or at least from the peril of shipwreck—for my Liberator. In this work, I have attempted to designate, as far as I was permitted, what is right, what is off the path or devious, and what of good or evil is to be found in such ways. I do this for the caution of those who are of a freer disposition and who aspire toward truer things, being **slaves to no man's opinions** <note>original: "nullarum ullius cogitationum mancipia." This reflects the early Enlightenment ideal of intellectual independence from scholastic or ecclesiastical authority.</note>. 

If I should be of benefit to some, there will be cause to give thanks to the **Author of all good** <note>God.</note>. If not, it shall suffice for me to have candidly intended something of good, and to have taken that occasion to testify publicly that I cherish a Prince who is a lover of solid and fruitful **Truth**, while I truly profess myself to be,

*Most Illustrious Prince,*

->*Your Most Serene Highness’s*<-

->*most humble and most observant Devotee,*<-

->**P. POIRET.**<-

<summary>In this conclusion to his dedication, Poiret presents his philosophical work as a "votive tablet" offered in gratitude for being saved from intellectual error. He emphasizes his commitment to independent thought and his admiration for the Prince's love of truth.</summary>

# A D M O N I T I O N S . <note>original: "Monenda." These are points the author wishes the reader to keep in mind before starting the text.</note>

My Reader, do not be frightened by the bulk of this book. It is a great evil when a subject, often explained elsewhere, is continuously encrusted only by an increase in words, or is re-presented with the order reversed and interpolated. *Perhaps here, where the subject matter is not so common, you will find nothing of the sort. In the meantime, he who is free from prejudices <note>original: "praejudiciis." In this context, Poiret refers to preconceived notions or biases inherited from traditional schooling.</note> might, for the sake of brevity, skip the entire first book and several chapters of the second; for they are spent more on destroying [old ideas] than on building up [new ones]. It is not a pleasant thing to clear away mud; I know that it was done there not without tedium, but also not without necessity—indeed, even by compulsion.* I have sometimes, though rarely, recounted the opinions of certain philosophers for no other reason than that their fame makes their harmful prejudices influential among many. I had to descend into **Scholastic** <term>Scholasticism: A medieval method of learning that emphasized dialectical reasoning and often became bogged down in complex, abstract categories.</term> trivialities several times so that those hindered by them might be set free. For it is especially for such people that these things were written. In other matters, I do not follow individual persons, but the signs of truth engraved by God in the depths of minds and leading to God—not so that I might subject Him, who is incomprehensible, to reason, but rather subject reason to Him, so that the testimonies of Himself which He left within reason may be revealed to His glory.

Therefore, I pay no heed to those who think it is not the role of genuine **Philosophy** to rise from natural notions and things to the knowledge and love of God. A diabolical strategy!—so that everyone aspiring to knowledge might vanish far away from God. I have attempted here to render that strategy void. Regarding the subject matter I have undertaken, I have written things which, back when I was still ignorant of them and was distressed by opposing prejudices and difficulties, I would have wished had been shown to me by others.

Furthermore, I care nothing for the thinness or, if you prefer, the **barbarity of my style**. <note>The author is apologizing for his "New Latin," which may lack the elegance of classical Cicero but is functional for philosophical debate.</note> I did not write for the ears, nor for those gasping for verbal tricks and feeding themselves on them, nor even for the contentious, who—simply because certain words are used in different senses in various places—have no grounds to claim either a contradiction or an ambiguity; since care was taken so that from the flow of the **discourse** <note>original: "discur-". This is a catchword, an 18th-century printing convention where the first syllable of the next page is printed at the bottom of the current one.</note> itself...

<vocab>Lector (Reader), Philosophia (Philosophy), Scholastica (Scholasticism), Deus (God), ratio (reason), scientia (knowledge/science), praejudicium (prejudice/preconception)</vocab>

<summary>In this preface, Poiret warns readers not to be intimidated by the book's size, explaining that much of the early text is dedicated to dismantling flawed Scholastic philosophy to make way for a God-centered "genuine philosophy." He defends his plain writing style and argues that the ultimate goal of all knowledge should be the love of God.</summary>

# A D M O N I T I O N S .

*...so that through the discussion, the unambiguous meaning of the term might be clear. If any further difficulties occur, I am certain that they—or at least most of them—will vanish upon repeated meditation. If anyone thinks they detect errors in these **demonstrations** <term>demonstration: In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to a rigorous logical proof that leads to a certain conclusion, often modeled after mathematical or geometrical reasoning.</term> and truly proves it, I will not resist; for I desire to love the truth because of its Divine source, without regard for myself, even if it opposes me. But I am certain that its more important parts are contained here. If you, Friend, can be carried toward God by these means, use them for this purpose; but if other ways are more convenient for you, and this one is not suitable, choose those others. But do not wish to disparage <note>original: "traducere." Meaning to misrepresent or speak ill of the methods used.</note> these means—which you might not be familiar with and which perhaps, contrary to your opinion, might be true and good—lest you thus oppose the many and genuine testimonies that are presented here concerning God and His wonders. Let this be said for the sake of truth itself. Farewell.*

->*Written at Annweiler <note>A town in the modern-day German state of Rhineland-Palatinate, near the Trifels Castle.</note> in the Palatinate-Zweibrücken <note>original: "Palatinatu Bipontino." A historical territory of the Holy Roman Empire. "Bipontinus" is the Latinized name for Zweibrücken, meaning "two bridges."</note>,*<-
->*November 30, 1675.*<-

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS
### ON
# GOD, THE SOUL, AND SIN.
## I N T R O D U C T I O N.

*1. The dignity and difficulty of the primary subject to be treated. 2. Diverse means. 3. Of which the latter belong to this place. 4. Things to be admitted. 5. Things to be excluded. 6. Division of the work into four Books.*

I. If it was well and wisely warned by the Wise King <note>A reference to King Solomon, the traditional author of the biblical book of Ecclesiastes. The specific reference is to Ecclesiastes 5:2: "Be not rash with your mouth... for God is in heaven and you are on earth."</note> that we should not be hasty with our words when we intend to speak before God, there is no doubt that when we must speak not only before Him, but also *about* Him, our thoughts and words must be most seriously weighed and cautiously uttered. To err in these matters is certainly no light thing. For what else could it be to attribute imperfections to the Supreme and Most Perfect Being <note>original: "Enti Summo, Perfectissimoque"</note>—which is no different from erring in these matters—than to deny His Nature, or to transform Him into an idol and cover Him with dishonor? To present God as deformed to oneself or to others is more serious and absurd for a person than if they were to present themselves poorly formed before God; which latter act, at the very least, is held as a fault of rashness.

II. There is no doubt that those who have followed God with due honor have also acknowledged Him as is fitting, and have strived to make Him known more and more to themselves and to others. But among the means by which they promoted this, they carefully distinguished those which consist of internal work and affection from those which are accomplished by reasoning <term>reasoning: "ratiocinio," the systematic logical process of reaching a conclusion.</term> and discourse, and they placed the former above the latter. Having embraced God in their own minds, they presented Him to others through similar labor to be accepted,

<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: qua-</meta>

<summary>The author introduces his philosophical inquiry into God, the Soul, and Sin, emphasizing the gravity of speaking accurately about the Divine. He distinguishes between internal spiritual devotion and logical reasoning, signaling that this work focuses on the latter.</summary>
<keywords>Theology, Philosophy of Religion, Solomon, Supreme Being, Divine Nature, logical reasoning, introduction</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the Introduction from page 1, completing the second point regarding those who have known God through inner experience and moving into the third and fourth points, which establish the author's philosophical approach and the scope of the work.</meta>

## I N T R O D U C T I O N.
<meta>catchword: similar,</meta>

insofar as—even without rational discourse—their way of living (a sign and effect of the internal influence and work of the Divine <term>Numen; a Latin term for the divine power or the presence of a deity</term>) was such that it revealed the beauty and decency of God (its efficient and exemplary cause), as well as the way of embracing and knowing Him, and the most certain way of advancing in that knowledge. Other things, if compared with those to which they devoted themselves continuously and without interruption, they used only rarely and occasionally, as being less primary and required. Indeed, it is notable that the few discourses they left behind are such that they cannot be rightly understood by those whose minds have not first been touched by the influence and operation of the Supreme Deity, and who do not seriously offer a mind ready to follow God so that they might later know Him more clearly. Therefore, whereas in that former way [of inner experience] there is all-encompassing security, in the latter way [of rational discourse], by contrast, much uncertainty and danger are often encountered by both the speaker and the listener of the arguments. For unless both are disposed as just mentioned—or at least strongly desire to be so disposed—it is true for both that *they became vain in their reasonings and discussions.* <note>original: "In ratiociniis & dissertationibus suis evanuerunt." This is a reference to the biblical Book of Romans 1:21, suggesting that intellectual inquiry without spiritual grounding leads to empty results.</note>

III. Nevertheless, it does not follow from this that we are so removed from God that we are not permitted to engage with Him through reason and speech based on innate principles. Rather, let us be stirred to compose our minds so that we may make the best and most useful use of these faculties, which He Himself certainly did not grant in vain. And since God Himself, the source of all good, wishes to grant such a thing: once the mists and clouds of corporeal phantasms <note>The author refers to mental images derived from the physical senses, which were thought to clutter the mind and prevent the perception of pure spiritual truth.</note>—and things even worse than these—have been driven away from the minds of those who are hindered and overwhelmed by them in conceiving spiritual things (and are sometimes quite troublesome), those things may be drawn out from the hidden depths of the mind which may serve, to some degree, in building or decorating a tabernacle for the uncreated mind <note>The "uncreated mind" refers to God, while the "created mind" refers to the human soul.</note> within the created mind.

IV. My intention in the following words is to briefly enough encompass those things which may excite clear ideas or concepts of God, the Supreme Being, and of His most excellent work, our soul, as well as of our perpetual adversary and enemy, namely evil or sin. However, it will not be necessary to recount every single detail in these matters, which would be a task of the greatest labor. Therefore, to keep ourselves within narrower limits, the following shall be excluded: (1) Regarding God, a formal demonstration of His existence (for which Descartes' *Meditations* <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), whose "Meditations on First Philosophy" was a foundational text for 17th-century thinkers. # I N T R O D U C T I O N.
<sig>A 2</sig>

...similar things, viewed more particularly in relation to things as they now exist:
(2) Regarding the **created mind** <note>The "created mind" refers to the human soul or intellect, which the author distinguishes from the "uncreated mind" of God.</note>, because it is not the primary object of this work, there will be no detailed explanation of its faculties, especially those that must be considered in relation to the body to which it is joined. V. These things being thus excluded, we take up God and those of His **attributes** which—if you except power in a certain sense—are conceived in such a way that, in conceiving them, one does not necessarily need to focus on the actual existence of creatures and their current state, even if the opportunity to think about them arises from considering such creatures. In this way, whatever is said about the created mind is mostly to be viewed insofar as examining it provides an opportunity to know God more clearly. Thus, there is no need for us to wander long outside our own mind and the ideas of various things within it; for whether they exist or do not exist outside of us is now a matter of indifference, since the notions of them alone, of which the mind is intimately conscious, are sufficient for our purpose. Regarding evil or sin, those things will be discussed separately which follow from what was said before and in a more general manner of treatment.

VI. To maintain some order, these matters will be arranged so that first, the clouds which prevent the mind from forming a true idea of **spiritual things** are cleared away. Once these are overcome, a general notion of both minds—namely, the uncreated and the created—will be proposed, along with the method of recognizing them in general, including their perfections and any imperfections. Third, this will be followed by a more specific derivation of God and the Created Mind, leaving the discussion of sin for the final section. These four topics, contained in four Books, will be presented as it pleases God.

III. Truly, it is a prejudice held by many that spiritual things are **unthinkable** <note>original: "incogitabiles"</note>—that is, they are of such a nature that they cannot be represented by thought, but exist beyond all thinking. Hence, whatever can be thought (precisely because it is being thought, and clearly so) is denied by these people to be part of the nature of spiritual things. The result is that, for them, a "spiritual nature" is nothing other than that which is neither conceived nor can be conceived. Of such a thing, I admit, no knowledge can be given. 

This is exactly the same way that the "forms" of bodies—which they call **substantial forms** <note>In older philosophy, "substantial forms" were the inner essences that made a thing what it was, often considered mysterious and hidden from the senses</note>—are imagined by their defenders to be so unthinkable that whatever is clearly conceived in bodies is denied the status of being a "form." Nothing remains but a void that cannot be known, decorated with the empty name of "forms," which they even admit are unknown to them. 

One may note (and I will occasionally follow this method of deriving less abstract points here and there, lest the rest of the work seem too thin and of no use), one may note, I say, the contagion of this disease in many people. For even in **Theological** matters, if something is explained in a way that can be understood with a new and easy clarity, some will often fear—because of that very evidence of clarity—that the truth might not be found there. Yet they persuade themselves that truth is present when obscurity and clouds of terminology wrap the matter so tightly that it cannot be understood, leaving room for an undue state of awe <note>original: "stupori", a state of being dazed or stunned by something incomprehensible</note>. 

So it is in practice: a very simple life—which is removed from the confusion of the crowd and from craftiness, just as clear ideas are removed from confused ones—is considered by the common folk to be "no life" at all. In general, anything clear, plain, easy, and simple—which, because of its natural harmony with our ability to understand, does not strike, disturb, or move us violently—is considered worthless. Instead, other unknown things must be substituted for reality, as these can be presumed to be greater and more wonderful. 

Although such a boast of **ignorance** might perhaps please some because it seems to have the appearance of sincerity, humility, and modesty (since it confesses its own defects so openly), if we are to speak the truth, it is to be feared that this is a sign of a mind that is both profane—not caring (to use sacred words) *to have God in its knowledge* <note>A reference to Romans 1:28</note>—and also proud and crude. Such a person, failing to notice the things that are within themselves, not only refuses to seem inferior or even equal to others who do know these things, but even wants to seem superior. They rejoice in trampling every kind of knowledge and saying to everyone: "You not only know nothing, just like me; but I have this advantage over you: I know that you and others know nothing, whereas you do not even know that."

...because they cannot know them in the same way they know bodies. When these people wish to rise to a knowledge of minds, out of a bad habit they immediately imagine some subtle bodily thing <note>This likely refers to the historical "ether" or a gaseous "spiritus" that occupied space, which the author argues is a category error.</note> which they take for the nature of the mind or spirit (for we use these words interchangeably). V. Finally, there are those who, because they see they cannot comprehend with the intellect all that is in minds, or can be in them—for instance, all the perfections in God, and all the faculties and variations in a created mind—denied for that reason that any knowledge of them exists. In this sense, it must be admitted that knowledge is not possible—not only of minds, but of any tiny body <term>corpuscula: literally "little bodies," referring to the smallest particles of matter</term>—if by "knowledge" one means something so adequate <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "adequate" knowledge meant a complete, exhaustive understanding of a thing's essence and all its properties.</note> that we are conscious of everything that is and can be in a thing. For perhaps not even an angel could determine all the particles of the smallest speck of dust, its motions, their degrees and paths (including possible ones), and similar things belonging to it. God indeed has adequate knowledge of it, since He perfectly knows every single thing within it and every way in which it can be affected. But since there is no reason to think that whatever knowledge a created mind can have of any thing should be considered as perfect as that which God has; and since God’s knowledge is adequate, there is no reason why any knowledge a created mind has should be presumed to be adequate. (But on this matter, see Book III, where God's knowledge is discussed). 

Just as it does not follow—even by their own admission—that no knowledge of bodies exists simply because they are conceived inadequately, so this reasoning does not prevent us from asserting that knowledge of spiritual things is possible. It may be a modest <note>original: "mediocrem"; meaning middling or moderate rather than "poor quality"</note> knowledge, not extending from first principles to the furthest recesses, but it is nonetheless truly knowledge, and not mere ignorance. It is a sign of pride to be unwilling to remain within modest limits, and to disdainfully reject everything unless it is granted to you to possess the highest degree.

VI. ### CHAPTER II.

*1. The second opinion, which is partly that of Hobbes. 2. It is refuted from his own hypotheses. 3. And from the truth of the matter. 4. Its cause and many effects, so that it might be countered.*

<margin>(a) See his Logic, chapter 11. Also Leviathan chapters 1, 11, 3, 34, 45, and in the appendix. And briefly, On the Citizen (De Cive) chapter 15, section 14.</margin>
I. Among those who harbor the opinion just rejected, Thomas Hobbes, the English Philosopher, stands out significantly. He denied not only the knowledge but even the existence of spiritual things, asserting that all things—even God himself—are bodies, or "extended" and measurable things, as he clearly states in the appendix to his *Leviathan*. <note>Hobbes's materialism argued that everything in the universe is physical matter. "Extended" refers to the philosophical concept of *extensio*: taking up physical space.</note> This man clung so stubbornly to his error (by which all true knowledge of God and piety is overturned) that he defiled all his writings with it. But since nature cannot be so thoroughly foresworn that it does not "return even if driven out with a pitchfork," <note>original: "furcâ expulsâ recurrat." This is a reference to the Roman poet Horace’s famous line: "Drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will ever hurry back."</note> it is for this reason that he discourses on these matters everywhere. Truly, he does not speak with one voice, but as if groping in the dark, he mixes diverse ideas so that if some are refuted, he might thrust others forward—as if from one severed head of a hydra, seven others might be reborn. He says that logical reasoning <note>original: "notitiam discursivam"</note> occurs through the combination of names, and that names are signs of thoughts; further, that all thoughts are either sensation or imagination, and that God is known by neither. Yet, he asserts the exact opposite where he affirms that God is a body, that every substance is a body, and that we move in God as an extended thing moves within another extended thing—all of which are things that *can* be imagined. Nevertheless, he still attributes names to God. He wishes these to be "insignificant voices" to which no thought corresponds; he claims that terms like *incorporeal substance* or *immaterial* (a) belong to this class of meaningless words, as can be found more than once in his work. Since these ideas have been a constant obstacle to a man considered so very subtle, it will be worth the effort to remove them, lest they also hinder others.

II. If any share this same opinion with him, they are easily convicted by their own hypotheses. Hobbes himself would not deny that spiritual things exist if he were reminded that nothing else is understood by them than "thinking things." Whether these differ from the body or not is a question for another place; let it suffice here to prove from his own words that the things known about them through reasoning or other means are not mere words. The argument is as follows: First, he says that words or names are signs of the mind’s thoughts. However, he attributes many such signs or names to God. Therefore, the knowledge of God (as a spiritual thing) consists not in words, but in thoughts. It no longer matters whether those thoughts are perfectly similar to God or not: whatever they may be, they are something beyond mere words. Nay, what is more, since he admits that God is not known by sense nor by imagination, it follows that that which is in the

# OF GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL

## CHAPTER II.

->*1. The second opinion, which belongs in part to Hobbes. 2. It is refuted based on his own hypotheses. 3. And from the truth of the matter. 4. Its cause and its many effects, which must be addressed.*<-

<margin>(a) See his *Logic*, chapter II; likewise *Leviathan*, chapters I, II, III, XXXIV, XLV, and in the appendix. And briefly in *De Cive*, chapter XV, section 14.</margin>

I. Among those who favor the opinion I have just rejected, Thomas Hobbes, the English Philosopher, stands out significantly. He denied not only the knowledge of spiritual things but even their very existence, asserting that all things—even God Himself—are bodies, or things that have extension and size, as he clearly states in the appendix to his *Leviathan*. This man clung so stubbornly to his error (an error by which all true knowledge of God and all piety is overturned) that he defiled all his writings with it. But since nature cannot be so thoroughly renounced that it does not "return even if driven out with a pitchfork," <note>original: "vel furcâ expulsa recurret." This is a reference to a famous line from the Roman poet Horace: *Naturam expelles furca, tamen usque recurret* (You may drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will always hurry back).</note> it happens that he discourses on these matters at length in many places. However, he does not stick to one story; rather, as if groping in the dark, he mixes together diverse ideas so that if one is refuted, he may thrust forward others—much like the heads of the Hydra, where if one is cut off, seven more are born in its place. He claims that logical reasoning occurs through the "combination of names," and that names are merely "signs of thoughts." He further claims that all thoughts are either "sensations" or "imagination," and that God is known by neither. Yet, he contradicts this when he asserts that God is a body and that every substance is a body, for he says we move in God "as extension moves within extension"—things which are certainly imaginable. Nevertheless, he still assigns names to God. He intends for these names to be meaningless sounds <note>original: "voces insignificantes." Hobbes argued that terms like "incorporeal substance" were literally "insignificant" or "meaningless" because they combined contradictory concepts.</note> to which no actual thought corresponds; he places terms like *incorporeal substance* or *immaterial* into this category, and such phrases (a) can be found in his work more than once. Since these ideas have been a constant obstacle even to a man considered to be most subtle, it will be worthwhile to remove them so they do not hinder others.

II. If there are any who share his opinion, it is easy to convince them using their own starting assumptions. Even Hobbes himself would not deny that "spiritual things" exist if he were reminded that we understand them to be nothing other than "thinking things." Now, whether these thinking things differ from the physical body or not is a question for another time; for now, let it suffice to prove—using his own logic—that the things we know about them through reasoning are not "mere words." The proof is as follows: First, he says that words or names are "signs of the mind's thoughts." Yet he attributes many such signs or names to God. Therefore, the knowledge of God (as a spiritual thing) does not consist in words alone, but in the thoughts those words signify. It does not matter now whether those thoughts are perfectly similar to God or not; whatever they are, they are something beyond mere words. Indeed, what is more: since he admits that God is not known by the physical senses or by the imagination, it follows that that which exists in the mind...

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...is in the mind, and signified by a name, to be a thought purer and higher than sense and imagination. Secondly, he asserts that the fact that God exists is known by nature: but no names, even the name of "God," are known by nature, or are demonstrable. That is to say, it is not evident from an inspection of nature by what specific sound God ought to be designated; and all names, as he says, exist by agreement. Therefore, that which can be known about God by nature is something beyond a mere name. Thirdly, since he says it is certain by nature that God exists, yet elsewhere—namely in his objections to the third of Descartes' *Meditations* (where, by comparing those objections with his other writings, it is clear he speaks his true mind)—he concedes it is uncertain whether any bodies, any sensible things, or any things fashioned by the imagination, actually exist. Since he says of all those things which are called into doubt by the Skeptics, *we acknowledge the truth of this meditation*, <note>original: "veritatem hujus meditationis agnoscimus." Hobbes is here agreeing with Descartes’ famous "Methodical Doubt," where one questions the existence of the physical world.</note> it follows that the knowledge of God which is certain to him is not contained in uncertain, corporeal words, provided that their very subject—all matter—is itself uncertain. From what has been conceded, we may, fourthly, conclude that there exists a knowledge not only of God, but of many things which are clearly not bodies, and that this knowledge is not merely verbal. A person knows for certain that he thinks, wills, and refuses (which is common to many), and meanwhile he does not know whether bodies, sensible things, or imaginable things exist, and consequently, neither does he know if voices and names exist. Therefore, there is a knowledge of a thing without a body or a name. Indeed, he is convinced by his own words that reasoning exists without sense, imagination, or names: *if we follow our senses without any other reasoning, we shall rightly doubt whether anything exists or not. If reasoning were the consequence of names, names of imagination, and imagination of senses, how will you demonstrate that certain things exist by not following the senses alone?* <note>The author is pointing out a "circular logic" trap in Hobbes's work: if all thought comes from senses, but senses are unreliable, we could never "reason" our way to certain truth.</note> Reasoning, therefore, does not belong to words—which are merely sounds and the movement of bodies—otherwise, in wishing to prove these points, you would presuppose the very things you are trying to prove through your reasoning, which would itself be a mere consequence of the senses. Nor does reasoning belong to the imagination, which he calls "decayed sense." But enough of these *ad hominem* <note>A Latin term meaning "against the man," referring to arguments that use an opponent's own specific claims against them.</note> arguments; indeed, I fear that these points, perhaps tedious to some, might discourage them from what follows, as if the rest of the work consisted only in the discussion of such trifles. Yet, because so many are deceived along with him, these things had to be said. Whatever else could be said about this Philosopher’s opinions regarding sensory and imaginary knowledge has been more than sufficiently refuted by these points, so there is no need to review them anew in the following sections.

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.
->B<-
<meta>catchword: words</meta>

...by application to paper? It is the behavior of brutes and parrots to produce sounds without a mind; such sounds have no use unless you become conscious of some thing through the occasion of them. But how often, during sleep or even while awake, do we find within ourselves a consciousness <note>The Latin *conscientia* here refers to "internal awareness" or "consciousness" rather than a moral conscience.</note> of many things without any words? This awareness, when we recognize it, exhibits both a spiritual reality and a non-verbal form of knowledge. And although the knowledge in our minds can be advanced or hindered by words, it is not proven that knowledge is completed by them. Rather, words serve to mark something that already exists in the soul; that internal thing is often stirred when words are present and remains quiet when they are absent.

IV. Among the chief causes of this mistaken opinion <note>Referring to the nominalist view that thinking is just "adding and subtracting names."</note> is that the mind does not pay enough attention to itself and its own actions. Instead, it flies out of itself with a certain levity and wanders among external things. Living among these externals, the mind hears nothing more highly praised than "knowledge"—especially regarding spiritual matters. Yet, because the mind cannot grasp this knowledge due to a lack of attention to its own nature, it comes to believe that knowledge exists only in the words it hears. From this source arises the fact that many people place their piety and their supposedly "spiritual" rituals in little prayers <term>preculis</term> <note>original: "preculis." A diminutive of *precibus* (prayers), often used dismissively to describe rote, formulaic, or superstitious recitations.</note>, or in words that must be bound to a specific time, number, or manner of being pronounced, chanted, or heard. It is also why we attempt to overwhelm the minds of infants with words from their very cradles. Furthermore, the countless quarrels of the learned and the excessive study of languages—so that a man might be able to name a thing in ten different ways without having truly understood it even once—flow from no other source.

From this also arises that never-sufficiently-deplored fact: that almost no one seeks knowledge (especially the knowledge of minds) within themselves. Instead, they think all knowledge lies hidden in books and in the authority of human words, which are the very foundations of scholarly brawls. When they desire to know something, they do nothing else but seek to burden their minds with the sayings and voices of others. They never return to themselves through pure, free, and unconstrained meditation, which is the goal of all study. Although those external things might sometimes contribute to meditation, they cause the greatest harm when one clings to them—just as standing still forever on a road prevents one from reaching the destination.

If anyone wishes to avoid these inconveniences, it is absolutely necessary that they abstract themselves from words. This is necessary not only when one wishes to attend to the private thoughts of one's own mind, but even when one attempts to calmly gather some fruit from the writings of others. For since people sometimes represent two different thoughts with a single word, or one thought with many different words, they often seem to be in opposition regarding the same matter when they are actually only fighting over words. Therefore, one should not pay as much attention to the words as to the thoughts the authors likely held, even if they did not express them aptly. Generally, it is almost certain that those who disagree about first principles, ideas, and their differences, are clashing only...

<header>RATIONAL THOUGHTS</header>

...to disagree in words, which would be most easily revealed if definitions were sought for the terms they use—definitions capable of exciting a clear idea in the mind. For example: **Hobbes** <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), an English philosopher famous for his materialist view that only physical matter exists.</note> says that there is no such thing as an *incorporeal substance*; we, on the other hand, say there is. Let us grant him his words for a moment, but let us pay attention to what each man actually has in his mind. He understands by "substance" a "body," or an "extended thing": in that sense, I grant you that there is no such thing as an "incorporeal body." But by those same words, I mean that there is "something," or a "not-nothing," which is *conscious* of the things that are within itself—and you do not deny that such a thing exists. You say that this very thing (which I call the "mind") does not differ in reality from the body, while another affirms it does. But do you mean that an idea, or a concept, or an act of attention cannot be had regarding *thought* without also simultaneously having an idea of *extension*, and vice-versa? <note>"Extension" is the philosophical term for taking up physical space.</note> So that one cannot be conceived without the other? So that to be conscious of one is, by that very fact, to be conscious of both? He does not say this. Well then: this is exactly what we call "differing in reality and substance." Unless you are a difficult student, you should not refuse this phrasing, having now been taught its true meaning. But if you wish to use the word *mind* to designate a "body" or an "extended thing," you are simply expressing well-conceived ideas badly or in an unusual way. And so it goes with other terms, which ought to be presented in dictionaries in such a way that they serve to distinguish thoughts, rather than teaching almost nothing beyond the pronunciation and substitution of words.

> *1. The absurdity of the third opinion, which claims that knowledge of spiritual things must be acquired through the senses, and its consequences. 2. I. Regarding touch, taste, and smell (to use this popular division), I believe there is no need for debate. # ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...even if they conceive of these things as splendid, beautiful, and most exquisitely suited to the senses. For this reason, many people place the governance of their mind toward God—that is, **Religion**—only in outward appearances. They are entirely occupied either with the "titillation of the ears" or the "delight of the eyes"—with colors, shapes, movements, the presence of certain physical materials, their use, or even with seeing and touching. Because these outward forms vary among all nations, they have divided mortals into mutual hatred and slaughter. They have led people away from the true kingdom of God—the primary subject of which they do not understand—because they are ignorant of the qualities proper to both the uncreated Mind <note>Referring to God.</note> and the created mind <note>Referring to the human soul.</note>, and because they substitute sensory things (which are necessarily manifold and diverse) for intellectual things.

II. However, so that something certain and clear can be determined in this matter, we will consider the senses insofar as they exist in the body, so that we may then see what results from them in the mind; and we shall see whether the knowledge of minds is derived from the senses. One thing can be said to arise from another in three ways: as if from an *efficient cause* <note>The agent that brings something into being.</note>, as if from an *exemplar* <note>A model or pattern that something mirrors.</note>, or as if from an *occasion* <note>A trigger or starting point.</note>. In which of these ways, then, can it be asked whether the knowledge Minds have of themselves or of others proceeds from the senses?

But since the senses in the body are nothing more than the motion of matter or of the organs, and since motion can produce nothing except a motion of the same nature (which is merely the separation of surfaces), while the mind is incapable of receiving such physical motion, it is clear that no knowledge can be produced in the mind by the senses. In fact, nothing at all can be produced there by them, not even the smallest bit that can be imagined.

Furthermore, it is easy to notice that within the mind, neither the mind itself nor any other efficient cause produces anything "drawn" from the bodily senses as if the senses were acting as a model or exemplar. This is because sensation itself, or perception, simply does not exist in physical bodies. Indeed, the ideas of *extension* <note>The quality of taking up space.</note>, *motion*, and *shape*—which we think we receive through the bodily senses to know physical objects—are such that, if we wish to speak with exactness, we must judge that the reality in the bodies themselves is entirely different. 

Otherwise, because only the outer surface is presented to the "sensory idea" (if I may call it that), we would have to believe that bodies have only a surface and no depth; likewise, we would perceive no motion except in a <term>rough, unrefined way</term> <note>original: "crassa Minerva" — a Latin idiom for a plain, common-sense understanding that lacks mathematical or scientific precision.</note>, and we would see no truly regular shapes. This is because the true instruments and vehicles of motion, and the exact geometric shapes of bodies, are completely hidden from our eyes. If we did not already possess much purer and more orderly ideas of bodies, shapes, and motions in the mind from another source, or from an earlier time, we could know nothing truly about physical objects. Much less should we believe that the perceptions in the mind—such as Light, colors, sounds, and the like, as well as heat, pain, and so on—have a physical model among bodily things to whose likeness [they correspond...]

III. It remains for us to see whether the senses are the *occasion* <note>The trigger or external circumstance that prompts the mind to act.</note> of the knowledge which the mind acquires concerning spiritual things. It must be noted that ideas of two kinds are excited in the mind upon the occasion of the senses: Some we shall call **primary**, or **immediate**, because they are not formed through the intervention of our will, and they chiefly concern the state of our body which excites them, insofar as it must be joined to certain surrounding bodies for its own preservation, and removed from others—which is their primary function. For the bodily senses were not given—as is evident in brutes <note>Animals or irrational beings.</note>—for the knowledge of the truth of things, which is the object of the **intellect** <term>intellectus: the faculty of understanding and reason, distinct from sensory perception</term>, not the senses; but rather so that the entire system of the bodily organs might be preserved. Hence, those primary ideas which are immediately excited by the senses in the mind are not to be thought of as "schemas" <note>Accurate models or outlines</note> of things: they are confused and tumultuous perceptions which, according to the varying degrees of pleasure or pain, indicate the different condition of external objects, of food, of the blood, and of the **animal spirits** <term>animal spirits: in early modern physiology, these were believed to be very fine fluids or vapors that traveled through the nerves to communicate between the brain and the body</term> in relation to the structure of the whole body. Thus, to external things correspond light and colors, sounds, odors, tastes, and the so-called "tactile" qualities (or rather, ideas); to food, thirst and hunger; to the blood, the passions; and to the animal spirits or their small vessels, the more vigorous pains and titillations. Since the bodily senses are neither the *efficient* nor the *exemplar* causes of all these things, but merely the *occasion*—having nothing in common with them beyond being positioned alongside them—and since these ideas, even if they are in the mind, are not in *every* mind, nor are they there by choice, nor are they present at all in the Divine Mind; it is clear that from these, the occasion for knowing minds can be had only most imperfectly. From such things, one can only know that the mind is a thing that sees, hears, perceives hunger, feels pain, rejoices, and the like. This is a most inadequate knowledge—not of the nature of the mind, but of certain of its accidental modes—and it applies not to all minds, but only to certain created minds; this knowledge is produced by the mind's own attention to itself on the occasion of the body. Therefore, there is nothing in these things that contributes to the knowledge of the nature of the mind viewed in itself, and especially not of the uncreated Mind <note>Referring to God.</note>. There are also other ideas which [arise] from the occasion of these earlier ones, and consequently...

<note>original: "sensuum corporeorum..." This page begins mid-sentence, continuing the thought that sensory ideas are not the source of truth.</note> ...of the bodily senses, are excited in the mind, which we can therefore call **mediated** or **secondary** ideas. For instance, when light reflected from this paper moves the eyes in various ways and excites in the mind the ideas of colors—by which characters <note>The letters or written symbols on the page.</note> are variously represented—there subsequently follows an idea or thought concerning God, the soul, or other matters. Or, when a certain sound is heard, a thought enters the mind, and from there comes the knowledge of many things, as often happens. Or, when feeling hunger, I consequently think of my own mind's poverty and God's most ample abundance. Or, when I am sad or in pain, I attend to God’s most wise **providence** <term>providentia: the protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</term> over all things.

Regarding these ideas, one might ask—since they truly pertain to the knowledge of minds, and we experience them following the perception of a color or sound, or some other feeling prompted by a bodily sense—is the knowledge of spiritual things so bound to the senses that they are its "occasion"? That is, must the senses be present as a trigger so that the subsequent knowledge may follow, just as was said regarding the primary ideas?

The answer is that the matter is entirely different with these latter [spiritual] ideas than with the former [sensory] ones. Indeed, the primary ideas are placed in the mind immediately, even against our will, once the movements of the senses occur. This is not so for the latter ideas once the former are present. How many infants, common folk, slow-witted people, or barbarians are able to hear or see these very words, or similar ones, yet no just perception corresponds to them in their minds? 

From this, one may confidently assert that if nothing more perfect than what is in the senses and their ideas were to come from elsewhere, no one could ever happen upon the knowledge of God or of minds through them. It would be more likely that we, if we were deprived of the faculty of hearing, could come to a knowledge of sounds through the vision of colors alone; for one could imagine more **analogy** <term>analogia: a similarity or shared proportion between different things</term> or parity between colors and sounds than between bodily things (or their sensible ideas) and God. 

The ideas of spiritual things must be present from elsewhere. The mind must contemplate these ideas attentively, discovering many things in them through much study. Finally, through labor and industry, the mind binds these ideas to colors, characters, words, and sounds. This is done so that, although the mind is often called away and hindered from spiritual things by the corporeal, it may sometimes be less hindered by them than by other things, and may in this way remember its own **return to itself**. 

If this were not so, all effort in reading or listening would be a waste. Wagons of external words do not, by their mere presence, bring in "internal words." These internal words are the only true words, which no man is capable of instilling in another by speaking. Rather, God—the author of minds—alone has imprinted them. To grasp these, the mind must be collected; leaving all other things aside, one must attend to them in earnest.

For the senses hinder the mind in many things and help it in none for perceiving those ideas. Nothing prevents all men from noticing that they possess these ideas equally, except that they are too occupied in perceiving the images of corporeal <term>corporeal: relating to the physical body or material things</term> things. Let us therefore remove those images, whether they are presented by the imagination (as will soon be said) or by the sense (as has already been said); and let us notice in passing that if even the knowledge of bodies does not come from the senses, much less is the spiritual and divine knowledge of truth and goodness—indeed, the very enjoyment of them—linked to the grossness of the senses. Thus, it is far from the case that by laying the senses aside like the discarded remains of the body, we should suffer any momentous loss.*

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...falsely held as axioms, which supply nourishment and strength to those same errors.

II. It is impossible for a distinct knowledge or idea of God or the created mind to be held, as long as the mind is not liberated from imaginary or <term>corporeal: relating to the physical body or material matter</term> ideas. These ideas have held onto the mind so stubbornly from birth that, by force of habit, the mind persuades itself that nothing real and nothing perfect can be conceived without them. Everywhere, even in those very things which it rightly or wrongly judges to be spiritual, it mixes in <term>extension: the quality of taking up physical space</term>, space, and very often motion, along with other corporeal properties. By this mixture, everything is corrupted. Therefore, it is worth the effort for everyone to resist, with their greatest struggle and with arguments sought from every side, such a stubborn inclination toward the corporeal. This inclination does not only stain and ruin philosophical speculations, but also the knowledge of the Divine and religious worship, through the intrusion of what is foreign to them. External idolatry—where material statues are worshipped in relation to God—comes from nothing other than the fact that in conceiving of God and minds, the human soul has turned itself toward things that can be imagined. From there, it did not hesitate to express the images it fashioned within itself through an external model. Even without such a model, there is an internal idolatry: wishing to perceive God through the faculty of the imagination, whether you fashion God in a human likeness, or under the idea of some "subtle extended thing" <note>This likely refers to the "ether" or a gaseous substance that fills space—a common misconception of spirit in the 17th century.</note> that permeates all things and has no end or limit. Augustine confesses this error among his own <note>In his *Confessions*, St. Augustine describes his struggle to conceive of God as anything other than a physical substance filling the universe.</note>, and it is truly the "changing of the incorruptible God into the likeness of a corruptible creature." <note>A reference to the New Testament, Romans 1:23.</note> Furthermore, if you apply this to the created mind, to represent it as a thin or slight thing defined by space is a denial of its nature and of the true Divine image.

III. To expel this evil, it would be useful to carefully study the First of the *Cartesian Meditations* <note>René Descartes’ *Meditations on First Philosophy* (1641), a foundational text of modern philosophy.</note> along with part of the Second. For since all the objections of the Sceptics are proposed there for those who do not yet know how to solve them, they may develop a habit contrary to their previous one: the habit of removing from their concepts all images of bodies, extension, figure, motion, and space. This allows them to conceive of the mind more easily and safely, without the danger of mixing anything foreign into the idea of it. Indeed, to avoid admitting foreign elements, they will be led to suppose for a time that nothing corporeal, nothing extended, nothing occupying space, and nothing moved exists—in a word, that nothing offered by the imagination exists. Indeed, they should suppose no place and no space exists, so that the troublesome phantasms <note>original: "phantasmata"; refers to mental images or "ghosts" of sensory perceptions.</note> flying about in their thoughts may better recede and leave the mind to itself.

...are anything at all, they are uncertain and obscure—who could even count them? Namely, that this knowledge is not of complete certainty when it is possible to conceive of its object not existing; nor is it of the highest evidence when obscurity remains even in those things claimed to be the clearest. From these two disadvantages, which cling to all imagination, the intellectual knowledge of minds is set free. For with the same absurdity that one would assert a triangle could exist without a shape or <term>extension<note>In 17th-century philosophy, "extension" refers to the essential property of matter: occupying physical space.</note></term>, one would equally contend that while I am thinking, I either do not exist, or I do not possess the faculties of willing and the like, nor the ability to know them. For if I were to deny these things, I would by that very act admit that I *will* to deny them, and that I *know* what I am denying. Thus, the intellectual knowledge I have of myself as a thinking being—which is as far removed from all imagination as possible—is of the highest certainty.

It is not so with the knowledge of bodies, especially that which is claimed to be produced by the imagination. For it is possible for me to conceive, while I am thinking, that no bodies, spaces, or similar things exist, or that it is possible they do not exist; yet my knowledge of myself as a thinking being does not become more uncertain because of this. Such a supposition is neither impossible to conceive nor absurd, unlike the preceding examples. Furthermore, in the imagination viewed by itself, there is always an inherent obscurity and confusion. For while it claims to present all things to itself as if they were present—things consisting of extension, shapes, and motions—these things are actually indefinite, even in a single <note>original: "corpusculi"; a tiny body or atom</note> minute particle. Consequently, the imagination necessarily fails in the attempt; if it thinks it has grasped anything, these are merely confused masses that weary and deceive it.

The philosopher *Hobbes* <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), an English philosopher known for his materialism, which the author is here critiquing.</note> provides an example of this in his own work regarding physical things that are otherwise very clear and easy to know. From this, it is evident how troublesome it is to rely on and use the imagination even in material matters. For that imaginative man, because he wished to measure the principles of Geometry by the imagination (just as he did with everything else), slipped right at the threshold in the little book he wrote on the principles and reasoning of geometers. Wishing to grasp a point, a line, and a surface through the imagination, he attributed parts to the point, width to the line, and depth to the surface, from which he then imagined many other absurdities. 

It is not so with intellectual knowledge, especially when it is concerned with minds. What it conceives, it truly reaches in its own way as they are, and as they are distinct from other things that are not themselves—as is clear to anyone paying attention to the examples already given regarding the "thinking thing." Nor is it necessary for it to grasp everything contained within its object; it is enough if the few things it does reach, it reaches truly as they are in themselves and how they truly behave. VII. If all these things are carefully observed, they will not only pave the way for the knowledge of minds, but they are also fit to demonstrate that the nature of minds is foreign to everything imaginable. We will not pursue this further here, as it has sufficed to propose those things which might recall us from the habit of turning toward imaginable things and lead us to more sublime matters. But if anyone wants to turn away from that habit in a tangible way and in few words, let him consider that all extension involves parts, and parts involve shapes and measurements. There is no space that is not endowed with extension, and consequently with parts and measurement in length, width, and depth. All motion happens in space, a part of which is left behind so that another may be acquired; therefore, every moved thing is also simultaneously extended. Furthermore, if he notices both that all of this is corporeal and material, and that it is irrelevant to attribute parts, shape, and measurement to the mind, he will easily be convinced by that very fact that all occupation of space, motion, and all imaginable things must be banished from the concept of the mind.

### CHAPTER V.

*1. The four pillars of the imagination that are mixed into spiritual matters. 2. The first is explained: "What is nowhere, does not exist." 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. This is destroyed by many arguments, and its opposite is proven.*

I. The root of this evil—namely, the use of coarse concepts when dealing with intellectual matters—lies in the habit of contemplating only corporeal things. But the nourishment and sap by which this habit is fostered is supplied by the prejudices born from it, because those prejudices first obtained the name of truths, and indeed of **axioms** <term>Self-evident principles that require no proof.</term>, among everyone, and they still hold it among many today. Among the chief ones are these:
*   That what is nowhere <note>original: "nuſpiam"</note>, does not exist. 
*   That God is everywhere not only by His operation, nor by His power alone, but also by His essence, by which He also fills the earth and the heavens. 
*   That the human mind is joined to the extension of the whole body, or at least of the brain. 
*   That the mind is moved along with the body when it is transported, a condition that is also sometimes said to be shared by the Angels. 

Although the responses that are owed to these views (and will be provided) may seem like digressions from the main purpose, and indeed rather long and

II. Let us return, then, to those aforementioned axioms—for so we shall call them by habit, though they do not deserve the name—which cause such universal confusion. It is my intention to drive them out so thoroughly that they no longer have a place to stand in matters concerning the mind. The first axiom, since it is the basis for all the others, will be the first to undergo examination. It wants to persuade us that something does not exist if it exists in no physical space. The Schools <note>Referring to "Scholasticism," the traditional philosophy taught in European universities which relied heavily on Latin translations of Aristotle.</note> express this in their own tongue: *What is nowhere, is nothing* <note>original: "Quod nusquam est, id neque est."</note>. This is intended to be understood as a presence that occurs by way of extension or expansion in space. It is for this reason that the defenders of such an opinion spend so much effort constructing certain "imaginary spaces" that are infinite and extend beyond the limits of the world; they do this so that God’s presence is not limited by the boundaries of the physical world, which would result in a "limited God." They struggle no less with the space through which the mind is spread throughout the body. They ask: is the soul "whole in the whole" and "whole in every individual part"? Or is it only in one of them? And if it is granted that the soul is in each and every part, what happens if one of the body’s parts is cut off? Where does the soul go, which was previously "whole" in that limb? To solve this, they imagined a kind of "contraction," as if a snail were pulling itself back into its shell. But to season these crude imaginings with the dust of their own cleverness, they divided these ideas into three separate classes, which they shrouded in specialized vocabulary. They said that presence—which they also call <term>whereness</term> <note>original: "ubietas," a technical term for the state of being in a place.</note>—is of three kinds:

1. <term>Circumscriptive</term> <note>original: "circumscriptiva." The way physical bodies occupy space, with one part of the body in one part of the space.</note>, which belongs to physical bodies.
2. <term>Definitive</term> <note>original: "definitiva." The way a created mind or soul is "limited" to a body without taking up physical room.</note>, which belongs to created minds or souls.
3. <term>Repletive</term> <note>original: "repletiva." The way God "fills" all things simultaneously.</note>, which they attribute to God alone.

Truly, there is no need for us to waste time repeating their inventions and questions, such as: *Can an Angel be shrunk down into a single mathematical point? Can a Spirit be moved in an instant? Can it travel from one extreme to another without passing through the middle space? Where was the soul of Lazarus, for example, when he was later raised from the dead, while his body still lay in the tomb?* <note>Referring to the biblical story of Lazarus being raised from the dead by Jesus (John 11). Philosophers debated where the soul resided during the four days the body was dead.</note> Was it perhaps in...

All these things are forged from that false hypothesis: that whatever is not "nothing" must be "somewhere"—that is, it must be extended in space. <margin>(a) Bisterfeld, in *The Seminary of First Philosophy*, chapter 12.</margin>
There is someone (a) who is said to have provided a more accessible utility in place of their sterile thorns <note>Likely referring to the dense and "prickly" complexities of Scholastic philosophy.</note>. He counts Space—which he also calls <term>Ubietas: "Whereness" or the state of being in a place.</term>—among the common properties of being. He divides it as mentioned above and attributes it to both minds and God (including both imaginary and real space), adding the rule: *To be somewhere is a universal attribute of all existing beings. That which is nowhere, does not exist.* Augustine confesses that he also committed this very error, and that it kept him away from the knowledge of God, as can be seen throughout his *Confessions*, where, among other things, he describes his struggle against "imaginable things" <note>Images or concepts that the mind can visualize as physical shapes or sizes.</note> as follows:

<margin>(b) Augustine, *Confessions*, Book 7, Chapter 1.</margin>
> (b) *My heart cried out violently against all my phantasms <note>original: "phantasmata" — mental images of physical things.</note>, and with this single blow I tried to drive away the swarming crowd of impurity from the eye of my mind. But no sooner were they scattered than, in the blink of an eye, they gathered again, rushed upon my sight, and clouded it. Even though I was not thinking of the form of a human body, I was still forced to think of something corporeal as being spread through space—either infused into the world or diffused through infinity outside the world. I even thought this of that incorporeal, inviolable, and unchangeable thing which I preferred over the corruptible and changeable. For whatever I deprived of such space seemed to me to be nothing at all. And a little later: Thus, being "thickened" in heart <note>original: "incrassatus corde" — a biblical metaphor for being spiritually dull or overly focused on material things.</note>, and not even clearly visible to myself, I thought that whatever was not stretched out, or spread, or crowded together, or swollen, or did not possess (or could not possess) such qualities, was absolutely nothing. For my heart followed those same images through which my eyes were accustomed to travel (this is the root of the prejudice: namely, the habit of contemplating and imagining corporeal things). I did not see that the very mental act by which I formed those images was not such a physical thing itself; yet it could not form them unless it were something great.*

### III.
Now, let us examine the stated axiom. We concede that it is valid for every body, of whatever kind it is or may be imagined to be: if it is nowhere, or if it is not in space, it does not exist. For space is inseparable from the essence of bodies, nor is the body distinguished from it, since its essence consists in extension in length, width, and depth—which is the very idea of space itself. But if the axiom is applied to incorporeal substances, it surely fails. For it is utterly false that the mind does not exist if it is "nowhere" or in no space. Nor is there a need to be imbued with an exact and exquisite knowledge of minds before we can detect its falsehood and recognize the opposite truth; the notion most common to all mortals is sufficient, by which we understand...

...we understand that the Mind or Spirit cannot be measured by the foot, or the span <note>original: *spithama*; a measurement of about 9 inches, based on the reach of a hand.</note>, or the ell <note>original: *ulna*; a measurement roughly the length of a man's arm.</note>: nor can it be said that this mind, for example, is three ells long or wide, or fewer, or more, or even infinite. Suppose then—as the false rule to be refuted demands—that Spirit or mind exists in some space chosen at will; that space will be endowed with some extension, to which a certain measure, small or large, a palm or a rod <note>original: *pertica*; a surveyor's measuring pole.</note>, can be applied. Once applied one or many times, that measure will reach from one end to the other, by which means the space will be completed in one, ten, or a hundred measures. Or, if the same measure is applied to the first part of the space that presents itself and is doubled everywhere into infinity, it will never find an end: which is how they conceive of the space in which they imagine God to be. 

Each necessary consequence of their hypothesis is absurd. This latter one is unworthy of God, for from it would follow that God's essence is co-extended with space or measurable by a ten-foot pole <note>original: *decempeda*.</note>, with only this exception: that while being measured, one could never reach the end, since it is understood to lack one. For this very reason, they do not deny that they have imagined infinite spaces for themselves. <margin>(a) See Derodon in *Abridged Physics*, chapter on place.</margin> Indeed, some (a) have gone so far as to persuade themselves that space—which receives all things into itself and is the place of all things—is also eternal, and is God Himself insofar as He is immense; or rather, that it is the Divine immensity itself, which possesses various <term>virtual parts: "Virtual parts" (partes virtuales) refers to a philosophical concept where something is divided by its power or presence rather than by physical cutting.</term>, to which located bodies are differently applied and within which they exist (which surely means being capable of being measured and divided). Since this is neither a point, nor located in a point, it would have an infinite virtual extension. 

But let us hereafter omit that example concerning God, lest we seem to toy with Him by combining His nature with such great absurdities—although we do not put forward such absurd thoughts for any other purpose than to expel them, so that things more worthy and fitting of God may be substituted in their place. 

Let us proceed, then, assuming a created mind is in space. Therefore, such a space, defined by a certain measure, will be filled by the created mind whose substance is claimed to be present there—either in its entirety, or in part, or so clearly that the substance of the spirit spreads itself even further to certain limits, beyond which it does not exist, but precisely extends to a certain point. It will have so much extension, or, if you prefer, co-extension. Therefore, it will be measured along with space, and divided with it into parts—halves, quarters, and so on. Since this is rightly considered most absurd, one must admit that the axiom from which it necessarily flows—concerning the necessity of space for the existence of Beings and Minds lest they be nothing—is also most absurd. Nor is there any reason for them to say in words that the substance of the mind is in space, and yet not

yet it cannot be extended or measured with it: for there is a contradiction in the very words themselves, and they pile a new absurdity onto the previous one. For indeed, they admit that "being in space" <note>original: *τὸ in spatio esse*</note>, or space itself, belongs to the essence and nature of a spiritual thing (certainly, outside the category of the efficient cause <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being. The author argues that space is not just something that helps a spirit exist, but something they claim is part of its very "being."</note>, that without which something is not a Being, or ceases to be a Being, is most especially of its essence); or let them say, if they prefer, that it is an inseparable property. These same people acknowledge it is either essential or proper to space that it be extended, measurable, and divisible into two parts, three parts, and the like. From which it follows that, if space is inseparable from spiritual substance, the spiritual thing itself, or the Mind, is extended, measurable, and divisible into two, three, or more parts: for whatever necessarily and naturally partakes in a thing becomes, by that very fact, a partaker in all those things which are essential and proper to that thing—unless, for the sake of their previous absurdity, they would absurdly deny this first known principle.
