IV. Furthermore, not only the presence of the mind in space (which we have discussed thus far), but also the beginning of that presence—that is, its entry into one space by the desertion of another—and the duration of the presence itself, can convict that axiom upon which these imaginings rest of being false and absurd. For if I suppose the mind is not yet in this certain space, but in an adjacent one, from which it wishes to exit so that it may take itself to the next: how, I ask you, will you conceive of this exit and entry, unless by attributing parts to the Spirit along with divisible extension? I would like you to say in what space it is during that time—or if you refuse "time," during that moment—while it is changing the first space to fill the other? Where is it? For then, it was either in no space (which destroys the premise); or it was entirely in the first, or entirely in the second (which is not "changing," but staying, or having already changed). It remains for them to conceive (even if they deny it in words, because it is too crude to be spoken openly) that the mind is partly in one space and partly in the other, and is promoted as if successively from one to the other. And this is the same as attributing parts to the mind, at least in concept, or conceiving of the mind as divisible; which is openly absurd.

V. The same can be said of its duration in space, for it is of no use. For what purpose, I ask you, is space for the Mind? What bond, what necessity ties space to the mind, whether you look at its operations or its nature? Do the operations of the mind exist through space? Is space, and its extension, either their necessary object, or subject, or...

...either a principle, or a sustaining cause? For if you consider its nature—clearly spiritual and incorporeal as it is—what is there in it that would require space in order to begin or continue to exist? What is there in the entire structure of the mind that involves a necessary, or any other kind of relationship to the occupation of space? Rather, what is more opposed to the notions common to everyone regarding the nature of minds than such statements: that minds are divisible into parts, are extended and measurable by a palm's breadth, or a foot, or any other measure of extension? These conclusions flow necessarily from the axiom: *Everything that exists is somewhere, or in space*; which, because it leads to falsehood <note>original: *in falsa ducens*, literally "leading into false things." The author argues that because the premise leads to the ridiculous idea of a "five-foot-long soul," the premise itself must be wrong.</note>, is itself false.

VI. It can also be asked whether Thought, meditation, judgments of affirmation or denial, love, desire, hatred, and similar things, are nothing? If they are not nothing, where then are they? What space, and how much, do they hold? And since every space is divisible along with what is in it, as has been proven, can it be seriously said or conceived that a judgment, for example, is so many measures long or wide? Or that love occupying a certain amount of space is a thousand feet high; and when divided with that space into two parts, there remain five hundred on each side, and more of the same kind? Therefore, since these things are foreign to reason, they are not in space; yet they are not nothing. 

Nor should you object that these are faculties, operations, and accidents <note>In 17th-century philosophy, an "accident" refers to a property or quality of a thing that isn't part of its essential definition—like the color of a rose vs. the "roseness" itself.</note> of the mind, but not the substance itself; and that the Axiom speaks of substance, not of them. For first, thought itself, and the mind's faculties of intellect and will, are not really distinguished from the mind, but are its very substance, as will be shown in more detail below. Therefore, if these are not in space, neither is the mind itself. Second, one cannot truly conceive that operations—which they call <term>secondary acts</term> <note>original: *actus secundos*. This is a technical term in Scholastic philosophy referring to the actual exercise of a power, such as the act of thinking, as opposed to the "first act" or the mere capacity to think.</note>—of any thing that is by its nature in space, are not themselves in space, especially since they subsist in the acting thing and are immanent <note>An "immanent" action is one that remains within the person doing it (like thinking or feeling), whereas a "transient" action affects something else (like hitting a ball).</note>, such as those listed above. I ask you, how could operations that exist within a thing whose nature requires it to be in space, not themselves require or involve space and those things that belong to spatial objects? Finally, concerning all accidents, modes, and variations that affect any thing, it is affirmed that those whose subject is in space cannot be conceived without space, nor without divisibility. And so it is with everything that happens to a body; and universally, it is the nature of every mode and accident that it cannot be conceived without that which belongs to the essence of its subject—so much so that the subject would be nothing without it. For an "accident" is a certain change or, if you prefer, a certain variation of the substance of the being itself, or of its nature, or of that which is essential to the thing.

VII. There might, perhaps, be some who would say that the modes or accidents <term>accidents: in philosophy, these are properties that can change without changing the essential nature of a thing, such as the color of a leaf versus the "leaf-ness" itself</term> of a spatial thing are indeed spatial and divisible, but only "by accident" <note>original: *per accidens*</note> rather than "by their own nature" <note>original: *per se*</note>. Regarding these trifles—if indeed they deserve a response—it can be said that when applied to the present matter, they appear utterly absurd. For to claim that a judgment, or love, or other such things are spatial or divisible into parts "by accident" is a statement too harsh to be voiced. Furthermore, such speech is twice over self-contradictory: to say something is spatial and divisible by accident. For it is the same as if they said that the position and existence of that thing could, by its nature, be without space—which contradicts what they previously assumed. But it is also a contradiction to grant that something is "divisible by accident." For if it happens to something that it can be divided, it was of such a nature that division could happen to it; therefore, it was divisible by its very nature. One could indeed say, without contradiction, that something is "divided by accident" <note>An example would be a thought being "divided" only because the paper it is written on is torn in half; the paper is divided, but the thought itself is not literally halved.</note>, but not "divisible." Therefore, we conclude that since many aspects of the mind are conceived without space and divisibility—and they could not be so conceived unless their subject lacked that imaginary space—the most false axiom concerning the spatiality of all Beings collapses.

VIII. We shall add another point drawn from the consideration of the existence of space. I ask whether space, such as they attribute to the Uncreated Mind <note>The "Uncreated Mind" refers to God.</note> and created minds, is a mere nothing, or truly something real in itself? It cannot be said to be nothing, since it is extended, divisible, measurable, capable of being bounded in many ways, and of such a nature that infinite things can be demonstrated concerning it, even regarding the shapes possible within it. Truly, such highly positive attributes cannot be affirmed of "nothing." Add to this that if space were nothing, it would not exist; it would not *be*. For you might better say that what is nothing does not exist, than that what is "nowhere" does not exist. No mind, therefore, would be in it, because space would not be provided. Thus, we must admit space is something. Of this I ask again: was it created by God? Or does it exist of itself, independent and without beginning? Certainly, no one who attempts to venerate God as is fitting will assert this latter point. There remains, then, the former: that it was surely created by God. But what space did God, the eternal mind, occupy before space was created by Him? Where was He? Was He therefore nothing, since He was not in a space that did not yet exist and was not yet created—given the claim that "what is nowhere, does not exist"? But since He existed in the highest degree, and was nowhere, was He not also able to create other things—namely, to place minds (things consistent with His own nature, at least in being without space) when no spaces existed? Can He not now reduce all bodies and spaces to nothing, while still preserving minds? The fact that we here use the medium of divine power does not prevent things from being distinguished: for if one thing can be placed separately without another...

## CHAPTER VI.

*1. Regarding the second "prop" of the Imagination mixed into spiritual matters—namely, the obscure phrase that God is present even to corporeal <term>corporeal: having a physical body or substance</term> creatures by reason of His essence. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. What should be thought of this phrase based on the proper use of words? Having removed four scruples <term>scruples: here, it refers to intellectual doubts or nagging logical difficulties</term>.*

I. Since the other axioms proposed at the beginning of the previous chapter lean upon this one which has just been deduced, now that this prop has been removed, they appear—and indeed are—overthrown. However, because they have been brought forward in various ways (some of which are thought to be more urgent and forceful), and since it does not seem consistent with reason to deny that minds are present to bodies—at least certain minds to certain bodies—the idea of space (which is inseparable from the body) is again mixed with the mind; it will perhaps be useful if we attempt to avoid that confusion in the following sections. The second axiom was proposed in these or similar words: *That God is present everywhere—that is, in every space—not only by reason of His operation, nor by His power alone, but also by reason of His essence.* Everyone seems to embrace this opinion as far as the words go; hence the famous little verse known to everyone: *God is present within and everywhere powerfully* <note>original: *Enter præsenter Deus est & ubique potenter*</note>; but they fight over the meaning. Those who are imbued with a healthier Philosophy join a nobler meaning to those words, one superior to every spatial presence. Others imagine some sort of presence of essence through all things, as if by an immense diffusion or expansion permeating all things, filling the earth and heavens, and spreading beyond itself; they want God to be conceived as present by reason of His essence to all extended and located space before He is conceived by reason of His operation <note>The author distinguishes between God's "essence" (His actual being) and His "operation" (His actions or influence). He is critiquing the idea that God's being is "stretched out" across the universe like a physical gas or fluid.</note>. We think that axiom is obscure and improper in its wording; as for the meaning which these [later...]

> *So also I thought of You, the life of my life (God), as being vast and penetrating the entire mass of the world through infinite spaces on every side; and beyond the world, in all directions, through immense reaches without end. I thought the earth possessed You, the heaven possessed You, and all things possessed You, and they were bounded in You, but You were nowhere [bounded]. Just as the body of this air, which is above the earth, would not resist the light of the sun so as to prevent it from passing through, penetrating it not by breaking or cutting it, but by filling it entirely; so I thought the body of the heaven, the air, the sea, and even the earth were permeable to You, and penetrable in all their greatest and smallest parts, to receive Your presence, which by a secret inspiration governs everything You created from within and without. This I suspected because I could think of nothing else—for it was false: in that way, a larger part of the earth would contain a larger part of You, and a smaller part a smaller part of You.* <note>Augustine is describing his former mistake: thinking of God as a "stuff" or "fluid" that fills the world. <margin>(b) Chapter 5 of the same Book VII of the *Confessions*.</margin>

He adds: *“I was turning such thoughts over in my wretched heart, weighted down by the sharpest anxieties regarding the fear of death; and the truth had not been found, etc.”* <note>original: "Talia volvebam pectore mifero..." — Augustine, Confessions, Book VII, Chapter 1.</note> Similar are the thoughts by which people commonly represent the presence of God to themselves, except that they say God, as far as His <term>essence</term> <note>The "essence" of a thing is its fundamental nature; what it actually is in itself.</note> is concerned, is <term>whole in the whole</term>, and whole in every part of space, the world, and bodies. But what else is this but a multiplication of God, even if He is said to be one in essence? It is exactly the same as how the essence of space, matter, or body—which is one and can be measured—is nevertheless conceived of as being whole in the whole, and whole in every part of that space, matter, or body. This is just as the entire nature of the water of the sea, which is but one, was conceived by Augustine as being in that entire sea, and in the whole of a sponge, and that same whole in every individual part of the sponge. Although they might deny this logical consequence, I have no desire to chase them into every corner of their "spaces." It is enough to close the door on the imagination regarding the question of God's presence—a door which our second axiom <note>Likely referring to a previously established rule in this text that the mind or spiritual things do not occupy physical space.</note> stands to refute.

II. It is clear from what was demonstrated in the preceding chapter that God existed when there were no spaces, and thus His essence was present nowhere except in itself, without any space at all. Therefore, presence in space is not essential to Him; or rather, it is not part of the nature of His essence to be in space. Therefore, He clearly is not in it, nor can He be, because nothing is or can be in the essence of God except that pure essence itself. Furthermore, nothing "new" can happen to God in terms of His essence; for the things that are conceived to "happen" to God are only names derived from His external actions, or from things that are not within His essence. Therefore, setting aside the consideration of His actions (which one might call being present <term>operatively</term> <note>original: "operative" — presence through action or influence rather than by being physically "there."</note>), God cannot be said to be present to things distinct from Himself. Nor should it be said that "being present" properly happens to God by reason of His essence—as if He, who previously was present to no thing distinct from Himself by reason of His essence (since nothing else existed), had finally become present to every thing by reason of His essence. This was the point to be demonstrated.

III. But since the light of the opposite truth does not necessarily shine forth simply by refuting someone else's opinion, the whole matter must be explained here in a few words. It should be noted, first, that there is a foundation beneath both sides that is solid by everyone's agreement: namely, that since God created all the spaces in the universe and everything contained within them, and since He preserves, rules, and governs them all, He is most especially present to them all. This is certain. But something "made of straw" <note>A "straw man" or a flimsy addition to a solid foundation.</note> might be built upon this; therefore, we must note, secondly, what can be meant by the words *presence*, *where*, and *essence*. 1. Someone can be present to a thing only in the sense that the thing is the result and external operation of that person, who is then said to be present **operatively**; and this often occurs in moral matters—

<meta>catchword: happens (originally "rit" from "occurrit")</meta>

However, for the sake of distinction, he is present **actively** insofar as he thinks about that thing; but the thing which is in turn present, or even the person himself insofar as he is thought of by that thing or represented in some other way, is present **passively**. Finally, a thing can be said to be present to another in such a way that no regard is given to the preceding categories, but rather its connection (<note>original: "nexus"</note>) with the thing to which it is said to be present is conceived, as a kind of flowing into it (<note>original: "immeatio"</note>). Or, it can be asked in respect to a subject that *does* imply space, which is the same as asking, "in what space is the thing?" 3. Regarding **essence**, it will suffice here to note that a thing's essence, all its essential attributes, all its essential perfections, and the nature of the thing are one and the same. If someone folds all these concepts together well, they will easily be able to determine what is meant by the "presence" of any thing—whether that thing be a body, a mind, or its internal or external operation (for one can ask of all these things: *where are they?*)—provided they attempt to vary this question, *where is the thing?*, according to these distinct categories. This will be explained by one or two examples, insofar as it is useful for our purpose.

...to what space should the essence, or nature, or all the perfections and attributes of God be joined or inhere? Or is Space linked with the divine essence or attributes? This is ultimately the same as asking: is Space itself the Divine essence?

It is absurd to ask of the subject of the question—to speak **scholastically** <note>Referring to the tradition of "Scholasticism," the medieval school of philosophy and theology that used rigid logical categories to define the divine.</note>—a **predicate** <note>In logic, a predicate is a property or characteristic attributed to a subject. The author argues that "Space" and "God" are so different that one cannot be a property of the other.</note> of an entirely different category. It would be like asking about the **Mind**, what "shape" it has, or what "flavor" it possesses?

But if the question, **where is God by reason of His essence?** or "where is His essence?" refers simply to the *subject*—that is, to that in which the essence itself exists—the answer must be that it is in God alone. This must also be asserted for all His attributes (since they are not distinct from His essence) and for His internal operations. In this sense, He is present to no creature in the entire universe, but to Himself alone, and to the eternal Son and Spirit. 

Indeed, if God, by reason of His essence (which encompasses all His divine perfections and internal operations), were present to any creature—whether spiritual or bodily—that creature would "contain" God. The creature would possess and hold within itself everything that God possesses in His essence, for the essence of God would be within it. Nor does the distinction between **adequate** and **inadequate** <note>Scholastic philosophers used "adequate" to mean a perfect, exhaustive representation or presence, and "inadequate" for a partial or limited one. Therefore, let us do away with those sayings about the presence of God by reason of essence as being **"the whole in the whole world, and the whole in any part,"** <note>original: "totius in toto mundo, & totius in qualibet parte." It is believable that if men truly knew what God is, they would not dare to propose such things, lest they bring dishonor upon Him. They care little whether the things they attribute to Him are truly fitting for His Supreme Majesty.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

Based on the reasons regarding those things called internal <note>Referring to God's "internal operations," such as the relationship between the Father, Son, and Spirit, which were discussed on the previous page.</note>, let us now ask concerning external things: are there such things—pleasing to, known by, produced, sustained, and governed by God—through which God is represented? And are these things located in space? To this, anyone can see the answer must be that such things certainly exist, and they reflect God just as an image does. However, some of them are entirely devoid of space, such as **minds**, while others, such as all **bodies**, are not separated from space.

In this way, God is present to His creatures: namely, by reason of His most free operation and representation, which is itself a work of God, along with everything else that exists. Neither God Himself nor His works require any other kind of "presence." Not God (that is, His essence and internal operations), as we saw above; nor His works. For it is enough for the creatures if God has willed them, if they are known by Him, produced, and governed—and if they reflect His divine perfections as best as can be done, whether in the extension and motion of their parts, or in the nature and variation of their thought.

God is said to be "more" or "less" present to things depending on whether He produces more or fewer effects in them which depict His divine perfections, as if on a **painting** or in an **image** <note>original: "tanquam in tabula vel imagine"</note>. Thus, He is less present to bodies than to minds. 

In bodies, the number of parts is so great it cannot be defined, and the governance of their motion follows constant rules that never waver. These are clear enough images of God’s infinite perfections and His constancy. However, it is a fact that no new matter is created, nor do the primary modes of matter increase. (For **motion**—the source of all diversity in the physical world—does not increase in the universe; no body begins to move because of another without the second body losing just as much motion). Therefore, God seems to be present to and communicate Himself to bodies in a determined way, with a fixed measure, without the addition of any new operation.

This is not the case with **minds** <note>The author uses "mentibus" to refer to rational souls or spirits.</note>. These are created anew daily by His operation. Their modes and perfections increase as He works within them. For example, if one person acquires knowledge or other gifts from another, the first person loses nothing of their own learning or gifts. This is certainly a greater image and effect of divine power and goodness, and thus a greater "presence." 

But the highest degree of this presence shines forth in clear, holy, peaceful, and tranquil minds, such as those believed to be the "blessed." Sacred Scripture says nothing greater of them, when recounting their highest privileges, than that the **image of God**—not the *essential* image <note>The "essential image" is a technical term for the Son of God (Christ), who is considered the same substance as the Father.</note> (which is God Himself), but a produced, created, and renewed image—is within them by God's working. Indeed, Scripture says that God’s essence—or what is the same thing, God Himself by reason of His essence—is never "in" them. I know that certain holy men and [experts]...

This is because, since His presence is an external operation, such things are not His operation at all.

VI. There still remain some specific difficulties which it is right to try to remove, since they have troubled even men held in high esteem, causing them to use highly improper and deceptive language. **Descartes** himself (a), because he did not want to admit that God is everywhere as if His essence existed everywhere, said that God is everywhere by reason of His power, but not by reason of His essence. However, when he saw that God's power and His essence are one and the same, he first thought it better in such matters to reason about the created mind rather than about God. But when an opponent pressed him, arguing that God cannot be everywhere by power without also being there by essence—since God's power is not located outside of God or His essence, nor is it distinct from that essence—he responded by conceding that God’s essence must be present everywhere so that His power can act there, but not in the manner of an **extended thing** <note>original: "rem extensam." In the philosophy of this era, "extension" refers to physical matter that occupies three-dimensional space.</note>. This way of speaking is followed and even exceeded by **La Forge** in his treatise *On the Mind or Spirit of Man*, where he asserts (b) that God is present to all things by His omnipotence, essence, and substance; indeed, he claims that all creatures correspond to a certain part of the divine immensity in which they are all included. # RATIONAL THOUGHTS
<meta>catchword: present-</meta>

<margin>(a) Wittich in the *Peaceful Theology*. Chapter 15, sections 117, 118, etc. <note>original: "Theologia pacifica." Christopher Wittich (1625–1687) was a Dutch theologian who sought to reconcile Cartesian philosophy with Scripture.</note></margin>
...prepares the mind to imagine present things? Another very famous author (a), also using improper words (though in a healthy sense) which signify something else by common convention and thus foster obscure concepts, also says that *God is present to all things by essence, essentially, and by reason of essence*. He claims that all those called Cartesians <note>Followers of the philosophy of René Descartes.</note> assert this, and that the contrary cannot be proven either from Descartes or from the writings of those who correctly follow his way of philosophizing. I certainly strive to follow his correct way of philosophizing, but that does not prevent me from believing that those words—*that God is present to creatures by essence, or by reason of essence*—do not signify the truth if they are interpreted according to ordinary usage. And although these authors substitute a truth for those words, this does not happen through the common use of words, but from a disposition of the mind that resists the very meaning the words ought ordinarily to have.

It is clear enough from what was said above in numbers 2 and 4 that those words do not properly signify the truth. This will be even more apparent if we notice that the words *essence* and *by reason of essence* are not used by anyone, according to universal usage, except to signify something internal to a thing, natural, proper, inseparable from it, and—so to speak—identified with it. However, when there is a question of external relations, or of modes that do not constitute the essence of a thing, no one is accustomed to use those terms. 

For example, no one says a body is square or perceptible *by essence*, or *by reason of essence*. Nor is that essence itself said to be square or sensed, but rather *extended*; a *body is said to be extended by reason of essence*. Yet the body itself is said to be square and sensed (or perceived by the senses) because the word *body* is such that in common usage it does not exclude a relationship to particular modes and accidents, whereas the word *essence* plainly excludes it. 

So it is in divine matters: although *God and the essence of God* are one and the same, nevertheless, when we wish to express a concept where God is involved not as a subject in which a quality resides, but as an agent, worker, or disposer to whom a new external relation is added, usage does not permit us to use the word *essence*. Nor do we say that *God, by reason of essence, is the Creator, has spoken, was incarnate, suffered, died, etc.*, even though He was more "present" to those events than to any other creatures. We say such things of *God* because usage has included a respect for external actions under that name; but we do not say them under the word *essence*, by which word everyone expressly intended to exclude anything that is not one and the same being of the same nature as God Himself. Therefore, it is not accurately said that God is present *by reason of essence* to any thing other than Himself. 

But how should we respond to the argument raised above: that since God is present by His power as Creator, it follows that He is also properly present by His *essence, which is that very power*?

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...should it be said that He is present to them? It must be denied that it is accurately said that God is present to created things by reason of His essential power, *or*, what amounts to the same thing, that God’s essential power is within creatures, for the same reasons and in the same sense that this was denied above in numbers 2, 3, and 4. We indeed conceive of divine power as producing something, but we do not conceive of the power itself being inside the thing produced; rather, we see only its effect. God is present, but by the effect and operation of that power which exists in Him alone. If the name "power" is given to those operations themselves, it is better to look at it as a rhetorical figure of speech <note>original: "rhetoricum tropum"</note> than to conclude that the presence of an operation within a creature is the very power of God—or even His essence and nature, along with all His perfections. For a creature is merely an imperfect sketch <note>original: "tabula," meaning a painting or tablet</note> and an effect of those perfections. This must be the conclusion unless one wishes to embrace the creature in place of the Creator and deny Him that sacred praise: that He "dwells in unapproachable light" <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 6:16, a common scriptural defense for God's transcendence.</note>. Indeed, to put it briefly, whatever is said concerning the various modes of divine presence ought to be understood through His operation. Thus, when He is said to be present to all things through His wisdom, providence, care, and counsel, it is not being asserted that God’s wisdom, providence, care, and counsel are *inside* the creatures. They exist in the eternal God alone; in created things, there are only operations occurring at this or that time, surrounded by these or those circumstances, as it pleases God. This very arrangement of operations or things is that "presence of God" which is said to happen through His concurrence <term>Concurrence (concursus): the theological concept that God "runs alongside" or cooperates with created causes to produce every event.</term>.

VII. Another difficulty arises from the fact that it does not seem consistent with reason to assert that God, or His power, works in a place where He is not. God, they say, works either while present or while absent; He does not work while absent, therefore He is present by reason of His essence in that "where" <note>original: "ubi" — a technical term in logic for location or placement</note> in which He works. But what does this mean? Does it mean that God’s essence or God’s power must be inside that subject where His operation is taking place? *Or*, that God cannot work on a thing unless the nature of God is in it, or unless it possesses God’s essence? *Or*, that there is no external operation of God except within God’s nature and essence? (For all these phrases lead to the same point). Is this the meaning of the words, *God, or His power, cannot work where He is not?* All of these things are most clearly not true. What about the claim, *God does not work while absent, but while present?* Do they mean that God’s nature and perfections are present inside the thing where His external operation occurs? Truly, how mistaken they would be! The opposite is true: for whatever thing is an operation, or the subject of God’s external operation, that thing does *not* have the divine essence and nature within itself. You might persist: "wherever someone works, they are present, for there is no such thing as action at a distance <note>The principle that an object cannot affect another object without physical contact or a mediating medium.</note>; it is absurd for someone to be working or acting somewhere without actually being there" (namely, in terms of essence, otherwise...

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...nothing is objected.) *Response:* So that one may extricate himself from these difficulties, let him only examine the terms according to the distinctions made above. What, then, is that *where* <note>original: "ubi"</note>? Is it this: that in whatever subject or space someone operates, his nature must be in that subject or space? This cannot be said, not even of physical bodies, which act upon other things by touching them externally rather than by penetrating their space; and it is only concerning these [bodies], because of physical contact, that it is said there is no "action at a distance" <term>action at a distance: the concept that an object can be moved or changed without being physically touched by another</term>. 

But regarding Minds, the matter is entirely different. The reasoning proceeds thus: In whatever thing—whether it be extended in space or not—someone (if it be God) operates, His operation is in that thing; indeed, that thing is the object of His knowledge, will, and power, and everything within that thing depends entirely on the efficacy of this [divine power]: very well. One must beware of this sophistry: "Whoever operates in a 'where,' or is an agent, is certainly in that 'where'; for to be an agent implies 'to be,' therefore to be operating in a 'where' implies being in that 'where'." 

*Response:* To be an agent does not imply first being in a "where" and then acting in it. Rather, concerning God who is the agent, it says, first, that He wills something, and second, that something is placed outside Him, or outside His essence. To be clearer: *to be an agent* does not signify a connection (or presence) of the agent’s essence with the work or its nature, but rather a connection between the positioning of the will in the powerful agent and the positioning of the work outside of Him. In this sense, far be it that the presence of God is diminished; on the contrary, it is evident from this that God is more present to a creature than the creature is to itself, since the creature does not exist by its own power—that is, because it exists, it does not have a necessary connection within itself. Instead, it exists because the will for it to be is in God, and it has in all things a connection so necessary with the effective will of God that once the latter is positioned, the former finally exists. 

But these matters should be referred to the Lordship and power of God, which will be discussed in their proper place. No difficulties remain in these matters, provided everything is resolved into the simplest words. Meanwhile, there is reason for one to wonder why people have not rather said that all creatures are "in God" by reason of His essence, or that they exist within the divine essence—which would better agree with the imaginary idea of an extended immensity—rather than saying God is "in them" by reason of His essence; for the latter seems to imply something more imperfect <note>The author suggests it is more logical to think of the finite world being "inside" God's infinite power than to think of the infinite God being "stuffed" inside finite things.</note>.

# CONCERNING GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...more worthy; those which are even higher up, or which are considered the highest of all, are held to be the most worthy of all in the entire mass. However, this way of speaking about the **intellectual world** <term>intellectual world: the realm of spirits, minds, and thoughts, as opposed to the physical or material world</term> has been borrowed from the material world. In the intellectual world, there are minds whose state is vile and ignoble—namely the ignorant, the wandering, and those established in vices; others are washed clean from these filths in some way; others still are rendered more worthy by the enjoyment of the true and the good. But above all is the most pure, most holy, and most perfect mind of God. 

Would it then be unfair to understand, by the "highest heaven" in which God is said to dwell, the very state of His perfections: His purity, His Wisdom, His dignity, and the "inaccessible light" <note>original: "lucem... inaccessam"</note> in which He lives? Indeed, God Himself—who wishes to hold created minds in His knowledge, care, and love, and into whom those minds pour back their own thoughts—could be considered "Heaven" in this sense. 

Or, if the question concerns a heaven that is not so sublime but is a created thing, might not the pure and holy minds themselves, which are gifted with the image of God and contemplate and love Him, be rightly called that "Heaven" in which God Himself exists, at least as much as He can be within creatures? Might it not be said that these minds "enter" into that Heaven when they pass into a state so pure, purely spiritual, and most perfect (though not absolutely so)? 

On the other hand, should not those things which are deprived of truth and virtue be said to lie and be depressed "in the mud" <note>original: "in luto"</note> and in the lowest depths, each according to its own foulness and misery? Thus, the **state** of minds is designated, not a **place** or **space**, which minds lack. 

In the meantime, I would not deny that God is said to be in the "physical heaven" because of the revelation of His glory and power through special effects there. But any person who looks inward at themselves can notice that this is not enough, and that the mind is not satisfied by this sense alone. Why, in interpreting the "great works of God" <note>original: "magnalia Dei"</note>, should we be satisfied with physical things? 

Lest anyone think, however, that the interaction of bodies (which are united to minds) with the physical heavens is being denied here—since the mind is viewed here on its own, as if free from every body—it is otherwise easy for God to excite ideas within the mind without a body, "in the manner of sensible things" <note>original: "sensibilium instar"</note>. Through these ideas, those things which exist in the place destined for glorified bodies may be represented to the mind in that way—or even a more noble way—than the things around us on earth are represented to us through physical means. However, it is not as certain that this happens to the mind while it is released from the body as is that which has been stated regarding the spiritual state. But we have wandered too far.

IX. I would like it to be noticed, lest there be any room for suspicion, that this doctrine—which arises from the fact that every imperfection must be removed from God—has nothing at all in common with the heresy of certain people. These people teach that God, by reason of His essence, is not everywhere, but only present through His operation, because...

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...attribute imperfections to Him: namely, they have imagined God as some sort of corporeal <term>corporeal: having a physical body or material form</term> being, restricted to a certain place and space in the heavens, and thus limited in respect to His own essence. From this view, it would follow that He acts immediately only in the heavens where His essence is contained, but that things on earth cannot be attributed to Him except through the intervention of those things between heaven and earth. They think He needs these intermediaries to act on objects distant from Himself—acting through the heavens upon the sublunary <term>sublunary: the region "below the moon," a traditional term for the changing, material world of Earth as opposed to the "eternal" heavens</term> world, through these upon the earth, and through the earth upon animals and men. In this view, none of these things would exist through the sole power of Divine efficacy <note>efficacy: the ability to produce a desired or intended result; here, God's direct power</note>, but would require the intervention of means, as if God could achieve nothing in the furthest reaches without them. 

It would be like a man standing at a machine of many gears; he could not move the final gear far from him except by touching the first gear, whereby he would produce motion in the last through the intermediate ones. Those who imagine God to be present in operation but absent in essence <note>original: "essentia vero... abesse"</note> because of a physical boundary offer something absurd and blasphemous. But in the preceding pages, every relation of essential presence to any amount of space has been so thoroughly rejected that no one can complain that the idea of God is diminished or obscured—especially if they wish to examine what will be said about God in the Third Book.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*1. 2. 3. The third and fourth supports of the imagination collapse.*<-

<margin>I.</margin>
The remaining two axioms that favor the imagination <note>In this philosophical context, "imagination" refers to the tendency to think only in terms of physical shapes and images, which the author argues is the wrong way to understand spiritual things like the soul or God.</note>—which were listed above concerning the coupling of Minds with bodies—will have no strength for those who understand what came before, or at least for those wise enough to know that the nature of the Mind is fulfilled and contained in the intellect and the will. 

From this, one can easily conclude that since the Mind is to be united with the body in a manner consistent with its own nature (and not contrary to it), and must be presented as present to it, it cannot be present in any other way than by perceiving or understanding the body itself (or something belonging to the body) and by willing. Thus, there is no need for the nature or essence of the intellect and will to reside within the substance of the body (otherwise the body would be a mind); instead, it is enough if the mind conceives and wills certain things that concern the body (which you might call **objective presence**), from which certain operations in the body follow (which you might call **presence by reason of operation**). A closer connection between these things can also be given,

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument from the previous page, shifting from the nature of God’s presence to the nature of the human Mind (or soul). ### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

If indeed something is done in the body on the occasion of the mind, and also if something occurs and is perceived in the mind because of various movements in the body: then the mind is said to be "one" with the body, not by a transformation or mixing of their natures, but by a simultaneous arrangement of certain operations in both. For instance, if a specific thought occurs in the mind, a specific motion occurs in the body, and vice versa; these interactions can vary in countless ways. But since these are not connected by the inherent nature of either extreme, but occur together by the completely free choice of the Supreme Cause <note>original: "supremæ causæ placito," referring to God's will</note>, it is wrong to look back to the body when the nature of the mind is to be viewed separately—as if the mind's expansive and mobile nature participated in the physical nature of the body.

II. Beside the internal operations of the mind concerning its own ideas (which are spontaneously available to it), the mind has no others that are necessary by the reason of its nature; therefore, it performs nothing outside of itself by necessity. Indeed, since whatever God produced besides the created mind is not known to the created mind by the power of its own nature viewed separately—and since it is not in its nature to be conscious of other created things, just as their nature does not demand they be known to the mind—the mind would never act upon those things, as they would be unknown and unperceived. 

However, since it pleased the Supreme Cause that there be a connection between minds and bodies regarding their operations, He willed that when certain movements of some matter (for example, the human body or the brain) are positioned, a certain idea of sensation would be excited in the mind so that the mind might be alerted to the state of the body. This is what is called the "operation of the body upon the mind." Conversely, He willed that when a certain act of will is positioned in the mind, the motion of a certain body would be determined in a specific way. 

It does not follow from this simultaneous occurrence of actions and passions <term>passions: in historical philosophy, "passions" refers to "undergoing" something or being acted upon by an external force, rather than just emotions</term> of the body and mind that the mind participates in the nature or properties of the body. It does not mean the mind receives those properties into itself—such as having a specific physical position, being stretched out, standing, lying down, running, leaping, moving through space, or being contained in a specific area. One should only infer that the mind wills such changes in the motion and position of the body, and therefore those external operations are immediately set in place. 

Though, to speak of the matter as it truly is, the created mind does not perform all those things, nor are the senses in the mind actually produced by the body. Rather, the single Will of God produces everything through the mutual connection of both, so that the created mind is not "present" to the body except through the mediation of God’s presence, insofar as He willed to link His operations in the mind and body in this way. Thus "in Him we have life, motion, and existence" <note>original: "Sic vitam, motum & existentiam in ipso habemus," an allusion to the biblical book of Acts 17:28</note>.

III. Furthermore, if anyone still can hardly rid themselves of that imaginary "motion" of minds because their mind is joined to the body, where—

...and since that body is moved, it might seem that the mind must also be conceived as moving with it, provided it is always present to it. There is nothing more to be said to such a person, except that—setting aside for a time the consideration of the mind’s connection with its own body—he should turn his thoughts toward other minds that are not so shackled <note>original: "mancipatas," suggesting a legal or physical enslavement or being "handed over" to the body's control</note> to bodies, namely to **Angels**. These are sometimes joined to matter by a certain link, though not a link as tight as that which binds human minds to bodies; yet it is similar enough that in both cases, the connection is not part of the **essence of Minds**.

First, therefore, conceive, as best you can, an Angel who by his nature has no connection at all with matter, such that matter is not even an object of his thought, and he does not even know if any body exists. Suppose further that God wishes to give that Angel some knowledge of the existence of bodies, and that He does this by arranging it so that when various movements, shapes, and other manifold variations of a certain corporeal mass are established, corresponding thoughts or perceptions are placed in the Angel’s mind. These would be like the perceptions of light, colors, shapes, movements, and so on, which we experience while awake or sometimes while dreaming. Who would then conclude that the nature of that Angelic mind is therefore similar to those external things? Would anyone suggest the mind itself is light, or that it has a shape—round, triangular, or otherwise—simply because it perceives them? Or that it possesses movement and extension because the ideas of these things are present within it? Surely hardly anyone would reach such an absurd conclusion.

Thirdly, consider that God willed not only that the mind be affected on the occasion of that corporeal mass, but also that this mass be moved and affected in various ways on the occasion of the different thoughts and the pleasure <note>original: "placiti," referring to the will or choice of the spirit</note> of the Angelic Spirit. Thus, if the Spirit is endowed with the will that the mass be moved this way or that, that movement follows; if he wills that the mass assume a certain shape or position, it happens immediately on that occasion. Is it necessary here for anyone to imagine that the very nature of the Angel is moved or takes on different shapes? Is it not enough to conceive that all those corporeal qualities exist in the mass of the body, while in the mind of the Angel—aside from the perception and the will concerning them—there is absolutely nothing of those physical traits?

It is in these ways that Angels move bodies. They are said to "descend to earth" or "ascend into the physical heavens" and to move with very fast and varied motions. This is not because of their essence, nor does motion occur within their essence as if the essence were the subject <term>subject: in philosophical terms, the substance or "vessel" that possesses a quality</term> of these things. Rather, it is said in respect to those external operations performed on bodies on the occasion of the Angelic will, and also "objectively," insofar as objects in the highest or lowest places—this thing or that—are the focus of Angelic Thought. Finally, think of your own mind alongside the mind...

The author argues that thoughts and souls do not take up space like a chair or a stone does.</note>, nor moved, nor is it located in space, nor does it change its position—even though all these things happen to the body while the mind itself wills and perceives them. Indeed, to this extent our mind agrees with the Angels in the "assumption of bodies" <note>The act of a spiritual being taking on a physical form.</note>: although thereafter it differs in many things, and especially in this: that the perceptions of our mind which it has on the occasion of the body are many, vivid, powerful, and very urgent; whereas the impressions which the body receives from the will of the mind are fewer, weaker, and contained within a small limit. Thus, the body prevails more over the Mind than the Mind over the body. In Angels, however, the opposite occurs: they have more power over bodies than bodies have over them.

Hitherto we have attempted to remove false opinions concerning the more general knowledge of Minds, along with their causes, and to show that there is an **intellectual knowledge** given of an intellectual thing, without space and extension. This has been demonstrated both in general, regarding all spirits, and more specifically regarding God and the created Mind (from which even the concept of movement has been removed), so that subsequent topics should not be contaminated by those errors. But if this discourse should seem too long to some, let them consider that the intent was to remove the principal doubts even from the "weakest" <note>meaning those who struggle most with abstract concepts</note>. For this discourse is offered for their sake; it might perhaps have been shorter for others, if they were not still unable to be drawn away from material things toward nobler ones. For such people, nothing is more useful than to often revolve these ideas in their mind.

## The Uncreated and Created Mind, Their Perfections, and the Imperfections of the latter, are treated in general.

### C H A P T E R I.

*1. All bodily things having been set aside. 2. Thought remains, to be attributed to both kinds of Mind. 3. In that alone is the essence of the created Mind. 4. Six difficulties are proposed to be resolved hereafter.*

<margin>I.</margin>
I. <image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial C decorated with foliate and floral patterns</image-desc>Since, as stated above from the beginning, various opinions were reported concerning the knowledge of spiritual things, the fifth among them was occupied by the view that the things of the mind can be investigated by purer thought and intellect. We embrace and shall attempt to follow this opinion as being the most true, so that not only shall everything bodily, imaginable, and sensible be banished from the idea of the Mind; but indeed, we shall not even take the occasion for speaking of spiritual things (except perhaps very rarely and incidentally) from the existence or the consideration of bodily things. Instead, as if stripped of all those things, we shall strive to move from the contemplation of the **Created Mind** <note>The human soul or an angelic intellect.</note> to the **Uncreated Mind** <note>God.</note>. For although those among the works of God that are bodily are marked with many and distinguished characters, by which the perfections of their Supreme Architect are most significantly manifested; nevertheless, because nothing in common <note>original: "nihil communius intercedit"</note> exists between these things and the essence of God—since nothing bodily, insofar as it is bodily, can be attributed to the **Supremely Perfect Being**—and since, moreover, even if one pretends to know God from the inspection of bodies, it is nonetheless necessary for the mind to intervene; and since the Mind bears more and more distinguished characteristics of Divinity; nothing more useful can be done by the mind than if it reduces any material things to a kind of nothingness for itself, and regards them no more than if they did not exist. Let it also set aside those ideas of material things which it possesses, so that it may better and more purely attempt to rise to God from the inspection of itself alone. It is regrettable that this purpose, applied with utility by **Descartes** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), whose "method of doubt" involved setting aside sensory information to find certain truth in the "cogito" (I think).</note>, has displeased many: since, however, it serves not only for knowledge, but also

<margin>II.</margin>
II. The Mind, placed in this state and looking around at whatever remains in itself, finds nothing except **thought** which it can attribute to itself and to that other Being of whose existence it is certain. Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> clearly set this out in his *Second* and *Third Meditations*. Therefore, thought alone remains to be investigated, setting aside the imagination, so that through it and in it we may recognize the nature of the Mind—both the **Uncreated** <note>God</note> and the **created** <note>the human soul or angelic intellect</note>. This will be done in the following order: first, we shall see how the nature of both Minds agrees in that they are situated in thought. However, lest anyone think the creature is mixed with God as a result, we shall show secondly, in a more general way, how Thought or Mind differs in each: one by the excellence of perfections, the other by a limit and a mixture of imperfections. Lest anyone say these immense perfections attributed to God, or the limits of the perfections given to the human Mind (which might be presumed to reach divine heights over time, tending toward them as their goal), are mere fictions of free human thought, we shall propose thirdly a certain way by which the perfections of God, and the perfections and imperfections of the created mind—along with their limits, measure, and rule—can be safely recognized. With these three points, this Second Book will be completed.

<margin>III.</margin>
III. A more general and evident notion of both Minds, the Uncreated and the Created, cannot be given than if both are conceived as **Thought**. For this is the Essence <term>The fundamental nature or "what-it-is-ness" of a thing</term> or nature of both, which can easily be demonstrated for each once apparently opposing views are removed. And first, to deal with the created Mind (for this must precede as the occasion for speaking of the other), it is certain that the essence or nature of any thing consists in that which is so conceived in the thing that even if all other things were reduced to nothing, it could nevertheless be clearly conceived as existing—and indeed so conceived that from it alone follows a series of the thing's **attributes** <term>Essential characteristics that define what a thing is</term> and many **modes** <term>The specific ways or states in which a thing exists, like a specific thought or feeling</term> of which it is the immediate subject. ->RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

...[fixed] in me, even if all bodies along with my own—I say all things that are in the world—were taken away, I nevertheless, while I think, exist sufficiently; or, thought is enough for me for the consciousness of my existence. Thus, for the evident knowledge of this truth, *I am a thing* <note>original: "sum res"</note>, there is no need for me to attend to or turn myself toward anything else besides thought. I see that many attributes are involved in this position, and many follow from it which cannot exist in nothingness, cannot be conceived without thought, are immediately present in it, and which everyone recognizes as belonging to a spiritual thing. Thought, therefore, is the essence and nature of myself, or of my mind, or of that which is in me besides the body. 

But if thought were taken away from me, nothing at all would remain for me from which I might be conscious or perceive that I am not nothing; perhaps some most brute extended thing <note>A "brute extended thing" refers to mere matter—something that takes up space but has no life or consciousness of its own.</note> remains, of which someone else might perhaps be conscious, but what is that to the Mind? If thought is denied, everything in me besides the most brute mass is directly denied: all perception, will, and the foundation and act of judging, loving, and even imagining and sensing are denied. This is certainly the essence of that thing which exists in me besides the corporeal mass. That Thought is such a thing is most evident to anyone who pays attention. From this and the preceding reasoning, it must be concluded that the essence of the created Mind consists in this one thing: that it thinks. Or, to put it in one word, it is **Thought**: if its Author <note>The Creator or God</note> has given it this one thing, it needs nothing else besides this to be what it is.

IV. It has been observed that this conclusion is not equally accepted by many because of the following difficulties. Some argue: 
1. That thought is not something real enough to constitute the nature of the Mind. 
2. That everyone has many thoughts which they change very often, and therefore many different and changeable minds would have to be assigned to everyone. 
3. That thought is an action, which presupposes some agent. 
4. That thought is an attribute which requires a subject or substance where it may reside: for although the Mind is a thinking thing or substance, the question is not what that thought is, but what that thing or substance is in which thought exists? 
5. That the Mind must therefore have necessarily always thought from the time it was created—before the birth of the body in which it resides, and also in sleep—if indeed thought is its essence; but no one is conscious of the former, and not everyone, nor always, of the latter <note>The author is addressing the classic objection to Descartes: if the soul's essence is thinking, why don't we remember thinking before birth or while in a deep, dreamless sleep?</note>. 
6. Finally, that thought could be a mode or temperament of the body, as in brute animals, and not really differ from it; indeed, that the body itself could think. 

All these objections shall be removed so that the truth of the following opposing points may become clear: namely, that Thought is the most real of all things; that it is a single thing...

## CHAPTER II.

->*1. Among all things, thought is the most real. 2. It is one, fixed, and persistent. 3. It is the principle of everything in the Mind.*<-

<margin>I.</margin> Those who admit that the Mind is the most real of all things—as it truly is—are hindered from believing it is Thought itself because "thought" seems to indicate something not quite so real. But they will easily allow themselves to be satisfied if, once they have explained what they mean by "real," they are willing to observe that, in whatever sense something is called "real," thought surpasses everything else in reality. Do you wish to define "real" as that which is certain and unshakable, which cannot be denied, and which is the opposite of a chimera <note>original: "chymærico"; a chimera refers to a mythological creature, used here to mean a mere figment of the imagination or a fabrication.</note> or a total fiction? What is more real in this sense than thought? I can suppose that all bodies are denied and are nothing: and how often are those things, which are represented to me as being outside of myself, nothing but figments, chimeras, and the play of dreams? But, even in the dreams themselves, it is certain to me that I am thinking: as long as the Mind lives and can say "I am," it is so certain that I think that I cannot deny it without contradicting myself. Or is "real" the same to you as "evident and clear"? Certainly, thought holds the first place among these. Who can clearly perceive everything that is actually in a physical body—such as the exact number of its parts, or the precise measurement of its motion or shape? But everything that is now actually in my thought (as anyone can assert for themselves) I see clearly. I cannot even deny it without simultaneously affirming that I clearly perceive what is or is not in my thought. If "real" to you means that which is permanent and does not vanish into thin air: in this sense, the human body would not be very real, because its substance "flows" so continually that in the body of an old man or an adult, there may not remain a single particle of what was there when he was born as an infant; after a short time, it ceases to be what it was, and whose it was. Nothing would be less real than the Mind if it were conceived as a thin breeze, vapor, or breath <note>The author is arguing against the ancient materialist idea that the soul is a physical 'pneuma' or "breath"; he argues that if the mind were a physical gas, it would be less "real" and permanent than the act of thinking itself.</note>.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS
<meta>catchword: actually,</meta>

But thought is constantly Thought; it does not vanish so as to become something else, or something belonging to another. Finally, if—in what is the primary sense—the "real" and the "perfect" are synonyms to you, you will recognize from this the greatest reality of thought. Reality must truly be defined by perfection. That which is nothing has no true reality, because it has no perfection. A tiny speck of dust is something real because it is endowed with some perfection. God is the most real because He is the most perfect. Therefore, if we look at created things, which is more perfect: brute extension <note>term: extension; in 17th-century philosophy, "extension" refers to the primary attribute of physical matter—the property of taking up space and having dimensions.</note> or vivid thought? To be moved and to have parts, or to understand, to will, and to possess so many noble faculties? If we consider their modes <note>term: mode; a "mode" is a specific state, form, or quality of a substance, such as a specific shape of a body or a specific idea in a mind.</note>, is there greater perfection in certain arrangements of physical particles (which make up the various wonders we admire in different bodies) than in the sublime arrangement of thought? For thought vividly presents all things to itself as present; it judges them soundly, reasons correctly, spontaneously approves or disapproves, lovingly embraces, joyfully delights, peacefully rests, and performs almost infinite similar acts. These are certainly so perfect, and present thought to us as so real, that other things of a different kind hardly seem real in comparison. 

But how highly does God Himself prize human thoughts above all else? Inasmuch as He alone wishes to possess them and, as much as possible, be possessed by them; since He seeks them with jealousy <note>original: "Zelotypia"; here referring to a divine, protective zeal or "godly jealousy" for the soul's devotion.</note>, and because they had strayed from Him, He performed wonders to lead them back to Himself; since He works His greatest deeds within them in the most excellent manner; and finally, since He has included every commandment and sacred duty within the act of thinking well! Therefore, among all created things, thought is the most real.

II. The second objection arises from the ambiguous meaning of the word *thought*, which is sometimes used in a more general sense and sometimes in a more specific one. For if by that word we wish to understand the various applications of our perception to various objects—say, now to physical things, now to spiritual ones, to the earth, to heaven, to God, to ourselves—then it is indeed true that there are many interrupted thoughts in any mind. But it was by no means in this sense that it was stated that the nature of the Mind is thought. For it is not of its essence, viewed generally and more confusedly, to be applied to one certain object to be perceived over another. Even though the mind, being of a finite nature and unable to perceive all things at once, is necessarily applied to some one of all those things—indeed, more determinately (which we shall refer to below regarding its more specific form) it tends toward one certain thing above others. Therefore, so that the nature of the Mind may be denoted by the word *thought* without ambiguity, Thought must be understood as being limited (because it cannot perceive all things at once), but not as being fixed to a specific thing, because it has no [restriction] in any...

## ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL

...actually <note>original: "actu"</note>, as a simply conscious thing, [the mind has no] necessary connection with any more specific object—indeed, not even with itself, insofar as it could reflect upon itself. And in this sense, Thought is something more general than in the previous sense, and it must be said to be singular in the Mind; for it is the intimate perception of those things, whatever they may be, which are within it. For though the objects may be diverse, and even perceived through various applications, they nevertheless return to this one thing: that they are perception—that is, one thought, varied in different ways. 

This matter will be easily understood by a similar example: namely, it is certain that a small piece of wax <note>original: "ceræ frustulum"; this is a classic philosophical illustration, most famously used by René Descartes to show how we perceive the "essence" of an object even when its physical qualities change.</note>, for instance, can be varied into many figures, yet it cannot be said to change its single nature for that reason. Whether it becomes round from triangular, or square, or assumes any other figure through internal heat, the same nature nevertheless remains and persists. In exactly the same way, the nature of the Mind remains one fixed Thought, though it is continually changeable by the diversity of objects and its application to them.

III. In a similar way, the third difficulty can be resolved, by which the nature of the Mind was denied to be Thought on the grounds that this was an action, not an **Acting Thing** <note>term: Res agens; the substance or agent that performs an action, as opposed to the action itself.</note>. For (not to dwell now on the fact that not every thought is an action, but there are also many **passions** <note>term: passions; in 17th-century philosophy, "passions" refer to states where the mind is passive or "acted upon," such as receiving a sensation or feeling an emotion, rather than actively reasoning.</note> therein), it should be noted that the word "action" commonly designates a certain application of a thing to some individual object. In this sense, it cannot be said that thought—taken broadly as noted just now and signifying the nature of the mind—is an action; since it is rather both the **acting principle** <note>original: "principium agens"</note> and also the subject admitting the passions. 

This, moreover, does not prevent Thought—insofar as it is considered a specific application to some object—from being called an "action." But in that case, as we have seen, it does not belong to the essence of the Mind or to fundamental Thought; for we do not possess perception or consciousness simply because there is an application to such-and-such an object, but rather the opposite. Therefore, in this sense, the nature of Thought is not an action. Furthermore, just as words in themselves are quite indifferent and possess no significance worth considering beyond the voluntary meaning assigned to them, if anyone wishes—contrary to common usage—to call Thought "action" (as it is asserted here to be the nature of the Mind), let them call it so as much as they like; but then they must deny that the thing they so name "action" requires another, different thing from which that action might be conceived to emanate as if from a principle.

### CHAPTER III.

->1. 2. 3. 4. *Thought is the very substance, nature, and essence of the Mind itself.*<-
->5. 6. *And it is inseparable from every Mind.*<-

I. When the Mind is free from material Phantasms <note>original: "Phantasmatibus"; in this context, these are mental images or "pictures" in the brain derived from the senses, which philosophers of this era often viewed as obstacles to pure rational thought.</note>, it will not be hindered by the fourth difficulty that has been mentioned. Even if thought is considered an attribute of a thinking substance, it should not be inferred from this that thought is something in reality distinct from the thing—or substance—to which it is attributed. On the contrary, it ought to be conceived as the very thing and substance itself. For it is not required in every attribution that a distinction must exist between that which is attributed and that to which it is attributed. This can be seen in the divine attributes, which are not something distinct from God himself. There is also such a thing as an "attribution of identity," so to speak—that is, a way of speaking by which we show that what is understood by two or more words is actually one and the same thing. This is the case in this matter, where the Mind is called a "Thinking Thing," or a substance that thinks.

II. The difficulty lies in this: when people wish to conceive of "substance" precisely and in a general sense, they nevertheless—because that concept is incomplete—unintentionally slip into thinking of a specific substance. When they later wish to add "thought" to this substance, it becomes clear that their concept of that substance (before considering the attribution of thought) was actually the concept of a *body*. For there is no specific or truly existing substance distinct from thought, other than a body. This leads to those absurd demands for an explanation of the nature, not of Thought, but of the substance—that is, the "trunk" or "stump" <note>original: "trunci seu stipitis"; the author uses these words to mock the idea of a soul as a lifeless, underlying "object" that exists separately from the act of thinking.</note> distinct from thought, in which thought resides. It should be noted, therefore, so that no one becomes entangled in these verbal technicalities, that the name "substance" is used in different ways. Sometimes it denotes an incomplete concept of a thing, and sometimes a complete one—that is, the thing itself as it exists outside of our concepts. Lest these ideas evaporate into excessive subtleties, they will be more easily understood through examples, which should put an end to all word-battles <note>original: "logomachiae"</note>.

If I am told that God will create or has created a certain thing which would still exist even if all other things besides it were reduced to nothing, the concept I have from this occasion is the concept of a "substance." However, I cannot know for certain from that alone whether that thing is a body or a mind, whether it is extended <note>original: "extensa"; in 17th-century philosophy, "extension" refers to the primary quality of physical matter: the fact that it occupies space (length, width, and depth).</note> or thinking. I do not yet conceive of thought or extension as having been produced by God; my concept of that thing is "indifferent," ready to receive either the idea of thought or the idea of extension to complete itself, and...

...up to that point, it is not determined toward either attribute. A substance is said to be "incomplete" <term>incomplete substance: a philosophical term for a concept that provides only a partial definition of a thing, lacking the specific details that make it a real, existing entity.</term> in this sense, which does not look at the thing as it is in itself; for no thing produced by God exists outside of my concept that is indeterminate between thought or extension <note>original: "extensionem"; in 17th-century philosophy, "extension" refers to the primary attribute of matter—the fact that it occupies physical space.</note>, or which involves neither, or which corresponds to that general concept of mine. Rather, that "incomplete" label refers only to the concept, and an imperfect one at that. 

However, when I say, "The Mind is a substance," by the word "substance" I now mean something different than the idea that the Mind is some indifferent thing waiting to receive either extension or thought, or involving neither. Instead, by that word, I designate something actually existing outside of a concept and endowed with thought. In the first (general) sense, thought differs from substance, but this is only in the concept, not in the reality itself. That is to say, when I attend to the "thought," I am thinking in a different way than when I attend to the "substance" taken in the first way. The concepts are different and distinct; more is conceived in one than in the other. 

In the second (real) sense, however, Thought *is* the substance. That is, in the thing itself, there is no diversity at all between that thinking thing—which can exist even if all other things were missing—and Thought itself. That thing is thought itself. Thus, it would be absurd to seek some other underlying thing of a different kind. 

Furthermore, there is a common saying that a substance is not known by itself, but through its attributes—indeed, some claim that only "accidents" <term>accidents: properties of a thing that can change or be removed without the thing ceasing to be what it is (e.g., the color of a chair).</term> are known. From this, they conclude that Thought is not the Substance itself, since Thought is easily known. This can be easily resolved if one pays attention to what has already been said. It is true that when someone conceives of substance in the first, general sense, they do not necessarily know that a thing of a determined nature (either thinking or extended) exists outside themselves, as we saw in the example. It is also true that thought is not such a general and abstract substance; therefore, in this way, a (specific) substance is not known "by itself" (that is, through the general concept of substance). 

But when thought becomes a certain and determined substance in the second sense, it is entirely false to say that such a substance is not known by itself, but only by its accidents. For that would be the same as saying that the mind or Thought (and you could say the same of the body) is not known as such—as a specific and certain substance—and is not known through the concept of itself, or is known only as an accident. On the contrary, accidents, being indefinite, are not as easily known as the substance to which they belong. Nor are they known by themselves; rather, in every concept of an accident, the concept of a substance is necessarily involved, even if indirectly. For example, in the concept of "shape" or "motion," the notion of extension (space) is underlying. 

From this, it can be proven by a new reason that thought is the substance of the Mind: namely, if in perceiving the "modes" <term>modes: the specific ways or states in which a substance exists (e.g., "hoping" is a mode of "thinking").</term> or accidents of the Mind—such as judging, denying, feeling sad, hoping, fearing, or reasoning about anything—one asks...
