# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...the concept of the subject in which these modes <term>modes: in 17th-century philosophy, "modes" are the specific forms or states that a substance takes, such as a specific idea being a "mode" of the attribute of Thought.</term> are present is discovered, and this subject is necessarily present when these are conceived: for besides Thought, nothing else will be found; and therefore, Thought is the Substance of the Mind.

III. From what has been said, it is clear how we should understand the point that was causing difficulty—namely, that "Thought is in a substance." It should be understood as follows: to the general concept of substance, the concept of thought must be added to represent the nature of the Mind, so that the concept conforms to the thing (the Mind) as it exists outside of our mental concept. We should not think that the thing or substance exists first and is then later "clothed" in thought as if thought were something different from it. Thought is that very substance itself, which requires only the concurrence of God <note>original: "concursu Dei"; a philosophical doctrine suggesting that God must continuously "cooperate" with or sustain created things for them to act or exist.</note> and absolutely no other created thing in order to exist. Since it subsists by itself, it requires no subject other than itself to exist within.

IV. Therefore, it would be ridiculous for someone—as if to mock this idea that thought is the substance itself—to take the phrase *a substance that thinks* and flip it into the paraphrase: "Thought that thinks." 

First, if we consider the "indeterminate" concept of substance (as I warned before), this phrase simply means: a concept of substance that is indeterminate in itself, to which the concept of thought is added to complete and define it. Second, if we look at the actual thing existing outside of our concepts, then these words mean one and the same thing, so there is no need to repeat them. Finally, if we consider both together, it is the same as saying: "a thing that thinks," or "Thought." It should not be conceived as an "accident" or a "mode" that cannot exist except inside another created thing, but as a being independent of every other creature in its existence. 

In all of this, there is nothing absurd. I will pass over the fact that one can even reasonably say "Thought thinks," by which we mean that perception—which by its nature is not limited to specific objects—determines itself toward those objects and thus produces specific, individual perceptions. We can also say that "thought is in thought," meaning that any particular thought exists in us only because there is one overarching perception in us in which all individual thoughts reside. But enough about words for now.

V. The fifth "scruple" <note>scruple: here used in the archaic sense of a small doubt or a nagging objection that prevents someone from accepting an argument.</note> touches upon the matter itself, not just the terminology. For it is certain that the nature or substance of the Mind is not Thought if the Mind has ever existed, even for a single moment, without Thought. However, we deny that the Mind, from the moment it was created, was ever non-thinking. Since the Mind is not "nothing," if you take away thought, there is nothing left that you can claim about it; thus, by removing thought, you reduce the Mind to nothing. For if thought is removed, what remains to assign to the mind—especially as its very essence?

G

You will say: "It is the faculty of thinking." <note>original: "Facultas cogitandi"</note> Well and good, if by that faculty you mean the power of determining an *existing* Thought toward various objects. But this very point implies that thought is actually existing; for that which does not exist cannot be determined by itself or by another. But if by this you mean that the mind is devoid of actual thought, but can recover it at a certain time or on some occasion, you are speaking nonsense. For anything that exists possesses something in actuality, or else it is nothing; it is not enough to possess something "in potential," since a thing does not truly possess that which it is said to possess only by potential—a state that excludes the actual. To assert that the Mind possesses the faculty of thinking in actuality would be the same as claiming that a body is endowed with a "faculty of extension" <term>extension: in 17th-century philosophy, "extension" is the defining characteristic of physical matter—the fact that it takes up space.</term> rather than with extension itself. Indeed, it should be noted that every faculty presupposes something real and actually existing in which it resides, unless one wishes to attribute faculties to nothingness. And what else is a faculty, if viewed in the thing itself outside of our concept, but the variable thing itself? What is the "faculty of receiving shapes" in a body, if not extension itself, insofar as it is capable of being limited in various ways? What is the faculty of thinking, if not thought itself, insofar as it can be applied to various objects and in various ways? Can anything else be conceived in the thing itself? Or if you do conceive it, express it in words that mean something certain and clear; for it is certain that nothing distinct can be alleged without resorting to trifles.

VI. Perhaps, however, it might happen that some who hear that the nature of the mind is placed in Thought—which is always present—might imagine that this must be interpreted as sublime meditations or discourses concerning the things of this world, or perhaps even spiritual matters. Since infants are devoid of these, they would thus be deprived of the nature of a Mind. But in truth, there is no need for thought to be restricted to these objects and modes, since the immediate perception of what is within us no more denotes exquisite meditations and reasonings than does the sense of pain, pleasure, joy, sadness, love, aversion, colors, sounds, tastes, and the like. All of these can arise in newborn infants—and in part even in those not yet born—by occasion of the body and its nourishment. Nor is it necessary for this truth that the Mind remember that it has always thought, or that it be mindful of all the thoughts it ever had; for it does not even remember intellectual thoughts unless it has applied itself to them both vividly and for a long time. For as far as those thoughts are concerned which have some connection to the body, their remembrance <term>remembrance: "reminiscentia," the process of recalling or retrieving a memory.</term> requires that while the Mind perceives something and notices (by reflecting on it purely and attentively) that it is new to it, it must use a brain that is well-prepared, firm, and calm, so that the traces <term>traces: "vestigia," the physical impressions or "footprints" supposedly left in the brain matter by sensory experiences.</term> of this thing may be easily impressed and constantly preserved. <header>RATIONAL THOUGHTS</header>

For this reason, it is no wonder if not only infants, but even grown men themselves, do not remember all their prior thoughts. No one can ever enumerate every thought of a single week or day, even if they are certain that that time was spent in thinking. From these points, therefore, it follows that the act of recollection <note>original: "reminiscentiæ"</note> of all acts of thinking is not the nature of the Mind; yet the fact that the Mind is thought itself remains, thus far, unshaken.

## CHAPTER IV.

*1. — 13. It is demonstrated that Thought, or the mind, and the body are distinguished from one another as much as possible. 14. — 17. No body is able to think, even if a single composite were to be made from mind and body. 18. The use of these points.*

I. Since it has been demonstrated that Thought can be conceived and can exist without the body, and that it is a substance <term>substance: in 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is something that can exist on its own, needing nothing else to exist.</term>, the last hesitation vanishes—the doubt as to whether thought might actually differ from the body, or if it were perhaps a "mode" or a "temperament" <term>mode: a quality or state of being (like "roundness" is a mode of a ball); the author is arguing thought is not just a property of the body.</term> of it. Could a body be capable of thinking? It follows from what has been said that Thought is a substance which is not a body, nor a mode of a body; and consequently, thought is not to be found among all the modes of a body. That is to say: the body cannot think. Yet because this is a momentous matter, and one that troubles many people quite deeply, I will not be reluctant to demonstrate it systematically <note>original: "ex professo"</note> and to mark out, as it were, the boundaries of the difference between thought (or the Mind) and the body.

II. Lest we be played by a confusion of words with things, we first require that nothing in the created world be supposed to exist except the Mind. Meanwhile, let attention be paid to the patterns or "ideas" of creatable things existing in the mind. There are ideas of internal consciousness, of perception, of judgment, and of the affections <note>original: "affectuum," referring to emotions or mental states</note>, which can be varied in many ways, but which are all nonetheless reduced to the single heading of "thought." There are also ideas of "extension" <term>extension: the defining quality of physical matter—the fact that it occupies space (length, width, and depth).</term> consisting of parts; if these parts are conceived as clinging together differently according to length, breadth, or depth, they represent various shapes. If they are separated, they show the origin of every kind of variety; but all these, too, are comprehended under the single idea of extension. Finally, there are other ideas that seem so composed of these two—extension and thought—that neither can be separated from them. For example, the idea of whiteness (even if nothing similar exists outside the mind, as happens when it is present in dreams)...

III. Secondly, let us suppose more generally that we are notified, without any more specific designation, that certain things emerge from nothing independently of each other. Since all knowledge of a thing occurs through its own unique idea, and here no such idea can be turned to over another (since nothing certain is determined), it is clear that the knowledge we are to have on this occasion will be rendered incomplete by us, as we abstract from all special ideas. In this way, as has already been said, we will conceive of "something" subsisting by itself; that is, we will have the concept of **substance**, but so abstracted from all the listed ideas that it involves none of them. Nevertheless, later on, when we see that the things represented by ideas exist, this concept becomes common to all of them. In this sense it can be said that many things, even of different natures, meet in one substance, or rather in one general concept of substance—that is, to be conceived as a substance. 

But we are not asking about that unity of substance between *Thought* <note>original: "Cogitationem"</note> and the extended; nor are things one in themselves just because they are conceived in one most general way. For nothing that has begun to be is and remains "mere being"—that is, nothing can exist that corresponds precisely to that general concept without also having something more specific by which its nature is constituted. 

But if things were to be called one thing simply because they agree in one general mode of conceiving, it would follow much more strongly that, due to a diversity of concept, things must also be diverse in themselves. And so, when it is conceived of one thing—firstly that it is "something," secondly that it is a substance, thirdly that it has such-and-such a nature, fourthly that it now exists, and fifthly that it lasts in existence—it would follow, I say, that one thing would be cut into just as many things, and be diverse from itself. This is something that all those who call this difference a *distinction of reason* <term>distinction of reason: a "distinction of reason" (distinctio rationis) is a difference that exists only in our minds or our way of describing a thing, rather than a real, physical separation in the thing itself.</term> (because it exists in the concept alone) would deny. From these points, therefore, nothing can be concluded regarding the unity or diversity of things.

V. To satisfy this question, the agreement and disagreement of ideas must be more carefully observed. Then, we must see whether the things themselves should be judged based on those ideas.

VI. To one paying attention to several ideas—for example, <term>knowledge</term>, <term>doubt</term>, <term>affirmation</term>, <term>negation</term>, <term>love</term>, and the like—it is perfectly clear that they all agree insofar as they are all "thought." It is also clear that their disagreement arises from the fact that this single "thought" is conceived as being varied in different ways. For although thought can be conceived without this or that specific way (or <term>mode</term>), it cannot be denied the capacity to receive them; and if thought is assumed to exist, it cannot help but be actually affected by some mode. Thought underlies all of them, and they necessarily involve thought. 

Therefore, if (as will be established later) we should judge existing things by our concept of them, when I contemplate the ideas of knowledge, doubt, affirmation, and the others, I should not conclude that the thing which doubts, the thing which knows, the thing which affirms, and the thing which denies are diverse existing things. Rather, I should conclude that there is one "thought" manifesting in these different ways. Thus, these do not differ among themselves or from "thought" in the actual thing, nor even merely in the concept I have of them, but in the variety of their modes. This is called a **modal difference** <note>original: "differentia modalis"</note>, which is distinct from a **real difference** and a **rational difference** <note>A "real" difference applies to two separate objects; a "rational" difference is a distinction made by the mind for the sake of analysis; a "modal" difference describes the relationship between a thing and the various ways it can exist.</note>. The same can be said of ideas involving <term>extension</term> <note>The quality of taking up physical space.</note>, such as motion, shapes, and individual bodies: they are all variations of one single extension, and they do not differ from each other or from extension in reality, but only in their mode.

VII. Furthermore, when I attend to the idea of a single variable thought, I conceive not only that one "thought" can exist modeled after this idea, but also that it can be multiplied so that many individual **Minds** <note>original: "Mentes"</note>—or thinking things—exist. Although I conceive each of these through the same idea of Thought (which is called the <term>essence</term> of its substance), I do not think they differ in their essence or in the idea of their nature. Nevertheless, because I conceive that each individual one could exist even if all the others were reduced to nothing, I am prompted to see that those things are diverse from one another. Therefore, I must conclude that they differ from each other **really** <note>Meaning they are separate, independent entities.</note>, but not **essentially**.

VIII. Finally, when I attempt to reduce those two aforementioned ideas (to which all other ideas are ultimately reduced)—namely, **thought** and **extension**—into one single idea in such a way that each retains its primary characteristic (just as I did when I reduced the idea of knowledge or affirmation to...

<margin>Note here that the question concerns the **essence of substance** <note>original: "essentia substantiæ"</note>, not of **modes** <note>A "mode" is a temporary state or quality of a thing, like a specific thought or a specific shape.</note>; because when an "essential difference" is said to exist, as often happens among corporeal things, it is less than a "real difference" and less than the "essential difference" currently being discussed.</margin>
By detracting nothing from thought, I have seen that the idea of knowledge and the idea of doubt agree to the extent that both retain that which is primary in them—namely, thought. I clearly perceive it to be impossible to do the same here. If I abstract from both **thought** and **extension** <note>original: "extensione," referring to the physical world that takes up space</note>, an incomplete common concept of both is indeed formed, but it is one that cannot denote anything in reality that precisely corresponds to it. I simply do not grasp how thought *as such* could agree with extension *as such*. I conceive of thought separately without extension, and vice versa. I conceive of each as diverse from the other—indeed, even with the other denied. I conceive of them as having **modes** <note>variations or specific instances</note>; for example, a thought about God, or a reflection upon my own perception; or an extension of a thousand ells <note>original: "ulnarum," a historical unit of length</note>, or a circular motion. I see these not only as diverse, but even as opposite and contrary, such that I almost burst into sudden laughter when I think that such things could be imagined to be one single thing.

Hence I judge that if such things—namely thought and extension—existing outside my own mind are to be considered similar to the ideas I perceive, then they do not merely differ **really** <note>original: "realiter," meaning they are separate objects</note>, as I just said regarding two or more minds which are multiple things; rather, they are distinguished **essentially** <note>original: "essentialiter"</note>, by the very essence of their substance. This is the greatest distinction of all, since each must be conceived through a completely different and opposite idea, and therefore a different essence. 

I notice, however, that it is possible for thought and extension (which differ in their essence, in themselves, and in their modes) to agree in such a way that when a certain variation occurs in thought, a variation in extension follows at the same time, and vice versa. In this way, their specific modes vary, are established, or cease simultaneously. Indeed, I easily conceive it possible for the **Author of Minds** <note>original: "Mentium Authori," referring to God</note> to will that no new thought or mind be established unless a certain physical body is arranged in certain ways. If these things should happen, I would nonetheless perceive these things as always remaining really and essentially distinct, even though they would then be "one thing" by composition—that is, a single composite—because they are established together and change together. The fact that the variation of one is linked to the variation of the other does not change the essence of the things themselves. I have clear ideas of all these things within me, and I am conscious that I perceive and conceive all of this most clearly and distinctly.

**IX.** Now, when I suppose myself to be warned that there are things existing that correspond to my ideas, should I judge their distinctions and agreements according to those differences and agreements I just clearly perceived in those ideas? Who could doubt this? For this is the most intimate, primary, and certain notion of all; if it were denied, then everything I think regarding myself, God, and the world...

For they are held precisely because the **ideas** <note>original: "ideæ"</note> of them are conceived clearly, vividly, and distinctly. How else do I know that a thought is not a lantern? How shall I demonstrate that God and the world exist; or how shall I believe the vast heavens are not merely a drop of water; if we must listen to the claim that these things are indeed so in the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectu," the faculty of understanding</note>, but not in the reality of the thing itself? If a thing can be otherwise than it is evidently perceived, then I, perceiving myself to think, could nonetheless in reality not be thinking: which reveals itself to be vigorously false. For by the very act that I would deny there is thought in me, even if I perceive it, an act of thinking—namely, the negation itself—would be placed within me. But since all men without exception are inwardly persuaded that it is possible to judge correctly concerning the differences of things, at least the more general ones; I would like to know whether that ought to be done without **perception** <note>original: "perceptione"</note>, or against perception, or according to it? The first is ignorance and rashness; the second, error and absurdity; there remains, therefore, the third: that the difference of things is perceived by me through perception itself. And yet, those very things by which objects differ from one another are not formally in my thought, but in the things themselves; and I am taught nothing concerning things except through ideas, which act as proxies for the things: even those things in the senses (from which some derive the distinction of things) that strike my **Mind** <note>original: "Mentem"</note> most closely are ideas. I am referred back, therefore, to the perceptions of ideas, among which there can rightly be no doubt that the clear and distinct ones are to be preferred over the obscure and confused when a judgment must be made.

The thought of my imperfect Mind about a perfect God, or about some other most excellent object, is not a swift motion of a small extension toward a large extension. Attention fixed upon an object, and the sticking together of one extended thing to another extended thing, are plainly different. Love, hate, etc., are not the bringing together or separation of various extensions: the subject which is varied in those ways is thought (let <term>Hobbes</term> <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), an English philosopher who argued for materialism—the idea that even thoughts are just the result of matter in motion.</note> call it a **phantasm** <note>original: "Phantasma"</note>, or whatever else he wishes) not extension. Thus, to be extended, to be small, to be thick, to be shaped in this or that way, to be moved through these or those channels—I conceive these to be plainly something else than thinking, and—in this or that way—to be conscious of this or that idea. These things, and very many of this kind, are conceived as being **worlds apart** <note>original: "plus toto cœlo differentia"; literally "differing by the whole sky," a Latin idiom for being diametrically opposite.</note>; and so I conclude the following about the things which are represented through them.

XI. First, Thought—or the substance of the Mind—is of an essence most distinct from extension or matter, and therefore—which amounts to the same thing—it is not material, but **immaterial**. For what is common in their ideas? Is it repugnant to conceive one without the other, or even to conceive either existing without its companion? Certainly you would judge it less absurd for the heaven to be the earth, and fire to be water, and a man's body to be made of glass, and a tree to be the city of Rome, and a triangle to be a circle, than for thought to be of a material nature. For those things just brought as examples are said to be distinguished in reality, yet for no other reason than that one is conceived without the others, and in each case there is something that is not common, however many common things they may have—for example, that they are extended, mobile, endowed with shape, and other things of that kind. What then of thought and of body, in whose ideas all things are plainly diverse, and nothing at all is common?

# RATIONAL REFLECTIONS

...each cannot be conceived except through one and the same idea of thought; but the **thinking thing** <note>original: "res cogitans"; the mind or soul.</note> and the **extended thing** <note>original: "res extensa"; physical matter that occupies space.</note> are not only conceived separately as existing things, but even if I wish to conceive of each as it is in itself, different kinds of ideas must necessarily be used, and one idea cannot completely represent both. Therefore, there is a greater distinction between any body and my mind than there is simply between any two other physical things.

XIII. It follows, thirdly, that **Thought** <note>original: "Cogitatio"</note> differs more from the body than it does from **nothingness** <note>original: "nihilo"</note> itself. In other words, it is "further" for the Mind to be material than it is for the Mind to be nothing; and extension (the nature of bodies) must be removed from the Mind's nature even more than nothingness itself. To be sure, if we consider **substance** <note>original: "substantiæ"; here meaning something that exists independently.</note> in its most general sense, thought does not differ more from body than from nothing: that is, it is more accurate to say thought and body share the trait of being "something" that exists on its own than to say thought is nothing. 

But if we look at the things themselves—where one is Thought and the other is Extension—the former is further removed from the latter than it is from nothingness. Indeed, one must deny that thought is "extension" even more than one denies it is "nothing." Once, all created Thought was nothing; even now, its essence stands alongside nothingness insofar as it "participates" in it—because it is not the **Supreme Being** <note>original: "summum Ens"; i.e., God.</note>. It is part of the very essence of a created mind that it involves many imperfections, and these imperfections are, in a sense, a form of "nothingness." It is impossible to have an idea of a created Mind without this "nothingness"—that is, imperfection—being essentially involved in it. 

But who would tolerate someone saying that the idea of extension, matter, and body is so involved in the idea of thought that it is impossible to conceive of the mind without the body? On the contrary, the opposite is clearly true to anyone paying attention. Therefore, thought differs more from matter than from nothing, just as a thing is more distinguished from its **opposite** than from something that is merely **different**. It is like how knowledge differs more from error than from simple ignorance; or how a true path is further from a path going the opposite way than it is from simply standing still; or finally, how virtue is further removed from vice than it is from insanity, stupidity, or a state of sleepiness.

XIV. Fourthly, it is concluded that **no body can think**. That is, whatever things are understood through the body and the things within it—such as extension, quantity, shape, motion, rest, the arrangement of parts, and whatever arises from the various combinations of these—do not have within their essence anything of that which we conceive as "thought." Their very "idea" contains nothing of the sort. One only needs to pay attention. Give to matter whatever shapes and parts you like; heap them up, pack them together, move them, divide them, crush them, and even, so to speak, refine them to the highest degree—must we then conceive that "thought" has suddenly appeared? If you take a heavy mass of matter and give it some shape...

...if you assign a shape to a mass, whether it be round or any other, will it think for this reason? You say no. But if you gave it a more complex form—if it were granted to you to give it the figure of a human body and all its limbs and vessels, inside and out—can you conceive that this mass would then begin to think? Or, if you prefer to look at finer matter: if a mass as thick as the first were divided into ten or twenty parts, would you believe it thinks for that reason? If into a thousand, into countless myriads, however subtle, endowed with any shape or motion you like; if you poured all these most subtle and agile parts into the vessels of the previous mass, so that they were introduced and moved through them—through the windings and paths of the brain—this way or that, straight or crooked, between these bodies and these walls rather than others, so that outward movement of the limbs follows—will thought now be present for this very reason? 

I ask you, why wouldn't the infinite parts of that matter—the **animal spirits** <note>original: "spirituum nempe animalium"; in early modern science, these were thought to be very fine, fluid-like particles that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note>, of course—which constantly evaporate from the body, as happens, and are dispersed into the air, also think? Is it simply because they happen to be driven in a more straight motion through a different kind of extension <note>The physical world that takes up space.</note> (namely, the air), while the other parts remaining inside—because they move through a different extension (namely, the brain) along a different path and perhaps with a more crooked motion—will therefore think, be conscious of themselves, of God, and of many things, and will judge, love, hope, and be strong in virtues or vices? 

Who would ever believe that God, when He commands us to contemplate, know, praise, and love Him, is actually ordering us to ensure our blood, or its most subtle part, is endowed with this or that temperament—that it be thin or thick, fast or slow, much or little—and that it move or rest in this or that way? The same can be asked of all thoughts, since they are all of the same nature. See how liable the minds of men are to folly, since almost everyone from their youth fashions such phantoms, and as adults they cherish them, and only with great effort do they finally let them go.

Following the previous page’s discussion on why the movement of "animal spirits" or the complexity of the brain's shape cannot produce thought, the author now addresses the common counter-argument: that physical illness and bodily fluids (humors) clearly affect our ability to think.</meta>

<page-num>58</page-num>

<header>RATIONAL REFLECTIONS</header>

For does a vapor from **black bile** <note>original: "atra bile"; in the ancient theory of the four humors, black bile was associated with melancholy and madness.</note> weaken thought, or does an excessive **humor** <note>The "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> soften it in those whose blood is thicker or thinner, slower or faster, more abundant or scarcer than usual? Do these things not seem to argue either that thought depends on matter, or that in many respects it is one and the same thing with it? 

I respond: the ideas of the senses were not given to us to be the true models of the nature of things (as a thousand experiments can prove), but rather the ideas of the intellect are; though a certain truth corresponds to the ideas of the senses, as will be seen. By the intellect, however, we clearly perceive thought alone and body alone, separately; from which we conclude they are distinct things. We evidently conceive that motion is linked with **extension** <note>A term for the physical world, which "extends" in space, as opposed to the mind, which does not.</note>, and thus they are not diverse things—the same holds for love being linked with thought. But we do *not* understand that thought and extension are inseparable or one and the same thing. 

Second, we understand it is possible for the **Author of all things** <note>Meaning God, as the creator of both mind and matter.</note> to cause variations in the Mind’s perception to occur certainly and simultaneously as a certain physical mass is varied in different ways. Yet, although those variations occur together and I am conscious of them together, I nevertheless perceive the essence of the varied things to be diverse, just as before; they do not become one and the same simply because they happen together, for the ideas of thought and extension remain always diverse. 

Now third, taught by the experiments of the senses, I understand that this is not only possible but is actually the case. For a sense of variation in both thought and extension is placed within me simultaneously. This sense, while presenting nothing clearly to me, indicates most confusedly though vividly a common benefit or harm to both the physical thing and the thinking thing, depending on the condition of either. 

Since I see that such a vivid perception exists in my thought only simultaneously with such a sense and perception of extension; and finally, since I know I must judge things based on ideas, and that my **Author** is not a deceiver who would have placed that connection of ideas in me in vain (however confused it may be); I conclude that the matter also holds outside my own concept. I conclude that a certain physical mass really exists, and its beneficial or harmful condition is linked with the beneficial or harmful sense in my thought. That is, I know I have a body. 

Just as I judge other things to exist, I also judge that they are not so closely united with me, because I have perceptions involving extension which I feel as being *outside* my own mass. And finally, when I observe that my body settles into sleep, yet I still have perceptions—though they are fainter and have less similarity or connection with those I observe vividly and ordinarily (which is what distinguishes waking life from dreams)—I notice that the thing whose immediate change causes my perception to change is not among external things. Nor is it the entire mass of my body, but rather a part of it, which I perceive to be in the **Head**.

XVI. And thus the fifth conclusion follows from what has preceded: that **Thought** and **extension** <note>extension: the physical property of occupying space, which defined "matter" in Cartesian philosophy.</note> are one—not in their reality and essence, which are understood as being most diverse, but in their composition and simultaneous existence. They are one insofar as certain variations of extension and thought are positioned together, being felt simultaneously in a single act and even captured by the imagination. This is precisely what the ideas of the senses, and even the imagination, teach us; in these, perception and extension are confusedly, yet also inextricably, folded together. Thus, judgment concerning these things should be made in conformity with the ideas we perceive through the senses; nevertheless, the essence of thought remains as remote as possible from every nature of the body. 

Regarding **brutes** <note>brutes: a common historical term for non-human animals, here argued to be biological machines without souls.</note>, however, what we observe in them are not thoughts but motions. These are not like the motions we notice in our own bodies or those of others—motions commanded by thought, which are the most certain signs of thinking. Instead, these are entirely irrational motions, arising from the sole disposition of matter without the perception of any idea, as <term>Descartes</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), who famously argued that animals are "automata" or complex machines.</note> most clearly demonstrated in *On Man*, and as <term>Forgeus</term> <note>Louis de la Forge (1632–1666), a physician and follower of Descartes who wrote influential commentaries on his work.</note> showed in his notes on that work. 

But even if you should strongly contend that thought or perception exists in animals, and this were granted to you, you could still conclude nothing in favor of the "materiality" of thought, so to speak. Rather, by the force of the preceding arguments, it would simply follow that such thought would be a substance distinct in essence from the body. It is, however, very easy to prove that such a principle neither is, nor ought to be, present in animals. 

The objection concerning humans, who think differently according to the different **temperaments** <note>temperament: the balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, etc.) believed to determine personality and health.</note> of their bodies, proves nothing more than that thought is varied in different ways according to the manifold variations of the body. Thus, if the movements in the body or its humors are sluggish, thick, confused, or turbulent—or conversely, orderly, easy, and agile—the thoughts of the mind are also varied in a sluggish, confused, stupid, or disorderly manner, and other ways that have a connection with bodily change. This is just as different thoughts follow within us—true, false, doubtful, sublime, light, joyful, or sad—based on the varying arrangement of certain external **characters** <note>original: "characterum"; referring to written letters or signs which, when read, trigger thoughts without the ink itself having the power to think.</note>. Yet, we do not judge that the faculty of thinking resides in those characters; the same judgment must be made regarding the body. Nor does it matter if it is said that those characters were arranged in such a way by a thought; for just as the thought remains nonetheless distinct from them, so it is distinct from the body. This is to say nothing of the **Divine Thought** <note>God's intellect.</note> having so ordered all bodies, and furthermore having established laws concerning the connection of thought with the various motions of those bodies.

XVII. We have lingered somewhat longer on this matter of the distinction between the **thinking thing** and the **extended thing** <note>original: "rei cogitantis à re extensa"; the core Cartesian distinction between Mind (Res Cogitans) and Body (Res Extensa).</note> because, as it seems to be of great importance, it must be asserted with evidence, as I believe has been done. But if it pleases some—

<header>RATIONAL THOUGHTS</header>

To strive further with words is unnecessary; there is only one more thing to consider here. Namely, that in this business, we should not pay much attention to words, but rather to **ideas**—especially the simpler, more complete, and primary ones. One should observe whether a thing is conceived under one or more of these ideas. For if someone were to say that **Thought** is one substance with the body, but differs from it "modally" <note>modally: a philosophical term meaning a difference in the *way* something exists (like a shape is a "mode" of a piece of wax) rather than a difference in the *thing* itself.</note>; and if by "substance" they mean that general concept of a "being existing through itself" which can refer to both the Mind and the body—and if it pleases them, contrary to common usage, to call the way that concept is filled to represent a mind a "mode"—we should not resist them too much. This is provided that they only disturb the names accepted by custom, and do not thereby confuse the things themselves. 

For it will nevertheless follow that what they call a "mode"—namely **thought**—and on the other hand, **extension** <note>extension: the physical property of taking up space.</note>, do not agree with each other except insofar as they are "something existing through themselves." They differ in such a way that each is conceived and known as entirely diverse from the other, even when the other is set aside or denied. From this, we conclude that those two, by whatever name they are marked, are as distinct from one another as any one thing can be conceived to be distinct from another. Let such a person call thought "material" if they like; if they say that with this new naming they are expressing that thought varies in many ways according to the variation of a certain matter, and they manage to get others to accept this term, we should congratulate them. But if they wish to betray the fact that the ideas of the "thinking thing" and the "extended thing" are necessarily and essentially one, they contradict their own concept.

### XVIII.

Nothing would be added to the completion of this chapter, except that—as noted before—from the substitution of bodily things (whether through the senses or the imagination) for intellectual things, a foul depravity follows in practice: specifically in the Mind's conduct toward God, and in the way most people think they should worship God. It seems necessary now to warn in a single word how this can be avoided by observing the distinction between **Thought** and all **bodies**. 

For what has been said about the difference between the thinking thing and the extended thing must be said, all else being equal, about the distinction between the "modes" <note>original: "modorum"; the specific ways or states in which a substance exists.</note> of each thing. It is certain that Minds and bodies, when they are related to God, do not set aside their nature or essence; rather, while retaining it, they behave in another way, or acquire new modes which truly agree with their essence. Therefore, when a superstitious or perhaps weak person embraces bodily and external things—motions, words, and the like—instead of divine, internal, and spiritual ones, they wander from the path. For just as the Mind is as distinct as possible from the body, so the modes of the mind (among which are those things that are truly spiritual and internal) are distinct from the modes of the body...

It argues that although mind and body (and by extension, the spiritual and the physical) are fundamentally different, God links them through His sovereign will to allow for communication and worship.</meta>

-> ### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL. <-

[Spiritual things] are as far removed from all external things as possible. Just as the **Mind** differs more from the body than it does from another **Mind**, so also truly spiritual matters differ more from external, bodily things than they do from <term>Mathematical Science</term> <note>The author views Mathematics as a bridge because it deals with pure abstractions in the mind, unlike physical objects.</note>. For mathematics agrees with spiritual things only insofar as it exists in thought; but this is not the case for external things, which differ in both reality and essence. Indeed, just as the **Mind** differs more from the body than it does from nothingness itself, so also spiritual things differ more from bodily ones than from the pure ignorance and neglect of external things. And since no body is capable of thought, no external things—if viewed alone and in themselves—will ever reach the point where they can be mistaken for things that are truly and properly spiritual and divine. For whatever can be pleasing to God within the realm of spiritual things arises from something other than the external.

However, for the same reason that the <term>Author of all things</term> <note>A common philosophical title for God.</note> does not wish to establish a Mind unless a specific body is first established—namely, because of His own <term>pleasure</term> <note>original: "placitum"; referring to God's sovereign will or decree rather than a casual whim.</note>, rather than because the nature of either thing requires it—He likewise ordinarily arranges matters so that internal divine actions and spiritual operations are not present unless external things are also present. Yet, those internal and spiritual operations are not produced by the force of those external things, nor do they have a necessary connection rooted in the things themselves; rather, the entire power of the connection lies in **God's sovereign will**.

Furthermore, just as once a Mind is established, bodily things are then perceived by it, and the Mind uses them while it teaches itself and others—employing them as signs and reminders by which thoughts are stirred up in itself and in others—it even arranges them so wisely that it is easily judged by others who experience the same thing that the Mind, along with those external things or their material principle (namely, the body), composes a single unit. This is true even though each retains its own distinct nature separately. It is exactly the same for spiritual and internal operations: when they are present within, then external things are useful; they assist, remind, and serve as signs. Nor can it happen otherwise than that the mind disposes of all external things over which it has power in such a way that it will be easy—not for earthly and <term>brutish</term> <note>In this context, "brutish" refers to minds that are driven by animal instincts or physical senses rather than reason.</note> minds, but for spiritual ones—to judge that a spiritual principle is truly present in that external <term>governance</term> <note>original: "regimini"</note>. Thus, the spiritual and the external together constitute a single whole—namely, **one true worship**—notwithstanding the separation or distinction that exists in their fundamental natures, which remains even while they are positioned together, at least as long as we are not purely spiritual minds. Many more excellent conclusions can be deduced from this by those who consider the matter more attentively alongside what has already been said.

<header>RATIONAL THOUGHTS</header>

### CHAPTER V.

1. 2. 3. *In God there is something analogous to ourselves, and that is Thought.* <note>The author uses "analogous" to mean a shared quality that exists in both God and humans, though to vastly different degrees.</note>
4. *Hobbes is refuted, who denies that we perceive anything that exists in God.* <note>A reference to Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), the English philosopher who argued that because God is infinite, we cannot truly "conceive" or perceive His nature, only His power.</note>
5. 6. *It is demonstrated that the Essence of God consists in Thought, to be expressed hereafter in more specific terms.*

I. Having shown up to this point that the essence of the human mind is Thought itself, it remains to be proven regarding the essence of God that it is also Thought in its very self <note>original: "ipsissimam Cogitationem"</note>. This should frighten no one at first glance, as if we were asserting by this that either the created Mind enjoys the Divine Essence, or that God possesses the same essence as the created Mind. Such a notion is as far from the truth as it is from our own meaning. Nothing else is intended by these words beyond what is commonly said by everyone in other terms, when they all assert that the human Soul is a Spirit, or enjoys the nature and essence of a Spirit, and that God is also a Spirit in His essence. From this, no one has ever concluded that they all intended to either change the nature of the human soul into God, or God into the soul. Thus, by substituting the word **Thought** for the word **Spirit**, nothing else is asserted here except that all things in the human Mind are to be referred to thought, and the Mind is that very thought; and all things that are in God are Thought, and God is that very thing—namely, Thought or Perception. But He perceives things in Himself in a far different way and manner than in other Minds, and we perceive the <term>Divine Thought</term> <note>original: "Cogitationem Divinam"</note> to be of an infinitely higher kind than our own. Thus an infinite distance is recognized between them, which will become so clear from what follows that no one will be able to complain that God is being mixed with the creature.

II. It matters little, it seems to me, to dispute with great effort whether there are concepts so abstracted from God and the Creature that they can be common to both, or predicated of both. These matters, which are much disputed, are obscure, and they almost vanish due to excessive abstraction and subtlety. The matter will be grasped more clearly and firmly if it is noted that the concepts themselves are not common or specific to things, but rather the things represented by the concepts are. In all acts of conceptualizing, things are not represented entirely as they are—that is, completely. Hence our intellect, which because of its weakness cannot properly apprehend the complete state of a thing in a single act,

...cannot [do otherwise], it applies itself to that thing through divided acts; and if it relates to two things in the same way—even if those things are extremely different—nevertheless, because of that similarity in the way it conceives different things, that concept is called "common." Things are then said to be grasped by the same concept. In this way, a **correspondence** <term>convenientia: a shared suitability or agreement between two different things</term> is signified in the modes of thinking or perceiving different things.

Therefore, the whole question comes down to this: In the way a finite concept deals with God, is there not some similarity with the way it deals with created things? This is too evident to be denied. However, if we are looking at the concept itself, this concludes nothing about the reality of the matter unless there is elsewhere a positive foundation of similarity in the things themselves. Without such a foundation, those general concepts which are called "common" would be false. For if absolutely no similarity exists between objects—as between God and **nothingness**—a common concept cannot apply to both. Therefore, we must return to the correspondence of the things themselves to prove that the essence of God is not poorly designated by the name **Thought**, a term he shares with the created mind.

### III. 

For even if—as will be seen more specifically hereafter—nothing can be said of God and creatures **univocally** <term>univocal: using a word to mean exactly the same thing in both cases</term>, or, although it is true that nothing is in God in the same way it is in a creature (and vice versa, the creature possesses nothing in the same way and sense that God Himself does), there is nonetheless between them a certain **analogy**, or similarity, or correspondence, much like that between a model <note>original: "typum"</note> and the thing represented.

For, **first**, those real things that exist in the created Mind **formally** <note>formally: as they actually exist in their own nature and form</note> are indeed in God—though not "formally" (that is, in the same form or same way), but in an **eminent** <note>eminent: in a higher, more perfect, or foundational way; for example, a composer "eminently" contains a song before it is written</note> and more perfect manner.

**Second** (which involves the proof of the previous assertion), what exists in the created mind not formally but **objectively** <note>objectively: existing as an object of representation or an "idea" in the mind</note>—that is, what is represented through the most perfect perception of the specific ideas that the creature contemplates—that is indeed in God not only "objectively," but also "formally." That is to say, God actually possesses those perfections of which the ideas are the objects of our thought.

Now, those real things that exist in us formally are, as has been proven, **thought**, **perception**, and **will**. Conversely, those things which are most real in our ideas as representations are **Thought** itself in its most perfect form, and perception and will subject to no defects. Therefore, despite the infinite disparity <note>original: "disquiparantia"</note> between God and the created Mind, there is a similarity which must be presented using the same words—namely, **Thought** or **spontaneous perception**—by anyone who attributes all perfections to God. Someone might ask: "How do you know that those things you conceive as most perfect regarding Thought, regarding voluntary Perception, and if there are any...

-># RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

...similar things exist in God, and not other things which you simply do not know? I respond that this is proven when His existence is proven: for by "God" we do not usually mean something that is entirely unknown, but this very thing which is represented through the idea of **most perfect thought**; or, if you reject the name "Thought," then the **Most Perfect Being**, or the one possessing all perfect things most perfectly, is what is denoted by the word *God*. Truly, that which would possess all the most perfect things, but would in some way not possess itself, would not be most perfect: indeed, that which does not perceive itself, and is not conscious of itself, does not fully possess itself. You must therefore necessarily conceive that this very thing, if it is indeed most perfect, possesses thought, and indeed the most perfect [thought]. This concept could not have been placed in you by something that itself lacked that quality. Furthermore, since this concept involves existence—if indeed to conceive of most perfect thought is to conceive of an existing thought—it compels you to judge that it exists. Yet, the fact that things are similar to our clearest and most distinct concepts and judgments is the first thing known; if this were denied, you could conclude that you yourself do not exist, even though you conceive and judge that you do. There exists, therefore, with God and in God a **Thought** <term>Cogitatio: here used to mean a conscious, spiritual activity of the mind</term> which is God Himself.

IV. Consequently, the things which **Hobbes** <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), an English philosopher famous for his materialistic and often controversial views on religion and the state.</note> teaches—dangerously, as he does almost everything—are far from the truth. He claims that when we attribute to God the things we conceive of Him, we ought not to think that these terms signify *what He is*; but rather that they only denote our admiration, obedience, and humility. He argues that there is no idea or concept of God, and similar claims, by which men are called away from the knowledge and study of God; for He is held to be not only unknown, but even unknowable. All the things he throws together here and there, mixed with absurdities, are often refuted by the very things he proposes in those same passages. For example, consider in passing one passage among many, in which all his errors on this matter are briefly gathered, which is found in Chapter 15, Section 14 of *De Cive* <note>original: "de Cive," Hobbes's work "On the Citizen" (1642).</note>. There, it is absurd that *he wants what cannot be conceived to be understood by "God"*; that *by "understanding" he understands a disturbance of the mind stirred up by external organs*; and *by "idea" or "concept," an imaginary phantom*. Contradicting these is his claim *that there is something in God analogous to our will*, for this destroys his preceding points and opposes what he adds—*that we nevertheless cannot conceive of it*. On the contrary, it is impossible to judge the **analogy** <term>analogia: a comparison between two things that are different but share a similar proportion or relationship</term> of things unless they are first conceived, both separately and together, so that it may be judged how they differ and how they do not. To this point belong the things he adds: *when* (he says) *we say that something* (namely God) *is infinite, we do not signify anything in the reality itself, but rather an impotence in our own mind, as if we were saying that we do not know whether or where it is terminated.*

An excellent analysis! <note>The author is likely being ironic here, mocking the logic of his opponent (Hobbes).</note> I say that God is infinite; yet it is the same as if I do not say God is infinite, for I do not know whether He is infinite, I doubt whether He has boundaries and where they might be—I wish, in this respect, to remain ignorant. Does he think, as he indeed pretends, that God is worthily honored in this way? Finally, he refutes himself:

1. When he says of God, in that same place, those things from which it follows that God is the **Creator**, **Eternal**, **Omniscient**, the **Ruler of all**, **Omnipotent**, **Infinite**, **Immaterial**, **One**, and **Blessed**.

2. When he says we ought to admire Him and obey Him with humility: for what would you admire most highly if you could not affirm that the thing is not, in itself, a brute <term>brutam: a "brute" thing refers to something unconscious or lacking reason, like a stone or a mindless force</term> object, but is truly endowed with thought? Indeed, what kind of "admiration of God" is this: *I admire the eternal, greatest, and just God, yet I doubt—or rather (as he says) I am unwilling to say—that He is such a thing, lest I circumscribe Him within the limits of my own imagination*? But if God is not such a thing, then you are merely admiring your own fictions and yourself, the one who forged them. Furthermore, heartfelt obedience, of the kind he understands, is not offered except where there are laws; and laws are the signs and effects of thought. Nor do we carry ourselves humbly from the heart before anyone unless we judge that person to be conscious (**thinking**) of their own Power and our weakness.

3. Finally, when he confesses that one name is significant of the Nature of God—the meaning of which properly and in reality belongs to God—namely **Existing**, or **Being**, or simply **Is**, he swallows up everything he previously said. For in this name, by which God Himself designates His own Essence, everything is included that can be attributed to God: for He who is **simple** <term>simplex: in philosophy, "simple" means not made of parts; a pure, unified essence</term> and pure **Being** lacks no manner of being, no pure being; therefore, He does not lack Himself—that is, He is conscious of Himself, or He thinks. The same applies to the other most perfect attributes, which there is no need to list here; if He lacked them, He would certainly not be a simple being, but an imperfect being, composed of *being* and *not-being*.

V. It is therefore proven—since those who deny it have existed—that there is something in God consistent with our concepts, and that this is represented by the most worthy idea of **Thought**. From this, it is easily deduced that the Essence of God, and the most ample concept we can have of God (embracing all things, to which all things are reduced, from which they flow, and without which God cannot be conceived—which is truly the concept of His essence), consists in one **Divine Thought** which is conceived by us according to our limited capacity. Nothing is lacking to the most perfect Thought, therefore it embraces all things; thus, one Thought is all. From this comes **simplicity**, which is this very thing itself, and which some say should be considered the final attribute of God; in truth, it is the first, for the knowledge of it must be presupposed...

[This concept] must come before a specific knowledge of other things, and be involved in the concept of each, without which you will conceive no attribute worthy of God: although after the examination of all [attributes], you can once again reflect upon it more attentively and clearly, in the sense that you might call it the ultimate attribute. 

But let us proceed. That which is all things in God is, without doubt, the Essence of God; therefore, **Thought** is the essence of God. To this, whatever things are in God are reduced, for there is no thing in God of which God is not conscious through that very thing: otherwise, there would be things in God devoid of perception which God would perceive through a thought different from them; they would be "brute" <term>brute: irrational or mindless, like a stone or a physical force</term> and unthinking things, which is blasphemous, and a concept worthy not of God, but of an imperfect idol. From this also flow all the other attributes. Once most perfect Thought is posited, it follows that it knows itself, which is *Intelligence*; that it possesses itself simultaneously, which is *Eternity*; that it subsists by itself, or is self-sufficient, which is *Sufficiency* or *Independence*; that it rests content in itself, which is *Felicitas* <note>original: "Felicitas"—this refers to a state of perfect happiness or blessedness</note>; that it approves of itself, which is *Justice* and *Holiness*; that it does not will or think anything in vain, which is *Power*; and so on for all the rest. 

Deny whatever you wish regarding God, so long as you grant a single Divine or most perfect thought, all things remain, and the most sufficient foundation of all God's attributes remains; but without it, no attribute of God can be conceived, nor God Himself. I can conceive that God could have not been the Creator, or not the Redeemer, and such things; I can thus conceive of one attribute of God without another attribute, so that in its concept the concept of the other is not formally present: but it is impossible for me to think of a God who is without Thought; it is impossible for me to conceive of any of His attributes in whose concept thought is not formally present, whose basis and foundation, positive reason, and—if I may speak thus—immediate subject, is not most perfect Thought itself. Nor do I see what more could be required to conclude that the Nature and Essence of God is Thought itself.

## CHAPTER VI.

*1. 2. The first difference between Created and Uncreated Thought, with the definition of each and some consequences. 3. 4. The second difference is likewise proposed. 5. 6. The third: but all in a more general sense.*

I. First, when I look into my Mind or my thought, I discover that it is indeed one regarding its subject—that is, the immediate consciousness itself within us, which we might call the matter or material of thought; yet that one thing is highly variable in the forms it successively takes, in perceiving innumerable objects, in judgments, and in many passions. I do not perceive all these things at the same time nor in the same way, and if I were to list them one by one to show how created thought differs, their number would overwhelm me. However, I notice that all of them can be reduced to this one thing: they are the **variability of thinking**. Thus, the first distinct notion I form of my mind, as it exists in its current state, is this: that I am a **Thought that is variable** through the multiplicity and the repeating of acts of thinking. This is the first general form of the Created Mind: namely, a susceptibility to innumerable forms or modes of thinking in terms of number, time, and manner. 

This imperfection is essential to every <term>Created Mind: a mind brought into existence by God, such as a human or angelic soul</term> to such an extent that, although in the future—by the grace of the <term>Uncreated Mind: the eternal, self-existing Mind of God</term>—it may happen that the created mind becomes "fixed," so to speak, upon one object, and remains with it uniformly and most constantly, there nevertheless remains both the repetition or succession of that same act (or its foundation) and the capacity for inconstant variation. Further, when I ask: from where does that variability in my Thought arise? I see it is because my Thought is limited; it does not embrace everything thinkable at once, but only a certain thing at one time, so that if I wish to attend to another, the first ceases to be perceived by the mind. 

Hence, the second notion that occurs to me, by which I know the created Mind more distinctly, is **limitation in Thinking**. Therefore, that the Created Mind is **mutable and limited Thought** is its first and most general definition. This definition denies more reality than it affirms; for it cannot be otherwise than that whatever is not the <term>Supreme Being: original: "Ens Summum," referring to God as the highest reality</term> must necessarily involve in its nature, and therefore in its definition, many defects. It is clear that these defects are essential to it, because when these qualities are placed within Thought, it is established as such.

II. From these points it is clear that in uncreated substance, all things are the substance itself, or simply the thing itself. But in a **Created Substance**, there is indeed something fixed and single, by which the substance is fixedly and constantly distinguished from nothingness, and from any other substance (if such exists). However, because that fixed element, which is the substance itself, is not simply perfect, it must be "mobile" or variable. These variations are called <term>modes<gloss>The specific ways or "shapes" a substance takes, such as a specific thought in a mind or a specific shape in a body</gloss></term>. Thus, in the mind, **Thought** is that fixed element which is always and constantly present; but in how many ways is it varied and limited? Likewise, in a body, there is fixed **extension**, but it is varied in innumerable ways. 

It is also clear that the knowledge of God is easier than the knowledge of the created Mind: for to know the one God, the contemplation of Thought is sufficient—that Thought which is simply Thought, without any limitation, discrimination, addition, or restriction. **Pure Thought** knows all things at once, encompasses all things, and even brings into being outside itself all things that it wills. For pure Thought thinks itself to be most efficacious <note>that is, perfectly powerful and effective</note>; otherwise, it would lack this thought, and thus there would be "non-Thought" within it, and it would not be pure Thought. It also thinks things to be exactly as it pleases to think them: for if they were otherwise, Thought would be determined and varied by external things, and thus it would no longer be a "pure" thing. If, indeed, they did not exist at all, it would be limited, for it could not think what it willed with truth—which is foreign to pure Thought. (I have noted this here specifically regarding **Power**, because it is easier to see with the other <note>divine</note> attributes that they are all contained under "Thought" in the absolute sense; and perhaps this will be shown elsewhere.)

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

While in knowing God we can fearlessly pour out our thoughts, having broken all barriers, here we must proceed one drop at a time. Just as the general points already stated provide a specific knowledge of God (since He is one), so too, to arrive at a specific knowledge of a particular created Mind, it is enough to have the notion of **variable and limited Thought**. 

For even if you know in a general sense that a lack of knowledge and a lack of consideration follow from its limitation, while knowledge of a few things follows from its capacity; and that the <term>faculties<gloss>facultates</gloss></term> attributed to it are not something different from the mind itself, but the mind itself considered insofar as it is variable or to be changed by many causes; and that to attribute an <term>act<gloss>actus; the immediate exercise of thought</gloss></term> to it is nothing more than to view it as changing or while it is being changed; and to attribute a <term>habit<gloss>habitus; a disposition or settled state of mind</gloss></term> to it is to view it as already changed and ready to repeat the act—(for everything that can be reasonably designated by these words is Thought itself considered in this way, from which it follows that such things must be removed from our concept of God in this sense, which it is helpful to note here in advance of everything that will be said about God)—nevertheless, the soul is not satisfied here when the question concerns a specific mind in particular. 

Once again, ignorance, knowledge, and other things must be limited according to their objects, and in almost infinite other ways: which faculties pass into habits through acts; and out of the innumerable good or bad acts and habits—which no one can possess all at once—it must be designated which ones out of all of them a person has, and to what degree, for the variations go on almost to infinity. All these things are scarcely known even from the longest experience and familiarity. (Nor indeed are they required for living our lives with others, since in that case we must presume about the Minds of others—unless the contrary is clear—that God has worked good, or perhaps better things, in them as in us; a presumption that proceeds from love, rather than from scientific knowledge.) If these things are compared with Divine matters, they will most evidently prove that God can be known most easily of all things—even more easily than my own Mind, which is better known to me than any physical body.

I will attribute as little as possible to myself, so that at last that reality remains which is intimately innate to me from the nature of my created state. ### RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...[bo]dies indeed either clearly do not exist, or at least they cannot concern me. I also set aside the imagination for the same reasons. Furthermore, I lay aside thoughts of every created thing really distinct from me, whether it be a Mind or a body: for those things could not exist, and I could lack the ideas of them as things distinct from myself, while I nonetheless would still subsist. I also set aside aversion, sadness, hatred, and similar passions, even if they are viewed as purely spiritual: for it could have happened that nothing existed from which there was a need to turn away, to be sad about, or to hate. With these things dismissed, there remains however Thought tending toward some form by which it might be filled, toward some place where it might rest; this Thought is neither sense, nor imagination, nor turbulent passion. That is, what remain are Intellect and Love, or the intelligent seeking of <term>fulfillment<gloss>acquiescentia; literally "rest" or "repose," the state of the mind finding its end in truth or God</gloss></term>. My own Thought indeed remained as its own object, but by the very fact that it looks at itself, imperfect as it is, there is placed before it another, greatest object through the idea of an absolutely most perfect thought: namely God, whom the mind cannot but conceive as existing, as supremely powerful, and as the one upon whose will everything—and therefore the mind itself—depends. By comparison with Him, the mind is more and more convinced of its own imperfection—that of itself it is nothing, has nothing, and can do nothing at all. From this, if its Intellect and Love wish to embrace that which is in the self, insofar as it proceeds from the self, they are frustrated, for nothing of "me" is truly in "me." But if they are directed toward that which is from God in me, since this does not exist or subsist by itself, it leads by this very fact to God: the most perfect and powerful Thought, which is the one, proper, and most real object of Intellect and Love, by which they are filled with rest.

Therefore, having stripped away all forms as much as possible, there remains in the created Thought a "form" of itself that is not worthy of consideration or esteem—namely, that of itself it is absolutely nothing—but the form of God, or His image, remains, demanding and filling the intellect and love. And yet this is the gift of the created Mind; what could be more intimate or more suitable to it? So much so that those who fill their thought with alien forms and set aside this one, which is their own, are at fault and act against nature. For this is nevertheless necessarily involved in that definition of the created Mind by which that which is most positive and intimate of all in it is expressed. Specifically: *A created Mind is Thought tending toward God through intellect and love, with a disregard for itself.* <note>original: "Mens creata est Cogitatio intellectu & amore ad Deum tendens cum sui despectu." Now if in a similar way I attempt to know the Thought which is God, in distinction to our own, I can also conceive of Him stripped of many forms that have a relation to external things, such as: being the one who decrees, the Creator, Sustainer, Pitier, Redeemer, Judge, and the like. IV. Certainly, in these things that have now been said about both Minds <note>meaning the Created Mind (human) and the Uncreated Mind (God)</note>, there lie hidden very many things of no small importance, of which it would not be entirely pointless to notice one or two. First and foremost, true Logic consists in this uncovering and separation of the forms of thinking, so that each may afterwards be better estimated at its just value, replaced in its proper order, and pursued according to its merit, lest life be wasted on trifles and unworthily. For it is not the task of Logic—that is, acting with reason—to seize upon the first form of thinking that either occurs or pleases (for example, about angles or circles, numbers, sounds, sensible things, or other matters regarding a brute and earthly life) and to spend all one's thought on them, even if with some order. Rather, we should first remove all these, so that we may then embrace the remaining one, God, as the most worthy; and thereafter resume certain others as accessories insofar as they are grounded in that most worthy one, are connected with it, and are referred to it. That, finally, is the true and Sacred Logic which God established along with man. The reason for the connection of the mind with the body cannot be given from the consideration of the Mind itself, or the body, but it must come from another <term>principle<gloss>original: "principio"; a fundamental source or cause, here referring to God as the coordinator of soul and body</gloss></term> freely disposing of these. V. Third, to return to the proposal: if I look at where those things happen to my Thought which are so limited? From where come so many forms? Why does it not rest in itself but strive beyond itself? I see it is because I am not from myself, nor through myself, nor for myself, as if I were a goal unto myself; I am nothing solid, nor representative of my own self. Otherwise, all things in me would be perfect, since they would have no other model, no other goal than themselves, nor would they depart from themselves. But on the contrary, I am from another, through another, and for another—like a shadow and an image reflecting another. These things, whatever they are in me, permeate and, so to speak, transcend and distinguish my Thought from that **Thought** which is such as I have said: which is from itself, through itself, and for itself, solidly subsisting, and representative of itself. From this also, whatever *that* Thought thinks is good and perfect, for it does not strive toward anything else from whose goal it might wander.

### CHAPTER VII.

*1. Three ways of knowing the perfections of God. 2. Only the way of causality is demonstrative. 3. It is proved that this way exists within the way of eminence, and a new argument for the Existence of God is proposed. 4. 5. 6. 7. The way of negation is either nothing, or it must be referred to the causal way. 8. Properties of the essential perfections of God.*

I. People commonly say that knowledge of God, both of a general kind and that which is more specific, is acquired by three ways. The first they name the **way of causality** <note>original: "causalitatis viam"</note>, where from the consideration of the effects that are visible in the world, one arrives at a knowledge of their first cause, which is God. They call the second the **way of eminence** <note>original: "viam eminentiæ"; the practice of taking a "good" human quality and projecting it to an infinite degree in God.</note>, namely, when after some created perfection has been thoroughly perceived, it is then attributed to God, but in the most eminent and highest degree. The third is called the **way of negation** <note>original: "negationis via"; also known as "apophatic theology," defining what God is *not* (e.g., "not finite").</note>, which occurs when the imperfections seen in creatures are removed from our conception of God.

II. It must be admitted that if the question is about the *occasion* <note>The specific instance or observation that triggers a thought.</note> by which we are stirred to think about God, then all of these are ways to his knowledge. And so, since all things can be considered either as certain effects, or as possessing perfections, or as being limited in their perfections (that is, having imperfections), just as I recently considered my own mind—but in reverse order:
1. as limited and variable (which belongs to the **way of negation**), 
2. as intelligently seeking to find rest (which belongs to the **way of eminence**), 
3. as not from itself, but from another (which belongs to the **way of causality**).
In this manner, all ways can be reduced to those three: causality, eminence, and negation. Thus, also in the following book, we shall take the opportunity to think about God more specifically by inspecting those effects within us, whether they are in any way perfect or endowed with certain imperfections. But if the question concerns the *method of demonstrating the certainty* of those things which are attributed to God—or if it is asked by what way someone might think about God and His attributes so as to be certain that the knowledge they have is true—then that enumeration of three ways is superfluous and flawed. For the latter two, insofar as they cannot be referred back to the way of causality, are of no strength—
