# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...ity for generating certain knowledge. For indeed, whatever in created things, especially in **Minds**, is not the effect and operation of God, that is all either mere nothing, or error, or sin: and conversely, whatever is neither error, nor sin, nor nothing, is the operation and effect of God proceeding from that supreme cause. But it is beyond doubt that everything from which the knowledge of God is derived in us is not nothing, or error, but some work: which, since it proceeds from nowhere but God, leads to the evident conclusion that God is recognized solely through those things which he himself has worked—that is, by the **way of causality alone** <note>original: "viam solius causalitatis"</note>. 

And one must be careful lest anyone understand "the works of God" here to mean only physical works; rather, having set those aside, one must attend to those which belong to a different order—namely to **thought**, and its immutable ideas, to which we can add nothing and from which we can take nothing. Above all, one must attend to the idea of a **Supremely Perfect Thought** <note>The author is likely referring to the "Idea of God" as an innate concept of perfection.</note>: for these are the operations of God from which we acquire our knowledge of him, insofar as they can be referred to God alone as their Author and Cause. Such were the solid demonstrations concerning God proposed by **Descartes** <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> in his *Meditations*. 

And although in the fifth [Meditation] that Philosopher seems to demonstrate the existence of God by a way other than that of causality and effects, nevertheless, to one who attends well to the order of things and to the things themselves, it will be clearly evident that the supreme certainty demonstrated there is drawn from what preceded it, and that all difficulties cannot be repelled unless one recurs to the **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the primary agent that brings something into being; the author argues that even Descartes' ontological argument (God's essence implies existence) relies on the fact that God caused the idea of himself in our minds.</note>. This could be shown at greater length, were this not an unsuitable place for commenting on the writings of others.

§ III. Indeed, concerning these three ways which others enumerate, there would have been complete silence, had not the necessity of showing that the knowledge and idea of God is not something fictitious and negative, but something true and most positive, required it. For these two ways—**eminence** and **negation**—insofar as they are distinguished from the way of causality, obscure the matter. For even if you increase a certain perfection which you recognize in creatures by many degrees so as to attribute it most eminently to God, how will you know from that point that the increased perfection is actually given in someone—namely, in God—unless you follow it by the way of the cause? 

Are you not taught by that way that the perfections which are in you and in your ideas must be from a **Sustainer of yourself** <note>original: "Sustentatore tui"</note> who truly possesses at minimum as much [perfection] as those ideas contain? Or, to speak more generally, that there must be a cause endowed with as much perfection in reality as you have in your representation? ...solid <note>The text begins mid-word, likely continuing "solidum" (solid) from the previous page.</note>, belonging to that class of arguments which return from the effect to the cause. And yet, nothing is more necessary for a judgment founded on the necessity of concluding that an effect proceeds from a cause—and indeed not from nothing—and that the perfect does not come from the imperfect as if from its cause. 

And it must be noted that "effect" is spoken of here not only as **Thought** <note>original: "Cogitationem"</note> viewed in itself and materially <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "materially" refers to the act of thinking itself, regardless of what is being thought about.</note>, nor only as something limited and variable in its nature, but especially as it is clothed in its own forms or ideas, or at least certain ones. The cause of these forms, or modes of thinking, is sought; and more specifically, the form or mode of thinking about the Supreme Being, or—what is the same thing—the idea of God. 

It is certain that the cause of this is not my own **Thought** considered most generally and materially. For if thinking, or being conscious, by itself implied the idea of God, then this idea ought to be present in all my modes of thinking, even the most imperfect ones, since **Thought** is present in them. Furthermore, if my own thought, or the concept of my own thinking, were completely sufficient to produce the concept of **most perfect Thought**, I could not help but conceive of myself as the most perfect thought whenever I conceive of myself as thinking. 

Nor can the sought-after cause be believed to lie hidden in my other modes and forms of thinking—which are less perfect than the form or idea of God—as if the form of the imperfect could possess within itself the form of the perfect (and I do not say this merely by way of comparison). Whatever is in me, however, is **Thought** along with its modes. Therefore, the required cause must be sought not in me, but outside of me; sought, I say, but in a thing regarding which I cannot allege the same disadvantages as I do for myself, because of which I saw that I am not that cause. 

Therefore, a **Thought** must be granted as the cause, in whose modes of thinking **most perfect Thought** is involved in all things, and which cannot but truly conceive of itself as the **most perfect Thought**—that is, which is **God**. From this, it is most invincibly concluded that God exists. 

This will be established even more clearly if a cause is sought not only for my modes of thinking, but also simultaneously for the thinking substance itself and its present duration. Indeed, the question of the cause of my **Thought**, viewed materially or substantially, leads me to the existence of God, as will be discussed when we treat the sufficiency of God. 

Finally, I would dare to say that by following the way of Causality, we can be made certain of God's existence best of all, if attention is paid to that rest <note>original: "acquiescentiam." This refers to a state of intellectual satisfaction or peace where the mind no longer needs to search for further causes.</note> in him who is represented through the most perfect idea. For that certainty regarding God which comes from the fact that the idea of God exists in our thought or intellect is indeed most firm; but it must be admitted that it is not infrequently fruitless and useless, or the kind that produces nothing but vain discourses and leaves its possessors as "practical Atheists." [In that Supreme Thought] I shall now and forever rest most fully and absolutely; I cannot but be most powerfully determined to confess from my whole soul that **Supreme Thought** <note>original: "Cogitationem illam Summam"</note> which is self-sufficient and at rest within itself. Even in myself, I understood nothing—nor do I yet understand anything—that is not (in respect to this rest) worthy of contempt or neglect, and incapable of establishing a foundation for rest. Therefore, God remains as the cause, or rather that **Thought** which I conceive to rest in its own knowledge of itself, and which I embrace as the ultimate goal and foundation of both striving and rest. If He did not exist, why would I be allowed to find rest in a mere fiction—which is what something that does not exist is—rather than in myself, who am a truly existing thing? 

However, when someone, setting aside themselves, truly rests in God, there is no need for many such arguments; for a brilliant and unshakable certainty is immediately joined to that rest. This is why the upright, who have not been educated in the human sciences, are more truly and solidly certain of God than the **Theoretical Doctors** <note>original: "Doctores Theoretici"; a likely reference to academic theologians or Scholastic philosophers who prioritized logic over internal experience</note>. This is not because of what they have heard from others or read in a book, but because they feel the solidity of the foundation in which they rest most powerfully, effectively, and vividly. This is true even if they cannot express the feelings of their soul using the human method of the sciences, nor refute all opposing subtleties with composed words, as they are not accustomed to **metaphysical reflections**. 

But this is common to all: when they become certain of God’s existence and perfections from the consideration of **Thought**—whether it is viewed as an indeterminate substance, or as modified in the intellect through the idea of God, or in the will through rest in the thing represented by the idea—they all proceed by the **way of Causality** <term>via Causalitatis: the logical method of proving God's existence by treating Him as the necessary cause of the idea of perfection or the feeling of spiritual rest in the human mind</term>.

#### IV.
The same can be said of the **way of negation** <term>via negationis: a theological method that describes God by what He is not (e.g., "not finite," "not changeable") rather than what He is</term>. It can be shown that without the inclusion of causality, this way proves nothing at all regarding what it concludes about God. One must constantly return to a positive operation. And although it might not seem that a positive cause is needed to deny any imperfections in God, it is precisely in this that people are most deceived. They fall into an error so common, and at the same time so contrary to the knowledge of spiritual things, that the detection of its falsehood cannot be omitted here.

# ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

[perfe]ctions <note>The OCR begins mid-word with "ctiones," likely completing "perfectiones" (perfections) from the previous page.</note> which they noticed in themselves, they removed from God by denying them of Him; they also attributed to Him negative names, such as **immortal**, **immutable**, **incomprehensible**, **independent**, **infinite**, and similar terms. This happened primarily because the people who first used these names paid attention to and reflected on created things before they did on God. They desired to cling to and enjoy those creations more than God, and so they first assigned simple and **positive names** to them and their ways of being, however imperfect they were. Later, when God came to their minds and they noticed that such qualities in Him were not like those in created beings, but entirely different, they designated His perfections—which are distinct from those of creatures—using those same names with a negation prefixed to them.

They used a similar method regarding the **created mind** <note>original: "mentem creatam," referring to the human soul</note>, insofar as it is compared with bodies; for the mind was the final object of their studies and cares. They first called physical things, which they desired and sought after, by positive names; but finally, realizing that they were also endowed with something that was other than a body, and whose properties involved nothing similar to bodies, they named it after physical things, but with a negation prefixed: **incorporeal**, **immaterial**, **invisible**, **immortal**, etc. But if their minds had contemplated God and themselves first of all, it is believable that they would have arranged their naming in another way; the names of bodies would have been more negative than those of minds, and the names of created minds more negative than those of the **Uncreated Mind**.

### VI.

However, it would be a small matter if it were only about names. But when they try to conclude that because a name is negative, the concept corresponding to that name is also negative in itself—that is, encompassing nothing of reality and nothing positive—that is no longer a trivial thing. And this is exactly what many people claim: from the negative names attributed to God, they infer that God is known by us through the **way of negation** <term>via negationis: A theological method that defines God by what He is NOT (e.g., "not finite") rather than what He is, based on the idea that the divine essence is beyond human language.</term>. They argue that God, like our own Mind, is known by us not positively but negatively; that is, we know what they are *not*, but not what they *are*. If you speak to such people about our knowledge of God and other Minds, they will immediately cry out that you are being ridiculous and that your goal is impossible. For they will say that knowing what God is not, or what the Mind is not—such as knowing that they are not mortal, corporeal, material, or visible—is not truly knowing what they are. Furthermore, they argue that attributing negations is not the same as attributing perfections and realities that are positive; nor does the **idea of the infinite**, which refers to God, require a positive cause to have placed it in me (since they claim it is negative), nor is God said to be positively more perfect because of it.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...to be said. Through these and similar lines of reasoning, such men wish to destroy the knowledge of God and of spiritual things. They want this knowledge to be regarded more as a negation and ignorance than as true science <note>In this context, "science" (scientia) refers to certain, systematic knowledge rather than modern laboratory science.</note>, so that they can subsequently immerse themselves in bodily things—which, even in their own judgment, are known most easily, most perfectly, and most positively of all.

VII. But the contrary has, unless I am mistaken, been clearly shown from the beginning until now. It must be added, however, regarding this occasion of **negative knowledge**, first: it cannot be asserted without contradiction that something is known negatively. To be sure, one can know of a thing that its nature includes many negations of perfections; but knowledge does not stop there; rather, it proceeds to those things which are positive in the object. A purely negative knowledge is properly a **knowledge of nothing**, for we have no other idea of "nothing" in ourselves than through the negation of things. 

Nor is there any reason for them to retort that they do not conceive of "nothing" because they presuppose that what they claim to know negatively is "some thing." It is not so unusual to presuppose absurdities. That presupposition of "some thing" will be held as a supposition of "nothing" until something positive is recognized in it. A thing might indeed be conceived generally so that nothing more specific is affirmed of it; but what we are discussing here is not an abstract and general concept of a thing, but a **particular thing** <note>original: "re particulari"</note>, distinct from the body and—when God is the subject—distinct from all things that are not the Most High. You cannot remove every specific positive quality from such a thing without removing the thing itself, so that nothing remains.

Furthermore, nothing is a grosser error than to confuse what is positive in *words* with what is positive in *things and concepts*. This confuses grammar and the unfair usage of words with Philosophy and reason. Who does not know that what is truly **positive** is that which introduces and establishes reality and perfection? Conversely, who does not know that the **negative** is that which denies perfection or asserts imperfection? 

Thus, even if an "imperfection" is denoted by a word that is—if you look at the Grammar—positive, its assertion is nevertheless negative in both the thing itself and in the concept. On the other hand, the negation of an imperfection is positive and affirmative: for the positioning of an imperfection is the negation of perfection; and the negation of an imperfection is a true positioning of perfection and reality. Therefore, regard must be had for what is represented in the concept through words—whether they be denying or affirming—so that one may judge from the perfection they attribute (or the imperfection they remove) whether the question concerns positive things or not. In this way, we must examine whether what is expressed about God in words is positive or not. Certainly, the terms **mortal**, **comprehensible**, **changeable**, and **finite** <note>original: "mortalis, comprehensibilis, mutabilis, finitus"</note> connote imperfections; therefore, they are negative, for they take away reali- 

<summary>The author argues that negative terms for God (like "infinite") are grammatically negative but conceptually positive, as they remove limitations to reveal supreme perfection. He warns against "negative knowledge," which he equates to knowledge of nothing, asserting that true knowledge must be based on positive reality.</summary>

Therefore, they are most positive, just as everything included in the idea of God is. Certainly, the idea of God is positively perfect, such that it is the only positive notion we have; by inspecting it, we can judge what may be called perfect or imperfect in relation to God or ourselves.

VIII. Therefore, we conclude regarding God that everything leads occasionally to the knowledge of His perfections (which are all positive); but the path of causality demonstrates that they truly exist in Him. What kind of perfections these are should be gathered generally from the preceding chapter: namely, they are not variable and limited, but uniform and infinite; not tending toward something else, but resting in themselves; not taken from creatures, but existing from themselves. From this it follows that everything that exists <term>formally</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "formally" means the thing as it exists in its own right, rather than just as a concept in the mind.</note> in a creature—that is, everything so considered—if referred to the nature of God, involves imperfection and consequently must be removed from it. It also follows from this that the essential perfections of God do not consist in external things—whether in deciding, recognizing, or bringing them about. Rather, God, by the necessity of His own perfection, is <term>Indifferent</term> <note>This suggests God's will is perfectly free and not compelled by anything outside of His own nature.</note> to all things that might be established or decreed, or otherwise. If any difficulties occur in these matters, they are reserved for their proper places in the following Book, where we deal with the attributes of God in detail. But let us first look a little more deeply into the perfections and imperfections of the **created Mind**, lest we attribute more or less to it by being ignorant of its rules.

### RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...to propose more distinctly. <note>original: "ctius," completing the word "distinctius" from the previous page</note> Let us therefore establish, **First**, that the fundamental notion against which true and solid perfections are to be measured is that which simply and absolutely excludes nothing; this is what is signified by the idea of **Highest Thought** <note>original: "Summa Cogitatio"</note>, or the **Greatest Being** <note>original: "Ens maximum"</note>. For there is no "being" more simple; it is pure existence, which is most simply opposed to nothingness, without any restriction or any addition. From this, we know which perfections are to be attributed to God, and which imperfections are to be denied of Him—such as dependency, ignorance, doubt, uncertain or incomplete knowledge, having a goal other than Himself, being an image of another thing, and similar traits.

**II. Second**, let us note that the Perfections of God are not the rule by which we judge the Perfections of Created Minds and their imperfections in such a way as if those Minds were more perfect the more they shared in the nature or essence of Divine perfections, and more imperfect the less they shared. On the contrary, all created minds are infinitely and equally distant from the real possession of the essential attributes of God. Therefore, the fact that they lack these attributes certainly shows that they are not perfect with the perfection of the Highest Being, but it does not follow that they are not perfect with a **perfection suitable to themselves** <note>original: "perfectione sibi convenienti"</note>; for these latter perfections are of a different kind from the others. Therefore, not possessing the perfections of God—which would be an imperfection unbecoming to God—is not unbecoming to Creatures. Thus, things that would be imperfections in respect to God—depending on another, being referred to another, not knowing all things most perfectly, and other similar things—are not to be held as imperfections in creatures, at least not as imperfections unsuited to a creature. Rather, if they are indeed imperfections, we shall call them either necessary, stable, or becoming imperfections, according to the different ways of conceiving them; these are to be contrasted with imperfections that ought to be corrected, cast off, or which are truly unbecoming.

**III. Third**, it must be noted that although the nature of God is not the absolute rule of all perfections and imperfections (as has been said, because the being of God is in no way the being of other things), nevertheless, since it pleased God to will that there be something besides Himself—something that would be like a **shadow**, or a **mirror**, or a **tablet** where His perfections might be sketched through some likeness—this likeness is not essential to Him but "shadowy." Hence, this will (which was not necessary for God, but toward which He was entirely indifferent), this pleasure that He be represented, is the norm for the perfections becoming to creatures, and for the imperfections they should set aside—namely, to the extent that they conform to that representation or not. Nor is there any other way to the perfections of God, which are the rule of all perfection, though in a different manner...

### # ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...of approaching, than those. <note>original: "sunt, accedendi, quam ista," completing a sentence from the previous page</note> For the path of sharing in God's essence is impassable. Moreover, it is a mistake to think that the things found in creatures—or those concerning them—represent God directly without the intervention of God's will (which was not previously indifferent to this). It is as if the essences, ideas, and rules of creatures were necessarily tied to the simple Divine intelligence, and were exactly as they are without any decree or most free pleasure of God. That this idea is false will be demonstrated more fully when we deal with the Sovereignty of God. Therefore, there remains only the pleasure of God, by which He willed in some way, and by way of a shadow or a picture, to be represented by created things.

**IV. Fourth**, before these principles are applied more specifically to minds, it should also be noted that perfections are either **substantial** or **modal**. "Substantial" refers to the core essence, while "modal" refers to the *mode* or way in which a substance is arranged. Although these modal perfections cannot exist without the substance, they are nevertheless much more worthy and deserve more consideration.

The reason for this is that the **being** <note>original: "τὸ esse," using the Greek article with the Latin "to be"</note> of that shadowy thing (the creature) is not its own being; it does not exist for itself or refer back to itself—for such a way of being belongs to God alone. Rather, its being is relative and directed toward another. It does not exist "absolutely," but exists in "this or that way." Thus, its greatest perfection is not to be sought in its simple existence, but in the **modes of its being** <note>original: "modis τοῦ esse"</note>. 

This is clear from two perspectives:
1. **From God's own judgment**: He asserts that it is better for someone not to exist at all <note>a reference to the biblical sentiment regarding Judas or the suffering: "It would be better for that man if he had not been born."</note> than to be arranged in a truly wretched state. 
2. **From the inspection of things themselves**: For example, consider **Extension** (or physical body). Regarding its material essence, its "perfection" is simply that it is consistent in length, width, and depth. But this alone is merely a kind of chaos. The perfections that arise from the different *ways* matter is arranged—which result in the most beautiful and admirable system of the world and its parts—are what truly matter. Look at how excellently these are varied in the vastness of the heavens, the expanses of the air, the depths of the waters, and the heart, interior, and surface of the earth. The world is decorated with innumerable species of plants, animals, and other wonders, all of which are held together and preserved by links so tight and fitting. Does not this excellent order surpass an orderless chaos of matter by many **leagues**? <note>original: "parasangis," an ancient Persian unit of distance used here metaphorically to mean "by a great distance."</note> This is why philosophers spend almost all their time and effort studying the perfections that depend on the *modes* of matter, while barely caring for the essential perfection of matter itself, since it is not the most important aspect.

Why should we not act the same way when trying to understand the **Mind**? Certainly, in searching for its perfections, there is no reason why we should cling solely to the one perfection of its substance—its "matter," so to speak—which is **thought, consciousness, or being conscious**. This quality exists even in the most wretched and imperfect minds. Let there be no question about that basic existence now; instead, let us look at the perfections seen in the modes and forms...

**V.** Finally, it should be noted that we are not asking here about the perfections of Thought or the **Created Mind** as they might be folded together, or how some might be based on others. Rather, we are looking at how each perfection stands on its own. For otherwise—just as in the signs of nature, the growth of certain plants or animals is considered a great perfection if it comes from a healthy climate of air and earth (even if the things themselves are lowly)—so too the **sensual mode of Thinking** (hearing, seeing, or imagining) is a great perfection insofar as it arises from and is wrapped up in the most noble principle of the **love of God**. However, if that sensual mode is viewed by itself, it should not be considered so highly. Here, the question is more general: we are looking at the simpler and truer perfections of thinking in the created mind, not the complex and sometimes ambiguous ones.

**VI.** Having noted these things in advance, we say first (which is easily gathered from what was said here and in chapter VI) that the **Perfections of the Mind** do not consist in those modes of thinking by which material things are represented. It does not consist in the Mind seeing, hearing, tasting, or touching whatever exists or could exist, nor in feeling pleasure or imagining. These things are external; they do not reflect God's pleasure regarding the representation of His own perfections in the mind. Therefore, a Mind that desires to be clothed in true perfection should not be devoted to them. Indeed, it should often strive to be withdrawn from these **coarse densities** <note>original: "crassaminibus," referring to the heavy, clouded nature of material sensory perception</note> in favor of a more excellent good. It should be ready to be stripped of all these things and clearly divest itself of what is properly used by sight, hearing, and the other senses, along with the emotions and the imagination. This noble study of **mortification** <term>mortification: the practice of subduing physical desires and the ego to focus on spiritual growth</term> does not itself create true *Philosophy*, though *Plato* asserts in this sense that the **meditation on death** is *Philosophy*; rather, it prepares one for true *Philosophy*. For this is the way one goes toward the true perfections of the Mind, the study of which alone deserves to be called true *Philosophy*.

**VII.** Furthermore, it is also manifest that the perfections of a mind—which, having been stripped of all imperfections, is left with **intelligence and love** (or an intelligent state of rest)—do not lie in being filled with its own self-consideration and complacency, or in being satisfied with itself. Since the mind is **nothing by itself**, is not sufficient to preserve itself, is not its own goal, and does not represent itself, such a "perfection" would be based on a total falsehood. Therefore, it would be a most imperfect state; that is, it would not be a perfection at all. From this, it is clear that for one aspiring to true perfection, the bond of self-attachment must necessarily be dissolved through a complete **setting aside of the self**.

**VIII.** But indeed, the perfections of the **Mind** consist in those modes of thinking, acts, and habits that tend toward God, which are called the intelligence and the love of God, or finding rest in God <note>original: *acquiescentia in Deo*; a state of peaceful contentment or satisfaction in the Divine</note>. Since these are innumerable, they cannot easily be listed, yet they cannot be ignored whenever they present themselves. The proof of this statement is found in the chapter just cited, where it was seen that nothing in the Mind is more **positive**—that is, more perfect—than the knowledge and love of God. Since it was also mentioned there among the imperfections of the mind (though they are not dishonorable ones) that a diversity or repetition of acts in terms of number is found (which arises from habit and creates it), this perfection of the created Mind, of which we now speak, is by that very fact extended to countless acts and habits. However, a few things must be added here so that the fulfillment and the limits of these perfections may be defined.

**IX.** In the **Mode of thinking about God** there is indeed true perfection of the mind, yet not insofar as the Mind, reflecting upon its possession of that mode, clings to it, considering itself as "intelligent," as "learned in Divine matters," and "skilled in knowing the idea of God." In such a case, the mind is pleased with itself for being so great and such a kind of thing; it exalts in itself, applauds itself, and inwardly bestows upon itself the highest testimony of its own worth. This would be, properly speaking, to admire and adore one’s own **Thought** about God—or to adore oneself insofar as one thinks of God—and to find rest in oneself. The **Idea of God** which is within us is not God himself, but a mode of our mind; and that love of ours, or that contentment, is not the supreme being. Therefore, it would be a horrifying thing to rest in those things and to adore them in such a way. This is the worst and most subtle form of all pride and idolatry. It must be noted, therefore, that the ideas and perceptions of things do not lead back to themselves, nor do they represent themselves as they are "modes of thinking" in the thinker; rather, they represent the things themselves which they imitate, and lead toward them. For a painted panel does not exhibit itself, but shows something else; nor does a vision signify that it is a mode of thinking in the Mind, or even that it arises from a certain motion of the parts of the brain; instead, it carries the thought to the object which is outside itself. Thus, the Mind ought not to embrace the very mode of **Thinking about God** through knowledge and love insofar as it exists in the Mind, but should be carried outside itself into the object represented by that mode. God made me of such a nature that what is to be desired, and what is to be embraced as good, must: 1. be known by me, and 2. its knowledge must excite a grateful, alluring sense, driving me toward it. That knowledge and that sense ought not, indeed, be rejected, but sought and taken up—yet only insofar as they are **vehicles** to the goal, which is God, and not for their own sake or so that one might cling to them.

...[what has] been said concerning [this dependence]. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely finishing a thought from the previous page regarding how the mind's perfections are spoken of.</note> What indeed is this, to strive toward God? Is it that we ought to conceive of God as if in a target, or at one extreme, and ourselves at the other, from which we must depart and progress through a middle ground more and more, so that we might finally arrive at possessing those perfections which are in God? This would be to desire to become God, and to wish to thrust God down from His own throne—than which nothing can be imagined not only more impious, but even more absurd.

In the created mind, it is a natural and stable **imperfection** to depend on another, namely on God. If I should desire to depart from this, I would contradict my very self: I would desire that I be perfect, that is, that I at least be *something*; and yet I would wish that I did not depend on God, that God did not sustain me—which is to say, I would desire that I be *nothing*. This is contradictory, for that which does not depend on God is nothing.

And yet, in truth, this imperfection is becoming <note>original: *decens*; meaning appropriate or fitting for a creature's nature</note> and, if one may say so, "perfect," for it is the foundation of all other perfections in a creature: that the creature depends most absolutely upon God. Thus, it is not fitting to wish to abandon these stable imperfections and strive toward independence, omnipotence, and other perfections essential to God. For, as has been warned, these are not the goal and measure of our perfections. Nor does the representation of God consist in this: that His shadowy and painted image should possess everything that is in the original. Such a thing is not even required in the images of other things; otherwise, the image itself would be the original. Instead, it is enough if such lines and features <note>original: *ductus lineamentaque*; refers to the "sketch" or "outline" of God's nature imprinted on the soul</note> are within it, by which the nature of the original can be recognized. Such independence in an image would deform and destroy the original—and even the image itself—rather than representing it.

Furthermore, that mode of "progressing" is absurd. For even if you were to increase your perfections unto infinity, they would never reach the point where they are essentially the same as the Divine perfections. No matter how many degrees you amplify a created perfection, it will never, because of that, become Divine. Nor should it be thought that the "way of eminence" <term>Way of eminence (via eminentiae): A theological method of describing God by taking a human perfection (like wisdom) and projecting it to an infinite, supreme degree</term>, by which one reaches God through the perfections of creatures, is such that the created perfection (which is said to be amplified) remains as a foundation upon which you build countless degrees, so that it might eventually become worthy of being attributed to God. Rather, nothing is achieved by that gradation unless one "leaps," so to speak—by an **infinite leap**—all at once to something entirely different from the created perfection previously established. In this new state, the created perfection is not spread beneath as a foundation, but serves only as the occasion for thinking.

Therefore, that striving can be nothing else but this: that the intelligence and love of the **Mind** may be filled and occupied, not by themselves or by the Mind itself, but by another object—namely, by God. In this sense, what *Descartes* expresses in his *Third Meditation* must be accepted as true:

->## ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.<-

*When I turn the gaze of the **Mind** <note>original: *Mentis aciem*; literally 'the sharp edge of the mind'</note> upon myself, I not only understand that I am an incomplete thing, dependent on another, and a thing that indefinitely aspires toward greater and greater or better things; but at the same time I also understand that He on whom I depend possesses all those greater things in Himself—not indefinitely and merely potentially, but in actual fact infinitely—and thus that He is God. Otherwise, these expressions are unsuitable.* <note>The author suggests that without recognizing God's actual infinity, our language about "bettering ourselves" lacks a true foundation.</note>

XI. Here again there is a need for limits and caution: for we must not aim to thoroughly know everything that is in God. That would be a matter of curiosity, rashness, and pride—not only if one considers the nature of God itself, but also if I were to desire to know and understand whatever God has decreed, arranged, and known concerning others. Nor is this love a union of the **Mind** with the Nature of God such that a created Mind would judge it appropriate to its own nature to possess it. For since this love is not a blind affection or a brute impulse, but is primarily intellectual, it perceives that a mixing with God’s perfections does not fit its own nature. It understands that a knowledge of all that is in God, or what God wants for others, does not suit it; therefore, it is not drawn to those things in that way.

But I could say that this <term>Intellectual Love</term> <note>a concept common in 17th-century philosophy, describing a devotion to God based on rational understanding rather than mere emotion</note>, if it is in me, is a surrender of myself to God Himself—to Him who determines whatever He pleases concerning me. Through this surrender, I find peace and delight in the fact that God is what He is, and in what He has revealed of Himself. I desire that He be represented and known in me and in others just as it is pleasing to Him. 

Here too, there is no place for that speculation in which a lover considers himself and the beloved object as a single whole of which he is some part—a part which, if smaller than the rest, should be subordinated to it by loving the whole more. For I ought not to look upon my **Mind** as a "particle of the divine breath" <note>original: *Divinæ auræ particulam*; a classical phrase used to suggest the soul is a literal piece of God</note> or some portion of the Great God, and be drawn to God more than to myself based on this imaginary fiction. Rather, if any regard is to be had for me, I am to be considered as the smallest particle of the innumerable objects of His pleasure and of His immense works—all of which, however, are only His shadow. They have nothing solid in themselves, nothing subsisting, and nothing truly their own. I am a thin point within this great shadow; my entire reality exists in that pleasure of God, by which He Himself willed to be overshadowed in this way, because it pleased Him to so will it—for He is the Lord. Thus, one must finally come to God Himself and find peace there.

And so, even if (as could happen) He were to behave toward me in a completely different way, and were to work other things in me, or work...

...it would cease to be [judged], because even if it were solely from God’s **pleasure** <note>original: *placito*; in this context, it refers to God's sovereign will or what He has decided is good.</note>, one must still **acquiesce** <note>original: *acquiescendum*; a technical term in 17th-century philosophy for finding peace or resting in a truth or a divine decree.</note> to it for this reason, and not indeed for any reason relating to myself. Indeed, those things which God’s pleasure did not want us to view as **indifferent** <note>original: *indifferentia*; things that have no moral weight or do not affect one's salvation.</note>, we ought not to view with indifference for the sake of that same pleasure; but rather, because God has testified that they please Him, we should embrace them for God's sake, so that we may be conformed to His pleasure. 

But as for those things which He willed to be viewed as indifferent in themselves—such as (in a certain way) the connection of myself with the body, and its duration, whether anxious or easy, pleasing or unpleasing, long or short; the way others may treat me, whether harshly or gently, and countless other things that can happen to me—these must be viewed with such indifference, and, when it is clear that they are God’s pleasure and decree, they are to be so received that we would not even want to change anything, even if we could, nor resist them in the slightest, whatever they may be. To do otherwise would be to embrace our own pleasure over the Divine. However, it is fitting that we be ready to experience the opposite as well, if that should seem right to God.

XIII. It is evident that this acquiescence is the highest and most fundamental perfection of the **Mind**, because it represents God best. For there is no doubt that the pleasure of God, by which He willed to be represented by His creatures, represents Him best. Nor is there doubt that the highest perfection of a creature lies in the representation of that pleasure. Such intelligent acquiescence best represents God's pleasure; it reflects it and proves how it pleases God, which is the **highest imitation of God**.

XIV. That highest perfection can permeate all other perfections of the **Mind**, even the most diminished or the sensual ones, and be found within them. But men are often deceived in this, believing it is present where it is actually absent. A more certain sign and proof of it is not found where all things smile upon us, where the senses are touched by no discomfort, where the body lacks nothing, where the imagination is soothed, where companions and others either flatter us or do not oppose us, and where the **Mind**, reflecting upon itself, thinks of itself as understanding and loving God, and as acquiescing to Him with a most pleasing feeling, from which comes delight and great joy. 

For in those very things that God wills and which touch the **Mind** with sweetness, it is to be feared that the **Mind**, in embracing them, does so for its own sake. Thus, contrary to what was shown above, it would consider itself its own end and its own representative. But when all these things happen in a most adverse way, and the **Mind** itself languishes as if parched, without the joy that arises from the sense of God's love (which is then suspended), and yet the **Mind** acquiesces to that pleasure of God—however harsh—simply because it is from God, without affectation, ready for either the most pleasant state or whatever state shall please God, for the sake of His pleasure, whether...

<summary>This page defines the "highest perfection" of the human mind as an intelligent acquiescence to God's will, regardless of personal comfort. It warns that true spiritual devotion is proven not in moments of joy and ease, but in the steadfast acceptance of hardship and "spiritual dryness."</summary>

Now we must deal more specifically with those things that are to be observed within the **Idea of God** <note>original: *Dei Idea*; the mental concept or representation of God</note>, which do not involve a relationship to the particular and present state of creatures or their specific governance, even if some of these things relate to the essence of creatures, some to their general existence, and some to their connection. However, so that we may proceed in some sort of order, and so that the things to be said about God may be simultaneously illustrated, we ought to reflect upon our own mind. In this way, from the things we contemplate within the mind, we may be led to consider the **perfections of God** <note>The author follows the "via eminentiae," a philosophical method where one takes a positive human quality and projects it to an infinite degree in God</note>. For since we cannot grasp in a single glance everything that can be known by us concerning God, there is no doubt that we are permitted to attempt and carry this out in various ways, designated by different names. When we look at God alone, He appears to us as such a **Simple and uniform Thought** <note>original: *Simplex & uniformis Cogitatio*; the theological concept of "Divine Simplicity," meaning God is not composed of parts</note> that, beyond what was expressed in His definition, no order, no distinction, and no "before" or "after" can be found in Him. Therefore, setting other things aside, we shall not without reason derive an occasion for arranging our thoughts about Him in some order from an inspection of our own mind. We shall omit the distributions of God’s attributes into negative, positive, communicable, incommunicable, and other such categories <note>These were standard scholastic classifications: "communicable" attributes (like wisdom) are shared by humans, while "incommunicable" ones (like eternity) belong to God alone</note>, because they are not without difficulties and are often disputed; nor do they illustrate what must be said about God as well as those points which come from a consideration of the Mind. Perhaps we shall bring those other categories up at the end. Otherwise, from those things which we have noticed in our Mind—

II. To achieve this, bidding farewell to terms sought out with much subtlety, and leaving aside for now corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> and other created things (although I will occasionally contemplate their **Ideas** <note>original: *ideas*; the mental representations or concepts of things</note> in my **Mind** <note>original: *Mente*</note>), I turn to my own Mind. (1) that I think:
(2) that I, as such, have nothing besides thought:
(3) that I do not possess that very power of thought from myself:
(4) that in me are so many dispositions or aptitudes for thinking in diverse ways,
(5) that I cannot enumerate or even conceive them all, so that to that extent I am unknown to myself;
(6) although I am the closest observer of all the objects of my thought,
(7) I easily conceive many things different from myself, some of which are my equals:
(8) I notice also that among them there can be some greater than me, and some inferior,
(9) but that I cannot add or subtract anything from the ideas and properties of all those things:
(10) and that I would attempt this in vain: from which my **sterility** <note>original: *sterilitas*; here meaning a lack of creative power or the inability to change the objective nature of things</note> in respect to other things is clear:
(11) Indeed, I know it is not even within my **will** <note>original: *voluntate*</note> to place those things, especially those greater than me, in myself in a more convenient way, so that I may enjoy them properly and as I rationally desire;
(12) nor does it depend on my will that they exist outside of me;
(13) nor do I hold in perfect **knowledge** <note>original: *cognitione*</note> how many they are, what their nature is, what their rule is, and other such matters;
(14) I notice, however, that I am permitted to arrange those thoughts of mine about them in whatever order I please, although a proper connection of the first with the last, and a deduction of the last from the first, is very difficult; and often in so arranging them, unexpected and unlooked-for things arise, and what was intended does not follow.

## CHAPTER II.
# (1) L I F E .

### §. A.
#### *1. The natural Life of the Soul.*

I. The very first thing that occurs to me about myself is that I **Think**, as I have already noticed above: and I see that thought is so closely connected to me that I cannot be what I know of myself without it. Once that innermost consciousness is established—once it is established that I am conscious—there exists a sufficient foundation on my part to believe, know, and feel that I exist, that I am active, and that I can be more and more perfected. This is precisely what I can properly call the *natural Life of my Mind*, and therefore I can affirm that the Mind, by the very condition of its nature, is a living thing. I leave aside other meanings of this word "life," especially those that apply to bodily things; nor do I yet attend to that most noble life which occurs when my thought is brought to its highest level of perfection <note>The author likely refers to the "Beatific Vision" or spiritual perfection in the afterlife</note>. Rather, I am dealing with that life which is natural to the Mind, and I see that nothing else can be designated by it than **Thought**, or, being actually **Conscious**. If all other things that lack this consciousness are compared to it, they can be said to be dead. Hence, I am more and more persuaded of what I mentioned above—namely, that the Mind is always thinking. For since the nature of the Mind is living, it is therefore by its own nature actually acting (in a broad sense that includes vivid experience), since to be living is to act, and life is not a **faculty** <note>original: *facultas*; a power or potential to do something</note>, but an **act** <note>original: *actus*; the actual state of doing or being</note>. Now, what is there, besides thinking, because of which the Mind can be said to act? As for a "faculty," that which lives only by faculty or potential is actually dead, and is not called living; nor can a faculty be taken for life itself, nor be distinguished from the Mind insofar as the Mind is and exists, unless you admit the Mind is a thing in itself dead and senseless. Whatever might be alleged regarding the dormant life of certain tiny animals <note>original: *animalculorum*; likely referring to microscopic organisms or insects in states of hibernation or suspended animation</note> has no bearing on this matter.

->RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

As long as the primary object of thought and the mode of thinking itself are not limited, it is a true perfection; therefore, He who is conceived as the most perfect being is not deprived of it. God is, therefore, a thinking being, conscious of Himself and of all things (if any such things exist), and thought is inseparable from His nature. This is precisely what is called the attribute of *Life*. Regarding its excellence, nothing more specific will be added here, since everything already said and everything yet to be said pertains to it. 

However, I will add this: just as in a created mind—indeed, in all living things—life is the foundation upon which everything else stands, and which, if destroyed, causes everything else to collapse; so also must the Life of God be placed beneath all His attributes and be found within them all. For all things involve life, nor can they be conceived unless it is expressly included in that concept that they are living. But what is it that can be assigned as the first and, as it were, the foundation of all things, besides thought considered in its simplest form? Rightly, therefore, this ought to be called the Life of God.

III. I would like it to be noted, so that there may be some fruit from these reflections, that this very concept can be well understood whenever mention is made in the Sacred Scriptures of the Life of God or the *Living God*. For although in some places one should perhaps attend to the fact that God cannot fail or cease to be, or that He is a most powerful agent (which will be referred to hereafter under immortality and power), nevertheless, the fact that God is conscious of Himself, of His perfections, power, and goodness, etc.—indeed, conscious of all things that happen—is what is most often being considered. 

For this reason, God is most frequently introduced as "living" when dealing with people who either do not pay attention to the fact that God is conscious of His own justice and power (as well as the things they themselves do or say), or with those who do pay attention or ought to pay attention to it. This is the source of the formula for swearing an oath: *God lives and your soul lives, etc.* <note>original: *Deus vivit & anima tua vivit* — a common biblical oath found in books like 1 Samuel and 2 Kings</note> as if they were saying: "God, who is conscious of His power to avenge evil, knows that I think this or that (whatever is at issue) sincerely; may you be as persuaded of this as you are conscious of your own thought." 

But God also interposes Himself as living when He wishes to make men more certain of what He Himself truly thinks and of what He is conscious. For example, in that illustrious protestation: *As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live, etc.* <note>original: *Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur & vivat* — a reference to Ezekiel 33:11</note> This is said lest the sinner, terrified by his sins, should think to himself: "Since I am not worthy of God's love, but on the contrary, worthy of His desertion, it follows that He thinks not of reforming me, but rather of leaving and deserting me in my sins as I deserve." It is what I might think, or be conscious of—that He does not wish me well, that He is not conscious of any goodwill toward me, or at least, I doubt and do not know if He wishes me well. To this, God opposes: *I Live, I do not wish the death of the sinner.* These words can be taken as if He were saying:

Who has known the Mind of the Lord, or who has shared in consciousness with the Lord? <note>original: *Quis novit Mentem Domini, aut ejus præ Domino conscius est?* This is an adaptation of Romans 11:34: "Who has known the mind of the Lord? This is my mind and my thought; and as certain as the former is—that I am conscious of my own mind—so certain is this latter. And this is the highest foundation of our certainty regarding God's goodwill toward us: His protestation by the very life of God. <note>The author refers to the biblical oath "As I live, says the Lord," suggesting that God’s mercy is as inseparable from His existence as our thoughts are from ours.</note>

IV. Concerning itself, the created Mind should consider everything that dulls thought (which is its life) as enemies of life to be avoided. All things which are not thought must be viewed as dead in themselves; even the letter which is called "sacred" is dead. Only the *Spirit*, or the thought which is from God and reflects God, brings life. <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note> Finally, since the mind lives in the act of thinking, and since in thinking it desires to live well, effort must be given so that it thinks well; and the whole skill consists in this: that Thought be clothed in good forms.

### CHAPTER III.
### (2) SPIRITUALITY.

->§. A.<-

->1. *Spirituality*. 2. *Spiritual life.*<-

I. I shall not here repeat, except in the mind, those things which were demonstrated at length in the previous book: namely, that Thought is so much within me that, besides it, there is nothing that pertains to the essence and nature of myself (as I now consider myself), so that my entire nature is included in that alone, to the exclusion of all other things. This complete notion of a thing or of a certain nature which is finished by thought is properly called *Spirituality* <term>Spirituality: In this philosophical context, it refers to the quality of a "Spirit"—a being whose entire existence consists of thinking, without physical matter.</term>, because of which I assert that my mind is a *Spirit*.

II. Among the many things that can be gathered from this, let this be noted first: that a mind is said to live a truly spiritual life when all its thoughts are directed toward thought in such a way that they find their final boundary there, find everything within it, and find their rest in it.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

->§. D.<-

->3. 4. *Pure Thought is God’s Spirituality.*<-

III. In God, when I turn my attention to Him on this occasion, I also notice that thought exists in such a way that His entire Nature consists in that alone, excluding all other things that can be conceived besides thought. If this were not the case, there would be many things in God that differed from one another in essence; for whatever is not thought possesses an essence diverse from Thought. In that case, God would be composed of parts, one of which would exclude the other, and the reality and perfection of one would not be found in the other. In this way, God would be conceived as imperfect and not simple. <note>The author is defending the doctrine of "Divine Simplicity," which argues that God is not made of parts (like a body is made of limbs) but is a single, unified essence.</note> However, the contrary was demonstrated above, where this very point that we now assert concerning God—namely, that He has nothing in His nature besides thought—was proved, I believe, with firm arguments; these will relieve us of the labor of demonstrating the same thing here. Let it therefore be noted that all things which will be attributed to God in the following sections are nothing other than pure Thought.

IV. From these points, it is easy to conceive what the Spirituality of God is: namely, that God does not merely think, but that all things which are in His nature are pure thought. Thus, God is Spirit.

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND THE EVIL ONE.
<meta>catchword: re- (likely referring to "rebus" or "rem" from the bottom of the previous page)</meta>

...to those who are eager, some may attribute absurdity and falsehood to the most true opinions.

II. When any thing exists, or is known as existing, two questions can be proposed concerning its existence. The first has regard for our knowledge of it, as when it is asked: *Why do you assert that you know this thing—for example, <term>God</term> or a <term>finite mind</term>—exists?* To this, it can be answered without difficulty: regarding the finite mind, from my own experience; regarding the infinite, however, from the reasons by which its existence is demonstrated. The other *question* that can be formed regarding the existence of a thing does not look so much at our knowledge, or the assertion by which we say we know a thing exists, as it does at the thing itself considered in itself: as when it is requested, *Why is that thing not only possible, but also existing?* Why does it have actual existence outside the boundaries of mere possibility, or how did it come into that existence? What cause, what reason, what perfection shall be alleged? 

This question can only be answered in two ways: for either one will not go outside the Thing itself, or it will be necessary to turn to another. The first occurs where the reason for the existence of the thing is given from the nature of the thing itself, which is perceived to be so perfect that it has no need to borrow existence from elsewhere, since the perfections of its nature are sufficient for this; they bring existence along with them, and thus they are the reason, the cause, the reality, and the perfection which satisfy the existence of the thing and the question asked about it. 

And note here that by the words <term>reason</term> and <term>cause</term>, a thing diverse from that which is being questioned is not designated, but rather that very same thing itself, insofar as its perfections are such that they suffice to exist without the intervention of another. To exist in this way is what is called <term>being from oneself</term> <note>original: "esse à se"</note>; the meaning of this formula of speaking is highly *positive*, because it poses or affirms the greatest perfections. 

The other way in which this final question is answered consists in this: that to assign a reason or cause why the thing is existing and not merely possible, we must turn to another thing different from the one being questioned. This happens when it is observed that the perfections of the thing in question are not so great that their nature implies existence—such that the concept of those perfections would be inseparable from the concept of existence or necessarily joined to it. In this case, it is asserted that the link between the nature of a possible thing and its actual existence, when it is present, is present because it was placed there by another thing, which is called not simply a *cause*, but an <term>efficient cause</term> <note>original: "causa efficiens"</note>. The first of these terms, namely *cause*, indicates that the reason for the sought existence is deduced from the assigned thing to which the name of "cause" is given; the other term, namely *efficient*, denotes that the assigned thing brings about the sought existence in such a way that it (the cause) is not one and the same thing as the result (whose existence is being questioned), but is something diverse from...

III. These things having been presupposed and, since they are evident, granted, I return to myself, I who exist as a thinking thing, and I ask: not why I judge myself to exist as a thinking thing, but *why do I exist?* What do I judge to be the cause of why I exist? Am I from myself? Certainly, if someone were to suggest to me that I am from myself, and that this **being from myself** <note>original: *à me eſſe*</note> ought to be understood **negatively**—namely, in such a way that nothing else is signified than that I neither know nor can assign any cause of my existence within or outside myself—such a suggestion would be most foolish. For it would be the production of mere ignorance in the place of a reason. "I do not know any real cause of my existence within me or outside me, therefore none is given, or it is not to be sought, and thus I am from myself negatively"—this would be an absurd reasoning, concluding nothing about anything except the ignorance of the person reasoning thus; for our ignorance is not the rule of the truth of things. 

But that **negative** sense of the formula **to be from oneself** <note>original: *eſſe à ſe*</note> is not only a mark of ignorance when it is used to answer a question about something positive, but it is also a fountain of absurdities. For since <term>nothingness</term> <note>original: *ipſum nihil*</note> is "nothing" precisely because it has a cause of existence neither in itself nor outside itself (that is, a reason why it should exist), nor can it be conceived to have one as long as it remains nothing, then according to that "charming" doctrine, not only could it be said that **nothingness** itself is "from itself," but negatively (a way of speaking we need not contend over too much); but also, nothing would prevent **the "nothing"** <note>original: *τὸ nihil*; the author uses the Greek article 'to' with the Latin 'nihil'.</note> from being held as a positive thing, since the same cause regarding the reason for existence would be alleged for it as is alleged for a positive thing. 

Therefore, I might more conveniently ask: Am I from myself **positively**? In which question I observe that the notion of an **efficient cause** likewise finds no place. I would be asking absurdly: Am I the **efficient cause** of myself? For in that way, I would suppose that I could differ from myself, and that I am not my very self. For a thing is not properly named an efficient cause unless the thing differs from the effect, and vice-versa, where the effect is supposed to be distinct from the cause. "Efficient" implies that of two things, one possesses something before it gives it, while the other has nothing before it receives it, but finally begins to have something when a distinct cause, existing prior, is determined toward giving it. Indeed, none of these things can be conceived, or even asked with reason, about me or any other thing, since they cannot be conceived in any way. It remains...

And so, there is a positive meaning of **existing from oneself** <note>original: *existendi à ſe*</note>, in respect of which I ask: am I from myself? Positively, that is: are the perfections which are in my nature such that they imply my own, or—which is the same thing—their own existence?

IV. Indeed, I am unable to assert that at all if I carefully observe what it means **to be from oneself** <note>original: *eſſe à ſe*</note>. It means to possess necessary existence; to possess perfections so complete and real that, when they are carefully considered, their existence cannot be denied without contradiction; to include existence within its essence and concept; to be such a thing that when one asks why it exists, a solid answer can be given from the consideration of the thing alone, setting all else aside. Finally, it means to be conscious (for we are dealing here with a **thinking thing** <note>original: *re cogitante*; a reference to the Cartesian *res cogitans*, or the mind</note> and with actual existence) that one is sufficient for oneself, and in reality finds satisfaction in oneself—nay, that one possesses by one's own power, whether in oneself or outside oneself, whatever one pleases.

If I examine these points one by one to see if they are in me, I find them all foreign to me. My existence is not necessarily joined to my essence, or, to speak with the <term>Schools</term> <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the traditional philosophical method taught in universities which combined Christian theology with Aristotelian logic.</note>, it is not "of my essence." To speak more clearly, the idea or concept which anyone could have of my nature (which is called <term>essence</term> <note>Essence is the "blueprint" or definition of what a thing is, regardless of whether it actually exists in the world.</note> in created things) is not such that one must necessarily conceive and judge the thing to exist outside the concept just as it is understood within the concept. 

For indeed, before I existed, it could easily happen that I might be conceived as possible, but not yet as existing, since in reality I was not yet; therefore, my nature is not such that it is inseparable from existence and implies it, since at one time it was actually separated from it. Nor are the perfections in me so great that they cannot be denied in any way, or even that, if they are to be truly conceived, one must establish that they exist. For I represent to myself innumerable minds of the same nature and condition as my own, yet my concept of them does not require me to establish that they enjoy existence; I can remove existence from them without contradiction, since I am permitted to consider them clearly, distinctly, and without any internal conflict in the concept as non-existing, but only as possible. 

Furthermore, since there are many things in me which are not really distinct from me, but are distinguished by a <term>modal distinction</term> <note>A "modal distinction" is a philosophical term for the difference between a thing (a substance) and its "modes" or states of being, such as the relationship between a mind and a specific thought.</note> insofar as they are my modes—yet the reason for these can never be given from the consideration of myself alone—such as the notion of a being greater than myself, the desire for perfections exceeding my own, and the search for satisfaction beyond those things I already possess in my nature, for the cause of which I must look toward something other than myself; much more so must I return to the consideration of a thing different from myself to assign a cause for my existence. For if the very mode of thinking is not from me, much less is the substance itself, the thought itself. For what is that power of mine by which I might place myself into existence? If my thought were not spontaneous, it would not be mine, but another’s. However, to think spontaneously and by will does not "place" me in being. Indeed, I exist willingly, but when it comes to the question of *why* I exist, I cannot rest upon my own will; for that will is not "real" enough <note>In this context, "real" refers to the philosophical "reality" or "perfection" of a thing's essence.</note> that, in conceiving it, I should judge existence to be inseparable from it, as has already been noted. Nor does my will "place" or establish me in the way I would wish regarding my various modes of being, as has been said. While I am attending to myself, I am indeed what I wish to be; but I also exist when I am not thinking about it. Nay, I can experience this: if I did not wish to exist in order to avoid mental anguishes, I would not therefore cease to exist. This cessation would occur if that absurd fiction—that I exist by my own will—held any ground. From this it follows that I exist because of another, who is He whom I call **God**.

V. Before I pass on to Him, however, I will note what flows into all things from what has just been said:

(1) It is manifest from this that not only I, but also all things in which there is even the least imperfection, do not exist from themselves. For if their essence does not exclude that imperfection—however small it may be—which they possess, and if it does not include the reality opposite to that smallest imperfection (which would itself be a very small reality), how could it exclude that greatest imperfection, **non-being** <note>original: *τὸ non esse*</note>, and include the first and foremost reality of all, **to be** <note>original: *esse*</note>? How could a thing include that which is greatest in the category of Being, yet exclude (in order to come into being) that which is smallest, and which is suited to its nature, and the lack of which is its imperfection? Thus, a thing would be both most powerful and most powerless in respect to itself; for it could place the greatest perfection in itself, but could not place the smallest, which is a contradiction.

(2) Therefore, if anything exists **from itself** <note>original: *à se*; referring to the concept of Aseity.</note>, it has no imperfection—not even the smallest—and consequently it possesses all thinkable perfections, none of which is greater than that which brings about existence through itself.

->§. D.<-

*6. 7. That God is from Himself positively, which is His Sufficiency. Two causes omitted by the Metaphysicians. 8. God’s Sufficiency as expressed in the Holy Scriptures.*

VI. Now, passing from the consideration of these things to God, that supreme Thought, I not only know Him to be the reason and cause of my existence, which I can call an efficient cause <note>In traditional philosophy, an "efficient cause" is the agent or designer that brings a thing into being, such as a carpenter making a chair.</note>, since I am His work, differing from Him and placed outside His nature; but even more, gazing upon that Divine nature and His perfections, I perceive Him to be "from Himself" <note>original: *à se*. This refers to the concept of "aseity," or self-existence, meaning God does not depend on anything else to exist.</note>, not negatively—as if the reason why the supreme being exists were merely that I did not know of anything else from which He might come, or as if His reason or cause were a negative thing or some imperfection—but most positively of all. 

That is, the reason, cause, force, efficacy, and power <note>original: *virtus*</note> that is conceived in God and understood to exist, is the most positive, real, and perfect thing of all. So much so, that He must be said to exist by the force and efficacy of His own nature, or of His perfections, which are so great, so abundant in reality, so full, and so complete, that their existence—and thus God's—is not to be summoned from elsewhere, since nothing from elsewhere can be added to them. 

Therefore, while all other things exist through a cause different from themselves (which for that reason is called "efficient"), God alone exists through Himself and for the sake of Himself and His perfections; that is, because He is the Most Perfect Being. And this notion of cause—namely, when one does not go beyond the thing proposed because such great perfections are found within it that they suffice for the thing’s existence—is prior to the notion of an efficient cause; indeed, it is its foundation. For how could He, whose existence had to be taken from elsewhere than from the consideration and power of His own nature, be the origin of the existence of others different from Himself? Therefore, God is "from Himself" in such a way that the reason or cause by which He exists is a cause preceding all others, primary and radical, from which also the existences of all other things sprout, even if through another cause, which is that of His good pleasure <note>That is, the "cause of His good pleasure" refers to God's sovereign will to create.</note>. And from this it is clear how meagerly the common Metaphysicians <note>The author is likely critiquing the Scholastic or university philosophers of his day for their overly narrow definitions of causality.</note> philosophize regarding causes, even if they pretend to transcend all things,

# RATIONAL REFLECTIONS

...since they have said nothing regarding this most noble and first [cause] of all, which—if it were to be expressed by an unusual term—could be called the cause of Identity or Selfhood <note>original: *Suitatis*; a technical term used by the philosopher Francis Bacon to describe the essence of an individual thing</note>; nor have they spoken of the cause second to this in nobility, which they were entirely ignorant of, yet by which the truths and essences of things are not so much "effected" (as that term usually refers to physical existence) but are *established*, and which therefore ought to be called the *establishing cause* <note>original: *causa statuens*</note>. Concerning this, I shall speak more below regarding the Dominion of God.

VII. But—to return to our path and apply what was assumed above to God—I say that the nature and perfections of God imply existence, such that they cannot be conceived as not existing; existence cannot be denied of them without contradiction. That God must be affirmed as being "from Himself" <note>original: *a se*; the philosophical concept that God’s existence is not derived from any external source</note>, requiring only Himself and being self-sufficient, will become most evident upon close attention to Him and those things which are in Him. Let Him be considered as pure being, or as **pure Thought**, and all will become clear. **Pure Thought** is Thought without any limitation. Thought without any limitation possesses existence within itself; otherwise, if existence had to be sought outside of it, that Thought would be limited, since something it needed—and which it would lack in itself—would exist outside it. The same result is achieved if we use the terms "Supreme Being" or "Most Perfect Being," for it is a contradiction to wish to conceive such a Being as not existing, or to judge—in a way that fights against the very concept—that it does not exist. I will add no more. See Descartes’ *Fifth Meditation*, along with the first set of replies, where he pursues the matter at greater length, which I do not wish to repeat here.

VIII. And this prerogative and perfection of God is what is meant when *Sufficiency*—or independence in existing—is attributed to Him. In this sense, the Holy Scriptures say that *beside Him there is nothing*, signifying that His existence is not drawn from anything distinct from Himself, but that He suffices for Himself, as well as for all other things which are nothing without Him. And here, in addition to the name *Shaddai* <note>Hebrew: שדי; traditionally translated as "Almighty," but here the author links it to "sufficiency"</note>, which everyone knows designates sufficiency, we may most aptly refer to that response of God when Moses asked who or what God was. He answered by making Himself known: **I am who I am.** "I am"—that is, my essence—"who I am"—that is, it is my nature to exist; my existence is that which is inseparable from existence itself. I am so perfect that the reason for my existence is I myself, not anything different or separable from me. To this we can also refer the *tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often translated as "The Lord," which is derived from the Hebrew verb "to be"</note>, which signifies both "to be" and "to exist."

# CHAPTER V.
## (4) ACTIVITY.

->§. A.<-

*1. The many faculties of the Mind. 2. Whether faculties for good exist in an evil mind? 3. Faculties hinder pure activity. Spiritual Memory. Habits.*

I. After the preceding observations regarding myself, this fourth observation occurs to me: when I endeavor to make myself better known and more familiar to myself—to know who I am and simultaneously to gather and embrace all the more specific qualities that can exist within me—then an almost immense capacity for thinking in countless ways occurs to me. I would not dare to reasonably fix certain limits to this capacity. For my thought cannot be varied in so many ways that I cannot easily conceive it being varied in even more ways by the One from whom I exist. Since He can excite new and ever newer thoughts in me without end, I see that I am <term>indefinitely variable</term> <note>meaning the mind has no set limit to the types of thoughts or states it can experience</note>, or rather, that I am endowed with countless <term>faculties</term> <note>original: *facultatibus*; here used to mean the inherent "power" or "capacity" to do or undergo something</note>. For this very thing is a "faculty" in the created mind: namely, an aptitude or capacity for a certain variation. It was proved earlier that a vast number of these are possessed by the mind, where it was asserted that it is the nature of the Mind to be indefinitely variable, even though the actual variation itself—or the "act" of the faculty—is not present unless a cause is also present.

II. Regarding these matters (to mention this in passing), it will not be difficult for those who are attentive to extricate themselves from certain difficulties that trouble some people. For example, it is disputed whether <term>fallen humanity</term> <note>original: *homo lapsus*; referring to the theological state of humanity after the "Fall" in Eden</note> possesses the faculties of <term>repentance</term> <note>original: *resipiscendi*; specifically the act of "coming to one's senses" or changing one's mind</note>, of believing, and the like. A "faculty" is variability, and the Mind is not invariable—as that belongs to God alone. But can that form of thought which constitutes repentance, faith, etc., happen to a thought or to the Mind? Does it agree with the mind, or is it repugnant to it, or does it destroy it? Not at all. In this sense, why should the mind not have these faculties? If, however, one looks toward the "act" or to the variation of the Mind itself, the question would be either: *Can such variations happen to the Mind without a sufficient cause?*—which would be absurd to assert—or: *Can the Mind be so changed, provided that a sufficient cause is present?* In this sense, again, all Minds have both these and many other faculties; that is, they can be so changed and placed into those states by a <term>sufficient cause</term> <note>original: *causa sufficiente*; a philosophical principle that nothing happens without a reason or cause enough to explain it</note>. But if it is now asked, whether that change...
