# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...of variation is something other than God, or whether a reason for this position can be rendered from a consideration of the nature of a thing that is not God? From the preceding chapter, and from those following, it is manifest what must be answered to this. In these matters, therefore, as in almost countless others, there is no difficulty once the terms have been weighed. But if, in these things, some profess that they understand *by a faculty* a cause by whose force a thing is varied—since that force is in God, and nothing that is in God exists subjectively within creatures (as has been demonstrated)—it follows that all creatures are destitute of such a power. To us, however, a "faculty" is precisely what we have already stated: <note>The author previously defined a faculty as a passive aptitude or capacity rather than an independent active power.</note>.

III. Since I have noted above that I—or my Thought—do not exist of myself but from God, I must conclude that by my nature I am a truly passive thing, or rather, a being that receives from elsewhere. This is now clearly evident from those faculties within me, which are indefinite in number; all of them are capacities for receiving that which is not yet actually within me. Whether this receiving happens by way of an action or as a passion <note>original: *passio*; in a philosophical sense, this refers to being acted upon by an external force</note>, I do not examine now. But whatever the case, I infer from this that I am not a purely active thing. I will draw the same conclusion from those things that result in the Mind after these faculties have been brought into "act" <note>or "actualized"</note>. These results include <term>spiritual memory</term>, which is the mind's capacity to think back on the fact that it once thought attentively and purely about certain things; and <term>spiritual habits</term>, which are an aptitude of thought to receive, more easily than all other forms, that specific form which has been present to it on repeated occasions. Although these habits are often confused with "faculties" in speech, they must not be confused in our concepts, for habits always presuppose the faculties and the capacity for receiving.

->§. D.<-

4. *The nature and will of God can receive nothing from elsewhere. How the Activity of God is to be conceived as distinct from Impassibility.*

IV. Regarding God, I perceive no such thing; no faculties, no intellectual memory such as I described, no habits, nor any capacity for receiving anything into Himself. Instead, He is conceived by me as <term>pure act</term> <note>original: *purus actus*; a theological term meaning God is fully realized and has no "potential" to become something He is not already</note>, which is exactly what I wish to indicate when I attribute "Activity" to Him. Mere thought actually includes within itself everything suitable to itself and has it from itself; if it were capable of receiving anything, then a state of "not-yet-actual thought" (or un-thinking) would have had to exist in it previously, which is repugnant to the very concept of <term>pure Thought</term>. But what would it be that I could conceive God being able to receive, and from where? Certainly, it could not come from another. That idea is too crude to require an express refutation. Therefore, could God receive something from Himself? But what? Himself? And yet He already [has] himself...

IV. Response: What should be thought regarding questions proposed about what God "could" do will be discussed elsewhere. But to the matter itself, I respond that there is a contradiction in the terms. This concept is most absurd: to represent God completely and adequately, yet not formally but objectively; since that complete representation of God is of the form, the nature, and the essence of God, and thus is inseparable from Him, nor possible outside of Him. Adequate knowledge of that supreme object is that object itself; otherwise God, adequately knowing Himself, would have knowledge or **Thought**, which was not Himself—which is proven to be an absurdity. In a word, it is a common notion that an adequate representation is not given through a thing of a different nature—a notion which is left to be weighed by anyone paying attention in meditation and illustrated by examples of all things in the world.

explanation: for it might perhaps happen that a malicious conclusion could be drawn from this—that I assign the first place to the Creature <note>original: "Creaturæ"; referring to any created thing, such as a human being</note> over the Creator, and propose that the creature's existence is more certain than the existence of God himself. Nor: what is in itself more certain, more constant, more necessary, and more existing? For these things have already been seen above. Rather, the question is: what is prior in our cognition <note>the process of knowing or perceiving</note>, and specifically in a "confused" way? And what is first known to exist in that confused manner? Certainly, it is beyond doubt that the knower is prior to the known in terms of logic and concept. Therefore, created Thought, which is the knowing subject, and whose nature consists in being conscious of its own existence, is in this sense prior to that which it knows afterward, namely God. For the mind is actually conceived to think, and to be conscious of this thinking, before it is conceived as thinking about something different from itself.

As for the objection that the existence of God is thus being made dependent on the existence of the created mind, or that His certainty is made secondary to the mind and supported by it—from which it would follow that if the created Mind were failing or removed, the certainty of God's existence would be shaken and unsettled, if not utterly overthrown—how absurdly that would be objected is clear from this: we are not dealing here with the actual existence of God, nor with His subjective certainty or the power by which He stands in Himself, but rather with the knowledge which I can have of myself or of Him, and with the certainty of this knowledge of mine whose object is His existence (which is, in itself, most certain). Indeed, the certainty of my knowledge of His existence completely collapses if I do not exist; I cannot have that knowledge unless it is first established that I am, and that I am endowed with perceptions that immediately bring with them a sense and certainty of themselves. But if one asks what is prior in dignity or even in "distinct" cognition <note>clear, logical understanding as opposed to "confused" or basic awareness</note>, far from myself or the knowledge of myself preceding, I would clearly not even know how far I am perfect or imperfect unless I first cast my eyes upon God, the most perfect Author. From Him, I would gather that I am more or less perfect according as I more or less represent His perfections.

Having first contemplated this Being and then returned to itself, the mind afterward knew itself and its own perfections more distinctly.

4. *God's understanding of Himself is, primarily and completely, Himself; it exists in Him alone and concerns Him alone.* 5. *The object of the "Knowledge of Simple Understanding" is God alone, not things that can be created or are possible.*

IV. Having already demonstrated above the Living Being <note>Referring to God as the "Re vivente"</note>—who is pure, self-sufficient, active, and understood by Himself alone—it is easy to perceive what must be noted regarding God from this sixth consideration of my own mind. Namely, first: He thinks or understands in such a way that He Himself is His first and nearest object; for He is a **thinking thing** <term>res cogitans: a philosophical term for a being whose essence is thought</term>, in which the very first requirement is to be conscious of oneself. Second: that His knowledge of Himself is perfect, most clear, and complete in itself, so that He does not need to attend to anything different from Himself, since His thought is pure and self-sufficient. Third: that His act of intellect or "Understanding" does not differ from His **Essence** <note>In God, being and thinking are the same; His existence is His act of understanding</note>, since it is a most perfect thought. From this it also follows that this understanding is so natural to God that it cannot be shared with any creatures, as they are not capable of the most perfect understanding; rather, anything that completely understands God is God Himself. Finally, that knowledge which God has of Himself is the only knowledge that is essential and unchangeable to Him. If He knows things other than Himself, He does not know them by necessity, but by His own pleasure <note>original: "ex placito"; meaning by an act of His will</note>, since He could have chosen not to know them just as He now knows them. However, one cannot conclude from this that there would have been ignorance or change in Him, for in that case those things could not have been called existing, true, or even possible, as will be demonstrated later.

V. This complete knowledge of God about Himself alone—which exists in Him alone, is Himself, and is the only knowledge essential, natural, necessary, and unchangeable—is what is denoted by the word ***Understanding*** <note>original: "Intelligentia"</note>, even in the Holy Scriptures. This same knowledge alone should be called ***Knowledge of Simple Understanding*** <term>Simplicis Intelligentiae: a technical term in scholastic theology referring to God's knowledge of His own nature, as distinct from His knowledge of created things</term>, or simply *Knowing Knowledge*. With all due respect to those who think otherwise, this does not regard any things that could be created, any essences of things, or any abstract truths. For God, in the simple act of understanding, is sufficient unto Himself; it is not necessary for the completion of His Understanding that He look toward other things, although if He is pleased out of His abundance that something besides Himself should exist

...the positioning of [individuation], it brings about a positioning as if another, as a part, did not exist outside of me as the whole: I—or rather, the work of God within me—I, the thinking "I," am indeed something, I am not nothing, but I am not everything; I am not everything that can be created, nor am I the representative of everything that is God, as is easily demonstrated from the power of God. And so, I do not exclude infinite others similar to me and of the same nature as myself; nothing prevents me from clearly conceiving an innumerable plurality of them.

IV. I will not now deduce more specifically everything that follows from these points—which to some might seem sterile, or perhaps even inept (for why should I prove that I am not someone else, or that others who are not me can exist?). Yet, these consequences are indeed momentous. Contained within them are the foundations of all unity and communion in any things whatsoever, and even of diversity, with a most evident example to which all things can be compared. From these things, it becomes clear what the <term>principle of individuation</term> <note>original: *principium individuationis*; the philosophical concept of what makes an object unique and different from others</note> is, as they call it (about which they make so many sounds without meaning), and the principle of plurality or multiplicity.

It is also clear from this example that the <term>individual essence</term> <note>original: *essentia individualis*; the specific nature of a single, unique being, like "this specific person"</note> is known before an abstract concept is held, or before the <term>general essence</term> <note>original: *essentia generalis*; the shared nature of a category of things, like "humanity" in general</note> is known. The latter arises because the individual does not possess every perfection; therefore, regarding the most perfect individual <note>Meaning God</note>, a general essence is not conceived, but only an individual one, since that individual is conceived to exhaust (so to speak) all solid reality. This is different from created things, where the reality perceived in them—and its cause, God’s pleasure—can be perceived as extending to others, notwithstanding the position and essence of any one of them (which concept is called an "abstract" or "universal essence").

From this it is also manifest that the well-worn saying is false: **that one must begin from the knowledge of universals, not particulars, in the discovery of truth; and that there is no knowledge of particulars, but only of universals.** <note>The author is attacking a standard Aristotelian and Scholastic rule of logic which claimed that "science" (scientia) only deals with general categories, not specific individuals</note> On the contrary, one must begin from individuals (and would that in spiritual and practical matters everyone would begin from the inspection of their own individual self!), and a proper and, as far as possible, complete knowledge of them is given. But because any single individual is not everything, or does not exhaust all reality, but can be reduplicated and multiplied—that is, similar things can exist—I can therefore extend the knowledge I have of one to those others. Yet it is not as broad, but more restricted, because I know more circumstances regarding the one, which are variable, than I do regarding the rest. Hence, I have a more complete knowledge of my own **Mind** than of the idea of the mind I have abstracted. This is our "evil"—that in all things, even in divine matters, we abstract everything from ourselves, and we contemplate their ideas like phantoms flying outside us in the air, so to speak...

*5. The concept of multiple Gods is an absurd and contradictory fiction. 5. 6. 7. 8. Demonstrations concerning the unity of God. 8. 9. Polytheism, Atheism, Deism, Trinity, Unity.*

V. If I now try to apply things similar to what I just said about myself to God—to see whether another being of the same nature as Him could exist, equal to Him, and yet differing from Him just as "I" differ from another Mind of the same nature as myself—then everything I said about myself completely collapses and behaves differently in respect to Him. If I wanted to conceive of several Gods, it would be a fiction, and indeed an absurd one in terms of the reality of the thing. That is, I would be joining the idea of a plural number with the Idea of God in such a way that the consideration of the very idea of God would convince me of the absurdity and refute the figment of my judgment, as something contrary to the nature of the thing being conceived. 

I say that such a judgment would be a figment: for all the reasons that lead me to judge that God exists require and imply the existence of only one God. Once this is acknowledged, all the difficulties that distressed me—unless God were known—are plainly settled, so that one is allowed to rest solidly in the existence of one God. From this it follows that seeking or establishing others is done without necessity and without cause or reason; nor can it happen except from the sheer petulance and fiction of the mind, which can demonstrate the existence of nothing it has imagined. 

But I say, moreover, that this fiction is absurd and contradictory: for since by "God" we understand the <term>most perfect being</term> <note>original: *ens perfectissimum*; a standard philosophical definition of God in the 17th and 18th centuries</note>, since God is everything perfect in the category of absolute perfection, and since He Himself is all things that are most real, it follows from His definition—with Him alone being conceived and existing—that every conceivable perfect thing and every absolute reality that could be said to exist is already conceived and established in Him. Therefore, His concept and essence formally exclude anything "most perfect" existing outside and beyond Himself. That which is "absolutely everything" excludes everything else from being "absolutely everything," otherwise that which is "absolutely everything" would not be "absolutely everything." Therefore, God is unique.

# ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...[the single divine] essence are said not to agree, they are therefore not all truly Gods; if they are said to agree in one essence, then they also agree in one existence, and thus they exist as one, or God is one: for in the most Perfect Being, Essence is existence (which is evident from the demonstration of Divine Simplicity <note>original: "Simplicitate" — the philosophical doctrine that God has no parts and is identical to His own attributes.</note> in Book II, chapters 5 and 6, and will be further illustrated hereafter). Furthermore, existence (from what was said above) is individual, since the existence of one exhausts and encompasses all and every reality or perfection.

VI. The same is also demonstrated from other things that have been more generally proven about God—for example, from the fact that God is Pure Thought <note>original: "Cogitatio mera" — a concept likely influenced by Aristotelian or Cartesian philosophy where God's nature is the pure act of thinking.</note>. If, however, another God were given, then each would be an individual of that species *God*. In this way, neither would be God, for neither would be the "non-part" <note>An entity that cannot be divided or seen as a component of something else.</note>, or the whole, or a pure thing. Pure Thought knows nothing similar to itself besides itself (according to the principle of Intelligence). Therefore, nothing similar exists besides itself—namely in regard to essence. For if it did exist, and Pure Thought did not know it, then Pure Thought would not be Pure Thought, since there would be ignorance or "non-Thought" within it, and thus God would not be God, which is a self-destructive contradiction. 

Or, to put the matter more clearly: suppose there are two Gods. I say that they must either know each other by necessity, or not. If they do not necessarily know each other, they are not necessarily perfect, and they are (or can be) ignorant; therefore, they are neither Gods nor multiple Gods. If they know each other by necessity, then the Thought of one concerning the other is a Thought of the other that is necessary to that Being—which is repugnant to Pure Thought, since it is completed by itself alone. 

Furthermore, that necessary thought of one God about another would either depend on and come from that other being—which again does not befit a true God <note>A true God cannot be dependent on an external source for His knowledge.</note>—or it would depend on the very one who is thinking about the other. In that case, the one thinking about the other would judge within Himself: *I, contemplating myself, conceive that I am not all-perfect, but that besides me there is another equally perfect*, which is a concept foreign to God. Nor could the knowledge of one regarding another equally perfect being come from anywhere except from that other: just as I, a created Mind <term>Mens creata: the human soul or intellect as opposed to the Divine Mind</term>, could not know that other Minds similar to me could exist, unless I had that knowledge from the notice of another, namely from the power of God. But if one being, in perceiving Himself, is imagined to perceive the other by that very act (and vice versa), so that the thought, knowledge, and thus the perfection of one is the thought and perfection of the other, then they will not be perceived as two, but as one. Therefore, one must arrive at Unity from the consideration of the Intelligence of God.

VII. We are brought back to this same conclusion by His self-satisfaction <note>original: "acquiescentia in se" — the state of being fully at rest or satisfied within one's own nature without needing external things.</note>, without which the concept of Pure Thought is destroyed. Pure Thought finds satisfaction in itself: that which finds satisfaction in itself does not necessarily require the knowledge or the presence of another thing different from itself. Therefore, it excludes the necessity of another being; therefore, [there] is not given,

-># RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

...is given, nor can another God be given; otherwise, another would necessarily be given, since God is a "necessary being" <note>original: "ens necessarium" — a philosophical term for a being that must exist and cannot not exist.</note>. This same Unity of God remains to be demonstrated from His sufficiency and other attributes, since those things addressed so far are sufficient.

IX. No greater distinction can be conceived in God than that which exists in one and the same Thought, and that the most perfect one; otherwise, Polytheism is introduced, which is a heresy worse than Deism <note>Deism is the belief in a creator who does not intervene in the universe; the author here argues that believing in many gods is more logically flawed than believing in a distant single god.</note>. For, as is evident from what has been said, the positioning of multiple gods is not only a fiction of the Mind—whence those who worship many gods are called idolaters, worshippers of themselves or of the fictions of their own Minds—but it is also a denial of God, a destruction of the concept of God, and a negation of this truth: God is the most perfect and pure Entity or Thought, or "God is God." Hence, those tainted by Polytheism are truly guilty of Atheism, which cannot be said in the same way of Deists and those who call themselves Unitarians <note>A Christian theological movement that believes God is only one person, rejecting the Trinity.</note>. 

But neither do these [Unitarians] have anything from the principle of unity with which to defend their error; for the distinction that is conceived in God is not of such a kind that it is opposed to His Unity, but rather it is that which best agrees with it. God Himself, on account of His Supreme Perfection, supremely loving and seeking Himself, attempted (to speak in a human manner) to multiply Himself as much as He could, so that He might find and love Himself as the most lovable being possible. This He indeed performed outside of Himself by placing His shadows, reflections, and images [in creation]; since one of these was not enough to overshadow His admirable perfections, He produced innumerable ones, diverse in every kind of variety. Yet while He multiplied Himself within Himself through the venerable generation which exists in the Trinity, because He is thus expressed most perfectly, He did not depart outside the unity of His individual nature, since outside the one most perfect being, no other can come to be. And those who note that this one Thought includes an "acquiescence" <note>A state of rest or satisfaction.</note> in its own Intelligence through a tendency or most perfect love, and who meditate on these things together with what has been said regarding the Incomprehensibility of God, will not take occasion from the Unity of God to doubt the Trinity, but will rather become more certain of the latter from the former—which is for anyone paying attention to observe.

X. Finally, let it be noted that God is "one" in such a way that the unity in Him is stricter than in my own individual Mind; the plurality and diversity in me is more separated in its own sense than it is in God. In my Mind, there are many and diverse acts of thinking that are separable from each other; often my Mind does not attend to itself, it is in a way absent from itself, unknown to itself, and interrupted in its most intimate modes of thinking, demanding one thing from itself [while doing another], even though it is numerically one. But all these things are plainly removed from God, who is unique in number, essence, and concept.

## CHAPTER IX.
### (8) LOFTINESS.

->§. A.<-

*1. 3. The Mind is superior to some things and inferior to others. 2. Its greatest humiliation occurs when it is made subject to a tiny body which, in proportion to everything else, is smaller than a mathematical point.*

---

I. Furthermore, among the things represented to me as being different from myself, there are some I notice to be lesser than me, and others greater. There is no need, for the sake of proving this more clearly, to bring up God as an example—for in the presence of His essence, everything that His good pleasure has bestowed upon me vanishes into nothingness. Rather, even among those things conceived as distinct from Him, I can conceive of **Created Minds** <term>Created Minds: In the philosophy of this period, these are spiritual beings like angels or higher intelligences that exist without physical bodies.</term> that are far more perfect than my own Mind. These beings think more vividly, purely, and extensively; they are more active, more self-aware, and they surpass me by a vast distance in every quality I have noted or will note hereafter. They are more exact images of the Divine will, in whom God chose to effect things indefinitely more excellent than in myself. Thus, I realize that among beings of my own kind—namely, created beings—I am in the middle rank, or perhaps even among the very lowest.

II. It is true that my perfections could surpass those found in other beings, should it please my Author to work more and better things in me than He does in them. Indeed, I am already more perfect than any **extended thing** <term>Extended thing: A translation of the Latin *res extensa*, a term used by philosophers like Descartes to describe physical matter, which takes up space but lacks the ability to think.</term> (the idea of which I shall now contemplate to some extent), and this is regardless of any reckless comparison to other minds. I say this because a thing that is conscious of itself, of God, and of His wonderful attributes and works, is far more noble than any extended, moving, or shaped thing, all of which are "brute" or mindless. Yet, if I compare these very physical things to myself—insofar as I am now in some way bound and subjected to them—I am also convinced of my own extreme insignificance through them. I think, to wander there for a moment, of the immense extension of the universe, to which I cannot assign limits or boundaries in my concept without reaching an absurdity or contradiction. Thus, the starry heavens that we see—in which countless myriads of stars are uncovered, such as in the so-called **Milky Way** <note>original: "via lactea"</note>—must truly be conceived as being like a single point when compared to that immense space of the universe which is conceived to extend beyond and in every direction without any concept of an end.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

->RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

Although the distance from the Sun—which for us is the center of this point—to Saturn (which they say consists of five or six thousand Earth diameters) is rightly thought by the more skilled to be tenfold if it were to be adapted to measuring the distance of the stars closest to us, and that same distance should be repeated a hundredfold, or rather substituted a thousandfold, if it were to be applied to the more remote among the visible stars. 

I consider, furthermore, that this visible sky of ours, which extends to the **firmament** <term>firmament: The sphere of the "fixed" stars which, in the cosmology of the time, formed the outer boundary of the visible universe.</term>, is again but a point; and that the space described by the Earth being carried annually around the Sun (a necessary, clear, and demonstrable truth in all of **Physics** <term>Physics: Here referring to natural philosophy or the study of the physical laws of the universe.</term>, if there be any, without a spirit of quarreling) is again but a point. This is evident from the apparent equality of the horizon and the lack of **parallax** <term>parallax: The apparent shift in position of a star when viewed from different points in the Earth's orbit; its absence suggested to early astronomers that the stars were incredibly far away.</term> in the stars. 

Further, I consider that within this point—or the sphere which the Earth's circle around the Sun is conceived to cut into two parts—the Earth itself is again a point, since it does not relate to that sphere as even one relates to three thousand times a thousand thousands. (For assuming the diameter of the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: The path of the Earth's orbit; the author is using the diameter of this orbit as a measuring stick.</term> contains 1,500 Earth diameters, the cubed ratio, which is the volume of the Earth compared to the volume of the sphere it circles around the Sun, comes out to 3,375,000,000. But if the Earth's diameters are taken as 1,550 for the maximum, as the more exact observers count it, then the proportion of one of these points to the other will rise to 1 to 3,723,875,000.) 

What, then, in comparison to these things, is a portion of the Earth’s surface? What is a region? What a city? What a house? Are they anything but particles of particles of a tiny point? And what is even that tiny **clod of mud** <note>original: "glebula luti"</note>, that little speck of dust in which the Mind is held (as is known) like a captive and a prisoner? It is so bound, indeed so depressed, that very often, whenever one sleeps or is more violently ill, the Mind itself with all its faculties is found as if swallowed and absorbed—and that against its will. Very often, too—which is the most base dejection of all—it happens by the Mind's own will, as it overwhelms itself with the burden, care, and singular cultivation of its own little speck of dust. This it does even though it knows that the stability of that vanishing clod is measured in moments (of which one does not guarantee the next), and that all things will scarcely last until that point—on whose surface-speck we rest—has completed a few of its revolutions. These revolutions are themselves very few in respect to the whole universe, just as the state of the Earth is not thought to be durable compared to the state of the heavens. Nor is this latter state to be compared at all to true **Eternity**, or to the expressed image of Eternity as much as can be given in a created Mind.

And yet, what is this madness of yours, O man? You think these thinnest vanities are the greatest and most serious things, for the sake of which—with a ridiculous and execrable daring—you must leave and despise God, and throw all things into turmoil and violation; and you yourself...

Do you seem to yourself a man to be magnificently esteemed? # ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

You seem to hold yourself in such high esteem, O man—you little gnat, you tiny worm like a beetle in dung, a mere speck of a speck taken from the shadow of a larger point! You pile up and stir the shavings of vanishing dust, building your tunnels, your thrones, and your triumphs there, only to be trampled underfoot in that very place! From this, I saw myself positioned as if in the middle between two things: superior to physical things in my own perception, but with no reason to prefer myself to other minds (which may exist) or even to consider myself their equal, since minds superior to me can be conceived by me.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...Supreme, not only in some respect, as is the case in the category of created things, but most absolutely, above all things that can be conceived by anyone. These things have not even the least thing in common with Him in a univocal sense <term>univocal: using a word in the exact same sense for two different things; here, it means "existence" or "perfection" applies to God and humans in fundamentally different ways</term>, as has been demonstrated elsewhere; whereas even the smallest among created things possess something in common with the larger ones.

VI. Here a difficulty arises, which must be examined because it seems to proceed from the Atheists, and—if it is cleared away—it helps to illustrate the following six attributes as well as the preceding ones. Since, they say, certain things are not only conceived but are said to exist that are "lesser" than God (as everyone affirms regarding their own existence), it seems one must conclude that there is no God, or Most Perfect, Supreme, and Infinite Being. For just as it is concluded that multiple Gods cannot exist because one, being infinite, already contains whatever there is of existence and perfection and excludes every other being distinct from Himself; so also, they say, one could not exist who is infinite and most perfect unless He possesses every possible perfection and existence in such a way that He excludes anything existing independently outside of Himself. For that which is infinite and most perfect in the category of Being excludes any other Being; otherwise, it could be said that He does not comprehend all things, nor is He all things, if besides Himself something were given which was not Himself. Thus, He would not be infinite and most perfect. From this they conclude: If an infinite Being exists, nothing different from Him exists; but many things different from Him (namely, ourselves) do exist; therefore, an infinite Being does not exist.

VII. I will not repeat the responses with which Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> refuted this foolish sophism <note>sophism: a clever but false argument</note> in his *Replies to the Second Objections*. I will note here that it is entirely false, indeed contradictory, to assert that an infinite, supreme, and most perfect Being must comprehend in Himself and in His own nature and essence every kind of perfection, reality, and existence different from Himself. To suggest He must contain these inferior things formally <term>formally: having the properties of a thing as it exists in reality (e.g., God containing "heat" by actually being hot)</term>—that is, exactly as they are and as they are conceived—is an error. Since these things are imperfect in themselves and in relation to the infinite Being, if the Infinite possessed them in Himself in that same way, He would contain imperfections. Thus, the infinite would not be infinite, the most perfect would not be most perfect, and the Supreme would possess things that are not supreme, which is a contradiction. Since, therefore, the nature of the infinite does not comprehend those things in itself and formally, it follows that the existence or standing of the Nature of the infinite, supreme, and most perfect Being is not cancelled out by the existence, or even the concept, of things different from Him. Therefore, the conclusion should have been: That an infinite, most perfect, and supreme Being is not given whose perfec-

# ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...[created or finite things] <note>original: "nes creatas vel finitas"</note> should formally include within themselves, or formally exclude from themselves: which is freely granted. For just as the **Most Perfect Being**, because He encompasses every infinite perfection in His nature, therefore excludes every other infinite perfection outside and beyond His essence; so too, because His essence and existence contain no finite perfection, His essence and existence therefore exclude nothing outside Himself, nor do they necessarily prevent a finite perfection from existing outside Himself.

VIII. Therefore it is absurd to say that God would not be the **Highest** and the **All**, if some reality or perfection existed which He Himself was not—on the grounds that something, namely this perfection, could then be added to Him. For God is not called the "Highest" or "All" because His essence possesses all finite and created things **subjectively** <term>subjectively: here meaning "as part of His own internal nature or substance"</term>, or because He is those things themselves; otherwise He would be imperfect, and finite things would be God. This is the same as what was said before: He is not said to be "everywhere" because His essence is literally in every location. Rather, in Himself and subjectively He is "all"—namely, all things that are absolutely perfect—and thus He is "all" to Himself alone, just as it was said that He is "present" to Himself alone. However, with respect to created and finite things, He is called "all" **operatively** <term>operatively: acting as the cause or power behind all things</term> (as noted above regarding *Location* <note>original: "Ubi"</note>, and for the same reason, for God’s "being" and "being in a place" are one and the same) and **representatively** (speaking here and elsewhere occasionally with the *Scholastics* <note>original: "Scholis"; referring to the traditional medieval university theologians</note>). Or rather, He is called "all" because the perfections of all things are derived from Him alone, and they reflect Him in such a way that they point toward perfections in Him that are infinitely greater. We should not say, then, that God would be imperfect and not-Supreme if He were formally lacking created perfections within Himself, or that He could become more perfect or greater by the addition of those things. On the contrary, the very concept of perfection and true Loftiness is destroyed if one imagines these finite perfections being mixed with Him. 

From this it is clear what should be thought of that maxim: *The Infinite in the category of Being or Perfection excludes any other Being.* This is either a fiction—namely, if an abstract concept is made of all "Being," called a "genus," and then applied to every Being and specifically to God with the word *Infinite* added, imagining that God encompasses everything to which that abstract concept could extend. But such a "Being," such a phantom, is not God. If, however, by "category of Being or perfection" one understands something involving all perfections, both finite and infinite, this is again a fiction; for it was demonstrated elsewhere—where it was proved that God and the creature have nothing **univocally** <term>univocally: having the exact same meaning or nature when applied to different things</term> in common—that no such thing exists. The maxim is only true if understood this way: an infinite Being does not allow anything else to be infinite within itself that is distinct from itself, nor...

...outside and beyond itself there were another infinite thing, another **Highest Being**, existing of itself and truly solid through itself: He truly denies and excludes every such thing. ### RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...represent things lesser than me, or concerning the ideas of any things—whether already created or capable of being created—which, since I can neither take anything away from them nor add anything to them, I see do not depend on me in any way. For although in thinking about material things, for example, I may seem to fashion manifold shapes for myself **at will** <note>Latin: *ad lubitum*; according to one's own pleasure or choice</note>, these are not properly from me, nor should they be called my inventions. This is because there is none of them which, if viewed solely as a concept, does not include very many truths that are immutable in respect to me, and which therefore does not come from someone other than myself. And although I may actually conceive now this image, now that one, or another which perhaps I have not yet noticed in myself—even if you were to call it a **chimerical** image <note>Latin: *chymericam*; referring to a "chimera," a mythical hybrid creature, used here to mean something purely imaginary or fantastic</note>—this is in no way a matter of inventing, but of varying a concept and applying it alternately to ideas whose truths and properties do not depend on me. It would be a **figment** <note>Latin: *figmentum*; a mere invention or fiction of the mind</note> if I were to judge that something similar existed outside of me simply because I conceive of them in that way. But that is not asserted; on the contrary, just as the **created Mind** <note>Latin: *Mens creata*; the human intellect as opposed to the divine intellect</note> has no right, no dominion, and no authority over any ideas, forms, natures, essences, properties, or truths of things (as will soon be shown), so it has none over their existence, as will be demonstrated hereafter. Whatever the created Mind judges to be positive in things—which is not there beforehand by some source other than itself—that is a false figment and not truly positive. A created concept is not so effective, powerful, and perfect that it is the true author of any reality; for all reality that is not God cannot but exist by **God's pleasure** <note>Latin: *à Dei placito*; by the decree or will of God</note>.

II. Regarding myself, I indeed experience that my mind looks upon the ideas of things—whether their essences or their natures, and their properties and truths, whether those things are spiritual or **extended** <note>Latin: *extensæ*; a philosophical term referring to physical matter, which takes up space</note>—in such a way that the mind is drawn toward them spontaneously, fits with them, agrees with them, and approves them as being most true. Yet, those things do not behave in that way, nor are they true, simply because I assent to them, conceive them, or approve of their being true. Whatever I have demonstrated regarding the created Mind thus far, and will reveal hereafter, does not depend on me; just as whatever truths can be stated regarding the nature or essence of bodies, regarding motions, and their rules, do not depend on me. All such truths concerning numbers and all figures are exactly as they are, such that I have contributed nothing to them; and they will remain so, along with everything that rightly bears the name of truth and is endowed with a certain nature and essence, whether I am willing or unwilling. For I can introduce no change into those truths, just as I contributed nothing to establishing them. Therefore, that **superiority** <note>Latin: *præpollentia*; dominance or excellence</note> of Minds over extended things, or of certain created Minds over me, or of myself over certain others—that superiority, I say, which I mentioned above...

# RATIONAL REFLECTIONS

indeed, that which consists in the Knowledge of God and of the principal realities, or truths and operations established by Him, must be held as most true, to which I trust the things present here can also be referred; but [there is] a certain other [science] which concerns the most universal **Being** <term>Ens: "Being" in its most general sense; anything that exists</term>, **Essence** <term>Essentia: the "what-it-is" of a thing; its core nature</term>, and the transcendental attributes—the One, the True, the Good, etc.—so that this science abstracts from the Knowledge of God and other things, indeed, it precedes it: whence its conclusions can be attributed to every being, whether created or uncreated, the lowest and the highest. 

As if indeed any truth, or goodness, or essence could be known whose essential foundation and true, solid reason was not God's **pleasure** <note>original: *placitum*; a technical term referring to God's sovereign and free decree</note>! As if truth were to be considered as positively independent, or could be distinguished in opposition to dependence on God and His will; when it is this very thing! It is horrible that it should be taught that something true to be predicated of creatures afterward should be considered as transcending respect for dependence on God and His will or pleasure. These are "transcendental darkness," and it is a harmful **figment** <note>original: *figmentum*; a mental invention or fiction</note> that such a truly founded knowledge of a real thing exists—or such a science, and the first of all, concerning Being, Truth, Goodness, etc.—by which men might thus become more and more accustomed to looking at all things as not dependent on God. Since, however, every truth is from God, and all its certainty and demonstration is founded in the knowledge of God. 

I implore any sensible persons: have they ever brought back any light, fruit, or use—outside of quarrels and darkness—overflowing into those things which concern God or men, from these transcendental trifles? That falsely named science mixes the **Creator** with the **creature** in advance of all things, as if they had certain things of entity, truth, goodness, causality, etc., in common **univocally** <note>meaning the terms apply in the exact same sense to both God and humans</note>, which will soon be more fully evident from every side to be most false: or indeed, let them confess that their pretended definitions and scientific pronouncements concerning Being, the One, the True, etc., since they do not apply univocally to created and Uncreated Being (for absolutely nothing real, whether subjectively, causally, or effectively, is common to God and creatures in a **univocal sense**), they are only distinctions and definitions of an **equivocal** <note>a term that sounds the same but has different meanings, like "bank" of a river and "bank" for money</note> name, and those definitions (if they leave the equivocation behind) are most inept; for nominal matters produce no science. 

It is pleasing to dispel this darkness with an example. When they say, *"Being is that which is,"* or when they wish to explain the name of "Being"—which is equivocal as it is common to the Highest and Uncreated and to the lowest or dependent—through less equivocal words, so that it does not remain ambiguous, as if they were saying: *"By the word Being, we denote that which is its own existence, or that for whose essence and truth the reason is in itself, and ought not to be sought beyond itself"*; how will they show that they designate God and exclude the other member, namely dependent being; which

IV. The first person by whom those shadows of this century were somewhat dispelled—shadows which had spread from Philosophy into <term>Scholastic Theology</term><note>The traditional school of philosophy and theology dominant in universities, often associated with Thomas Aquinas and formal logic.</note> and everywhere else—was the celebrated Descartes. But since these things were proposed by him only briefly, occasionally, and in passing (a), and were not set forth with total exactness—nor, as far as I know, has anyone else done so more exactly—yet because they are most worthy and contribute greatly to acknowledging and celebrating the Supreme Majesty of God, which is infinitely elevated above all things and Ruling over them, it is worth the effort to explain them more diligently. Otherwise, we might continue to attribute our own imperfections to God. We are people who want Him to conceive truths which He Himself did not first determine to be so, but rather truths He found already determined; meanwhile, in our daily lives, we act as if our own wills or desires toward an object actually "create" the truths and qualities we want to be there. Thus, in theory, we give to God what belongs to us (limitations), and in practice, we try to seize for ourselves what belongs to God (the power to determine truth).

V. I say, therefore, that God necessarily conceives, by the necessity of His own nature, those truths which are about Himself, and which immediately regard His nature, essence, and attributes; He was never <term>indifferent</term><note>In this context, "indifferent" means having the freedom to choose otherwise. The author argues God cannot "choose" His own nature, but He does "choose" the nature of everything else.</note> toward these. But the same is not true for those truths that concern the ideas, essences, and properties of all things that are *not* God Himself—whether they actually exist or are only imagined, and whether they refer to the nature of Minds or to bodies, their motions, their laws, or to shapes, numbers, or anything else. For God conceives and thinks of them as such for this reason: not because they are such in themselves...

### VI.
God is one. God would not be one if He conceived anything diverse from Himself and yet <term>univocal</term><note>Meaning something that shares the same fundamental nature or category of being as God.</note> to Himself, or possessing a property fundamentally and essentially similar to His own. Therefore, beyond Himself, He conceives no necessary truth, and none that is immutable through itself.

### VII. 
God alone is most perfect. Therefore, His Essence alone is supremely and absolutely necessary: for simply absolute necessity is the highest perfection. The absolute necessity of the Thought of a most perfect object excludes the absolute necessity of the Thought of an imperfect object, for He has no need of it, and it would be imperfect if He did have need of it. Furthermore, absolute necessity cannot be attributed to finite or less-than-perfect essences and truths without attributing to them one of the highest perfections, and consequently all of them—which is an offense against God. From this it follows that all of them, being finite, are not supremely and absolutely necessary; that is, they are not absolutely and necessarily what they are, and therefore, speaking absolutely, they could have been otherwise.

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

VIII. God alone is <term>from Himself</term><note>Latin: *à se*. This refers to the concept of "aseity," the idea that God contains the reason for His own existence within Himself and does not depend on anything else.</note> in a positive sense; that is, He alone is the one who possesses such a nature, essence, and such properties and truths, that the reason for them can be provided by considering the thing itself, so that there is no need to refer to another object or to appeal further. However, this attribute would be snatched away from Him and given to another if we were to imagine that certain essences, truths, natures, etc., apart from Him, were such that if it were asked why they were so, or why they were true, it could be answered from an inspection of these things alone: that they are such because their nature is such; that they are such from themselves from eternity; and that God conceives them as such for no other reason than that they are such in themselves. You might as well say that there are essences, natures, and truths independent of God, but dependent on themselves or self-sufficient. This is so insulting to God that I do not think anyone who understands these things will hereafter approve of them, for these ideas imply that God depends on things that are independent of Him.

1. The fulfillment of God’s thought would not depend upon—or arise from—His own intelligence alone, if there were something else that God necessarily required besides the knowledge of Himself: namely, the ideas of things and those truths which are called "necessary." But that which lacks what is necessarily required would not be complete, and thus the fulfillment of Divine thought would depend on certain things which are not God’s nature, which are imagined to be independent of His will, and which He could not do without.

2. He would not be a <term>Being satisfied in Himself</term><note>Latin: *Ens sibi acquiescens*. A being who finds all happiness and sufficiency within his own nature.</note>, rejoicing in Himself alone, if there were some truth besides Him which He was necessarily bound to enjoy.

3. He would not be independent of a goal or motive distinct from Himself, if He knew and willed something as true and good for the reason that it had already been so beforehand.

4. Finally, the knowledge and perception of God, along with His very Nature, would depend on those things which are not God. For from where does God, who knows these essences and truths, obtain His knowledge of them? Is it from them, or truly from Himself? Who would say that God derives His knowledge from them? It is clear that we must return to God Himself. But we fall into the same absurdity—indeed, into a greater one than we were trying to avoid—unless we return to God as the most free cause of those things, and as being plainly <term>indifferent</term><note>In this philosophical context, "indifferent" means that God was not compelled by any external necessity; He was equally free to make a truth "true" or "false" until He willed it so.</note> to them beforehand. To assert that God conceives these things necessarily because He conceives His own nature—to the point that they are so connected to the necessary concept of His nature that they are included within it—would be the same as asserting that God’s nature cannot be conceived without them. Consequently, anyone who denied those truths would also take away the Divine nature and essence, just as when one perfection of God is denied, the others are also denied. IX. And these are the origins of all ideas and truths distinct from the nature of God, whether they concern material or spiritual matters. Although, in respect to God, these cannot properly be called <term>innate</term><note>Born within or inherent from the start.</note> or naturally impressed upon His concept, they are nonetheless innate to every created Mind. They are naturally carved into the mind in such a way that it can in no way conceive of anything different from them. Just as some King is able to devise a new currency or establish new laws, which, if he were able, he would imprint on the minds of his subjects so that they would be held as self-evident and innate; so too nothing prevents God from having fashioned and devised all ideas and truths, along with their laws, according to His pleasure. He has so inscribed them upon our minds that they cannot be conceived except as true, innate knowledge; and their contrary cannot be held as anything but false by anyone paying close attention—that is, as something not ordained by God. 

And just as a skilled Painter sometimes freely creates noteworthy fictions for his own delight; so it seemed good to the most Blessed Mind—which is entirely self-sufficient—to <term>play</term><note>Latin: *ludere*. In this playful manner, He fashioned things that He might contemplate with delight in His own concept, later to exhibit outside of Himself through His power certain specimens of His "playful fictions." These creations are such that they perfectly suit a Mind that is most perfect, most sufficient, most intelligent, and most wise—a Mind whose <term>foolishness</term><note>Latin: *stultitia*. ### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL

**X.** Perhaps several difficulties will occur to those who have not yet scrutinized these matters more deeply—difficulties that might arise from the consideration of God as He conceives and decrees, as well as from the things conceived and decreed by Him. We will attempt to remove the principal ones from our path. These arise from our perspective of God.

**XI.** First, it seems it should not be denied that God knows what He can or wishes to decree, or otherwise; and thus, knowledge or conception precedes the decree. But those who say this presuppose that there is something distinct from God which, before God’s decision or <term>pleasure</term><note>original: *placitum*. In this context, it refers to God's free determination or choice.</note>, possesses truth and possibility on its own account. This is a <term>fundamental error</term><note>original: *πρῶτον ψεῦδος* (proton pseudos). This is a Greek logical term for a primary falsehood or a "first lie" from which all other errors in an argument follow.</note>. "Let God be something," they say, etc. But what is that *something*? Nothing is given or conceived before God’s pleasure. It is absurd to say that God conceives or knows that which depends on His decree before it depends on it, or before it is conceived as depending on it—as if it did not depend on it. It is absurd to know it as something preceding His pleasure, when the very idea of it is a consequence of that pleasure.

**XII.** Second, from what has been said—that God was most <term>indifferent</term><note>The author uses "indifference" to mean that God was not compelled by any external necessity or logical rule. He was perfectly free to choose otherwise.</note> toward these truths and could have plainly not decreed them, and thus neither conceived nor known them—it seems to follow that if God could have been ignorant of all truths that exist outside Himself, then ignorance could have existed in Him. For the sake of removing this absurdity, the premise from which it flows would have to be rejected. But those who think this do not understand what ignorance actually is. Ignorance presupposes that there is a knowable and true object, and it does not exist where there is no such thing. Yet, no such thing exists before God’s decree, as has been demonstrated. He upon whose decree all truth depends, and who does not know what He has not decreed, is not to be called "ignorant"—any more than one could say there is ignorance in God because He does not know flies to be men, just as He does not know that all men will be eternally blessed. <note>The author argues that "ignorance" is the lack of knowledge regarding a reality that exists. If God chooses not to make something true, His lack of "knowledge" about it isn't a defect, because there is no truth there to be known.</note>

If ideas and truths could have been decreed and conceived differently by God, then God's conception would be mutable, or could have been different than it now is; thus, there would be a possibility of variety within Him. This would conflict with the previous demonstration concerning God’s activity. That concept of God concerning Himself could not and cannot be otherwise, because nothing new happens or could happen to God’s nature or essence, whether from Himself or from another. Indeed, I do not think in any way that any diversity can happen to God's knowledge or conception from elsewhere—for that would be contrary to His activity—nor can there be in Him either contraries or diverse things by way of succession. Indeed, the contrary view destroys both the activity of the Divine conception—for a conception that conceives a form and a truth different from itself, of which it is not the cause, and which it cannot absolutely conceive otherwise, is not active, but passive—and it also destroys God's freedom in producing things. For He could not have made those things exist in another way unless He could have conceived them as different in at least some way. If such diversity is not unbecoming to God's conception, then neither is that which we are asserting. To be sure, the power to be otherwise is a mark of imperfection in created things, because it implies receptivity and dependence. But in God's—I do not say nature, but—pleasure, or His conception regarding all things that are not Himself, there is pure activity and perfection, by which God conceives Himself to be bound by necessity to nothing besides Himself.

The root of the error lies in this: that we want to consider God's conception just as we conceive our own—namely, as a thing that receives. Yet His is a supremely active principle, or a most free pleasure, about which one might say this of Augustine <note>original: *Augustini*. XV. Finally, a difficulty could arise from the fact that God is proclaimed as **just** and **truthful**, which is taken to mean that God—while preserving His justice and truth—cannot arrange, judge, or decree otherwise than He does and will do, at least concerning most things. But, God’s **Justice** indeed means that those things He has decreed were established in a manner becoming to Him; His **Truth**, however, means that He will not change those things He has decreed to be and to endure in a certain way. But these do not imply that He was not previously the most free cause of these things, nor that He was not <term>indifferent</term><note>In 17th-century philosophy, "indifference" refers to the "liberty of indifference," the state of being completely free to choose between alternatives without being compelled by any external or internal necessity.</note> either to decreeing nothing, or to establishing other things that would have equally suited Him, and which—if it had pleased Him—would have been limited either at a specific time or not at all.

XVI. There are other difficulties that proceed either from the consideration of things, or from prejudices concerning the truths themselves, or from ambiguous axioms that are commonly understood in an inferior sense. Let this saying serve as an example of this last class: *The natures of things, whether essences or forms, are immutable and eternal*, proposed by <term>Descartes</term><note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the famous French philosopher. The author is referencing Descartes' *Meditations on First Philosophy*, specifically the idea that mathematical and logical truths are "true and immutable natures."</note> himself in his *Fifth Meditation* and defended in his *Fifth Replies*; this, however, seems opposed to what has been asserted so far. I respond that the axiom is true if it speaks of the **immutability** that God has decreed, namely while it pleased Him that certain things should not be changed. Likewise, in the common sense, things can be called **eternal** if no time preceded their positioning, or rather, things which the eternal God conceives without <term>succession</term><note>God's thoughts are traditionally understood as happening all at once (simultaneously) rather than one after another in a sequence of time.</note>, and which will never cease to be. But these do not destroy what was said before. For although God has conceived something from eternity and decreed that it would not be changed, it does not follow that He necessarily conceived and decreed it, nor that He could not have done otherwise. For example, He conceived me from eternity as I am, and decreed the **Mind** to be immortal; who would say because of this that He could not have done otherwise? Therefore, such reasoning has no weight in itself, and thus it should be applied not only to the existence of things, but also to their <term>essences</term><note>The "essence" of a thing is the set of properties that make it what it is (e.g., the essence of a triangle is having three sides).</note>. Only the nature of God is properly eternal, to the exclusion of all else, as will be more fully demonstrated when we reach the appropriate place with a clearer discussion of this difficulty. Only the **Divine essence** is absolutely immutable; nor is it in the nature of a truth distinct from Him that it be immutable. But if other things, and their truths and essences, are viewed absolutely—that is, without regard to the placement of the Divine decree and the connection of things among themselves (which is the effect of that decree)—God is no more attached by any greater bond to any specific things or forms outside Himself than He is to this truth: *I am thinking about the Mind*, or *I am reading*. For toward everything that is not His own nature, He is by His very nature <term>indifferent</term><note>In this context, "indifferent" means God was not compelled by any internal or external necessity to choose one thing over another; He was perfectly free to create or not create.</note>.

XVII. And so, it is a prejudice to bring forward as a law the idea that many truths flow from the nature of God, or that they represent God’s nature in such a way that they cannot be changed or denied without God's nature—the original and pattern of those images—being denied or conceived as changed. From the nature of God, nothing flows except God Himself—namely, the **Son** and the **Holy Spirit**. The Divine decree—which is beforehand indifferent, and not a matter of necessity—is the origin and life of all other things. Those things that represent God do so through the free determination of His decree. No matter is suitable in itself, and nothing is capable in itself of representing God; for outside of God’s necessary nature, there is the most universal *nothingness*. God has no shadowy image (I do not speak of the solid image, which is God Himself <note>The "solid image" refers to the theological concept of Christ as the perfect image of the Father.</note>)—He has no shadowy image, I say, out of the necessity of His nature. Rather, that image, along with its nature and essence, exists from the overflowing and gracious generosity and goodness of His most indifferent and free decree. 

If God had not wished to establish this [creation], it would only follow that He wished to please only His own nature, not that He was displeased with Himself. On the contrary, if He had established an image out of necessity, He would have shown that He could not be without something different from Himself, that He needed something, and thus that He was not fully satisfied in Himself, nor entirely pleased with Himself as He is alone. 

If any creature were now to deny those images which belong to God, they would not, to be sure, directly and immediately deny God's nature; yet they would deny God insofar as it pleased Him to represent Himself thus. For even if God has no bond with the truth or nature of another thing, He does have a bond with Himself and with His own decree, insofar as it pleased Him to determine Himself, and to will that something of that sort—true, good, and essential—should be and would be. That thing cannot now be conceived as being able or needing to be otherwise—not because of the thing itself, but because it cannot be conceived that God wills differently than He wills, or has willed differently than He has willed. It cannot be conceived that God does not agree with the consensus of His own decree, or that He is separated from it, as if He would bring about and place things differently than He willed to establish—even if He willed it freely and could have not willed it. Once we assume the <term>hypothesis</term><note>The "hypothesis" here is the starting assumption that God has already made a choice.</note> that He has willed it, because He is not separated from Himself as the one making the decree, the contrary cannot be conceived. XVIII. However, because from the consideration of individual things, infinite objections could be raised—leading to absurdities that might seem impossible to overcome—for example, if one were to ask: Could God, from that Highest Dominion and highest <term>indifference</term><note>In this context, "indifference" means that God's will was not compelled by any law or necessity to create the world in one specific way; He was perfectly free to choose.</note>, create a square circle, a round triangle, or a creature independent of its Creator? Could the hatred of God become good, and could His love be changed regarding its nature and become evil? Could a mind exist without Thought? And other things that cannot be listed and refuted one by one; it will be useful here to gather several observations from which less attentive readers might be able to free themselves from any difficulties. For otherwise, it can be clear to those who pay attention that the hidden refutations of all these objections lie within the preceding arguments.

XIX. Let it first be observed that, under the pretext of this most absolute Dominion over all things, many objections can be raised which, even if they seem to attack this doctrine, clearly do not concern it at all. For example, since God’s pleasure—which was previously indifferent—is finally determined, it is absurd to ask whether, once it is determined, it can be "not-determined" in the **composite sense**? <note>original: "sensu composito." A logical term meaning to consider two things together at the same time. The author is saying it is impossible for God to have decided something and *not* have decided it at the exact same moment.</note> Or, whether something determined as such is even now indifferent? No one, as far as I know, has put forward such an absurdity, though some believe they are attacking it. Yet those who ask whether God, from His absolute Dominion, could make it so that what has been done or decreed was *not* done, or that what was true for a time was never truly true at all, are presupposing this. This is to conceive of God as determined and not-determined by Himself, decreeing and not decreeing, willing and not willing, sustaining and not sustaining at the same time, approving and not approving, performing and not performing the same action. It would be the same as asking whether, by conceiving of God as currently the "placer" of some thing, we could by that very fact conceive of Him as the "non-placer" of the same thing; or, whether God is not decreeing while He is decreeing? These are absurdities, for which the things said above have given not even the slightest occasion. XXI. And so it must be noted thirdly (which follows from the previous observation) that to correctly perceive this doctrine, one must use a **universal abstraction** from every thing, idea, essence, nature, form, truth, and so on, which are not God Himself. For if anyone, while retaining some idea (especially a general one), wishes to ask whether—while this idea remains—the other particular truths (which undoubtedly involve it) can be changed, he will be unable to find any ground for objection. For the first absurdity of the objectors would return, as if it had been said that a thing is "not a thing" in the composite sense. Therefore, one must abstract in such a way that it is thought that God, out of His absolute indifference, could have established entirely other truths and essences than those we already have. Under this supposition, the truths that now exist would be absolutely nothing, nor could they be conceived of any more than those things which the Lord did not establish.

Thus, those objections concerning numbers, shapes, and the like collapse. For those who seek a difficulty in these matters presuppose the idea of **extension** <term>extension: In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to the fundamental property of matter—the fact that it occupies physical space.</term> and number, yet meanwhile they want that idea, which they consider as remaining fixed, to be excluded from its particular subjects. I do not think all the solutions to similar difficulties that he proposes there should be admitted. It is as if the ideas of numbers or lines remained separately on their own, while their combinations could behave differently; for their combinations are their very nature and ideas conceived together. Therefore, it would be the same as asserting that the nature of shapes and numbers remains, and at the same time does not remain. If this is resolved into God's **pleasure**, <note>original: *placitum*, referring to God’s sovereign decree or what He has decided is good.</note> it posits God as establishing and not-establishing at the same time.

The simple ideas of lines and numbers also vanish along with the rest before the absolute Dominion of God. Nor can it be said that it follows from what has been said that, while the idea of extension remains, the truths of shapes could be changed because they are not part of the essence of matter. They are indeed not part of its essence if matter is viewed more generally and indeterminately; yet they are part of the essence of matter as it has been determined by its Author. He is not called the Supreme Lord in this respect as if, while arranging matter in this way, He were by that very fact arranging it in another way—which is a wandering off track. -># RATIONAL THOUGHTS #<-

->136<-

God’s decree <note>original: *placitum Dei*</note> to represent Himself through a shadowy reflection <note>original: *cogitationem umbratilem*. The author likely refers to the human mind as a faint "shadow" or imitation of the Divine Intellect.</note> whose very nature is to tend toward God, as was demonstrated in Book II. Therefore, it is absurd for someone to presuppose that this reflection exists and remains, yet simultaneously wish to conceive that it does not exist—or to rightly claim the opposite in a **composite sense** <note>original: *sensu composito*. A logical term meaning things considered together at the same time. One cannot logically hold that a thing is both "A" and "not A" simultaneously.</note>. Love presupposes the nature of the Mind; the Mind presuppopes the will or decree of God to "foreshadow" Himself in this way. Once this position is conceived and established, it is absurd to use it to destroy another truth which can only be understood by abstracting from that very position. Such an abstraction is provided by the consideration of the Divine Essence alone—which is uniquely necessary and independent—and His indifference toward all other things. Through this indifference, God could have represented Himself through any other means He wished, rather than through the natures of all things as they currently exist.

XXII. I will insist on this more clearly, even to the point of exhaustion <note>original: *ad fastidium*</note>, so that no one fails to grasp it. Among those things we conceive of besides God, there are:

First, **primitive ideas**; for example, our ideas of Thought, extension or space, simpler shapes, numbers, and other concepts in theoretical matters; and in practical matters, the ideas of good, love, and the like.

Second, **first principles** or **axioms**, both theoretical—such as the axioms of geometry—and practical—such as moral principles or **syntheresis** <term>syntheresis: A term from medieval and early modern philosophy referring to the innate faculty of the human mind that perceives the basic principles of morality.</term>, as they are called. All of these are said to be **indemonstrable**, because they cannot be proven by anything clearer than themselves; and they are called **innate**, not only because they are linked in a certain way to the nature of our Thought, but also because God has so disposed the mind that if it thinks about them, it immediately sees them to be true without any intervening reasoning.

Third, there are **ideas composed from these**, and more specific conclusions, both in theoretical matters—such as geometric propositions—and in practical matters—such as moral conclusions. The truth of all these is not obvious at first glance, and therefore they could be considered false or obscure by an unobservant mind, though not by a mind that is attentive and reasoning.

Now, what I have said here regarding the dependence and mutability of all truths upon God should not be understood as if I were speaking only of the truths of this third class, while the first and second classes were supposed to remain fixed. For since these final truths are simply the first and second classes considered more deeply, a contradiction would be placed within God's own determination—as if God were simultaneously decreeing and not decreeing the same thing. Rather, what has been said must be extended to all truths without exception, even the simplest ideas and truths of the first and second classes. One must abstract from these—or rather, one must transcend them—so that a proper concept of **Divine Authority** over all things may be achieved.

->137<-

For I confess that I do not conceive of those other possibilities; for if they were conceived, they would already exist. Not to mention that my mind is determined by God toward those things which He willed to establish and which He willed me to partially conceive. Nor do I see what more can be required in this matter by those who look upon God as the Supreme Arbiter of all, upon whom everything depends.

XXIV. I do not know what others will judge of this doctrine. For my part, certainly, when I revolve it in my mind—not to inquire out of curiosity into God's concepts and Thoughts, but with the intent of celebrating His supreme Dominion, and of admiring His immense elevation above all things, and the insignificance of all things before Him—I confess that it seems to me I find therein that which impels me toward an intimate and ineffable veneration of His most magnificent Majesty, praise for His generosity <note>original: *liberalitatis*. Here meaning God's "liberality" or free-giving nature, which is not bound by any external necessity.</note>, confidence in those things He has sanctioned and promised, and a disregard for all things in comparison to Him. 

His unconfused Majesty—most distinct and separate from every thing by the incomparable excellence of His nature, truly an "inaccessible light" <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 6:16, describing God's dwelling.</note>, or such Truth that no other exists besides it—I gaze upon as best I can in my weakness, according to His good pleasure <note>original: *placitum*. This is a central term for the author, referring to God's free, sovereign choice or decree.</note>. I praise the generosity of His Goodness, which is all the more commendable because it is bound by no things whatsoever, and owes nothing to them, not even that which they are in their very idea. I rest upon the truth of His decrees; for if He willed them to be established when He was indifferent toward them, why should I now conceive that He would change those same things after having embraced them? 

Finally, I perceive that all things, in their most hidden depths and essences, in their Goodness and Truth, are not merely dust before His Divine Essence, but are absolute and pure nothingness. If I find anything besides God, I find it all in the abundance of the decree of His most free mind; outside of it, there is nothing. Therefore, there is no reason for me to seek or hope for rest outside the Divine decree. Let the best analysis and resolution of all things be not the "nature of the thing"—to which many wrongly appeal as the ultimate cause—but rather the decree of God, without which no nature exists. This decree (though let no one abuse this to commend their own fictions) should be the ultimate goal <note>original: *ultima meta*. The final boundary or destination of inquiry.</note>, not only in sacred mysteries but also in natural things—even if petty philosophers <note>original: *Philosophastri*. A derogatory term for those who pretend to be philosophers but lack true understanding.</note> do not soundly grasp it—and indeed even in those which are falsely called "transcendental truths" <note>In the Scholastic tradition, these are the most universal concepts, such as "Being," "One," and "True." The author argues even these depend on God's will.</note>. 

For this axiom, which they call the first—*Whatever is, either is or is not*, or *It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be*—is resolved into and founded upon this: God, willing and establishing this by His decree, is not Himself not-willing, not-establishing, not denying His own decree, nor differing from Himself as He wills. To such an extent is this true that nothing is its own foundation and reason except the one God, who so flourishes as the One in all things by His decree that His decree is the force of all things. I do not wish to say more, but let us remember these things for the future.
