### CHAPTER VII.
## (10) GOODNESS.

->§. A.<-

*1. The Mind, being sterile of itself, communicates nothing of truth or reality to other things.*

I. Since, therefore, every Idea of truth and reality depends upon God, there is no reason for me to pretend that I fashion anything out of myself that has any power within it. And just as nothing of mine is created by me, so nothing from outside of me is made by me; therefore, my nature and my <term>pleasure<note>original: *placitum*. In this philosophical context, it refers to a free, sovereign choice or decree of the will, rather than mere "pleasure" in a sensory sense.</note> are, in themselves, entirely sterile toward other things. And although I may investigate truth in the depths of my Mind, and sometimes find it, there is nonetheless no reason to think it is of my own manufacture, or established by me. Rather, I should think it has lain hidden like a concealed treasure, whose eventual discovery makes it known, but whose reality is not created by me. For all other Minds, however many there be, find the same truths in the same way when they seek properly in their own depths; this would not happen if those truths were fashioned by the <term>pleasure</term> of each individual. Indeed, out of a thousand figments made by different Minds from mere whim <note>original: *arbitrio*. Refers to the human capacity for choice, which the author argues is prone to inconsistency compared to God's established truths.</note>, scarcely two would agree. And although perhaps, if the nature of Minds had not existed, other truths about things besides God might not have been determined, this implies nothing else than that they were established *along with* Minds, but not *by* them.

->§. D.<-

*2. 3. The Goodness of God is the source of all. It is poorly conveyed if anything is taken away from it. 4. The Essential Goodness of God. 5. How would God be good if nothing existed besides God?*

II. What, then, prevents God from fashioning whatever things please Him, which, representing His pleasure, are therefore true and good? Likewise, since the ideas and truths of things are nothing beforehand, God cannot be hindered from acting here according to His pleasure. [consi]dered <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with *deratum*, likely completing *consideratum* (considered) or *desideratum* (desired) from the previous page.</note> as most free, determined by no necessity and no external motive—this is precisely what must be called Divine ***Goodness***. It is, as it were, the most fertile, most abundant, and most free fountain of all things that exist in any way besides God. From this fountain, all things draw their ideas, natures, essences, and truths; and if they exist, they draw their existence and duration from it as well. Through that Goodness, God communicated—not His own nature, but a <term>sketch<note>original: *adumbrationem*. Literally a "foreshadowing" or "outline." And this very possession is the communication or gift itself.

III. It is clear that this Divine Goodness is improperly represented when it is asserted that God gives His consent or pleasure to certain truths of things out of necessity, or that He could not have done otherwise, or that it was necessary for Him to give His approval to some things, or that certain things do not derive their nature from Him. It is a harsh thing to say that there is anything among created things that does not owe its form, nature, truth, its being, and its origin to His Liberality. But these notions have already been dismantled. A coerced goodness, a goodness not moved by itself, a partial goodness, a limited goodness, or a goodness without which there is some other goodness distinct from it—all these are foreign to Divine Goodness. Rather, every goodness of all things (which you might call passive goodness) comes from that Divine Goodness, which for that reason you would call active (a property belonging to God alone). Therefore, everything real, every established truth, every essence, every substance—whether <term>thinking<note>original: *cogitans*. A reference to the Cartesian "res cogitans," or mental substance/mind.</note> or <term>extended<note>original: *extensa*. A reference to "res extensa," or physical matter which occupies space.</note>—every mode and motion, whether in idea or in existence and duration, are good (as they truly are) precisely because it is God's pleasure that they should be. Thus, all things that are, and can be said or conceived, are heralds of the Goodness of God; so there is no need to heap up many words here concerning that which has its seat everywhere.

IV. Furthermore, there is in God an essential Goodness, which exists without respect to those things which are not God; this is when He communicates Himself to Himself most abundantly and perfectly, not out of indifference, but out of self-love. But here we have dealt with that Goodness which is relative, and which finds its fulfillment in those things which are not God. The former [essential goodness] does not reach toward creatures.

V. From this, it is clear what should be replied to this question: *How would God be good if no created things existed?* I add: *What if nothing at all had been decreed?* The answer is that God’s essential Goodness would remain whole and entire. Even if He then communicated nothing in Map according to His pleasure, He would nevertheless be such that, if it pleased Him to will to give something, it would happen for that reason.

# CHAPTER VII.
## (10) GOODNESS.

### §. A.

1. *The mind, being sterile of itself, communicates nothing of truth or reality to other things.*

I. Since, therefore, every Idea of truth and reality depends upon God, there is no reason for me to pretend to fashion anything from myself that has any power within it. And since just as nothing of mine is truly my own, so nothing is foreign to me; therefore, my nature and my <term>pleasure<note>original: *placitum*. Referring here to the mind's arbitrary will or choice as opposed to objective truth.</note> is a thing entirely sterile of itself toward others. And although I may investigate truth in the depths of my Mind and sometimes find it, I should not think it is of my own making or established by me; rather, it was hidden like a secret treasure whose discovery is finally made manifest, though its reality is not created by me. For all other Minds, however many there be, find the same truths in the same way when they seek properly in their own depths. This would not happen if these truths were fashioned by each person’s pleasure, since out of a thousand fictions created by different Minds from mere whim, scarcely two would ever agree. And although perhaps, if the nature of Minds had not existed, other truths concerning things besides God might not have been determined, this implies nothing other than that they were established *along with* Minds, but not *through* them.

---

### §. B.

2. 3. *The Goodness of God is the source of all things. It is misrepresented if anything is subtracted from it.*
4. *The Essential Goodness of God. 5. How would God be good if nothing existed besides God?*

II. What, then, prevents God from fashioning whatever things He pleases, which, representing His pleasure, are therefore true and good? The very nature of God does not prevent such ideas—even if they are distinct from the idea of His own essence—nor is it obscured by them, since they are conceived as non-necessary and dependent. ...that which was determined most freely, from no necessity and from no external motive, is precisely what we must call divine **Goodness**. It is the most fertile, abundant, and free source of all things that exist in any way besides God; it is the source from which everything draws its ideas, natures, essences, truths, and—if they exist—their existence and duration. Through that Goodness, God communicated not his own nature, but a shadow of himself according to his <term>pleasure<note>original: *placitum*. This refers to God's free decree or sovereign choice, rather than a mere whim.</note>, through his free determination, to those things that possess even the smallest shadow of truth. This possession of truth is itself the very act of communication or a gift.

III. It is obvious that this Divine Goodness is wrongly portrayed when people claim that God grants his consent or pleasure to certain truths of things out of necessity, or that he could not have done otherwise, or that he needed to grant his approval to some things, or that certain things do not derive their nature from him. It is a harsh thing to say that there is anything in the world which does not owe its form, nature, truth, being, and origin to his Generosity. But these [arguments] have already been refuted. A goodness that is forced, a goodness not moved by itself, a partial goodness, a limited goodness, or a goodness that exists alongside some other goodness separate from it, is entirely foreign to Divine Goodness. Rather, all the goodness of all things—which you might call passive—comes from that Divine Goodness, which you might therefore call active (belonging to God alone). For this reason, every real thing, every established truth, every essence, every substance—whether <term>thinking<note>original: *cogitans*. In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to minds or souls.</note> or <term>extended<note>original: *extensa*. Refers to physical matter that occupies space.</note>—every mode and motion, whether in idea or in actual existence and duration, are good (as they truly are) because it is God's pleasure that they exist. Thus, all things that are, or can be spoken of or conceived, are heralds of God's Goodness; there is no need to gather many examples of it here, for its seat is everywhere.

IV. Furthermore, there is in God an essential Goodness which exists without regard to those things that are not God. This is when he communicates himself to himself within himself, most abundantly and perfectly, not out of indifference but out of love for himself. However, we have been dealing here with that Goodness which is relative, and which finds its end in those things that are not God. The former [essential goodness] does not reach out toward created things.

V. From this, it is clear what should be replied to the question: *How would God be good if no created things existed?* I add further: *...if nothing at all had been decreed?* The answer is that God's essential Goodness would remain whole and complete. But even if nothing were then actually communicated according to his pleasure, he would still be of such a nature that, if it pleased him to will to give something, it would therefore <note>original: *eventurum*. The catchword *turum* completes this word on the following page.</note> come to pass...

### §. A.

->1. *Obstacles to Happiness. How Acquiescence and Happiness differ.*<-

I. Since I must take the occasion to speak of God from the consideration of myself and those things which I can observe in myself, I proceed, therefore, to return to myself. I remember that I noticed in myself the ideas of things greater than me, equal to me, and less than me, over whose natures and truths I had no right <note>original: "jus"; meaning legal or moral authority over the essence of things</note> to dispose of them according to my whim, or to conceive and establish them differently, or even to create new ones. The Mind has already entered upon the path to this happiness when it desires nothing besides God according to His pleasure, and, while awaiting the fulfillment of that Divine pleasure, embraces for God's sake whatever that same pleasure ordains for the present state of things.

<header>RATIONAL THOUGHTS</header>

III. What I stated in the second place—that God must be considered absolutely Happy because things distinct from Him can add nothing to Him nor take anything away—further demonstrates a truly singular kind of Happiness, of which there is no other example besides Him. Every kind of happiness known to us receives an increase (sometimes its entire basis) from something external or from another person. Thus, among men, those who are considered happy because of their power, knowledge, or some other quality, would not find themselves so happy if they were placed alone and deprived of everyone except themselves. They would easily notice that something pleasant comes to them from the society, notice, love, or praise of others. Indeed, there is no doubt that something is added even to the truer Happiness of the Created Mind <note>By "Created Mind," the author refers to the human soul or angelic beings as distinct from the "Supreme Mind" of God.</note>—which we just discussed—even if we suppose the mind enjoys that happiness alone. This increase comes from society with other holy minds; namely, when it knows and sees that it has pleased God to be loved by many others besides itself. But we must not conclude the same regarding God. For although He is known, loved, praised, and represented in a fitting manner by countless beings, He is not for that reason happier in Himself than if He were alone, or if those other things either ceased to be or were entirely different. If He willed to establish, effect, create, redeem, and adorn with benefits those who would love and praise Him, He did not do so to become more Blessed <note>original: "Beatior"</note>, but because it pleased Him to thus shadow forth His own Happiness, which is sufficient for Him, according to His own will. These points are clear enough from themselves and from what has been said before.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...that those things exist just as they are conceived by Him and are decreed to exist. I recognize in Him such a great efficacy of Thought or will that I fully rest in this conclusion: that things exist from the efficacy and power of God’s <term>pleasure<note>original: "placiti Dei". This refers to God's sovereign decree or goodwill; what He "pleased" to make real.</note></term>, or because it pleased God not only to establish them as true, or to conceive their ideas, but also to will that they should have in themselves that <term>shadowy reality<note>original: "realitatem umbratilem". A philosophical concept suggesting that created things are not the primary reality, but rather faint reflections or "shadows" of the divine archetype.</note></term> or representative reality of His pleasure. I will not now bring forth the Holy Scriptures to demonstrate the efficacy of this Divine Thought or will, for I do not wish to use that kind of argument here; nor will I rely solely on my own experience—feeling that I exist and knowing this comes from Him, as I have already seen. Rather, I shall clearly conclude this according to reason from what has been previously proven.

V. This power and perfection of Divine Thought, which brings about the existence of things exactly as it wills, could be denied by no one without also affirming that something is lacking in God—or that the <term>Most Perfect Being<note>original: "Ens Perfectissimum". A standard philosophical term for God in the 17th century.</note></term> is not the Most Perfect Being. For although the existence and nature of things—indeed even the concept or pleasure of God concerning them—are not part of the essence of God (and thus their denial does not in itself directly imply a denial of the Divine essence), nevertheless, from the hypothesis that the Most Perfect God wills them to be in this way, it follows either that they are so, or if they are not, He is denied to have willed them who is said to have willed them, which contradicts the hypothesis. Or if He did will it, He is denied to be the Most Perfect Being: first, because something would thus be established as lacking in Him—not that His Nature lacked external things (since they do not belong to His Nature), but rather that God, insofar as He willed to determine Himself thus, or God's will itself, would be judged to lack the efficacy of placing those things which He willed to be placed outside Himself so that they might be both signs of His efficacy and <term>shadowy sketches<note>original: "adumbrationes vel tabulæ". Literally "shadows or tablets/paintings"; images that represent a greater reality.</note></term> or depictions of His divine perfections. For indeed, how could He be considered most perfect in Himself, in His Nature, in His will, and in His thought, if He were said to be unable to place outside Himself even those things which are very imperfect? Second, it would thus be established that God tends toward <term>non-being<note>original: "non-Ens". Nothingness.</note></term>, and is thus alienated from Himself. God cannot desert Himself, and when He wishes to attend to things different from Himself, He does so chiefly for His own sake; He is His own goal, and He tends toward other things so that He might represent Himself through them according to His pleasure, and thus that there might be a return to Himself. But nothingness—indeed, such a nothingness that remains nothing against God's will—does not represent God's perfections. Therefore, because God does not desert Himself, it must be concluded that when He wills something to exist outside Himself, such a thing also exists in which the perfections of God are foreshadowed, and from which a return to God is made; therefore, it does not remain nothing.

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...or His <term>pleasure<note>original: "placitum". In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to God's sovereign choice or decree.</note></term>, whatever it may be and wherever it might be directed, is not fulfilled; such a thought must be removed from our conception of God, since He can in no way be called unhappy. Furthermore, what has been said of God until now, especially concerning His Altitude and Dominion, does not permit the establishment of those premises from which it would follow that someone Greater than Him could be conceived, or that His own concept could be restricted to nothingness against His will. But if that Supreme Thought did not bring about the existence of those things which it wills to think of as existing, a Greater and more perfect Thought would be conceived—namely another, at whose determination things would exist exactly as it pleased it. And since God wills to determine Himself to conceive something as existing, if it did not actually exist, then God would be determined by nothingness itself to conceive the opposite of what He willed; and His will would be forced to this: namely, to be content with what He does not will, and thus to be filled, bounded, and determined by nothingness itself—all of which are contradictory.

Nor should anyone say that God wills many things as existing which nevertheless do not happen, such as those things concerning the observance of His commandments, which even if He wills and commands them to be done by all, yet they do not exist in those people. For it is certain that this "will" of God is not some absolute pleasure of His by which He has decreed to fully effect, according to His divine strength and power, whatever can contribute to the production of this effect—otherwise the thing would undoubtedly exist so. Instead, it is a declaration by which He warns men that it pleases Him that they should not pretend to act by themselves according to their own <term>fantasies<note>original: "phantasmata". This refers to subjective human imaginings or delusions as opposed to divine truth.</note></term>, nor tend toward nothingness, nor abuse the gifts He has bestowed upon them, which is the purpose of God's commandments. But it is by no means to be concluded from these things that God has absolutely, and as fully as He could, decreed that no perfection should be lacking in anyone that could be in them. This would entirely destroy the idea of God, if God, willing thus, did not effect whatever He wills.

VII. Therefore, it is clear from what has been said that the force and efficacy of God's will is so great that, granted that He wills these or those things to exist in this or that way, by the very fact that He wills it, it follows that such things are established as existing, and not otherwise. This virtue of the Divine will we recognize in God by the name of *Power*. In order that we might say something more specific about it and come to know it, we shall consider it as related to various objects—not indeed to all individual things, for they are innumerable, but to more general ones. The Power of God is viewed as related to things that already exist; the same is viewed as having respect to those things which do not yet exist, and perhaps never will exist, which are nonetheless called "possible"; and finally, it is viewed absolutely, as not related to any things having either existence, or essence, nature, and ideal truth,

For whether I conceive that things exist; or whether I think things do not exist, but are only conceived or exist by God only as far as their established <term>ideas<note>original: "ideas". In 17th-century philosophy, "ideas" often refer to the eternal archetypes or blueprints of things existing in the Divine Mind.</note></term>; or finally, if I think that God could have brought nothing into effect and decreed nothing—and thus nothing besides God’s own nature would possess truth—nevertheless, I must still conceive of God as Powerful. We shall deal with these points in reverse order, beginning with this final consideration.

### VIII. God's Power
In the ultimate sense, which can be called **absolute**, God's Power is not so different from **God’s Supreme Dominion**. It is considered even before we conceive of God having established any specific thing, essence, or truth. To understand this, one must <term>abstract<note>To "abstract" here means to mentally set aside or ignore the physical world to focus on a pure concept in isolation.</note></term> from all existence, essence, idea, and truth of things. We must think that although nothing besides God existed, and nothing besides God was ever going to have existence, essence, or truth, God’s **will** would still be so perfect that if it pleased Him to decree certain things and will them to exist—whether they were to be similar to those things that now exist, or possessed of natures, essences, and truths entirely different from those we know (and thus unknown and unthinkable to us)—they would indeed be brought forth exactly as He willed. 

In this sense, therefore, God is **absolutely Powerful**. Nor is He <term>indifferent<note>original: "indifferens". This refers to "indifference of the will," a philosophical debate about whether God's will is "indifferent" (could choose anything) or "determined" by His own perfection.</note></term> to this, such that whatever pleased Him to will would be so or not be so just as He liked. For He is not powerful because He willed to determine Himself to these or those things, but He is powerful necessarily, for the reasons already stated: because He is most perfect, and His will cannot lack its intended effect. This will is not powerful because it was first seen as indifferent and then later determined toward this or that; rather, it is powerful because it is God’s—it is powerful prior to any determination. 

Consequently, **God can do more than He wills**; indeed, He can do other and different things than what He has willed and decreed to be true or brought into existence. This Power of His must in no way be limited by our consideration of the ideas, essences, truths, and the nature of existing things—as if God could not absolutely do what does not exist in them or what does not agree with them. To Him, everything except Himself is inherently "indifferent," since in themselves, all other things are nothing. Therefore, we should not define God’s **Absolute Power** in any way that limits it. Our mind is already determined to conceive of the things that exist (though, as will soon be seen, not even all of those); hence, it cannot conceive the full extent to which God’s Power might reach. A certain degree of mental attention is required to properly grasp these points and those that follow. Once these are understood, it will be easy to see what should be thought regarding the Power of God, or what should not. Furthermore, because these points almost coincide with what was said above regarding **God’s Dominion**, they are subject to the same difficulties:

### IX.
I come now to the second consideration regarding the **Power of God**. Specifically: Since God has determined to conceive certain **ideas**, **essences**, **truths**, etc., as it pleased Him, then wherever He wishes (if He so chooses) that all or some of these should exist outside of His own <term>concept<note>original: "conceptus". In this context, a "concept" refers to a thought or blueprint within the Divine Mind that has not yet been brought into physical reality.</note></term>, He is able to carry this out. That is, He is **Powerful** enough to place those things He willed to be conceived into a state outside of that concept. In this respect, God is said to be able to do those things which He wills and has willed; thus, His <term>efficacious will<note>A will that has the power to produce an actual effect or result.</note></term> regarding the existence of certain things (which we call His Power) does not come before the will that decrees their essence and nature. It would be ridiculous, in this sense, to assert that God could do things which He did not will, or which He did not ordain. This would be to say that He could grant existence to a thing for which He had willed no nature or essence. I note that this is the reason and the **Origin of the power or possibility of things**. For things are called "possible" because they were first established and ordered by God’s most free <term>arbitrament<note>original: "arbitrio" - a formal word for "will" or "choice," often implying a legal or sovereign decision.</note></term> regarding their natures, essences, ideas, and truths; if God’s pleasure regarding their existence were then added, they would exist, being fit to obtain existence because of His efficacy. This consideration of Divine Power commends to me the truth of the following Propositions, the first of which is:

### X.
*Of the Power of God, we can affirm all things which we evidently conceive.* This is clear if we assume these points—which can easily be demonstrated from what has been said, and will be demonstrated hereafter—namely, that God conceives what I conceive, and that my concept is a certain representation of the Divine concept. From this I argue: Those things which I conceive <term>evidently<note>In 17th-century philosophy, "evidently" means "clearly and distinctly," in a way that the mind cannot doubt.</note></term>, God also conceives; they are in His concept, and indeed they are in it more clearly and evidently than in mine. Furthermore, those things which God conceives, and which therefore have an idea, essence, and truth in His concept, are (based on what was said before) fit to exist through the Power of God. Therefore, whatever I conceive can exist through the Power of God, or God can bring about whatever I conceive with evidence.

### XI.
The second proposition: *Those things which I do not conceive, I ought not to deny regarding the Power of God.* I do not say that things which are <term>repugnant<note>Meaning logically contradictory or impossible within the framework of a concept.</note></term> to my concept and destroy its evidence should be accepted, but rather those things which **transcend** or "absorb" it, so to speak—these are not to be subtracted from the Divine Power. When God, out of those things which He conceived, brought certain things into effect outside of Himself—and thus also rendered me, whom He conceived, as an existing being—He impressed upon me certain concepts similar to His own, but He did not impress them all. Hence, I can indeed draw affirmative arguments from my concept, but it is not permitted to think: "I do not conceive this, therefore God does not conceive it, nor can He bring it about." It is a matter of the highest recklessness...

For an extension that is in itself truly and positively infinite excludes the possibility of any new addition, since this exclusion of further addition is the very concept of the infinite. What, then, can be determined here by our Mind? Nothing. Therefore, let the mind be convinced of its own weakness and the narrow limits of its own measure; let it not conclude anything from these regarding the Power of God. "I cannot grasp this, therefore the power of thinking in me is finite"—this is a sound conclusion. But "Therefore God cannot effect this"—that conclusion lies entirely outside the premise.

### XII.
The **Third Proposition** is this: it must never be supposed that **Divine Power is comprehended by us**, or can be comprehended, such that we might reason from that hypothesis. We know that God is **Incomprehensible**, and that He is a single **Simple Thought**; hence we see that His Power cannot be comprehended by a finite Mind. It is therefore often said—dangerously so—that "not even God can do this or that," as if the **Sphere** or measure of His Power could be grasped. Some, neglecting this caution, have fallen into foolish and absurd questions about the Power of God. <page-num>151</page-num>

# ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

Must we conceive and note such absurdities as belonging to the **Power of God**? Yet this is exactly what is done by those we are dealing with—namely, those who, having abandoned the old way of philosophizing <note>The author refers to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian philosophy taught in universities for centuries.</note>, embrace a new one, according to which they cannot reconcile their own views except through these absurdities. 

Namely, by their own admission, through a <term>voluntary decree<note>original: "voluntaria constitutione." The idea that the laws of physics or the nature of things are the way they are simply because God chose them to be so, rather than being necessary truths.</note></term> of God, space, actual extension, matter, and body are one and the same thing. And yet, according to these same people, countless spaces and <term>extensions<note>In Cartesian philosophy, "extension" refers to the quality of taking up space (length, width, and depth). Descartes famously argued that the essence of matter is nothing but extension itself.</note></term>—though diverse in number and set apart from each other—will not be diverse in their quantity of matter, but will be a single matter in number! They claim that other spaces will be added to one space, and yet nothing will be added to the body! Spaces will be diminished and removed, and yet nothing will be lost from the extension or the matter of the body. 

At the beginning, a small volume of bread will be present; the extension will remain the same, and yet it will be a large body—that is, an extension actually a thousand times greater! Its own extension will remain, and yet its own matter (which is the same thing to them) will not remain, nor will its actual extension! The same shapes of that extension will remain in the particles, in motion, in rest, and in arrangement; and yet the same particular nature will not remain, which—even according to them—consists in these very arrangements of particles! 

Either let them renounce their new principles about nature (which they hold as if founded on sound reason), which is to say they renounce what they think is sound reason; or let them admit that, according to those principles, they contradict themselves—which is likewise to deny sound reason. This problem is in no way cured by appealing to **Divine Power**. 

For indeed, in order to believe that God is Omnipotent, must they judge that God, while establishing and preserving the same extension, is *not* preserving the same extension—or, what is the same to them, the same matter? That He, while preserving that tiny amount, is in that very act not preserving the tiny amount, but a massive one? That He, while sustaining the same shapes and arrangements, is not sustaining the same ones—or (what they determine does not differ) the same specific nature of the body that was there before? 

An intelligent reader can hardly read without a laugh what the good <term>Descartes<note>Latin: *Cartesius*. René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher whose "mechanical philosophy" redefined matter as simple extension.</note></term> laboriously toils over in his *Fourth Replies* <note>Descartes' *Responsiones Quartae* (1641) were his responses to the theologian Antoine Arnauld, who had pointed out that Descartes' physics made the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist—where bread remains looking like bread but becomes the body of Christ—logically impossible.</note> regarding this matter. From his arguments, you finally conclude that God, while preserving the same internal and external extension of the bread or wine—namely the boundaries, limits, shapes, and arrangements—is nevertheless not preserving these very things, or the bread and wine itself. And yet, to Descartes, extension *is* matter; and those arrangements of particles are the very principle by which the **essence** of bread and wine is distinguished from the nature of flesh and all other bodies. Their essences, as they are distinguished from one another, are (according to him and his followers) nothing but those very configurations and modifications. What then, if God preserves the same extension along with all its modes, has been changed...

...what will they judge has been added from these principles (according to which all things that constitute nature remain unchanged and immutable) other than a different name, a different use, or different relations? But let them see where their own principles lead them. It is not, indeed, my intention to deal with religious controversies (which it would be better to suppress entirely) or to treat the dogma itself here by profession, nor to examine whether it can be explained by the principles of the **Old Scholastic Philosophy** <note>The traditional Aristotelian philosophy used by the Church to explain how the "substance" of bread could change into Christ's body while the "accidents" (look, taste, smell) remain.</note> (whatever they may be) or not. Let others see to that. 

But since the author of the not-uncelebrated work *The Art of Thinking* <note>original: "Artis Cogitandi," referring to the *Port-Royal Logic* (1662) by Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole, which attempted to reconcile Cartesian philosophy with Catholic theology.</note> triumphs rather prematurely and boastfully over his opponents regarding this matter—using the principles he himself established—I did not think he or his followers should be kept from seeing how effectively, according to the **Cartesian principles** which he proposes everywhere, his own opponents (whom he thinks he has so handily defeated) can prove the opposite of his assertion. This is so that he and his followers might proceed more cautiously in the future, or plainly leave off such controversies in philosophical writings (not trusting too much in their new speculations).

<margin>(a) *The Art of Thinking*, Part IV, chapter XI.</margin>
He says (a) *that the senses clearly teach that roundness and whiteness are present, but do not teach whether the substance of bread makes these things appear.* But how will his opponents respond according to his own principles? Surely, reason and the senses teach that the extension of the bread has remained, and that the arrangement of the particles of extension, the shape, the motion, the rest, and the position have remained; and you yourself admit that the nature and distinction of the essence of bodies consist in these very things. How then will you say that the substance of the bread has been changed? In your judgment, what is that substance besides **extension and modes** <term>modes<note>In Cartesian terms, "extension" is the essential nature of matter (taking up space), while "modes" are the temporary states or qualities of that extension, like shape or motion.</note></term> (which you admit remain) except an empty name, of which no idea is held? 

Why, given an idea which you call essential, and which remains evidently unchanged in both the senses and the intellect, would you substitute another thing which ought to be perceived through a completely different idea? Will you say that God placed an idea in me by which He wished me to conceive one certain thing, and yet by that same idea He did not want me to conceive what He willed, but its opposite—and that He thus positively aims toward non-being? 

The Author says, *that it is established by reason that neither can one body be in two different places at the same time, nor can two bodies be in the same place: but that this must be understood as the natural condition of bodies; otherwise, it would be a failure of reason if we thought our mind, being finite, could comprehend the Power of God, which is infinite.* At this, someone might ask: will I then remove the failure of my reason if I think that the **Infinity of God's Power** consists in this: that while He acts upon and sustains one thing, and exhibits a clear idea of its essence to me, it is nevertheless that very thing He is not sustaining? And that, while the prior essential idea remains unchanged, He is not exhibiting the idea of that thing to me, but of something else entirely, for which you admit you have established a completely different idea?

<header>ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.</header>

But I ask you: what else is that "natural condition of bodies in general" which our Author <note>The author of the *Art of Thinking*, Antoine Arnauld.</note> describes, if not the very constitution of their nature, if not nature itself, if not the bodies themselves, if not the decree and effect of God's will? It was God who willed bodies to be of such a nature, or willed that their nature be exactly as this Author conceives it to be. Thus, he contradicts himself by asserting that a body, while remaining a body, can change its natural condition or its corporeal nature. For if it did, it would be said to no longer be a body; and God would be seen as willing it to possess the nature of a body and yet not possess it at the same time—even while, by your own admission, it was and remained a body. 

But perhaps it would be better for our Author, and those who philosophize from the same principles, to conclude that God (as the one who poses, decrees, and wills something) would simultaneously approve and disapprove of the same thing. They would rather believe that God’s Power consists in this contradiction than admit they are mistaken in the principles they have accepted. For my part, I would more easily believe that there exists in our Author a "power" of saying and not saying the same thing, of decreeing and not decreeing—that is, a power of contradicting himself—than that there exists in God a power of simultaneously establishing and not establishing the same thing. It is impossible that God would decree (according to our Author) a certain nature for bodies in general and in species, and yet fail to preserve that nature while he preserves everything within them which (according to our Author’s own philosophical musings) constitutes that very nature. No more splendid contradiction than this can be found.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

What, from these principles (according to which all the things that constitute nature remain unvaried and unchanged), will they judge has been added, other than a different name, a different use, or different relations? But let them see where their own principles will lead them. It is not my intention to deal with religious controversies (which would be better suppressed entirely) or to treat the dogma itself here as a professional task, nor to examine whether it can be explained through the principles of old Scholastic Philosophy <note>The traditional medieval philosophy based on Aristotle, which used the concepts of "substance" and "accidents" to explain how bread could become the body of Christ.</note> (whatever those may be). Let others see to that. 

But since the author of the well-known work *The Art of Thinking* <note>The *Port-Royal Logic*, a famous 17th-century textbook by Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole.</note> triumphs quite prematurely and boastfully over his adversaries regarding this matter according to the principles he has set down, I did not think he or his followers should be kept in the dark about how effectively his own adversaries—whom he believes he has handily defeated—could prove the opposite of his assertion using the very Cartesian principles <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, which reduced the physical world to "extension" or measurable space.</note> he proposes throughout. This is so that he and his followers might proceed more cautiously in the future, or entirely leave off such controversies in philosophical writings, rather than relying too much on their own new speculations.

<margin>(a) *The Art of Thinking*, Part IV, chapter xi.</margin> He says (a) <note>original: "Sensus evidenter docere adesse rotunditatem & albedinem, sed non docere an has faciat apparere panis substantia"</note> *that the senses clearly teach that roundness and whiteness are present, but they do not teach whether it is the substance of bread that makes these appear.* 

But what will his adversaries respond according to his own principles? Surely this: reason and the senses teach that the extension <term>extension: the property of taking up space, which Descartes argued was the very essence of matter</term> of the bread has remained, and the arrangement, shape, motion, rest, and position of the particles of that extension have remained; and you yourself admit that the nature and distinction of the essence of bodies consist in these very things. How then will you say that the substance of the bread has been changed? What, in your judgment, is that substance besides extension and its modes (which you admit remain), if not a hollow name of which no idea is held? 

Why, when an idea is posed which you call essential, and which remains clearly unchanged in both sense and intellect, would you substitute another thing which must be perceived through an entirely different idea? Will you say that God placed an idea in me by which He wanted me to conceive something as certain and as one specific thing, and yet by that same idea He did not want me to conceive what He willed, but rather something else—and thus that He positively moves toward non-being? 

The Author says, <note>original: "ratione constare nec corpus unum tempore eodem in locis duobus diversis, neque duo corpora in eodem loco esse posse: at vero id esse intelligendum de conditione naturali corporum: alioqui defectum fore rationis si putaremus mentem nostram, utpote finitam, comprehendere posse Dei Potentiam, quæ infinita est"</note> *it is established by reason that neither can one body be in two different places at the same time, nor can two bodies be in the same place; yet this must be understood as the natural condition of bodies; otherwise it would be a defect of reason if we thought our mind, being finite, could comprehend the Power of God, which is infinite.* 

But (someone might say) will I then remove the defect of my reason if I think that the infinity of God’s power consists in this: that while He acts upon and sustains one thing, showing me a clear idea of its essence, He is nevertheless not sustaining that very thing? And while the previous essential idea remains unchanged, He is not showing me its idea, but the idea of something else entirely, whose idea you admit you have established as being completely different?

But I ask: what for our Author is that "natural condition of bodies in general" which he describes, if it is not the constitution of their nature, if it is not nature itself, if it is not the bodies themselves, if it is not the decree and effect of God’s will—a will that intended bodies to be of such a nature (or intended their nature to be such as this Author conceives it to be)? ...in the sense (which finds a place among the Sacred Authors) the **Creature which is in Christ**, that is his **humanity**, which is most strictly joined to the **Divinity** and is the head of all creatures, is to be **adored**, as is clear from the very meaning of the words provided. And these points are agreed upon by everyone. It is also agreed that God, in the primary sense <note>The author refers here to *latria*, or the worship due to God alone.</note>, is to be adored whether his body is present or absent, and regardless of whether it is truly present or merely thought to be so. Now, if someone should think the Lord’s body is not present, yet still confesses Divine adoration in the primary sense, but is unwilling to exhibit the act of adoration in the secondary sense <note>The secondary sense refers to *hyperdulia* or veneration, which is honor paid to Christ's human nature because of its union with the divine.</note>—or rather, is unwilling to acknowledge with his mind and gestures that a certain creature (for instance, the **Eucharistic bread**) is that most noble creature which God united to Himself (which, if he believed it were present, he would indeed adore in that second sense already mentioned, just as he confesses it ought to be adored)—then it is clear that such a person cannot be accused of impiety or the rejection of God, as is often done by those who are blindly fervent. 

For, although he might be in error, his error would not be about the things themselves—namely, about that adoration which concerns the **Divinity**, nor about that which regards the **humanity**, which he admits in the stated sense. Instead, his error is only about a **circumstance of the matter** concerning the location of the humanity: Is that humanity, which he would certainly adore (according to the second definition) if he believed it to be present, actually in this place, or not? Why then such great hatred? 

If, however, someone thinking the humanity were present were to adore it alone as a creature and viewed without the Divinity according to the first sense of adoration, he would indeed be substituting or acknowledging a creature in place of the Creator, or erring in the object of the primary adoration (and I would not wish to excuse this). But if someone, focusing on God, offers Him primary adoration in the presence (even if only supposed) of His humanity—which he also honors with its due (secondary) adoration, though he would omit this if he thought the humanity were absent—he ought not to be accused by those who think him mistaken of any crime other than that he is "wandering in thought" <note>original: "hallucinetur"</note> regarding a circumstance of the matter, namely the location of the humanity. 

Nor do the dissenting parties have anything greater that they can clearly reproach each other with; and as much as one errs in the opinion of the other, so too does the other err in the opinion of the first. Thus the "crime" is reciprocal, such that one side cannot, in its own judgment and opinion, make the other's crime seem heavier without representing itself to the other's opinion as the more gravely erring. The crime, however, is merely a question of **external circumstance**. 

But what kind of crime is it, if someone, thinking the Lord's body is present, takes from this an occasion for loving God, considering that He condescends so far (so to speak) to human infirmity and accommodates Himself? Or if someone, thinking the Lord's body is absent, thinks this happens so that he does not cling too much to an external presence, and thus seeks to be united purely through love with the **Spirit of Christ**? 

Behold, where we would have arrived if they had used restraint <term>moderamen: a legal and philosophical term for the "management" or "tempering" of a conflict</term> and reason! For...

These points are clearer than the midday sun. But perhaps they are hated by those who love factions and would wish the excuses for hatred and quarrels to remain forever. For the sake of any sensible person, there is no reason to please such people to that extent. But let us return to the matter at hand, namely, the Power of God.

**XV.** It remains for me to consider Divine Power in relation to the existence of things. Although God's Power is an essential and necessary attribute <term>attribute: a fundamental quality or characteristic that belongs to God's very nature</term> of His Nature, one must not think that the things which exist through that power are absolutely necessary, or exist by necessity. For even if, when thinking about these things, I must necessarily judge that—given God wills something to be—the efficacy of His will is so great that it suffices to bring that thing into existence; nevertheless, it is not necessary that God willed such a thing rather than another, or even nothing at all. 

Therefore, just as I said above regarding the essence <term>essence: the "whatness" or definition of a thing, regardless of whether it actually exists</term> and truth of things, I now say the same regarding their existence: even if no thing existed, nor were ever to exist in the future, God would nonetheless always be Powerful. This is because this perfection and efficacy is inseparable from His will—meaning that, if He wills it, things will come to be. Note in passing that since all things, in terms of their essence and existence, could have been "nothing" for all eternity, we see the necessity and sufficiency of God alone. 

Just as it is within His Power that if He wills things to exist, they will therefore come to be, so also I say conversely: If things—whatever they may be—exist (as many indeed do exist, the structure of which is called the "world"), they all exist through this force, reason, and cause: because God willed them to be so. Or: *Everything that exists is produced by God's effective will or Power.* 

This is deduced from what has been demonstrated as follows: 
1. If God wills something to exist, the thing will exist because of that very "willing." 
2. But God wills all things to be as they now are: for if He willed them to be otherwise, and yet they were not so, His will would not be powerful. 
3. Therefore, the fact that God wills all things to be what they already are is the cause, reason, and force behind the position or existence of all those things. 

Furthermore, no things besides God exist necessarily or have the reason for their existence within themselves, as was seen in the section on the Sufficiency of God. Therefore, all things must have the reason for their existence elsewhere. But "elsewhere," beyond all things, there is nothing but God. And since we consider God's Nature to be content in itself alone—from which nothing proceeds except God Himself—and then consider His "indifferent pleasure" <note>original: "placitum indifferens." This refers to God's total freedom of choice; He is not forced by any outside necessity to create the world.</note> in deciding upon external things, it follows that this pleasure (or this will) is the reason and cause of the existence of things. Without this, things would be nothing at all, as they would lack both an internal cause (namely, the necessity of essence and existence) and an external cause (namely, the efficient producer). I will not bring forth more proofs of this truth which [arise] from other [attributes] of God...

### XVI. 
When I said that all existing things, as they are now, are established solely by the efficacy of the **Divine pleasure** <term>Divine pleasure: from the Latin *placitum*, referring to God's sovereign will or decree rather than an emotional whim</term>, it is well understood, first, that this must not be extended to error and sin. For these are not "things" but **defects** <note>The author follows the classical philosophical tradition (like Augustine or Aquinas) which argues that evil and sin are not positive "things" created by God, but rather a "lack" or "privation" of good</note>; they are not the existence of things or perfections, nor are they anything positive, and therefore they do not require a positive cause to be established. Second, it is clear through this that everything which possesses **reality** is included here, from the greatest to the smallest: the things themselves, substances, their perfections, properties, modes, and their duration—whether long or short. In a word, all things are as they are, they endure, they stand, and they are changed for no other reason than because **God wills it**. 

And this applies not only to the corporeal substance that constitutes the earth, the heavens, and everything within them—including all its particles, their shapes, motions, arrangements, and the directions of those motions (which, even if they are joined to the agreement of a created **Thought**, are nonetheless established by the Divine alone)—but this must also be extended to all **Minds** and their modes. It is a **childish prejudice** to think that the modes of thinking—this or that thought, knowledge, judgments, affections, habits, determinations toward these or those ideas, and all internal acts, insofar as there is something positive and "real" in them—depend less upon or are produced less by the **Power of God** than physical modes are. 

To be sure, when some physical body takes on new modes—as if clay were to take the shape of a human body, or if a mountain were transported from its place, or if the motion of the planets were turned in the opposite direction—then these are viewed as highly positive things and are referred to the **Greatest Cause**. Yet, would it not also be so when the modes of the **Mind** are changed and new ones are added? When an ignorant Mind becomes a knowing one? When it begins to know, desire, and love God? Should this not be produced by the **Supreme Cause**, or is it a small thing? For in this, there is a thousand times more reality or perfection than in the motions of the entire universe or their changes. 

It is the mark of children to judge that where nothing bodily is encountered, or nothing that affects us in a **forceful** <term>forceful: Latin *coactivo*, implying a physical or compelling force</term> way—as in those things that happen to the Mind with its own consent—that nothing great is being achieved there, or nothing at all. For this reason, some have failed to grasp that they are sustained by God, because they did not experience it acting upon them in a violent manner. But so that one may notice how great the perfections and realities are in the modes of minds, let him consider within himself that the entire matter of the whole universe, however perfect it may be, is not conscious of even one of its own perfections or imperfections—a perfection of which no mode of thinking is deprived. Let him then observe how great a difference there is between a stupid, ignorant, or vicious and wicked mind, and one that is skillful, dili-

Finally, thirdly, we must note that the object of **God’s Power** consists of the things I have mentioned: all corporeal and spiritual things and their modes, whether they are said to proceed from nature or from grace, and whether they are called natural, supernatural, or celestial. Or as if a creature in the state of nature depended less upon God than in the state of grace, contributing more of themselves in one state than in another. 

This distinction is wrongly made where nothing, in this sense, should be distinguished. Everything and anything that exists outside of and apart from God is nothing in itself; it cannot exist except by the will of God, and only because and for as long as He wills it. Is there even the smallest positive thing that exists apart from and beyond God’s will? Is anything given besides God that could be the cause and reason for its own existence, and which could say: "God did not establish me; I established myself independently of Him"? Certainly, to seek the cause of even the smallest positive thing outside of God is a **denial of God**. Indeed, if it were thought that anything could be conceived as independent of God, I wonder why this is not claimed for more perfect things—such as the highest knowledge, learning, happiness, and preservation of life that a human can possess—rather than for lesser things, such as walking, speaking, and other natural or political actions, which must be recognized as having less perfection and power within them. If you wish to attribute self-existence to anyone besides God, you ought logically to judge this of the more perfect things rather than the imperfect.

XVII. Having acknowledged God's power over everything that exists, we must investigate certain matters more specifically: namely, how does He actually bring each thing into being <note>original: "actu rem quamque ponat"</note>? Does He cause things to exist absolutely, or rather under a certain condition? Thirdly, why are some things said to exist contingently <term>contingently: something that happens but could have been otherwise; not strictly necessary</term>, while others exist necessarily? Finally, a word or two must be said about creation and preservation. Regarding the first question, it would be superfluous to say anything after what has already been said regarding the efficacy of the divine will, were it not for some who—preoccupied by troublesome prejudice and false reasoning—shroud a clear matter in darkness. They complicate it with obscure terms while imagining they are offering profound subtleties. 

For when anyone reflects upon themselves when they wish for certain external things to begin to happen through their own intervention, they can observe that their own power is not sufficient for the effect—either because they can only act in their own way, nor is it sufficient that they simply will or decree that the thing exist. Rather, it is necessary to deploy with these a singular exertion of strength and a mental "striving" <term>conatus: a focused effort or impulse toward action</term>, which others call a "commanded act" <term>actus imperatus: in Scholastic philosophy, an action performed by one faculty (like the hands) under the direction of another (the will)</term>. We all sufficiently measure the difference between this and a simple will to effect something through our own internal senses. From this, it follows that there is perhaps no one who has not at some point thought something similar about God bringing previously non-existent things into being—especially in those first judgments formed after childhood, which remain uncorrected in many people. 

I recall having seen, if I am not mistaken, such a prejudice confirmed by a similar line of reasoning somewhere: "Things do not begin to exist or be placed in being because God is Powerful, for He has always been so, yet things have not always existed—and by this reasoning, more things ought to exist than actually do. Nor are they brought into being because He is willing <note>original: "volens"</note>, for He is said to have been willing from eternity, yet things did not exist then; indeed, He wills many things that do not immediately arise for that reason, but only after many future centuries." Therefore, besides Power combined with Will...

...that things come into existence from nothing, they required something further, which, if I remember correctly, they called <term>actual efficacy: the active power or causal force required to bring a potential thing into reality</term>; and they believed that this, joined with Will and Power, places things in existence that were previously only possible. But there is no need for such crude subtleties. God is not like us, who experience such violent and transient efforts within ourselves and manifest them outside ourselves. The Will of the Powerful God alone suffices for things to begin to exist—not indeed at the same moment that the Will is conceived to be in God [eternally]; but at that time, moment, and in those circumstances in which God, before all time, willed such and such things to exist. Nothing is required beyond this: nor do the absurdities with which this was pressed have any force, if I say that God is so perfect a **Thought** <note>original: "Cogitationem"</note> that those things which He willed before time to think would be at such a time and in such a manner, therefore, because He willed it, they also exist at that same time, manner, place, etc., exactly as He willed.

XVIII. From these things, it is easy to deduce those points which satisfy the second question. Namely, if God wills things to be made under a certain condition and in such circumstances, it follows that things exist not absolutely, but under a condition; when the condition is met, the things are established, but when it is absent, they do not exist. And this is proved from all things whatsoever that happen and exist, whether bodily or spiritual, natural or moral. My body, for example, is not moved—*or rather*, is not determined in its motion in a certain way—except under the condition of the intervention of my will. The human Mind does not begin to exist unless a certain body is prepared to be united to it. In that same mind, God does not place knowledge and virtue except under the condition of attention, prayers, exhortations, etc., just as the body will not live except through the mediation of food and the help of men; and so with the rest. Yet it does not follow from what has been said that God depends on the creature, or subjects Himself to it, or is conceived as changeable, when it is asserted that truth is denoted by these and similar words: namely, "*if this had not been, neither would that have followed*"; if this had happened, this or that person would not have died, or something else—and such things as can be said about any events and are true. For these rules of acting, or conditions so that God may act, are not imposed on God by creatures, but God prescribed them for His own operations, insofar as He did not wish to operate except under these conditions. Hence He observes them constantly, and that not by necessity—as if He could not have done otherwise or could not do so now—but because, from the freedom of His own choice <note>original: "arbitrii sui libertate"</note>, having prescribed them, it constantly pleases Him to observe the same; except that, to show that He is not therefore bound by them, and that He depends on nothing, He occasionally brings things about somewhat differently, and then He is said to work **miracles** <note>original: "miracula"</note>, about which I shall speak shortly. But, what is most important to this matter, creatures [do not produce] the existence and circumstances of such conditions...

...establish the conditions, but God Himself establishes all of them together with everything else, as has been proven. Therefore, when it is said, "If such a thing had not been, then that which followed would not have been done," it should be understood in this way: If this had not been—that is, if God had not willed it and had not been able to do it—it would have been a sign that He did not will it, and would not have established that which followed. He is the Beginning, who establishes the prior condition <note>original: "antecedens"</note>; He is the Finisher <note>original: "Consummator"</note>, who establishes the result <note>original: "consequens"</note>. And when He does not establish the prior condition, by that very act He indicates that He will not establish the result. For the regular way in which He acts convinces us of the connection of His operations; since He observes this connection, we also ought to observe it diligently.

Nor can it be said that God seems more "needy" or less powerful because He works through many means <note>The author uses "means" (media) to refer to the intermediate steps or tools God uses to achieve an end, like using medicine to heal or seeds to grow a plant.</note>; on the contrary, He presents even more brilliant proofs of His Generosity and Power by effecting things through a great apparatus of means, since He brings the means into existence just as much as He does the results. However, He convinces man of his own tangible poverty and suppresses his pride by subjecting him to certain laws—of matter, of motion, and of the recognition of his own misery and lack—and to the petitioning for help from others, so that through these, the transition to his goal must be made.

### X I X.

By these principles, many thoughts are easily cleared away which trouble many who do not meditate on these matters as they should. These thoughts lead them to conclude that if God’s will is set on a result, then the "means" are negated—as if, when God wants to establish something by His pleasure, no means are to be employed. How often you hear among the common people: "If God wants them to stay alive for a certain time, then they should not want to avoid dangers (which are the conditions for the body's destruction)," such as places infected by contagion <note>The author likely refers to plague-infected areas, common in the early modern period.</note>, or places exposed to danger, and many things of this sort. This is a rebellion against God’s laws and a rejection of them, proceeding from a barbaric and ignorant pride—as if such a man were so great that God ought to abandon His own laws for the sake of his life and sustain him in an extraordinary way. Such an insolent thought is secretly underlying this view.

But you will say that this cannot be the case for moral means: "If God willed to bring about good and happiness in me, why do I need prayers and exhortations?" I respond that God wills these very things to be the essential means for the thing or the goal intended by God. For since true happiness consists in this—that I enjoy what is most opted for and desired (as we showed above)—therefore, when God wills to make me happy, by that very act He wills to make me one who supremely desires, one who longs, or one who prays <note>The author argues that prayer is not about changing God's mind, but is a necessary state of mind that God creates in us so we can appreciate the "good" He provides.</note>, and to place in me a fire for the true good, so that afterwards I may be made blessed by the enjoyment of what was desired. XX. I have just said that God sometimes effects something in a manner other than under ordinary conditions, and those effects are called miracles. I will now say something about these, and perhaps at some length, because until now I have not been able to find any source that could satisfy a discerning mind on this difficult subject. Some people flatly deny that miracles have been performed by God, or that they ought to be performed. Others debate whether those things said to be done through the mediation of evil Angels and wicked men are "true miracles" or merely "wonders" <note>The author distinguishes between *miracula* (miracles) and *mirabilia* (wonders). In this period, "wonders" often referred to amazing events that seemed supernatural but were actually just clever tricks or the result of hidden natural laws known only to spirits or demons.</note>. Now, if these are considered in relation to establishing doctrines in Religions, or the opposite, what a commotion! Here, to extricate myself from all these disputes, I will consider miracles first in relation to the natural state of things; and second, their use in those matters which pertain to the worship of God. However, as for the facts—whether this or that event narrated by this or that person happened exactly as they say—it is not the place here to inquire; nor will we deal with those things which God works in the minds of men when He turns them toward Himself, but only with those things which occur in bodily things. The distinction between "miracles" and "wonders," as it is sometimes used in this matter, is of the kind that some people use so that they can pretend to know what they are ignorant of, using words that signify nothing clearly to the unlearned.

XXI. For miracles to be judged well, it must be supposed that things remain, as much as can be affirmed, in their own state. Therefore, when a miracle is proposed, the way of explaining it that deviates least from the state of things and clearly satisfies the phenomenon <note>original: "phenomeno"</note> is to be preferred over one that disturbs the state of things more; and that explanation which completely subverts the very nature of things is to be flatly rejected. This is so clear that I shall refrain from proving it, especially after what has already been noted regarding the Dominion and Power of God. From this, however, two rules of the greatest use follow. The first is this: *Miracles are not against the nature of extended things, or, they do not destroy the ideas of matter, or extension or space, nor the ideas of motion, or rest, or the division of matter, etc.* <note>The author is using "extension" (*extensio*) in the philosophical sense to mean "matter" or anything that takes up physical space.</note> They do not cause these things to cease being what they are in their essence; much less do they cause things to remain in existence and yet simultaneously not remain, but be changed—for example, that a small extension should be a large piece of matter (or a large extension) and not a small one; or that the same extension and its mode remain, yet the same thing does not exist, but another, whose nature is a larger extension modified in a different way. Let all miracles upon which there is agreement be examined, and none will wander from this rule. # RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...as if they are the modes of the primary ones) are the positioning of rest and the determination of motion: from whose mixtures the diversity of all material things, particular nature, and every variation arises, as is most clearly evident—as if before one's eyes—from all the physical works of Descartes <note>original: "Carteſii." Referring to René Descartes (1596–1650), whose mechanical philosophy dominated 17th-century science.</note>. The law of these primary modes is this: that motion and rest, just as they now exist, do not perish, but remain in the same quantity and proportion. Thus, if some motion begins to exist afterward in a part of the matter of the universe where previously there was none, a reciprocal amount of rest begins to exist in other matter previously moved, so that the proportion is preserved exactly. Nothing has ever been observed in nature that cannot be explained while keeping this law intact—indeed, through it—as those know who have inspected God's ordinary works with some attention, outside the shadows of the pseudo-philosophers <note>original: "Philoſophaſtrorum," a derogatory term for those who pretend to be philosophers but lack true knowledge.</note>. 

But I also say, no miracle can be designated that can be said to have been done against this law. For even if motion suddenly began to exist in a body previously resting, and yet no other body seems to come to rest to preserve the proportion, or vice versa; it does not follow that some motion is newly made against said law. This is because (as happens in all motions of gross bodies) a certain subtle matter <term>subtle matter: In Cartesian physics, an invisible, fluid-like substance that fills all space and carries forces, ensuring there is no vacuum in the universe</term>, withdrawn from the senses, penetrating and surrounding all things, could have transferred this motion from itself into that body by receiving into itself an equal amount of rest. Thus far, therefore, it cannot be said that miracles are against the conditions or laws of nature. Their diversity from other operations of God must therefore be sought in the secondary modes of things, or their laws.

XXII. There are two kinds of laws for secondary modes: those which concern only modified bodies, and others which regard them insofar as they can be united to certain minds. We will call the first **Brute Laws**, and the others, **Rational Laws**. The brute laws concerning the determination of motion are: 
1. Direction in a straight line. 
2. Reflection. 
3. Refraction (which, to those inspecting closely, is truly a species of reflection.) 
4. Communication of itself to certain bodies according to a straight line, but by receiving—on account of what was already said—an equal amount of rest. 

These are observed most exactly in works in which no created thought intervenes, but not in those to which God wished to join created Thought: for it is certain that the motions of that body to which a Mind is joined, or of some of its parts, such as the animal spirits <term>animal spirits: Following a long medical tradition, Descartes believed these were very fine, active particles in the blood that acted as messengers between the brain and the muscles</term>, are not determined in this Brute way, but by the reason and choice of the created thought joined to it. This thought determines the motions existing there—if not all, then at least most—wherever it wishes, so long as they are in the sphere assigned to its action: for otherwise, when bodies are moved, namely the animal spirits,

# ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL

...masses <note>original: "moles," referring to quantities of matter</note>, have traveled from that location in the brain to another, and fill the muscles that push external bodies. These things, as they are now outside the sphere of the mind, are again subjected to brute laws <note>The "brute laws" are the mechanical rules governing non-thinking matter, such as momentum and collision</note>. And in all these things, whatever occurs—even if they are often called marvelous—is nevertheless recognized as natural.

But it should be noted that God has so arranged certain minds, which are called Angelic, that—even if perhaps not all of them, nor always—some at least, whether they be good or evil, are sometimes linked with a certain portion of matter that is in motion. From this it follows that the motion of this matter (which some call the first and second element <note>These are terms from Cartesian physics: the "first element" is a very fine, agitated dust, and the "second" consists of the spherical particles that transmit light</note>, and perhaps the subtler parts of the third) is not indeed produced, but determined <note>original: "determinari." In this context, it means the direction of the motion is changed without creating new energy or motion, which would violate the laws of physics</note> in a different way than if it were left to brute rules alone. Namely, it is directed according to the thought of the united Mind, just as the motion of the animal spirits <term>animal spirits: In early modern science, these were thought to be extremely fine fluids that acted as the medium through which the soul moved the body</term> is determined by the will of the human soul.

From this, there arise directions, reflections, refractions, and collisions into thick and sensible bodies of that most highly agitated matter—which is withdrawn from the senses (like animal spirits, though those are much coarser). Thus, sudden and manifold changes in these bodies occur. Because these happen beyond the ordinary and brute governance of the bodies around us, they excite wonder in us and are called miracles. Such examples include the darkness of Egypt, or the darkness in Palestine at the time of Christ’s death, which were an obstruction of the direct motion of the sun's rays and their reflection away from Egypt and Palestine alone. Likewise, there is the miraculous reflection in the Red Sea, in the Jordan, in the Babylonian fire <note>referring to the Three oily Youths in the fiery furnace who were not burned</note>, etc. 

There was also the miraculous refraction in the Dial of Ahaz <note>A biblical reference to the sun's shadow moving backward as a sign to King Hezekiah</note>, to which that stopping of the Sun and Moon in the time of Joshua could perhaps be referred. In that case, the planets indeed proceeded as before, but the rays of the luminaries were miraculously refracted and reflected toward the land of Canaan through many clouds arranged in an extraordinary manner over a long space and time, so that the day was thereby prolonged. Similarly, the "determination" of said matter toward other bodies can so scrape, change, shape, and compress their particles, and arrange them in such diverse ways—either in our body and its organs by which we perceive objects, or in the mediums, or in the perceived objects themselves (for it matters little where these things happen)—that great changes occur. For example, in external objects, particles of air might be gathered so that from airy things they become watery, or from watery things they become winy <note>A reference to the miracle at Cana where water became wine</note>, and similar things; and thus they change their particular nature. Consequently, they strike the senses differently than before; or, if those things which were first changed do not strike the senses immediately, they act upon others, and these perhaps upon others still, which finally cause some things to strike the senses in an extraordinary way. Nor is there any miracle that cannot be performed—and thus explained—in this way, if God so wills. For what need is there to establish that God [breaks] all the [laws] of the universe?
