# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...to overturn the laws most wisely established and founded by He Himself, when a way fitting for God can be conceived while they remain intact? Nor does it even appear that miracles—in the very thing that strikes the senses—occur immediately, or without the intervention of matter (corresponding to that by which our bodies and other things are moved) or without a certain mind determining the motion of that matter. What of the fact that in the miracles which Holy Scripture <note>original: "Scriptura S."</note> recounts, almost always one or more Angels are narrated to have intervened? Or at least human Minds, which can be called Angelic because of their office—because they were sent by God for something special—and possess the same power as Angels? Or at least a power such that if they wish for something, the Angels must execute it, just as among human minds some are bound to operate externally according to the command or declaration of others.

XXIII. I will not dwell now on refuting those who would claim that almost nothing is attributed to God in this way, but only to Angels; for I have demonstrated above that all positive things in the means and effects, whether of minds or bodies, are produced by God alone. I will not reject the consequence that could be objected from what has been said: namely, that those things which happen through the intervention of depraved, diabolical, and impious Minds would be counted among miracles. Operations of this kind must certainly be called miracles, through whatever intervention of a Mind they exist, even if it be the Devil, or an Impostor, or a Magician. But to those claiming they would not be miracles because they occur so regularly and through means, I respond: miracles are not called such because God operates in a confused or disordered way that destroys nature and its laws so that only fools might be amazed. Rather, they are miracles because they are His well-ordered operations, which are determined around us by an intelligent principle in matters that would have happened differently through brute physical rules, or through the ordinary disposition of the human mind. And since these events are unusual and extraordinary to us in the way they occur, it must therefore be judged that they are performed by God for a grave and extraordinary cause. These things lead us to the end or use of miracles, which from these words is clear: attention to God the worker, and then also to the persons, and their actions or voices through whose intervention He works—yet only insofar as a return to God ought to be made from them. For to get stuck in the means themselves, or worse, in the operations, is wicked and the promotion of the mystery of iniquity <term>mystery of iniquity: A biblical phrase (2 Thessalonians 2:7) referring to the hidden power of lawlessness or evil working in the world</term>.

Since this Proposition is clear and not disputed, it needs no further proof.

2. Second Proposition. To examine or test whether those **who are no longer weak**, but—because of the truth in which they have often been instructed—**ought to be strong**, cling to God so solidly that they are torn from Him by no creature, word, or deed, whatever may happen, so that it may be clear that they cling to God alone with true love above all things; God wills that miracles be performed by Impostors, instilling false worship, so that they may attempt to turn man from God to creatures. 3. Third Proposition. So that those who **persistently resist the truth**, and are therefore unworthy of it, and **who seek lies and vanity**, may be punished...

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...either the worship of or clinging to the creature (since everything is entirely nothing of itself), and thus those who deserve to be enslaved to a lie; God wills that miracles be performed by which these stubborn people may be persuaded of their own lie and vanity. Therefore, held fast under the slavery of sin, they are severely punished by the just judgment of God for neglecting the truth. # ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL

...they will remain. I shall not elaborate on these matters any further. Let this suffice concerning miracles for now.

**XXV.** I now move to the third question regarding the **Contingency** and **necessity** of things that are said to exist. Concerning these, I say it can be asserted that *all things*, without exception, exist *contingently*, insofar as I consider them to have no necessity of existing within themselves; indeed, even insofar as God did not establish or place them out of necessity. But when I observe that all reality—which is and shall be—cannot be established except by God; that it is necessary for the determined will of God not to be frustrated; and that God, being the most perfect **Thought** <note>original: *Cogitatio*; in this context, it refers to the divine intellect or the attribute of thought.</note>, infallibly thinks and knows all that He has determined; I cannot help but be led to the conclusion that all things which exist do so *necessarily*, in this sense. For no greater necessity can be imagined in things than that which is the positioning and consequence of an effect from an efficient, effective, and determined cause. 

Yet if, among things themselves, some are said to exist and happen *contingently* while others occur *necessarily*, that "contingency" of certain things (as opposed to the "necessity" of others) denotes nothing other than our own ignorance. For instance, since we know by experience that God acts through certain things in a single way—for example, heating by means of fire—we can predict with certainty that this will happen once the fire is present, and we are not deceived; therefore, we say it happens *necessarily*. But since there are things through which God works in diverse ways—namely, through the **thought** of man—and He has not revealed to us which of several paths He will act upon, we are ignorant of it. Thus, because we cannot predict a specific effect with certainty, we say that whatever happens there occurs *contingently*. 

Even when we see all the causes of a thing present (perhaps because they fall under our senses), we say the thing happens necessarily—as when a body is moved by necessity when violently struck by a larger one. But we say a thing happens contingently when it is unknown whether the causes (or at least some of them which do not fall under the senses) are present or not. Hence, nothing is said to follow by necessity, but everything is said by us to follow "contingently," because it is unknown what will follow. There are those who also say that everything proceeding spontaneously from the **Mind** happens contingently; let us grant them their words, provided they acknowledge that the positioning of any reality whatsoever—even of spontaneity itself—is established infallibly by the most free and powerful will of God, which is subject to no defects.

**XXVI.** It remains that I should not pass over what I reviewed fourthly above. But since the matters have already been explained, what must be said pertains more to names. Namely, the first positioning or existence of any **substance** and primary **mode** <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "mode" is a specific quality or state of a substance, like a particular thought or a particular shape.</note> by the will of God is called **Creation**, at whatever time it may occur. Also, the change of modes in some extended or **Thinking** substance through ways...

### RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...extraordinary and miraculous ways, without which those modes would not have followed so quickly, or not at all, it is called **Creation**. Examples include the formation of the Sun, the shaping of the human body from clay <note>The author refers to the biblical account of the creation of Adam from the dust of the ground.</note>, the transformation of an ignorant mind that does not love God into one that knows and loves God, and other such things. However, the lasting existence of all these things is called **Conservation**, which does not really differ from Creation—neither in terms of the thing established (since it is simply the positioning of its existence beyond the first moment), nor on the part of God (since it is His single will that the thing be exactly as it pleases Him).

Therefore, when it is said that the moments of things' existence are independent of each other—and that as much power is required for the positioning of the second or third moment as for the first moment of creation—one must not think that the commanded act, the impulse from God mentioned above, or the divine will is repeated for each separate moment. One should not imagine that God wills a thing to exist at one moment, and then, as that moment passes and the thing tends toward nothingness in the next, God would again exert the efficacy of His will for the following moment, and so on continuously. This is what the term **concurrence** <note>original: *concursus*; a technical theological term describing God "running alongside" or cooperating with the actions of created beings.</note>—specifically **preceding concurrence** and **simultaneous concurrence**—seems to suggest. 

While this term is applied aptly enough to created things (since it describes how they "run," flow, and almost vanish, possessing nothing constantly), it is most inappropriately attributed to God. For God is not to be conceived as if He acts at individual moments, or as if His acts flowed from Him successively in a continuous duration, ending at each individual moment of a creature's existence. Strictly speaking, God does not "concur." That is to say, there is nothing in Him or from Him that, by enduring alongside the creature, causes it to exist and act; or rather, there is nothing from Him that coexists and cooperates with the duration of creatures. These ideas are absurd and contrary to the eternity of God, as will be seen in its proper place. 

One Powerful and simple **Will of God** <note>original: *Voluntas Dei*</note> that such things exist for such a length of time is so sufficient for all duration that no other thing is needed. This moment, and that moment, and every moment exists and is exactly as it is because of that one Powerful and Immutable Will, which decreed all moments at once. The signs of His single sufficiency or efficacy—namely, the actual existence of things—extend to all time; it is in this sense that He is said to "always be at work." 

Nevertheless, because these terms regarding **preceding** and **simultaneous concurrence** are in common use, they can be explained well in this way: No creature exists or "runs" by itself unless we first conceive of its cause—namely, the will of God—as being positioned and determined so that the creature runs or exists. Thus, God's will is conceived as that which presides or "runs before." (This they called **preceding concurrence**.) Then, since the creature exists at this specific moment, we conceive that God’s will is for it to be and run at this time rather than another; and thus it is considered

XXVII. If any reality, along with its duration and preservation, is established by the power of God alone in any state—no less in minds than in bodies—then all created freedom seems to be abolished. This would apply not only to what is called **freedom of indifference** <note>original: *libertas indifferentiae*; the capacity of the will to choose between two opposites when all conditions for acting are present.</note> but also to that which they call **freedom of spontaneity** <note>original: *libertas spontaneitatis*; an action that is free because it is done from one's own internal impulse without external force.</note>. Regarding the freedom of indifference considered in respect to evil (without which it seems nothing could be called evil), this will be discussed elsewhere. But if that freedom refers to the establishing of reality, or some physical good, or some other order, since it has been demonstrated that all reality is established by the Power of God alone, I do not see how it can be said that a human being is "indifferent" to establishing things that he himself does not establish. 

If anyone seems to themselves to be "indifferent" between two real options—this one or that one—let them only pay attention to what has been demonstrated. They will recognize that this does not arise because they act independently of God, or because God does not effect everything in the universe according to His will. Rather, it arises first from the fact that they do not know which of the two God will work in them in the following moment, and second because God does not act in and through them in a violent manner, but in a way that carries a certain consent along with it. Therefore, **spontaneous freedom** is not destroyed in this way, but rather is necessarily established, since a spontaneous effect cannot fail to occur where God powerfully wills it to be. Regarding all indifference, more will be said elsewhere.

Compensation from one creature to another is nothing; it is impossible. For all things that can be given belong to God; they cannot be taken away from Him, nor are they owed to any other. Therefore, all things are the Compensation or donation of God, and they are unearned, by whatever means they reach me. 

Nor does it follow that if God has worked some good in me, and through me in another place, He is bound to work another good in me subsequently through others. How far, then, have almost all people fallen from the truth, since no one allows their labor to be used for another unless they are spurred on by the motive of compensation, profit, or praise! Hardly anyone acts freely so that the Good Power of God might be made manifest in others through them.

You will say, then: is it not permitted to ask anything of a companion, to seek from him, to plead with him, to pray to him, to give him thanks, and things of that sort, since this would be done by acknowledging that it is or was in another’s power to act in a certain way, or otherwise? # CHAPTER XIV.
## (13) KNOWLEDGE or SCIENCE.
### §. A.

*1. 2. 3. Concerning the knowledge of the created Mind. Why it is not extended to all things. 4. The inadequacy and narrowness of knowledge. 5. Ignorance. Obscurity. Error. Reasoning. Uncertainty. Opinion. Evidence. Certainty. Science. 6. Nothing is to be determined regarding what will happen to our knowledge in this life.*

I. Whatever it was that I had to say concerning the Knowledge possessed by both Minds—the Divine and the created—I have deferred to this place; even though it could have been proposed before the preceding sections, I delayed it for no other reason than that its evidence and certainty might follow from what has already been said. For, to begin with my own Knowledge, after I saw the limits and imperfections of my knowledge in a few words from the thirteenth observation in my thoughts, I shall now perceive this very thing more clearly from the preceding and third-to-last chapters.

I know a particle so small that, if it were compared with the rest, it would not even be like a tiny point in respect to the immense space of the heavens that we imagine; and I do not know why I know this particle rather than another. Whether my knowledge of it is adequate <note>adequate: In 17th-century philosophy, "adequate" knowledge meant a complete and perfect understanding of a thing's essence, leaving nothing hidden.</note>, or whether it even can or cannot be so, is not something I should determine at first glance. Even the knowledge I sometimes wish to think I have concerning those things which are in that particle, or can be in it, is so uncertain and doubtful that it sometimes corresponds poorly to reality, and thus I am deceived. Finally, although I know my knowledge is to be increased in the future, I cannot determine how far it will proceed. But after I have perceived the preceding points, I am able to determine something certain about all these things—namely, about the perfection and imperfection of my knowledge. And first, indeed, since every perfection and reality of all things, and thus of my Knowledge, comes from the most free pleasure of God <note>original: "placito Dei liberrimo." This refers to the theological concept that the laws of nature and the limits of the human mind are chosen by God’s will rather than by logical necessity.</note>, it is clear that the measure of my Knowledge concerning things which are outside of God and myself is not to be drawn from a respect for the things themselves, but from the pleasure of God. (I do not indeed exclude the Knowledge I have of God and of my own Mind from this, but I neither include it nor look at it here, since it has been dealt with elsewhere.) Yet the very nature of my Knowledge could not determine God so that it would please Him for me to know all things, for the very nature and idea of created Knowledge depends on God’s pleasure; it could therefore please God that created Knowledge should not know all things, but only certain ones. However, God’s pleasure is not evident except from His effects; since I count my knowledge among these effects, and since I see it extended to only a few particles of things, to a few minds, and to a few bodies—while of the rest it knows nothing, except from the fact that, knowing the Power of God, it judges His innumerable effects to have some similarity with the ideas it experiences in itself—I conclude that it is established for me by a prior reason <note>original: "ratione à priori." A method of reasoning from causes to effects, or from self-evident principles rather than observation.</note> why my knowledge of things is not universal, but particular, and restricted to certain things, among which I must devote myself to those that are more intimate and intertwined with me. But concerning this choice, I shall speak elsewhere.

Therefore, all fantasies concerning the Power of Creatures in themselves vanish, so that God alone remains the Most Powerful and Best Governor and Author of All, in whom alone we must rest most calmly as the effects and instruments of His will. From others <note>meaning: other created beings or things</note>, however, who are powerless to establish anything of themselves, nothing is to be either hoped for or feared. Regarding the Dominion, Power, and attributes of God which are viewed in relation to created things, if more is said about these than about others, let us remember the sacred riddle <note>original: "ænigmatis sacri." This refers to Exodus 33:23, where God tells Moses he may see His back but not His face—implying we understand God through His effects in the world rather than His direct essence.</note> that God offers Himself to be seen from the back.

### CHAPTER XIV.
## (13) KNOWLEDGE or SCIENCE.
### §. A.

<margin>1. 2. 3.</margin> *On the knowledge of the created Mind. Why it does not extend to all things.* 4. *The inadequacy and narrowness of knowledge.* 5. *Ignorance. Obscurity. Error. Reasoning. Uncertainty. Opinion. Evidence. Certainty. Science.* 6. *Nothing is to be determined about what will happen to our knowledge in this life.*

I. **W**hatever it is that I had to say concerning the Knowledge possessed by both Minds—the Divine and the created—I have deferred to this place. Although it could have been proposed before the preceding chapters, I have delayed it for no other reason than that its evidence and certainty arise from what has already been said. For, to begin with my own Knowledge: after I saw the limits and imperfections of my knowledge in the thirteenth observation of my thoughts, I shall now perceive this more clearly from the preceding and third-to-last chapters.

I know a particle so small that, if it were compared with others, it would not even be like a tiny point <note>original: "instar punctuli"</note> in respect to the immense space of the heavens that we imagine, and I do not know why I know this particle rather than another. Whether my knowledge of it is adequate, or whether it can even exist or not, is not something I can determine at first glance. Indeed, I would sometimes like to think that I have knowledge of those things which are in that particle, or could be in it; yet that knowledge is so uncertain and doubtful that it sometimes corresponds poorly to actual things, and thus I am deceived. Finally, although I know that my knowledge is to be increased in the future, I cannot determine how far it will proceed. But after perceiving the preceding points, I can determine something certain about all these things—that is, about the perfection and imperfection of my knowledge. And first, indeed, since every perfection and reality of all things, and therefore also of my Knowledge, comes from the most free pleasure of God <note>original: "à placito Dei liberrimo." The author emphasizes that human capacity is a gift of divine will, not a biological or logical necessity.</note>, it is clear that the measure of my Knowledge concerning things which are outside of God and myself is not to be taken from a relationship to the things themselves, but from the pleasure of God. (I do not indeed exclude from this the Knowledge which I have of God and of my own Mind, but neither do I include it here, nor do I look at it in this place since it has been dealt with elsewhere.) Now, the very nature of my Knowledge could not determine God so that it might please Him for me to know all things, for the nature and idea of created Knowledge itself depends on God's pleasure; it could, therefore, have pleased God that created Knowledge should not know all things, but only certain ones. However, God's pleasure is not evident except from His effects; since I count my own knowledge among these effects, and since I see it extended to only a few particles of things, to a few minds, and to a few bodies—while of the rest it knows nothing, except from the fact that in knowing the Power of God, it judges that His innumerable effects have some resemblance to the ideas which it experiences in itself—I conclude that it is established for me by *a priori* reasoning <note>Reasoning based on theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note> why my knowledge of things is not universal, but particular, and restricted to certain things. Among these, I must occupy myself with those which are more intimate and involved with me. But regarding this choice, I shall speak elsewhere.

III. Certainly, at first glance, it does not seem to have been necessary to ascend so high <note>meaning: to refer to God’s supreme will</note>, since the mere inspection of created Knowledge is commonly thought to suffice to give the reason why it does not extend itself to all things: for it would be dissipated by a multitude of things, and thus would return into forgetfulness and ignorance, or into non-knowledge. Furthermore, they say, if created Knowledge embraced all things, it would be omniscient, which belongs to God alone. And they will say that this last inconvenience is not avoided by the reasoning I alleged, from which it could certainly be concluded that created knowledge could have been extended to all things from the indifferent pleasure of God, and thus could have been omniscient, Divine, and—

...to become God himself. But all these things are foolish, and arise from a false idea of the Knowledge of God <note>original: "Scientiæ Dei"</note>, and from a habit of thinking poorly about Divine matters. <term>Omniscience: the state of knowing all things</term> Omniscience, which belongs to God’s nature and is God himself, is solely the Understanding of God. This was discussed above in a whole chapter; God could have known nothing besides this if it had pleased him to decree nothing different from himself, as has often been demonstrated. The Knowledge which God has concerning things different from himself is proper to him only insofar as it comes from his pleasure alone, and is not dependent on any other thing. This knowledge, however, would not become common to a creature, even if it were said that God had given a creature knowledge of all things which he himself decreed and wished to set apart. For this knowledge would be established as merely depending on another, and therefore would not be the same as Divine knowledge. 

I do not indeed say that knowledge of all things which God can bring about is possible in a created mind, for thus one would eventually arrive at the question of the <term>Power of God: Latin "Potentia Dei," referring to God's ability to act or create</term> Power of God, and it would have to be said that this power could be comprehended by a finite Mind. But when it comes to things not that he *can* decree, but which he *has already* decreed, who could say that he cannot create a Mind to which, if he so pleased, he might make known all the things he has decreed? Certainly, one would rashly circumscribe the Power of God, or determine this negatively about it. As for the saying that the Mind is scattered or distracted by a multitude of things, that is true in this state of affairs which God has pleased to establish for us. But why could he not have done otherwise? Specifically, why could he not create a mind in which all ideas of things were gathered without such scattering? 

Therefore, the firm reason for my Knowledge being restricted to certain things remains—not because of the nature of the thing (which is nothing of itself), but because of the pleasure of God <note>original: "placitum Dei," a key concept meaning God's free and sovereign will</note>, which is the reason for all things and which quiets the mind. Since God may wish something different for Minds that are in a state different from mine—and I neither know nor experience what those states are—it does not permit me to determine anything about their knowledge. Regarding those minds whose state is similar to mine, the same conclusion can be drawn as for myself.

...or in another state, present or past, I perceive and acknowledge that it could easily happen that it pleases God to grant me a knowledge fully equal to those things. Thus, I could recognize certain things perfectly <note>original: "adæquate," referring to "adequate knowledge," a technical term for knowledge that contains everything within the object being studied</note> if God willed what I conceive He has the power to will. However, since it is not clear to me from my own strength whether it was God's pleasure that there should be as many representing forms in my thought as there are perfections and degrees of them in the object itself—for I do not match the Divine counsel in perfection—and since it has not been revealed to me by God whether He chose for there to be more in a thing than what I think I know best, I acknowledge the reason why I cannot be certain my knowledge of any thing is exhaustive. This was well observed by <term>the Philosopher: Referring to René Descartes</term> in his *Fourth Replies* <note>The "Fourth Replies" refers to Descartes' responses to the fourth set of objections to his *Meditations on First Philosophy*</note>. Nevertheless, I judge by the result that it is God's pleasure that none of those things from the tiny portion of the universe set before my knowledge be perfectly known by me, since I experience that my thought falls short in every instance.

I am ignorant of the past thoughts of some minds I have known, along with their present and future ones, their habits, and so on. Indeed, I do not even know my own thoughts which I have had in the past, or those I am about to have soon. 

Concerning <term>extended things: physical matter that occupies space</term>, I cease to wonder at many "miracles," since it is as much by God's pleasure that some things are hidden from me as it is that some are open to me; and so it is no less wonderful that I know some things than that I am ignorant of others. <term>Physicists: scientists or "natural philosophers" who study the physical world</term> Physicists exhaust themselves in trying to determine the extent of the universe. They do not dare to claim it is "positively infinite," fearing this would mean God could add nothing more to it; yet they cannot call it "finite" either, because if one were supposed to be at the very edge, a further space—that is, a further extension—would be conceived. 

In the same way, they cannot bring themselves to say of any particle of matter that it is divisible into "positively infinite" parts, lest a tiny grain have as many parts as the whole world. Yet they cannot say there is a "smallest" part that contains no others, because any shape we can imagine has a top, a bottom, and sides, and is touched by different things in different places. Here, then, they are caught between two opposites regarding the same thing—the finite and the non-finite. One of these must be true and the other false, yet they cannot embrace either without falling into absurdity. For what some suggest regarding "indefinite" parts or an "indefinite" number is simply a confession of their own ignorance; it is the same as saying they do not know how to define these things, which <term>Descartes: Latin "Cartesius," the French philosopher René Descartes</term> himself acknowledges. 

Similar difficulties return when asking about time: is it divisible into infinity or into "moments"? The same applies to motion and its highest degree of speed—does such a thing exist or not? This again cannot be answered without absurdity, nor can the question of its [extreme] slowness...

...from the final degree, it can be defined. It is not my goal to review these here at greater length. For centuries, Mathematicians have been searching for a straight line geometrically equal to a circular one, and they still dispute whether such a thing can even exist. The difficulties that arise—from a straight line touching a circumference <note>original: "peripheriam tangente," a tangent line</note>, from the comparison of a straight-lined figure with a circular one, from the proportion of the side of a square to its diagonal <note>Referring to the discovery of irrational numbers, where the ratio cannot be expressed as a simple fraction</note>, and many other instances—are so great that they stun the mathematicians themselves and any attentive observer. These difficulties make them admirers of their own invincible ignorance in matters so thin and simple. 

I, however, after observing that I ought not to claim any knowledge of things or its measure from my own strength alone, consider it a gift whenever any notice of things occurs to me by the pleasure of God. But when I have truly and clearly experienced the limit of my knowledge in any instance, I conclude that I ought not to stretch further, and I abstain from it as if from something forbidden. This constitutes part of that ignorance which is without shame and is called **learned** <note>original: "docta dicitur," referring to *docta ignorantia* or "learned ignorance," a concept popularized by Nicholas of Cusa suggesting that the highest wisdom is knowing the limits of one's own mind</note>. It is called this because the unskilled pretenders to knowledge <note>original: "scioli," meaning those with a superficial or "smattering" of knowledge</note>, who wish to display a universal and complete science of all things while truly knowing nothing, have not experienced how far knowledge extends in things or what limits it. Consequently, they do not profess any ignorance—not even this learned kind—but instead pretend to ignore nothing or rashly aspire to everything. 

Certainly, from the inspection of things which God has willed to set before my knowledge from whatever tiny portion of the universe, it seems to me it can be concluded that the principles, the extremes, and the greatest increases—whether the minimum or the maximum—of things (however well known), of substances, of modes, and of the duration of all these, are plainly hidden from me and those like me. Thus, nothing remains as an object of our science except a small portion of a **middle state** of a very few things, or a certain small stage of a massive course that runs from unknown starting blocks to an unknown finish line. 

This can also be experienced in sensory perception: the smallest things escape our senses, the greatest things destroy them, while middle things nourish them. Therefore, the **Human Mind** is like a tablet; just as a tablet does not reflect every solid body, nor every part of one, so the Mind represents neither all the originals (the **Divine ideas** of things) nor any first copies <note>original: "apographa," a Greek-derived term for a transcript or direct copy</note> of them (namely, the things themselves which most exactly reflect the originals) in every part. However, the mind excels brute creatures in this: that the representations it has of those divine ideas are vivid and bring with them a consciousness of oneself.

...is not known by the mind, just as when the method of formation—at least in its more general sense—of a plant or an animal is unknown. I call it "obscurity in the mind" when the mind wishes to reach toward those things which God has placed beyond the capacity of its own cognition, such as the difficulties already noted. For then, being destitute of those ideas which are the light of cognition, the mind can be said to be in darkness. However, I have referred this to those things which are not the objects of our cognition. For even if someone is said to grasp certain things more obscurely which another knows more clearly—and thus something that falls within the limits of human cognition—I would still prefer to consider that as ignorance, insofar as it does not reach all degrees of evidence; perhaps it could even be an error.

*But Error* (I am not speaking here of sin <note>The author distinguishes between intellectual mistakes and moral failings</note>) consists entirely in this: that I should think or judge that it pleased God to decree or perform certain things which He did not, in fact, establish; or conversely, that He did not decree or perform those things which He actually did decree and perform. Accordingly, every error concerning created things revolves around a "matter of fact," since all created things and truths, in respect to God, are not matters of <term>right|Latin "juris"; implying something that must be so by necessity</term>, but of <term>fact|Latin "facti"; implying something contingent on God's free choice</term>, which God, being previously indifferent, most freely brought about, as has been often said. 

For example, if I think the mind is corporeal <note>made of physical matter</note>, or that the body thinks, it is the substitution of one "fact" for another—as if God, in bringing about thought, were by that very act bringing about <term>extension|The quality of taking up space, which seventeenth-century philosophers like Descartes defined as the essential property of matter</term>, or vice versa. In the same way, if I were to believe that God, while preserving the extension and <term>modes|The specific qualities or appearances of a thing, like shape or color</term> of some substance—say, bread—was nevertheless not preserving that thing but another, I would err by assuming something else in God's work. This can be applied to all other things. 

Error arises from this: when it has pleased God to imprint certain ideas of things upon my thought—which, although He established them as true, He did not place all of them as existing outside of me—and since these ideas vary among themselves in infinite ways, and the things that exist according to them are also most diverse among themselves, I, while attending to one of these things, might judge that some reality represented to me by another idea is involved in that thing, or was placed there by God, when it is not actually there. It might be elsewhere, or nowhere at all, except perhaps as a possibility. Thus, I err because I think God willed to establish or perform things in one place which He willed to place either elsewhere or nowhere. 

Therefore, I will avoid error if I contemplate the ideas of things in my thought in such a way that I do not judge that anything similar exists or does not exist outside of me, or that this or that thing which I know to exist possesses or lacks these or those realities which are represented in any way by my ideas. Truly, however, this method of avoiding error does not advance knowledge, and it is inseparable from ignorance. Or, I shall have avoided error if—and this is especially important—I seek and find certain signs from which it is established that it was the pleasure of God that they should exist,

If, however, I find such indicators that have some similarity with those from which truths about God and the created Mind are demonstrated—as when, from the indicators of my own existing thought, I conclude that there exists a most effective decree, or someone effectively willing that I exist, or a most powerful being, etc.—or indeed indicators that have some connection with these, then *evidence* is present, and consequently there is *certainty* in the judgment of the knowledge of the thing, from which comes *knowledge* <note>original: "scientia"; in this period, "science" referred to systematic, certain knowledge derived from principles</note>. To deduce all these things more specifically would be a task of enormous labor. VI. Finally, regarding what I noted in the fourth place—namely, that I can determine nothing about the increase of my knowledge, or even its decrease, or any other change—this flows from the same sources as the points above. What I have just said holds true for the most part in the present time. But as for the future, since God’s will toward that which He has produced is not known, it follows that I cannot know when and to what extent my knowledge is to be increased, or whether it will extend to these same specific things or to others. [I cannot know] whether it will be adequate in the future, or on the contrary, whether it will be diminished or disturbed (as sometimes happens when, due to a brain injury, all the knowledge and learning of even the greatest Teacher vanishes into *sluggishness* and folly <note>original: "Socordia"; implying a total loss of mental faculty or professional competence</note>). All these things are to be calmly committed to the hidden will of God; if this should be revealed to anyone, let him count it as a gain.

...I preferred above to refer to the intellect. However, when I contemplate Divine Knowledge from the occasion of my own Knowledge, I recognize it to be **Free** and independent, universal, adequate, and finally certain and immutable.

VIII. For first, since God has so established and positioned every truth, idea, essence, and even existence which is not Himself, such that He was **indifferent** <note>In this philosophical context, "indifference" refers to the "liberty of indifference"—the idea that God's will was not compelled by any external necessity to create the world exactly as it is; He could have chosen otherwise.</note> toward not positioning them (which was established above beyond doubt), it follows that the Knowledge He has of them must be called **Free**, rather than natural. This is because God does not know these things simply because He knows His own Nature, but because He knows His own **free pleasure** <note>original: "liberums placitum"; refers to God's sovereign choice or decree.</note> concerning them. Furthermore, since all things in the universe outside of God's will are pure **Nothing**, and do not contribute anything that is real, it follows that God’s Knowledge is independent of any things whatsoever—independent of any foreign pleasure, of events, or of any indicators—nor is it produced through reasoning. God does not know things because they exist; on the contrary, they exist (I speak of real things) because it pleased God to know them. Therefore, **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose "Consolation of Philosophy" famously argued that God's foreknowledge of the future is like a spectator watching a chariot race: seeing it doesn't make it happen. The author here rejects this as making God too passive.</note> was not correct when, in order to explain the compatibility of human **Freedom** (whether he meant "indifference" or that which is called "spontaneous," he did not say) with divine knowledge, he used the example of vision. He argued that while vision perceives things, it does not (as anyone can experience) impose a necessary position upon the things seen. This is an **absurd comparison**. A human who sees present things does not "position" <note>i.e., create or establish the existence of</note> them, but receives them and senses them from something external; his vision of them depends on them. Does God, then, sense, receive, or know from something external? Not at all. As far as the knowledge of **evil** is concerned, since evil is not something **positive** <note>In Scholastic and Early Modern philosophy, evil was often defined as a "privation" or a lack of good, rather than a "positive" substance created by God.</note>, I conceive that God knows it insofar as He knows His own operation will not proceed further in something; or rather, that He wills not to work those things in a certain instance which, although He absolutely could, He nevertheless does not will to work there for a most wise and, for the most part, most hidden reason. But if even this explanation is not sufficient, it is not our place to inquire further: in these matters, the incomprehensible and most tremendously to be feared **Majesty of the Supreme Divinity** must be adored.

IX. Furthermore, since nothing is possible, true, or existing except that which it pleases God to conceive, establish, and position as such, it is rightly inferred that the knowledge of God is absolutely **universal**, and at the same time **singular** (that is, extending to individual things), and also **adequate**. This means that God knows all things and every single thing most perfectly in every state and circumstance, whether they have already vanished with time, or currently exist, or are not yet brought forth by time. ...and here or there, realities corresponding to this, that, or those of my ideas (which is *to reason* <note>original: *ratiocinari*</note>). But if I perceive either no indicators or equivocal ones—that is, the kind from which judgments can be made that are different from each other or from what I precisely intend, or similar to these but concerning other things—then *uncertainty* <note>original: *incertitudo*</note> arises. From this uncertainty, opinions proceed, and one has not yet reached the very "soul of the matter," so to speak. If, however, I find such indicators that have some similarity with those by which truths about God and the created Mind are demonstrated—as when I conclude from the indicators of my own existing thought that there exists some most effective pleasure, or some being effectively willing that I exist, or a most powerful being, etc.—or indeed indicators which have some connection with these, then *evidence* <note>original: *evidentia*</note> is present. Consequently, there is *certainty* <note>original: *certitudo*</note> of judgment concerning the knowledge of the thing, which is the source of *science* <note>original: *scientia*; in this period, "science" referred to any systematic, certain body of knowledge.</note>. To derive all these things more specifically would be a work of immense labor. Let it suffice if the reason is made clear in a general way as to why and how a few particular pieces of knowledge about small portions of things can be affected by all these variations.

VI. Finally, regarding what I noted in the fourth point—namely, that I can determine nothing concerning the increase of my knowledge, or even its decrease, or any other change—this flows from the same sources as the points above. What I have just said holds true for the most part in the present time; but concerning the future, since God's pleasure <note>original: *placitum*; refers to God's sovereign will or decree.</note> toward that which is His effect is not certain to us, it follows that I cannot know when or to what extent my knowledge is to be increased, or whether it will extend to these same particular things or to others. Will it be adequate in the future, or on the contrary, will it be diminished or disturbed? (As sometimes happens when the brain is shaken <note>likely a reference to physical trauma or illness affecting the mind.</note>, the entire science and learning of even some great Doctor vanishes into *dullness* and folly.) All these matters are to be committed tranquilly to the hidden pleasure of God; if this should be revealed to anyone, let him count it as a gain.

...I preferred to refer above to the intellect. However, when I contemplate Divine Knowledge from the occasion of my own Knowledge, I recognize it to be **Free** and independent, universal, adequate, and finally certain and immutable.

VIII. For first, since God has so established and placed every truth, idea, essence, and even existence that is not Himself that He was indifferent to not placing them (which was established beyond doubt above), it follows that the Knowledge He has of them must be called **Free**, and not indeed natural. For God does not know these things because He knows His own Nature, but because He knows His own free pleasure concerning them. Furthermore, since all things in the universe are pure Nothing outside of God’s will, and do not contribute anything that is real, it follows that the Knowledge of God is independent from any things whatsoever, from the pleasure of another, from events, or from any indicators; nor does it occur through reasoning. God does not know things because they exist; on the contrary, they exist (I speak of real things) because it pleased God that He should know them. 

Therefore, Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher famous for *The Consolation of Philosophy*, which attempted to reconcile God's foreknowledge with human free will.</note> was not correct when, to explain the compatibility of human Liberty (whether of indifference, or that which is called spontaneous, he did not say) with divine knowledge, he used the example of vision. He argued that while vision perceives things, it does not, as anyone can experience, impose a necessary existence on the things seen. This is an **absurd comparison**. The man who sees present things does not establish them, but receives and senses them from something external; his vision of them depends on them. Does God, then, sense, receive, or know from something external? By no means. 

As far as the knowledge of evil is concerned, since evil is not something positive <note>In philosophy, "positive" means having its own actual substance or being; the author here follows the tradition that evil is a "privation" or a lack of good, rather than a thing God created.</note>, I conceive that God knows it insofar as He knows that His operation in something will go no further, or that He does not will to work those things in a certain case—things which, although He could do absolutely, He nevertheless does not will to work there for a most wise and, for the most part, most hidden reason. If even this explanation is not sufficient, it is not our place to inquire further: for in these matters, the incomprehensible and most terrifying Majesty of the Supreme Divinity <note>original: *Numinis Summi*</note> is to be adored.

IX. Furthermore, since nothing is possible, true, or existing except what God pleases to conceive, establish, and place as such, it is rightly inferred that the knowledge of God is absolutely universal, and at the same time singular (that is, extending itself to individual things), and also **adequate**. This means that God knows all things and each individual thing most perfectly in every state and circumstance, whether they have already vanished with time, or currently exist, or indeed have not yet emerged into time. It may be asked: whether our thought, in order to imitate God’s Knowledge, should be applied (at least as much as can be done) to all objects that God knows, especially since those things are around us, and the means for knowing them do not seem to be offered in vain? Specifically, since the objects presented to us are either **necessary**—and those are the greatest, such as the **Most Perfect Thought**, or **God**—or they are **accidental**, and those are minute; since the condition of our **Mind** is such that when applied to some things, however small they may be, it ceases from others, which eventually becomes a habit; since, finally, its state is such that it dwells among corporeal things for a little while, soon to bid them farewell; there is no doubt that its application to knowing temporal things, compared with the occupation in which it ought to be engaged regarding the eternal object, should maintain that proportion which exists between the perishing and momentary and the perpetual and eternal; between the creature and God; or rather, between the use of tiny things out of the necessity of a mortal life tending toward something else and bounded by a short limit, and the **immutable rest** in the greatest God from whose pleasure all things exist. ### CHAPTER XV.

## (14) WISDOM.

->§. A.<-

*1. The Wisdom of the Soul: its source and imperfection. 2. A worthier, firmer, and more certain Wisdom.*

I. Having noticed those few things that come under my **Cognition**, I am conscious that they can be arranged in various ways in my mind at will; yet it is not so easily granted to achieve their correct arrangement. There is no doubt that things are linked together by a certain connection and order; it is a difficult task to imitate this in thought, establishing the notions of things in the mind in such an order that they agree with the connection of the things themselves. It is also possible—though only with the greatest mental effort—that just as some things serve as means for establishing others, I might propose in thought and in idea certain things as effects, and others as the means to achieve those effects, in such a way that if the means are actually put in place, the intended effect truly follows. This way of thinking about things is called **Wisdom** (I do not dwell on the definitions of the schools <note>original: "ſcholarum definitiones". A reference to the complex, often rigid definitions used in Scholastic philosophy taught in medieval and early modern universities.</note>), the entire certainty of which comes from the fact that God has imprinted in our thought certain ideas of things and their **modes** <term>modes: the specific states, qualities, or ways of being that a thing can have, such as its shape or motion.</term>, and thus also of their order; and from the observation of the outcome of things—by what means, circumstances, or rules God has placed this or that, and what has followed from them—it can be gathered for the future that such a thing will happen if such means are applied. This must ultimately be traced back to the **constancy** with which God operates in the same way. But since the knowledge we possess of things, means, and effects—and much more of the divine pleasure regarding the future—is not adequate but incomplete, liable to error, and uncertain, especially concerning **contingent** <term>contingent: things that happen by choice or chance and are not strictly necessary by logic or nature.</term> matters; since even the efficacy...

Although this last definition of wisdom is the most important of all, I do not wish to use it here; rather, I will use the former definition so that I may use it as an occasion to contemplate the **Wisdom of God**.

...it is permitted, while we apply ourselves to the multitude, variation, and connection of objects for the sake of contemplation, to conceive as if there were as many acts in the **Divine pleasure** <term>placito: refers to God's sovereign will or "good pleasure," the ultimate reason for His decrees</term> as there are things established. However, when one returns to the consideration of God, these must be reduced to a **single act**. By this act, all the truths of things—their natures, ideas, existences, modes, and governance—are so well disposed, connected, and linked together (or to put it in a word: "constituted") that nothing better or more fitting could be imagined by any created Mind. Thus, nothing disordered or incongruous is to be found there. 

The reason for this is evident: because the ideas of goodness, decency, fittingness, and order are not something absolute and independent from the perspective of the thing itself. Rather, they are the **Divine pleasure** itself, determined in the same way that those things are determined. Therefore, by the very fact that something is given by God, it is inherently good, beautiful, and fitting. Furthermore, the purposes God intends cannot be made void or delayed by anyone, since **Omnipotence** removes all obstacles and nothing unexpected can happen to **Omniscience**. 

Even the evils that He allows creatures to commit not only do not hinder the works of this Wisdom, but in their own time, they make it even more manifest and illustrious. From this, His Power is revealed, which is seen to extend beyond being and non-being (or beyond that which is simply negative), and beyond all the thoughts of men. He hides His wonderful ways of working from the "prudent" so that they remain unknown to them. From this also, His **Happiness** and **Goodness** are revealed; for evil is "evil" and "unhappy" precisely because it is a removal from God. It is easy for any attentive person to notice how the other attributes of God are further illustrated by the occasion of evil, so that even "darkness is light to Him" <note>original: "tenebræ sint ipsi Lux"; a reference to Psalm 139:12, suggesting that from God's perspective, even the "darkness" of evil serves a luminous purpose</note>.

V. One may ask: *Are all things so well established by God's wisdom that nothing better could have been made by Him?* I answer by remaining silent regarding the **Power of God** and the **Universality of things**, which I do not fully grasp. But regarding certain things that I do know, I can easily conceive that they could have been made better individually—that is, more perfect, possessing more degrees of reality—even though I conceive that God acted most wisely in each and every thing, such that it is not possible to think He could have acted more wisely. 

Indeed, the Wisdom of God in acting does not depend on the degrees of perfection that exist in each individual thing (which He can bestow more or less upon creatures); rather, it lies in the **most hidden reason of His pleasure** <note>original: "occultissima ratione placiti sui"</note> as to why He acts and wills in such a way. Therefore, God always does the **optimum**—that is, a good of such a kind that, while He could have granted it more "reality" <note>In this context, "reality" refers to the metaphysical "fullness" or perfection of a thing's nature</note>, it could not have been done with a better or wiser counsel, nor with a more fitting purpose. This is why He does not will that all possible goods should exist.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...why grant such and so many degrees of perfection to such a creature, but not to another? Why wish to represent Himself more in this one, and less in that one; to work more in this, and less in that? Why permit these evils, here, at this time, to this extent? And infinite other things besides, all of which are most wisely established and deliberated. No one is granted the ability to judge these matters more specifically except for the one to whom the purpose of the creation of all things and the entire Universe are perfectly revealed. 

For us, who are ignorant of both, it can happen that we judge something to deviate from the goal—a goal which we have merely imagined—which nonetheless agrees perfectly with the true goal hidden from us. Just as it is known to a man who understands all the conveniences of a house that a place which, when viewed in isolation, is considered most unsightly <note>original: *inhonestissimus*, meaning "dishonorable" or "unbecoming." In architectural metaphors of this period, this often refers to necessary but "unclean" areas like sewers or latrines which are essential for the health of the whole house.</note>, actually brings a greater convenience when the whole building is considered; it is more necessary and required than perhaps some more splendid walkway. In the same way, we are ignorant of the entire structure of the universe and are only conscious of some tiny portion of it. Thus, something can be regarded by us as very imperfect, useless, and to be rejected, which nonetheless—when the whole (which is unknown to us) is taken into account—will be more fitting and required than the things we judge to be more perfect. Therefore, one must not judge these things lightly.

### VI.
However, because the **Wisdom of God** is an impassable abyss, he who contemplates it must be careful not to fall into the crime of rashness. Two extremes must be clearly avoided: first, that it not be judged according to the external appearance of certain things; and second, that it not be explored too much, nor its judgments or impassable ways of acting be searched out. It should suffice for anyone to know that the **Most Perfect Thought** <term>Perfectissima Cogitatione: a philosophical term for God, emphasizing His nature as the ultimate, infinite Intellect</term> does nothing and permits nothing that is not most excellently and perfectly done or permitted.

### VII.
The first of these extremes is not without fault. Every single thing is a tiny particle of the whole universe and has a relationship to its whole. This can also be said of time, for its individual moments are connected with all preceding and following ones. Who, then, does not see that a person who passes judgment on the **Wisdom of God** from an inspection of things happening to a specific person, family, or region, at a specific time (all of which are merely a particle of the universe of things and time), is doing the same as one who tries to pronounce judgment on the **Skill** <term>Solertia: the expert craftsmanship, ingenuity, or cleverness of a creator</term> of a most expert **Architect** from a single stone of a building? Such a person does not look at the frame of the entire structure's construction, nor does he wait for its completion—though even a completed building would not exhaust the architect's skill. Or, it is like one who would pluck a small fragment from a most beautiful statue or painting to judge from it not only the whole work, but also the skill of the artist to pass—

VIII. But with no less recklessness, some might attempt to explore **Divine Wisdom** so deeply as to uncover its "bottom," so to speak. Those who inquire into the ends <note>original: *fines*, here meaning "purposes" or "goals."</note> and reasons why God created this or that thing seem to exhaust themselves in this occupation, so that they might support their demonstrations <note>In this context, *demonstrationes* refers to logical proofs or scientific explanations intended to show why nature must behave a certain way.</note> about the nature and modes of things from this imaginary knowledge. It is not easy to believe how many absurd and dangerous consequences arise from such rashness. From where else do so many complaints against **Divine Providence** spring forth? From where else comes the unfortunate work of those who, setting aside the known laws for conducting one’s life, peer into the secret decrees of God, especially concerning the future? 

For from the lust for knowing the hidden ends of the Divine Will, it is an easy transition to the desire for understanding the very counsels of God—those which have not yet been unlocked through their effects, nor revealed through Divine oracles. And if the enjoyment of the former is held to be possibly acquired—indeed, even held as a principle of proof—then one can be persuaded of the latter with no effort at all. Thus, many will be ready to resolve their practical demonstrations (or their reasons for how life should be lived) into that pretended knowledge of divine decrees. 

Nor does the frenzied reasoning of so many people flow from any other source—the kind they often use as a pretext for a wicked life. They say: "If God willed and decreed this concerning the state of my mind or body" (although evil does not come from God’s decree, as will be said in its proper place), "whatever I do in the future will change nothing; indeed, it will be according to the Divine decree." Yet God willed that His secret counsels be the limits of our thought, and that no Mind should presuppose a knowledge of them, much less govern itself by them as if they were known and understood. Certainly, if God had willed that our life be directed according to a knowledge of His decrees regarding what will happen to us, He would surely have manifested them to us. Since this did not please Him, it is a rebellion to wish to look upon them specifically as the principles of knowledge by which life must be ruled. The same can be said concerning demonstrations about the theory of things, which some wish to summon from the "end" <note>This refers to "final causes," the Aristotelian idea that we understand a thing by knowing its purpose. The author is arguing against using God's "goals" to explain physics.</note> that God proposed for Himself in things, as if they had thoroughly explored the Wisdom of God, in which those ends are hidden.

### RATIONAL REFLECTIONS

...commonly sought in **Physics** <note>original: *Physicis*; referring here to natural science or the study of the physical world.</note>, he rejected it as useless for demonstrating anything, believing that he could not without rashness investigate the ends of God <note>original: *fines Dei*; here meaning God's ultimate purposes or goals.</note> which are hidden in the treasury of His incomprehensible **Wisdom**. Nevertheless, I will not fear to say that this is most true not only regarding **Physics**, but also in respect to all things in the universe. It is an absurdity and arrogance to ask what end God proposed for Himself in the nature, state, and governance of things; for what purpose, by what reasons, and by what motive He arranged things so? 

And lest anyone more fervent should suddenly cause a disturbance here without reason, it must be observed that the **use** of things should not be confused with the **purpose or motive** for why the Wise God produced them. This could easily happen if these two very different things were designated by a single word, as occurs when the word *end* <note>original: *finis*</note> *sometimes signifies the use of a thing, and sometimes the motive for its production.* 

Therefore, to proceed clearly, if in the question—"Why?" or "For what end was such a thing made?"—one looks to the **use** of the thing (as if asking what the true use of this thing is which God assigned to it, and which He even decreed to assign when He produced it), then not only is this question just and fair, but it is also among the most necessary. For nothing is more useful than the knowledge of the lawful occupation and employment of creatures. In this sense, it can be affirmed that the end of the creation of men—that is, the use and occupation of their bodies, **Minds**, and all the faculties with which they were gifted by God—is to love God and to give Him this glory: that He alone is the one in whom, all other things having passed away, we must find our rest. Likewise, regarding material things, one rightly seeks the specific use of all and each of the bodies we encounter, but only insofar as they contribute to the necessity of this mortal life, which is to be dedicated to **Divine Love** alone; otherwise, these things are vain. 

If, however, in the same question—"Why?" or "To what end did God do something?"—one looks to the goal God proposed for Himself, or rather, to the **motives** and **reasons** that led Him to do this or that (for example, asking for what reasons God permitted the fall of the **Angels** or of men? what He intended? by what motive He allows so many men to perish? or why He created them all? why so many and not more? by what reasons He arranged the natures and state of things in this way?), this type of questioning is not done without rashness and impiety. For it dares to pry into those counsels and judgments of God which best reconcile things incomprehensible to us, while simultaneously being covered in a veil of worshipful obscurity. Therefore, there is no reason for us to torture ourselves in searching for reasons to answer these questions. Indeed, what answers could even be given? Let us examine, for example, that which is sometimes given as an answer to a similar question: namely, that the **Glory of God** is the end of the creation of things which

God, in truth, is not determined in acting by any thing which is outside of Himself. Whatever differs from Him is neither a motive nor an end for Him. Absurd external reasons are demanded, and it is asked by what rule something was made by Him, before whose pleasure no laws and no ideas of things are conceived. It shall suffice, therefore, in these matters to allege the one pleasure <note>original: *placitum*; often translated as "good pleasure" or "will," referring to God’s sovereign choice which requires no prior law.</note> of God, since that is Wisdom itself and the foundation of all things, beyond which to seek any reason for things is outrageous <note>original: *enorme*; literally "out of the norm" or "irregular," here meaning it is a fundamental error of logic or piety.</note>.

...rather, one can look at this single thing from a triple perspective, from which I take the occasion to contemplate three of God’s attributes: **Eternity**, **Constancy**, and **Simplicity**. I shall consider each separately, according to the different ways I observe this in my mind. II. Because all the objects of my thought are not equally necessary (as stated in chapter 14), and because my mind does not grasp them all at once (as is self-evident), Thought must therefore be divided into many particular thoughts. Each of these relates to a specific object, or to a specific difference within an object—or even to the degree to which an object is more or less necessary—according to the way we are drawn toward them, whether by love, joy, aversion, or some other passion. In this plurality, *Succession* occurs, by which one thought follows the first, and a third follows that, and so on. There also occurs a *continuation* or prolongation of the Mind, without which its succession of thoughts would be broken off. Finally, a certain *outflow* occurs, or a vanishing, as the earlier thoughts do not remain but disappear—often partially, sometimes entirely—as later ones take their place. 

And this is precisely what I call my "time" in other words; by this single process, I perceive its succession, its prolongation, and its flow. Therefore, to recognize the nature or measure of time, there is no need for me to resort to speculations about material things—such as how certain parts of a motion follow one after another as a body moves, or how the movement of a certain fluid matter (like water or sand) is delayed by a narrow space, as in a water clock <note>original: *clepsydra*; an ancient device for measuring time by the regulated flow of liquid.</note>, or how the states of certain bodies vanish or appear through decay, production, or other alterations. In these material things, many people wrongly place the nature of time, rather than just the measurement of it. The nature of time, which is proper to the created Mind in this state, is exactly what I have described. Every measure of time is recognized immediately and is ultimately resolved in the sense or perception I have of the change and succession of the objects of my thought, and the modes of thinking by which I am drawn to them. This problem exhausted Augustine through almost the entire eleventh book of his *Confessions*, as he himself admits.

III. I have said these things regarding the present state of the Mind. Regarding the state of the future life, nothing is certain without revelation, due to God’s hidden pleasure <note>original: *placitum*; referring to God's sovereign and inscrutable will.</note>. Nevertheless, I understand well enough that time as it is here—or such a mode of existence for my Thought—must vanish if it pleases the Best Mind <note>A philosophical term for God as the supreme Intellect.</note> who sustains me to join Himself to me according to the fullness of my Thought. # ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...for if every object were One and perfectly uniform, and if, with all the diversity of my faculties ceasing, my every Thought were a single Intelligence burning and fixed uniformly upon a truly single object, then surely every cause of succession would be removed. I would feel neither duration nor the "flow" of time; rather, all things would be a single moment—so to speak—or a single *present* to me. This one moment would be everything, insofar as it would exclude every cause of plurality, diversity, or variation. And from where, I ask, would the perception of variation be drawn, if all things are to think "one" in "one" way? This life, when it shall be granted as not temporary but eternal (though not with the eternity proper to God alone <note>The author distinguishes between God's absolute eternity—which has no beginning or end—and the "aeviternity" of created spirits, which has a beginning but no end.</note>), must be described as that state upon which the God-desiring Mind stays fixed. It pants until that day breathes and the shadows flee away, <note>A poetic allusion to the Song of Solomon 2:17: "Until the day break, and the shadows flee away."</note> until time flees, succession perishes, the "outflow" vanishes, and the very sense of duration—and duration as it now exists—ceases. Thus, nothing of temporary things would remain in the Mind, and nothing would remain by which it might differ from the true eternity of God (of which I shall speak shortly) except for these two things: namely, a single and total dependence upon God, and a uniformity of thought that does not arise from the perfection of its own nature, nor relates back to itself, but exists by God’s good pleasure and is directed toward God according to His will, with all plurality driven out. The sublimity of this subject and the incapacity of our present state forbid saying more. Indeed, these are difficult matters, neither obvious to the drowsy nor fully transparent even to the attentive; for as soon as thought has risen high enough to almost "taste" these things, it immediately falls back into the temporary and vanishing concepts to which it is subject in this life.

RATIONAL REFLECTIONS

...it should not be thought that the existence of the Mind established in that state is about to cease—though this might seem to follow to some—even if it cannot be said to be prolonged into the past or extended into the future. That Mind does not cease; rather, there is nothing in it that vanishes or becomes past, and nothing is lacking that could or should happen to it anew (and thus become "future"). Everything is present—but it is a present that does not exist by its own power (and thus in an absolute sense, is not), but exists from God, who alone exists simply and purely. That state draws its perfection from His good pleasure and from His <term>representative fullness</term> <note>The idea that God’s mind contains the perfect representation of all things</note>. Moreover, even if such a Mind were joined to a body—whose motion and governance cannot lack the distinctions of time—this would not harm that perfect state. Just as temporal things are subject to God and their concepts are in God, yet He Himself is not subject to time (as will be stated formally soon), because He is not distracted or hindered by those things from the uniform intelligence of Himself, in which He rests perfectly in a total, simultaneous present.

IV. To the person perceiving these things as much as is granted here, a concept of God must occur that represents His Eternity more truly and distinctly than is commonly done. This concept makes us certain that the existence of the eternal God has nothing in common with time. For indeed, as we have seen, all succession, extension, and the flow of time from the past through the present into the future belongs to a thing because of its dependence—specifically, a dependence such that its <term>representative realities</term> <note>The distinct "units" of thought or being that make up an experience</note> are not all established at once, but one after another, as it pleased the Sovereign Lord. ### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...at the same time they do not exist together, and thus it belongs to a limited Nature. For those whose Thought is prolonged, their existence—when viewed simply and in itself—is not necessary; or rather, it is not absolute, but exists under the condition that it be reproduced or replaced, without which it would vanish into nothingness. In the temporary flux from the past through the present into the future, there is infinitely more imperfection (or non-being) than there is perfection (and being): the infinite past no longer exists, the infinite future does not yet exist, and all that remains is the fleeting moment <note>original: *volucre momentum*</note> which the thing subject to these conditions actually enjoys. With what face could one attribute such things to Him who says in absolute truth, **"I am"** <note>original: *Ego sum*; a reference to the divine name in Exodus 3:14</note>, as if He were saying: "In me nothing is past, nothing is future; nothing is before me and nothing after me; I am at once and entire." The existence of Him who is most perfect can never become "past," nor is His present state so insufficient that it lacks something now failing it—namely, a future existence to be acquired later.

V. Since it is clear from what was demonstrated before that all these things are far removed from the Nature of God, it follows that the reason for His eternal existence is that **Pure Thought** <note>The author uses "Pure Thought" to describe a state of being that does not rely on external sequence or time</note> insofar as it possesses itself, or its whole essence, independently and most perfectly at once. In this way, the Eternity of God is exactly defined and is perfectly distinguished from that "representative and dependent eternity" which I noted above was possible for a created Mind.

<margin>(a) Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book V, Prose 6.</margin>
We omit Boethius's <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD) was a Roman statesman and philosopher whose definition of eternity as "timelessness" became the standard for the Middle Ages.</note> most celebrated definition (a) in which he says Eternity is *the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of an endless life* <note>original: *interminabilis vitæ totam simul & perfectam possessionem*</note>, as being less apt. He did not clarify the obscure and ambiguous word "life." Furthermore, the word "endless"—which he says can be attributed to the perpetual existence of the world according to Plato, and to God as well (but as possessing it all at once)—seems to give an occasion for thinking of God's eternity as a sort of contraction of infinite moments or infinite space. It is as if a very long, extended thread were wound into a ball so that it could be held all at once. However, no quality that truly exists or can be conceived to exist in creatures can be attributed to God in the same sense <note>A warning against "anthropomorphism" or "univocity," the idea that words mean the exact same thing when applied to God and humans.</note>, whether in part or in whole, separately or together, as must be done in proper definitions. Moreover, Boethius overlooked the <term>formal reason</term> <note>The essential defining characteristic</note> and fundamental concept of eternity—namely, God’s own independence or self-sufficiency—nor did he exactly distinguish eternity from the eternal life of created Minds, to whom his subsequent remarks on temporary life (which he proposes as the only thing distinct from eternity) do not apply. Perhaps some of these difficulties could be resolved by the word "perfect" which he inserts, but only by the use of many intermediaries and arguments which an exact definition should not require. But it is not my purpose here to discuss the thoughts of others.
