<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument from page 191, where the author began distinguishing God’s absolute, unchanging existence ("I am") from the fleeting, sequential nature of time experienced by created beings. Here, the author critiques common scholastic attempts to reconcile these two incompatible modes of being.</meta>

### RATIONAL THOUGHTS

VI. We must observe, however, that because of a poor understanding of God's Eternity, certain absurd questions, propositions, and expressions are commonly put forward—things that would never have been brought into the open if the speakers had conceived of a true idea of Eternity. For example, it is asked: how does Eternity coexist with time and its different parts—namely, the future, the present, and the past? Likewise: how do temporary things coexist with Eternity? Great effort is spent trying to satisfy this question, and to explain things as compatible that are in no way compatible, nor even understood by those who try to explain them. Some say that Eternity coexists with all the different parts of time because it is "together" with them, even though those parts of time are not "together" with each other. Another says it does not coexist with the future, but *will* coexist with it. Yet another says it coexists just as a column fixed in a marketplace <note>original: "columna in foro defixa"</note> coexists in its entirety with all the signs of the Zodiac as they follow one another across the horizon. <note>This was a common scholastic analogy used to explain how an unchanging God could relate to a changing world, imagining God as a stationary point and time as a revolving wheel.</note> This is nonsense; these are words without sense or clarity.

Yet it would have been easy for them to consider that the existence of Eternity is the very essence of Eternity. Therefore, to ask how Eternity is coexistent with time is the same as asking how it is co-essential with time, or "contemporary" with it, and how time is "co-eternal" with it. Or, it is to ask: how can the nature of Eternity and time be as one thing and agree in their essence? How can the nature of one be conceived under the concept of the nature of the other? Such absurdities should have turned them away from seeking a compatibility between things that differ by more than their entire category <note>original: "plusquam toto genere differunt"; a logical term meaning they are fundamentally different kinds of being</note> in respect to the very thing being asked.

Indeed, since we perceived above that the Eternity of God is the very essence of God (insofar as He exists most sufficiently from Himself), and that time is the created things themselves (insofar as they receive their limited perfections one after another), we believe that those who ask how Eternity coexists with time, or how the eternal God coexists with temporary things, should be answered in no other way than by sending their own question back to them with this added paraphrase: How does a most perfect thing—insofar as it is from itself, all at once and most sufficiently—agree with another, imperfect thing—insofar as this latter thing is not from itself, not fully, but is limited and exists in varying turns? How is the most perfect also the most imperfect? How is God not-God, but a temporary thing, and vice versa? It would be less outrageous to ask how the Mind is a body, or how Love is the "squaring of the circle." <note>original: "quadratura circuli"; a mathematical impossibility used here to denote a logical contradiction.</note> It is irrelevant to demand that one distinct thing be another distinct thing. Therefore, since these matters of Eternity and time in no way agree, nor can they be conceived as agreeing in existence (or as "coexisting") without being established as "co-essential" (or of the same essence), they ought not to be asked about with any expectation of a rational answer.

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of scholastic terminology regarding eternity. ### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

VII. But, while the existence of things was questioned with doubt, their essence has been confidently affirmed: they say the *essences of things are Eternal.* This is false. Consider whether the idea of any created thing involves the idea of true Eternity? Not at all. Therefore, Eternity is falsely attributed to it. But you will say, "it is eternal in the concept of God"; I am speaking of the essences of things insofar as they are conceived by God. What is this, really? *The essence of a thing is eternal in the concept of God?* Does this mean God conceives the essence of that thing—which is distinct from Himself—to be eternal? This is an abominable thought. You might say, "I would not mean that, but rather this: God conceived those essences from eternity, or, as has been said, He established, willed, and determined them by His pleasure; therefore they are rightly called eternal, just as God's decrees are everywhere called eternal." These are obscure and awkward expressions—to be "eternal" simply because of being conceived from eternity! Does a thing's essence involve eternity just because the thing was conceived from eternity? And further, what does this mean: *God conceived and willed these from eternity?* Does it mean "God, who is eternal, willed these things"? That is well enough, but in that case the existence of the world would have to be called eternal, since He who made it is eternal. Or rather, does it mean "God conceived these with an eternal concept"? Are they in God's eternal concept? No more convenient meaning seems possible. Let us examine this a bit to see whether it follows that Eternity belongs to the essences of things.

A "concept of God" implies three things: first, God Himself; second, an object other than God's nature; third, God's act. Now when a Divine concept is called eternal, to which of these three is Eternity to be attributed, and in what sense? If to God Himself, this does nothing for the essences of things. If to the objects themselves, or the ideas, these do not involve the idea of eternity, nor are they necessarily linked with it; absolutely speaking, they are not, and from themselves they are nothing. <term>see Chapter 10</term> There remains the *act*, which they will undoubtedly bring forward as the cause for their phrasing, calling it "eternal." I could respond by weakening the reasoning they must use: "The act by which the essences of things are conceived is eternal, therefore the essences themselves are eternal." I would counter: "The act by which the idea of a triangle is conceived by God is omnipotent and omniscient, etc.; therefore the idea of a triangle is omnipotent." <note>The author uses a logical technique called *reductio ad absurdum* to show that just because God's mind (which is omnipotent) thinks of a triangle, it doesn't mean the triangle itself becomes omnipotent.</note> But because these instances—though they convince by leading to an absurdity—do not bring enough light, I will say something else: namely, when the act by which things are conceived, established, and decreed is called eternal, should we think it means it is involved in God's Eternity, flows from it, and is so connected with it that if that act were denied, Eternity itself would be denied? That God's essence would not be eternal unless God had so acted, conceived, and willed things which are distinct from Himself?

That this is not the case is demonstrated by what has been said regarding the <term>Absolute Dominion of God</term> <note>original: "Dominio Dei absoluto"; a theological concept referring to God's total freedom to act according to His will without external necessity.</note>. The act of God, which is most free and most indifferent, has no...

->### RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

...we must conclude that whatever God was able to refrain from doing does not have a necessary connection with the essence of the Divine Nature’s Eternity. Nor can such a thing be called "eternal" except in a different sense: namely, insofar as things did not yet exist and yet were actually conceived by God, or insofar as the concept in God does not exist by way of succession <note>original: "successionis"; the idea of things happening one after another in a sequence</note> and a flow corresponding to time, but through another way which God alone knows. This "way" is certainly not the Eternity of His Nature, even if it is appropriate for Him whose Nature is eternal. It all comes down to this: **Only God’s Essence is eternal.** The act or pleasure of God, or His determination or concept regarding things (and, if you wish, the essences of things), are in Him freely, not by necessity. They exist before all time, yet without succession—as if some things in God preceded others while others followed. Finally, the works of God exist in time, even if, as has been noted, some of these might be considered outside of it. It is enough to conceive of things this way. Let anyone who wishes argue over words as much as they like; if someone refuses to grasp this, it is of no concern to me.

VIII. It is from a misunderstood idea of Eternity that some reason as follows: *“If there was no time when things did not exist, then Eternity must have existed, in which the world was made; but if there is no succession in Eternity, then all things must have been made all at once.”* These people imagine Eternity, and even time, as if they were something separate from the eternal God and from temporary things—an empty container indifferent to receiving God or objects, much like the way "imaginary spaces" are invented. We speak instead so that there is no room for this supposed difficulty: Things that are not most perfect did not exist, but the **Most Perfect Being**—existing most sufficiently and fully of Himself (this is Eternity)—did exist. While He existed, it pleased Him by His own choice (which was inherently free) to establish things that would receive their limited perfections one after another. This is certainly not a case of things "happening within eternity," nor is it saying all things were created at once. I see no difficulty in this, however much it might be muddied by obscure or meaningless words.

IX. To those who claim (such as *Plato* and *Aristotle*, so they say) that the world lacks a beginning to its existence, the objection was raised: *“If that were the case, then the world would be eternal.”* See how these men imagine Eternity as if it were merely an order of infinite moments lacking a beginning and an end! This is **true ignorance of eternity.** It is false to claim the world is "eternal" simply because it is said to have always existed, or because one cannot point to any single moment that was not preceded by another. For even if this were the case, the world would still be temporary and dependent, and this would not detract in any way from God’s Eternity or Power. Indeed, I do not defend that particular dogma <note>The "dogma" refers to the Aristotelian view that the universe has no beginning in time.</note>, but I argue that the objection used to attack it is foolishly...

-># ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL <-

I show <note>This sentence continues from the previous page's discussion on the misconception of eternity</note> that this arises from a false concept of Eternity. Perhaps, incidentally, it might be requested that this dogma be refuted using true principles, and that it be demonstrated that the world has not always existed. To satisfy this request as much as I am able, I will not be reluctant to interrupt the thread of my discourse with a small digression. To those who have long considered this matter, it is not as easy as it might seem at first glance—so much so that the supporters of the opposite opinion <note>Those who believe the world is eternal, such as certain Aristotelians</note> can be excused to some extent, provided they lacked revelation <note>Divine truth revealed by God, as in the Bible, rather than discovered by logic alone</note>. Certainly, while I was still writing these things—after I had seen that the extremes of things are hidden from our understanding, and that just as empty space cannot be conceived, neither can empty time (or a time in which nothing existed); and after I had found the reasons offered by others to be weak and had long sought others in my own mind—I thought that, setting revelation aside, it could not be demonstrated by the **light of nature** <term>lumen naturae: the capacity of human reason to discover truth without divine help</term> that the World is such that it did not exist previously. For if you go backward from this moment, to which the world's duration has descended, ascending as if to reach the first moment, you will never be able to designate any moment that could not have been preceded by another, and that by another, and so on to infinity. Since you can conceive of it being placed this way, how do you know, setting revelation aside, that it was *not* so placed? 

But afterward, it occurred to me that moments which are called "infinite," or particles of time whose beginning is not conceived, are not only to be considered separately one after another. Rather, if they are called "infinite" when collected into one, they must also be viewed in a single intuition, so that they may be observed all together to possess what belongs to the essence of each one separately. I observe, therefore, that the **present moment**, before it was present, was **to be** <note>original: "futurum"; that is, it existed only as a future possibility</note>; but that which was "to be" did not then exist, or rather, did not exist before. Therefore, by gathering however many moments through which the world has lasted—which you say have flowed by in an infinite number—the whole and entire past existence of the world, with all its parts, was "to be" before it was "present." This means that first it was nothing, and then it was. This, unless I am mistaken, demonstrates that the world has a beginning to its existence. 

Regarding minds <note>or souls</note> which we said in their own sense could be withdrawn from time (for some objection could be raised from the consideration of them), let it be known that they possess no more reality of themselves than temporary things, and perhaps all were previously subject to time. But let these things suffice. Let us return to those matters concerning Eternity.

Otherwise, even **wagon-loads of commentaries** <note>original: "commentariorum plaustra"; a common Latin idiom for an overwhelming or excessive amount of writing</note> would not suffice. ->## RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

...the materials <note>original: "teria"; likely the end of "materia" (materials/subjects)</note> sprout, so that once they are detected, those errors may be avoided with no effort. First, because men were foolish and—to use an **Augustinian** phrase—**thickened of heart** <note>original: "incrassati corde," a reference to St. Augustine’s description of those whose minds are too weighed down by material things to understand spiritual truths</note>, they substituted and thought of nothing for all things other than **divisible extension**. Specifically, they used the extension of **space** to represent the nature of things, and the extension of **duration** to represent actual existence. Second, when they later heard or perceived something from elsewhere concerning the Mind or God, they sought and assigned to them a certain **Where** and **When** outside of their own essence and outside of Thought, placing them within physical extension. Third, so as not to mix everything together but to distinguish them to some extent according to their own imagination, they first considered bodies. Just as they defined the extension of space by a certain shape and measure, they assigned that extension to the presence—or **the "Where"** <note>original: "$\tau \tilde{\omega}$ Ubi"</note>—of bodies and called it **Place**. In the same way, by limiting the extension of the duration of moments with certain boundaries at the beginning and the end, they said that this measure of the existence of corruptible things is **time**, which they specifically called **When**. Fourth, they further made the space of extension not exactly infinite, but they did not define its limits as they had for bodies; instead, they left it indeterminate in a middle state. They attributed this to the presence of **created minds** <note>such as angels or human souls</note> under the term **Where**. In this same way, although they had not removed all the limits of temporal extension, they removed at least some—namely the future ones—and adapted this extension to the existence of created minds. They did not wish to call this "time," but rather **eternity from the back** <note>future-eternal</note>, or an **age** <term>aevum: a theological term for a duration that has a beginning but no end, distinct from the absolute eternity of God</term>, being not at all concerned with the more worthy eternity of Minds. And fifth, just as they had relaxed the limits of spacious extension and conceived of it as infinite, attributing it to God’s presence and calling it **Everywhere** and **imaginary spaces**; so too, having rejected all limits of durable extension—both the earlier and the later—they referred it to God’s existence. That which was previously "eternity from the back" now became for them **eternity from the front** <note>past-eternal</note> as well, or simply **Eternity**, which they asserted as proper to God. But truly, by some stupendous contradiction, they mixed everything up again by enclosing the entire essence of God within the smallest space of all, claiming that God is present there according to His **immense essence**. Likewise, they went so far as to establish their **Eternity** within the smallest extension of duration, teaching that it exists in its entirety alongside any small particle of time, etc. These are ridiculous fictions and should be dismissed in the same way. For as we saw in the first book, the essence of God (which encompasses all His perfections) would be limited if it were in a creature—indeed, the creature itself would thus be God, since the essence of God would be in it. In the same way, if the Divine existence or Eternity were to coexist with time...

...and its differences <note>original: "que differentiis"; likely the conclusion of a word like "quibusque" from the previous page</note>, and if time were added to it, it would follow that this Eternity would be like a moment and would be limited along with it, since the whole of eternity, which is one, would coexist with that moment. This is what I have intended to present here. To one who meditates more and more on these things, the ineffable beauty of the Eternity of the Supreme Being will appear, a nature which can be common to no other, even if a representation of it is best found in those minds which, by thinking on that one Eternal object, we have seen withdrawn from time so that they might be devoted to eternal life. Would that these things were thought upon more deeply, until the preoccupation with temporary things—which disturb us while present for a moment, but once passed become incapable of affecting us—might utterly evaporate from the soul before a burning concern for eternal things!

...but [perceive] it as subject to much failure. Truly, by its aid, what I cannot perceive in the mind regarding some object in one part of duration, I conceive more correctly in the following parts spent on it; indeed, I direct the sharpness of my mind to other objects as well, which are very many. But because my knowledge <note>original: "Cognitio"</note> is partial, inadequate, and subject to obscurity, error, uncertainty, and other things—as I saw above—hence there is variety and inconstancy in the way I apply myself not only to many objects, but often to one and the same, and think about it. It often happens that I think about one thing, then later about many others, and then return as if in a circle to the first; although it is the same and has in no way changed its state, it is nevertheless treated by me in thought in a way that is sometimes opposite to the previous one, sometimes different from it. Thus, what was just now thought of as such-and-such—true, good, suitable, pleasing, to be acquired in such a way, handled, etc.—is a little later judged otherwise, even though the thing itself remains the same, but because of those defects of my thought I mentioned. And although another cause could come from the **will** <note>original: "voluntate"</note> (which we are not dealing with now), and although all inconstancy is usually attributed to the **affects** <note>Term: "affectibus." II. I know indeed that this defect of inconstancy could be driven out of me if He who holds me were to affix to my thought true and necessary **evident ideas** <note>Term: "ideas evidentes." But truly, if He denies those things to me as undeserved <note>original: "indebita"</note>, the inconstancy of my state is to be deplored.

rience <note>original: "experientia"</note> and Eternity considered together, or with no effort, from the fact that He is the **Most Perfect Thought**. For he who changes becomes to that extent different from what he was before; but that which is different from the most perfect is not the most perfect. Yet the most perfect does not become "non-perfect," nor can he, for this contradicts itself. Therefore, he does not become another, nor can he; that is, he is not inconstant, but constant, by the very essence of his nature. This is also easily concluded regarding his **pleasure** <note>Term: "placitum." In this context, it refers to God's "pleasure" or "decree"—the sovereign choice or will of God that determines the nature of reality.</note> or **will**, insofar as it regards the things established and created by him. For in him there is no succession or recurrence, such that a later application of will could be said to be different from an earlier one, and thus subject to inconstancy. Nor can it even be thought that God deserts one purpose and embraces another without supposing that God first proposed something which he himself later, completely deserting it, in no way approves—that is (since in God’s pleasure there is no "before" and "after"), without supposing that God simultaneously approves and disapproves of the same thing: which falls into an absurd contradiction.

IV. And these points are not hindered by that **indifference** <note>Term: "indifferentia." This refers to the theological concept of "indifference of the will," where God is free to choose between various possibilities without being compelled by external forces.</note> which we have often said exists in the Divine pleasure, provided that the Divine pleasure is considered then as indeterminate, but now as determinate. Nor does the inconstancy found in created things prove that He is less constant: for it constantly pleases God that things are and will be inconstant exactly to the extent that they are seen to change in effect. They change for this very reason: because the will of God that they should change cannot itself be changed. Furthermore, even in that inconstancy of things, excellent signs of Divine constancy are seen. First, while the substances of things themselves and their primary or immediate modes are preserved once they have come into existence—whence the substance of **Minds** <note>original: "Mentium"</note>, even the worst ones (namely, thought and its faculties), remain constantly. Second, insofar as change does not come to the state of things subject to inconstancy except according to the most constant rules, which are constantly observed in minds and bodies, as those who philosophize more specifically about these things well know. And although with respect to created minds—which God is said to approve, love, etc., more or less as they delight in good or evil—an inconstancy might seem at first glance to reside in the Divine will; nevertheless, if what has already been said is held firmly in mind—namely, that God embraces the state and duration of all things in a **single act**—the difficulty will vanish. It vanishes so completely that even if all things were changed, or indeed even if they vanished into nothingness, the evidence of reason would not allow any other conclusion than that the Divine pleasure—which saw fit that all things exist in that way, and for that long, and no further—is altogether immutable and constant.

...[prepar]ing <note>original: "parantibus." Truly, since the <term>divine pleasure <note>original: "divinum placitum." This refers to God’s sovereign decree or will which sustains all existence.</note></term> establishes and preserves all things, and since that pleasure—even if it is most constant—does not necessarily imply the constancy of the things which a man wants, or which God himself has established (perhaps only for a time), it is absurd for anyone to vow or promise themselves that God will do certain things (whatever they may be, without distinction) unless a declaration from God himself regarding the future outcome is held, or unless one already possesses the "first fruits" of all the effects of the divine pleasure, which are said to have a link established by God to their completion. It is even more foolish to vow in such a way as if the establishing or prolonging of any reality depended upon you. I can well assert the present state of my mind—that such and such a thought is indeed already in me, or such a desire, so that I now want this or that, or even crave that God might preserve this will in me. But what He will do regarding my inconstancy, or what He will permit concerning it, is something I ought to wait for between hope and trembling. Where, however, it is established by certain testimony that God will place good things in me, then when I vow that I will perform good works, my vows are not to be regarded by anyone in any other way than as signs of my confidence in Divine truthfulness, rather than as my own guarantee of my own proper constancy.

## (17) SIMPLICITY.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the limitations of the human mind compared to the nature of God. <page-num>201</page-num>
<header>->ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.<-</header>

[com]paring <note>original: "parandus." Completing the word from the catchword "paran-" on the previous page; likely "comparandus," meaning "to be compared."</note> it to a moderate vessel with a narrower mouth, which indeed admits liquid little by little, yet once admitted, it actually retains all that entered through various turns at the same time—insofar as what I have admitted into my thought at various turns does not all remain actually present; or rather to a narrow channel, through which a quantity of water or other liquids cannot pass successively unless the portions of liquids flowing into it push each other out and eject one another through continuous evacuation. For I experience my thoughts excluding each other in such a way that if one is present, it gives no place to the others; if any of the others are to be recalled, the prior one must be dismissed; and so it goes continuously. This happens not only when I think of things that are different from one another, but even when I turn toward the object that is most truly One, namely God, whose perfection I am unable to represent to myself in this state except through many acts of thinking. For even these thoughts are subject to this imperfection: while one is present to me, the others do not appear, nor are they thought.

II. And although I sometimes embrace many things in a single instance of thinking, I nevertheless do not conceive of them as completely and clearly all at once as I would if I took each one separately. Instead, I grasp them only to a certain extent, and more confusedly—no differently than if I were to capture masses of several liquids in a small channel at once. In that case, a tiny portion of each liquid having been admitted, their confusion and dilution would become greater the more liquids there were.

III. Meanwhile, I contemplate the diversity of the form of my thought with some wonder. Therein is limitation; there is no unity, but multiplicity; yet even this is not present all at once, but rather in parts that push each other out. To these points you may add, from what was said above, that any given part is not grasped with <term>adequate knowledge <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "adequate knowledge" refers to a complete and perfect understanding of a thing's nature and all its causes.</note></term>. Whether my Thought is one day to be reduced from this multiplicity to a greater simplicity depends on the <term>pleasure of God <note>original: "placito Dei." This refers to God’s sovereign and free will or decree.</note></term>. What He wills regarding this matter is left to be determined by revelation; what He is *able* to do is not determined, since the question is resolved into the Power of God, which can be grasped by no one. Nevertheless, whatever may happen, since the created Mind will never possess even a single perfection of God, let alone possess them all at once and indivisibly, an infinite distance must be acknowledged between the greatest simplicity to which a mind might arrive and that simplicity which is truly proper to God.

It does not stand in the way of simplicity. 8. Nor does the diversity of decrees. 9. How it is foreshadowed in material things and in minds.*

IV. Indeed, Divine *Simplicity* is inseparable from Highest Perfection, and we shall conceive of it best if we dismiss the trifles <note>original: "quisquiliis," referring to trivial or scrap-like arguments</note> by which it is commonly designated negatively—such as the denial that God is composed of matter and form, or of genus and difference, etc., things which one could even say about "nothingness" itself. Instead, let us think of God according to the way I just used in thinking about myself <note>Referring to the analogy of the mind's capacity on the previous page</note>. For in this way we will observe that all the perfections which God has, and which I can in any way think of regarding Him, are not only present at once in His Nature and indivisibly united so that none can be missing; but they are also so united that one is the other, and vice versa—indeed, one is all, and all are most properly one in essence. For example, Life is Spirituality, is Eternity, and others, and vice versa: life is all the attributes, and all attributes are life, and so with the rest. All of these are simply one and the same, or are a Single pure Thought <note>original: "Unica mera Cogitatio"</note>. That this is so in the most perfect Nature can be easily demonstrated, and it has been sufficiently demonstrated at the end of the second book, to which we refer the reader. This is also proved with no trouble from the other attributes—for example, from Sufficiency <term>Sufficiency: In this context, God’s "Sufficientia" refers to His self-sufficiency and the fact that He contains all perfections within Himself without needing external causes</term>. For if you say that one attribute does not possess the perfections of the others (that is, is not those very things), I ask: is God sufficient to give those perfections to that attribute? To say "no" is not permitted by Divine Sufficiency; if you say "yes," it follows that they are actually held by that attribute, since there is nothing passive in God <note>In classical philosophy, "passive" implies a capacity to be changed or to receive something one does not already have; God is seen as "pure act"</note>. This is also shown from His activity, which would be denied if it were established that one attribute could be separated from another, or that one lacked the perfections of another or of all; for then something in God’s nature would be conceived as "capable of receiving," or as not merely active. It is also proved from Unity: for that which does not exhaust everything can be multiplied; but if many "Sufficiencies" or "Eternities" could be given, many sufficient or eternal Beings would be given, and thus—because these are acknowledged to exist in God alone—many Gods would exist, which has been proved false. But, to pass over more points, this is also clear from the immediately preceding attribute, by which all diversity and capacity for diversity is removed from the Divine nature.

V. It must be confessed that several [difficulties] can occur in conceiving this...

...difficulties: First, because no example of such <term>Simplicity</term> <note>Divine Simplicity is the theological concept that God has no parts; He is not "composed" of different pieces, but is a single, unified essence</note> occurs in any other things. Second, because we are accustomed to numbering many <term>attributes</term> <note>Qualities or characteristics, such as "just," "all-knowing," or "eternal"</note> in God as if they were distinct from one another. Finally, because there are said to be in God many concepts of things—many statutes and decrees—which could have been absent from Him or could have been otherwise. But none of these things stand in the way of Divine Simplicity.

VI. For the fact that all things—whether <term>extended</term> <note>original: "extensa," referring to physical matter that takes up space</note> or <term>thinking</term> <note>original: "cogitantia," referring to minds or spirits</note>—are not simple in this way is because they do not exist by their own power, but by the will of another who gave them being through particles as He pleased. The reason why knowledge, justice, joy, and such things are not "one" in a human being is because not only are their objects different, but the Mind itself is variable in many <term>modes</term> <note>The different states or "ways" a mind can be in; for example, being "in a state of joy" vs. "in a state of sorrow"</note>. One of these modes can exist without the other; indeed, when the mind is set in one way, another disposition of the mind that would happen through a different mode is blocked. But since the causes of these things are not found in God—who exists of Himself and uniformly enjoys one unchanging object—it can be judged without difficulty that such effects are far removed from Him. Thus, His Simplicity is not called into doubt by them.

VII. Regarding the diversity or difference of the Divine attributes, as they are conceived and numbered by me, the matter stands thus: God is a single, pure <term>Thought</term> <note>original: "Cogitatio"</note>. However, the acts of thinking within me, or my thoughts about Him, are many; they are born from many occasions which often involve the different objects of the world. For sometimes I reflect upon Divine Thought because I did not create myself; at other times because I cannot do all things, or because I do not know all things, and so on. These reflections—which are called "Attributes" when considered in relation to God—cannot help but have some difference between them, since they involve a relationship not only to God but also to the diversity of my own acts, occasions, and objects of thought, and thus they embrace concepts of many different things. Yet this distinction exists in the plurality of the acts of *my* thinking self, in the occasions from which I think of God, and in the objects to which I relate my thoughts—not in God Himself. My one thought of God is not numerically the same as my other thought of Him. One occasion for my thinking of Him is different from another, and one object that I refer back to God is not the same as another object I might also refer back to Him. But whatever of God is involved in each and all of those many different thoughts—arising from different occasions and tangled with different objects—that something is one and the same, indissolubly uni-

and firmly observed in the Divine nature. Besides the arguments already stated, another proof of this truth is that no true and clear idea of any <term>attribute</term> <note>A characteristic or quality of God, such as His power or goodness</note> can be held if even one of them is denied. For example, if you deny eternity, you deny life, for "non-thinking" is "non-living"; moreover, where there is <term>succession</term> <note>original: "successio"; the state of things following one after another in time, rather than existing all at once</note>, and where all perfections are not present at once, there is a lack of thought and a lack of consciousness regarding them. VIII. As for the concepts, statutes, and decrees of God regarding a great variety of things, these do not belong to God’s <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature of what God is</note>, since they could have not existed, or could have been different. Therefore, one should not seek the Simplicity of the Divine Essence within them; nor, if simplicity is not found there, does it prevent all the perfections that can be thought of in the Divine Essence from being one and the same reality. Nevertheless, even these decrees have their own kind of simplicity among themselves, a simplicity that befits the decision of a most perfect Being who is <term>indifferent</term> <note>In this philosophical context, "indifferent" means God is not compelled by external forces but chooses freely</note> toward them. This is because they are all a single act, embracing all objects distinct from God, present simultaneously and constantly. But the Simplicity which belongs to a most necessary and perfect thing is of a different sort, and does not necessarily require the presence or absence of this other kind. The foundation for solving this difficulty more clearly is revealed most evidently in Chapter X; without that goal, I am certain it cannot be understood how the consideration of statutes and decrees—which could have been otherwise—does not conflict with the concept of Divine Simplicity.

IX. It has been said that no example of Divine Simplicity is found in any things besides God. This is true if we speak absolutely, for nothing is absolutely simple; rather, if anything is simple, it is so only in a certain respect, and thus it is not "simply simple." However, among things that are simple in a relative sense, some can be quite excellent signs and <term>patterns</term> <note>original: "ectypa"; a copy or image of an archetype</note> of Divine Simplicity, according to their own mode and nature. Take, for instance, the **nature of matter**, where length, width, and depth are so inseparable that each and every one exists in each and every part of the matter. Nor can matter be divided into parts where one part would have less than all three dimensions together. In the same way, the **direction of motion** along a straight line is a remarkable sign of the **Simple Maker**. Indeed, nothing is simpler than straightness, which is uniform in the whole and in its parts, and the entire nature of the whole is present in any part. Therefore, from the simplicity of operation that befits a Most Simple Being, we rightly derive the **Law of motion** regarding direction in a straight line—just as that other Law, that everything is preserved in its own state, was related to **Constancy**. <note>This text appears to refer back to the human soul or mind, as "creata" (created) is feminine in Latin, matching "Anima" or "Mens".</note> however, was created so that <term>Divine Simplicity</term> <note>The theological concept that God is not made of parts, but is a single, unified essence</note> might be reflected as much as possible. Since concepts of things different from God do not belong to the Simplicity of the Divine nature, it is likewise necessary for the created mind, in order to reflect that simplicity, not to cling to them. For attention to created things, which are manifold, scatters thoughts into infinite and diverse multiplicities. The first fruits of that <term>eternity</term> noted above consist solely in the straight, genuine, naked, and open direction of Thought toward the Simple God—without ambiguity, without concern for variety, without artificial preparation, without affected arrangement, and without the pursuit of accidental ornaments and <term>trappings</term> <note>original: "phalerarum"; literally the decorative metal plates on a horse's harness, used here to mean empty rhetorical flourishes</note>, empty shows and mere puppets <note>original: "pupis"; literally dolls or puppets, implying lifeless or childish distractions</note>, whether in words, in gestures, or in intellectual subtleties. This is a mode of acting in all things that seeks neither the appearance of variety nor of simplicity, nor fixes the mind to external and foreign formalities—which are only necessary outwardly according to the state of things—and thus becomes free from everything that a thing pleasing to God can do without. These things, I say, conform the Mind to Divine Simplicity, whereas contrary things are accustomed to remove it from the Simple God.

For the more a person possesses things that are distinct from perfection—that is, from that most uniform and constant thought which purely embraces God—and which can therefore be separated and dispersed, the more that person is composite, manifold, and divided. Such a person is less "Simple" and less like Him who is best represented by that from which nothing can be further separated, in whom all things are the <term>one thing necessary</term> <note>A reference to the Biblical phrase "unum necessarium" from Luke 10:42</note>, and where the "one" is all things. Just as we have already reviewed Divine Simplicity among those things which first occur in the knowledge of God, so also in a Mind approaching or closest to God, the first and chief requirement is this Simplicity, which seasons all things. Hence, this truly admirable Simplicity is the very form and Soul of the Divine Scriptures.

### CHAPTER XIX.

## (18) LIBERTY.

### §. A.

1. *In what does the freedom of the mind consist? 2. 3. Of Spontaneity. From where do the degrees of impulse arise? A caution. Motion dedicated to God. It is established by God, nor is it diminished by His Power, etc. 4. Indifference is granted. 5. Nor do difficulties stand in the way. 6. Should the Idea of created Liberty be called equal to the Divine, or is it to be called lesser?*

I. Having observed these cycles of variation, I encounter the more general ways they are established within me. I notice these are partly voluntary, partly forced or foreign, and partly mixed, according to how they relate to different classes of objects and the different communication of the Mind with those objects. And first indeed—which was the subject of the eighteenth observation—I notice those of my thoughts which concern the knowledge of truth and the possession of good (through judgments of affirmation or denial, through love, desire, and similar inclinations). These are not placed in me by an external force in such a way that I feel I am compelled to receive them whether I wish to or not. Rather, they enter into me so freely that they seem to proceed from me. This mode of thinking is called *Liberty* among Philosophers, though you might better call it *Spontaneity* <term>Spontaneity</term> <note>The quality of acting from one's own internal nature and will, rather than being moved by an external cause.</note>. Nor should this be confused with that other liberty mentioned by more Divine writers <note>A reference to theologians or scripture</note>, by which the Mind, released from sin, most freely clings to the Divine will alone.

II. However, just as the knowledge of truth and goodness is either clear or obscure (or clouded by ignorance), so too the thoughts by which I judge them or am carried toward them are either spontaneously determined and eager, or <term>indifferent</term> <note>A state of being "un-inclined" or balanced between two choices.</note>—that is, spontaneously undetermined and leaning toward neither side. For this reason, Liberty is called "spontaneous" by some and "indifferent" by others; though perhaps it would be more correct to say that Spontaneity is either *undetermined* or *determined*, which is the way of speaking we prefer to use. Concerning that spontaneous motion by which I am carried toward objects, I observe that the greater or lesser the clarity and extent of knowledge (and the perfection of truth and goodness), and the more or less they concern me or are necessary to me, the greater or lesser is the eagerness and impulse with which I rush there spontaneously and willingly. Thus, there are many degrees of *Determined Spontaneous Liberty*. Regarding this truth—that any two sides of a triangle taken together are greater than the third—

I move spontaneously <note>original: *sponte*</note> indeed when a truth is completely evident; however, since it is not among my primary concerns, the leaning of my mind toward it is quite relaxed. But in those matters which are greater—namely, those that have God and Divine things as their objects—a different vigor of the Mind is felt. One perceives a swift, joyful, and vivid movement or impulse of inclination, the most spontaneous of all. Whether I should attribute this to the spiritual passions of the soul, or to the internal senses (which some bring forward as the strongest arguments for truth after innate knowledge), matters little—provided that I apply diligent effort so that it is joined with a clear and evident cognition of truth. Otherwise, the greatest deception can lie beneath. The ignorant Mind might be carried away by a blind impulse toward its own chimeras <note>An imaginary monster; here meaning delusions or groundless fancies.</note> as if they were God or Divine decrees. It might imagine, from an internal sense of fervor and flow that penetrates, occupies, and carries away its whole thought at that time, that it is rushing most happily into Divine things; yet it must be "untaught" by the outcome when that fervor vanishes along with those phantasms.

Meanwhile, just as among the ideas which the intellect perceives, there is one certain idea—and that the most intimate of all—which is to be referred to God alone, so there is no doubt that among these movements of the will there is one which, moving the more secret roots and "bottom" <term>Bottom of the Mind</term> <note>Latin: *fundum Mentis*. A philosophical and mystical term for the deepest, most essential part of the human spirit where it is most capable of connecting with the Divine.</note> of the Mind, as it were, is excited by God alone with no mediating means. Indeed, this movement looks totally and immediately to God alone, whom God has chosen for Himself as His own secret place of operation and His own vehicle, incapable of receiving any disturbance from any created things whatsoever. Without this, it would be impossible for anyone to discern Divine operations, inspirations, the true touch of God, and the true conversion of the mind from the imaginary things by which so many are deceived; nor would any certain sense of true happiness, or even of misery, be given. But to draw these things out at greater length is not for this place. It will suffice to note that they rely on this principle: the Mind is fit to be intimately affected by the Almighty God alone in a way that is most different from those ways in which created means intervene, and so a way which created means cannot reach. In this sense, it is said to be "hidden" and "secret" from them, and the Mind is said to be touched in its most recondite "bottom" (because other things cannot reach there). And here, truly, the wonderful and ineffable works of God take place.

III. For all these things—to return to what has been said so far—I can offer no other reason than the Constitution of my nature, or that it was God’s pleasure to so constitute me; for this alone is the reason and cause of the essence of things and of their primary modes. Therefore, the Divine Power, the efficacy and force of His pleasure, and His Omniscience do not stand in the way of Spontaneous Liberty <term>Spontaneous Liberty</term> <note>The freedom of a being to act according to its own internal nature and inclinations.</note>, or determined Spontaneity; on the contrary, they help it. For since they are its causes, the greater their operation or effect is placed in me, the

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...there is a greater Spontaneity <note>original: *Spontaneitas*; in this context, it refers to the mind's ability to act from its own internal nature without external compulsion.</note> within me; and the more it pleases God to foreknow regarding my will, the more truly free I am. For it is self-evident that this Liberty is something positive, and it was demonstrated above that all things are established by God, and therefore liberty itself exists according to that manner and measure conceived by Him when He wills it.

IV. Regarding indeterminate Spontaneity, which exists in me when I do not evidently perceive what is true and good, and thus I remain spontaneously indeterminate, I notice that it is the absence of that spontaneous determination I just mentioned; hence the Mind is not carried toward an object by affirmation or negation, love or hatred. But furthermore, I observe a certain image of active, indifferent indetermination, by which the Mind seems to have the Power <note>original: *Potentiam*</note> of determining itself toward any object whatsoever from many opposites or diverse options—whether they be more or less good—as it pleases the Mind. It must be admitted that this is a profound difficulty. Evil would not exist unless indifference <note>The state of being able to choose either of two opposites.</note> existed or had existed. He who has done blameworthy things ought to have acted differently than he did; therefore, at least at some time, in some respect, and in some state, he was indifferent. For if he had no other goal, no other means, no other occasion, and no other principle before his determination than he had after it, then he did not wander from the goal, the rules, or the principle—from which it follows most evidently that he in no way sinned. 

Unless, perhaps, you were to say that sin consists in this: that he who acts, thinking he acts wrongly, acts against his conscience, not attending to whether he is determined to this or not—as if indeed, if someone persuaded himself that all things were indiscriminately good and that "fate calls each man to his own," he would sin less; and that sin would consist merely in the opinion that sin exists! (Which are the very principles of Libertinism <term>Libertinism: Here referring to a philosophical stance that denies moral responsibility by claiming that "sin" is merely a subjective opinion rather than an objective reality.</term>). But then, how would that opinion—that sin exists—itself be a sin, and thus blameworthy in those who held it, unless there had first been in them an indifference toward embracing or rejecting that opinion? Therefore, Indifference must necessarily be established within indeterminate Spontaneity.

V. Yet all things are not only determined by God, but—which increases the difficulty—they are determinately established so that no thing, even the smallest, can be established in any way by anyone other than by Him alone, who determinately ordained that He would establish all things. How are these things to be reconciled with the indifference of indeterminate spontaneity? But I recall that it is sufficient here for me to touch briefly on these matters from which I will take the occasion to speak of God, and that there is no need to discuss every single scruple, especially those that arise from the occasion of extraneous matter, namely evil. # ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

I put this aside until we must consider the nature of evil. However, I will briefly set down the principles from which all things are to be derived. If it is most certain (as indeed it is) that all positive things are established determinately by God, and yet a state of "indifferent indetermination" <note>A state where the mind is not yet decided or inclined toward one choice over another.</note> exists, then that indifferent indetermination is not some power or capacity of the created being to establish or not establish something positive and real. That is to say, it does not involve the presence of any perfection. Therefore, even if God determinately establishes all the positive elements within the Mind, this does not prevent something from being left behind that involves imperfection or negation. I have another argument for this point—namely, that indifference is a defect: when I long for perfection, I am conscious that I desire to be completely free of such indifference, just as I conceive the blessed souls <note>original: *Mentes beatas*; the spirits of the redeemed in heaven who see God clearly.</note> to be entirely stripped of it.

VI. As for the question of whether I can be said to conceive of my own Freedom so highly that I cannot grasp an idea of any greater freedom—not even the Divine freedom (which I will discuss shortly)—I consider such a question to be of little use, as well as troublesome and obscure. Freedom does not exist in all my thoughts. Those thoughts described as "free" through indifference are actually less perfect (I am not speaking here of the imperfection of sin) the more they are "free" or indifferent. Therefore, this degree of liberty cannot be compared with the Divine. Comparing my own spontaneous acts of thought, I see that some are less eager and vivid than others; what then if they were compared to God? Even that which is the greatest "willingness" <note>original: *lubentia*; a joyful, internal inclination toward an action.</note> in certain acts—how can it be compared to Divine liberty without the Divine being called greater? To be "greater" or "lesser" is properly said regarding the equality or inequality of degrees of reality in things or their modes—a comparison that has no place between the Creator and the created being. You might argue that compulsion—or rather, the *feeling* of compulsion—is no more absent from the Freedom of God than from the Freedom of a created Mind. Therefore, in this sense, one might agree with Descartes <note>referring to René Descartes’ *Meditations on First Philosophy*, Meditation IV, where he argues that the human will is equal to God's in its essential nature, even if it lacks God's power and knowledge.</note> that both forms of Freedom, when considered strictly in this way, are equal, with neither being greater than the other. I respond by admitting that these points are indeed true: all sense of compulsion is absent from God, and it is also absent from those thoughts of mine that are called free. However, because this absence does not arise from the same cause or in the same manner in both cases, and because that which is positively signified by the term *non-compulsion*—namely, either indifference or "pleasure"—is not the same in God as it is in the created being, I am unwilling to use comparative terms. For in no respect is there anything positive in God and in the creature that can properly be called precisely equal, nor greater, nor less; just as one cannot say that something in them is more or less eternal, or more or less omnipotent, or more or less...

God, etc. is appropriately said. These things of a very different kind do not truly allow for any parallelism. I add that it was not necessary for the Philosopher <note>This refers to René Descartes, whose "Meditations on First Philosophy" are being critiqued here, specifically his theory that error arises because the will is wider than the intellect.</note> to use that comparison of a certain reality between God and the creature in order to investigate the cause of error (which he was doing there); nor does he seem to have proceeded clearly in that place. Let anyone pay attention: for truly in that place, and in the subject matter he treats there, obscurity remains. He says that from evidence follows a *spontaneous liking* <note>original: *Spontanea allubescentia*; a Cartesian term for the will's natural attraction to a clearly perceived truth.</note> (which we have called the *spontaneous determination of thought*); that indifference (spontaneous indetermination) arises from ignorance or obscurity; that it is the lowest degree of liberty; and thus brings no perfection but rather imperfection or defect, even if it extends to those things which the intellect either does not know, or does not clearly know, and thus spreads more widely than the intellect. He adds that greater thanks should be given to God the more extensive that [will] is, or the more it extends itself beyond the intellect. This does not agree with what preceded, for here he supposes that magnitude to be a perfection, which he had denied above, and which is also false. Otherwise, an act fitting that magnitude—that is, a judgment extending itself beyond the perception of the intellect—would be a perfection (which he seems to have sensed in some way), and he would not be to blame, nor would it be an error. Which is absurd. It would have been enough to say that God, who owes nothing to the created Mind, gave it certain perfections, but not all those He could have; He thus left imperfections in it, among which is this: that while in the mind there is no spontaneous determination arising from evident perception, the Mind remains thinking spontaneously either in a *negative state* <note>Simply a lack of knowledge, like a stone not knowing it is a stone.</note>, that is, it thinks to itself that it does not know this or that; or in a *privative state* <note>A lack of something that ought to be present, like a person being blind.</note>, that is, it is carried toward a non-being as if it were a being, which is the source of error. These things will be further illustrated by what is to be said elsewhere.

### §. D.

->*7. In God there is a Liberty that is not Indifferent. 8. There is also an Indifferent*<-
->*liberty, which is positive, and the prerogative of God alone.*<-

**VII.** Although in Divine Thought there is no imperfection, I nevertheless observe in it a *Liberty* which has some similarity with mine, and that liberty is both merely *Spontaneous* (or most determined), and also *Indifferent* toward determination, according to the diversity of the objects, the truth, and the goodness of the things about which God thinks. I recognize Freedom in Him, not as a mere absence of compulsion, or as merely saying that the principle of Thinking is in Himself, but as stating that it is from Himself and toward Himself

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...Himself. I observe that **spontaneous Freedom**, or a determined *liking* <note>original: *allubescentiam*; a philosophical term describing the soul's natural attraction or "pleasing" toward a perceived truth or good.</note>, exists in God. This is by no means "indifferent" when His Thought is directed toward the object of absolute **Truth & Goodness**—that is, toward Himself. For without a doubt, God is not "indifferent" toward Himself, nor toward knowing, approving, or finding satisfaction in Himself, even though He is engaged in these acts with the highest degree of spontaneity and pleasure. It is just as much a part of the **Essence of God** that He is not indifferent to these things as it is part of His nature that He cannot be contrary to Himself, so that He is necessary.

There is no reason for anyone to take offense because I have classified this act—by which we conceive God moving toward the knowledge and approval of Himself—under the heading of **Freedom**. By using this word, I only wished to indicate that the source of the act resides within the being itself, and proceeds from the being itself. Nor is it a contradiction that I previously stated that God’s **Science** or Knowledge of Himself is not "Free" but "Natural," while only that knowledge which He has of other things should be called "free." In that earlier context, the word **Freedom** (which I am expanding upon here) was restricted to mean "indifference" <note>In the philosophical language of this period, "indifference" refers to the capacity to choose between two or more options without being naturally compelled toward one.</note>; thus, the dispute is merely a matter of terminology.

**VIII.** However, when I consider **Divine Thought** as it relates to natures, essences, truths, goodness, and other things that are not God Himself (since these are neither absolute nor independent), I judge that the **Divine will** has no necessary connection to them. Instead, He was "indifferent" toward them. This means He could have established, positioned, and preserved them, or not at all, or in this or that specific way; and whatever He determined, He determined from the mere "indifference of His pleasure." This was explained so extensively above in Chapter 10, and emphasized so frequently, that I would prefer the reader consult those specific sections rather than repeating the same points here. Yet I wish to note that this "positive indifference" is a privilege belonging to God alone, which cannot be shared with any creature, as it involves independence and the **Power**, or the **Force**, of establishing and decreeing reality.

There are certain things which—even if they are sometimes prompted by certain free Thoughts—are nevertheless joined to them against my will, so that this connection is not free. Such are some of the passions of the soul and turbulent disturbances, which sometimes follow certain free thoughts so closely that once the thoughts are present, the passions can hardly fail to follow. Nor can anything else be done regarding freedom in these cases, except that by spontaneously removing or placing the preceding causes, the following effects are removed or placed. This, however, does not hold true for all passions; for when they arise from a constant disposition of the "humors" <note>original: *humorum*; referring to the early modern medical theory where bodily fluids like blood and bile were thought to dictate a person's temperament and emotions.</note>, there is indeed more of an external and violent impulse present, even though they are partly felt as if they were in my mind. Finally, there are others which I perceive as if they come from bodies outside of my own, and as if they are located within them, such as light, colors, sounds, and the like. It is clear that these are present or absent against my will—and cannot be stopped or removed by the will—whenever the necessary movements [of those objects] are present or absent, very few of which are arranged by my own choice. From this it follows that I suffer many things because of things that are baser <note>original: *ignobiliorum*; literally "less noble." Indeed, [the soul] determines that these sensations become weaker and more faint. Where the cause is outside the body itself, the impulses are weaker; where it is partly outside and partly inside, the sensations are middling and mixed, terminating partly in the body and partly outside it, such as heat, hunger, and thirst. When that which is outside the body is further removed, or does not (and cannot) affect it vehemently, indifferent perceptions are excited, such as those ordinarily held through sight and hearing. 

But when something is presented as if it were about to strike the body easily and suddenly—either to destroy it or to perfect it—then more vehement agitations are added, by which the body is disposed toward meeting or fleeing external things. These general principles, if they were deduced more specifically, would present a marvelous beauty of <term>Divine ordering</term> <note>original: *Divinæ ordinationis*; the idea that the universe is arranged by God in a purposeful, rational way.</note> to those who contemplate them. There is also reason in these things for God to be praised: that through compulsions, disturbances, anxieties, loathings, the limitations of external things, and similar imperfections which occur in these states—and which call the mind back, as it were, from itself and from God—He has warned me that these are not solid goods. Thus, I should not seek to adhere to them of my own accord beyond the necessity of my connection with the body.

III. Therefore, the perfections found in these things, however limited and mixed with imperfections, are nevertheless not to be blamed. But it does not seem possible to place them so far beyond blame when they sometimes appear to deceive us positively and by the very condition of their nature. This occurs when either the passions or the senses recall the Mind to things that are either not as they are represented, or are going to be harmful to its connection with the body—such as when pain is felt in those parts that are actually missing <note>This refers to the "phantom limb" phenomenon, where an amputee feels sensation in a limb that is no longer there.</note>, or when thirst disposes a person with <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: *hydropicum*; dropsy (edema) is a condition of fluid retention; historically, it was noted that patients felt intense thirst even though drinking more water was harmful to their condition.</note> toward a drink that will harm him.

The question is: how can these and similar things, which are the operations of God, be reconciled with what has been demonstrated—namely, that God does not tend toward <term>non-being</term> <note>original: *non-ens*; in this context, it refers to falsehood, nothingness, or the absence of truth and reality.</note>, and that it belongs to His Wisdom to employ means that lead to a goal and do not deviate from it insofar as they are governed by Him? <term>Descartes</term> <note>original: *Cartesius*; referring to the French philosopher René Descartes (1596–1650).</note>, near the end of his **Sixth Meditation**, attempts to untie this knot; but, to express what seems right to me, he does not untie it. For he concludes that the nature of man, as a composite of mind and body, cannot help but be occasionally deceptive. The whole difficulty remains: Can the operation of God sometimes tend positively toward the false? Certainly, the reasons by which it is proved that it should not be thought of God that He ever tends toward non-being in any act...

...acting, or should produce deceptive operations, they are beyond all exception. Nor are the reasons which the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>original: *Philosophus*; here referring specifically to René Descartes (1596–1650), whose *Meditations* are being analyzed.</note> explains—namely, that the indivisible Mind is joined to a divisible body and to a specific part of it <note>This refers to the pineal gland, which Descartes famously proposed as the "seat of the soul."</note>, affected by neighboring parts, and that the fibers of the nerves are moved in the same way at their beginning, middle, or end—enough to suggest that sensation should be traced back to the extremities of the nerves rather than to their beginnings or middles. This is because it is usually to those extremities that the benefit or harm by which we are affected must be referred. Furthermore, from each motion, we perceive that one sense which most frequently leads to the preservation of a healthy person. These reasons, I say—even if they hold true materially or in the thing itself—do not have so much reality that this most real truth should be broken: ***God as an active agent never deceives in a positive sense***, or, ***None of His actions is positively deceptive*** <note>original: *Deus agens nunquam fallit positive*; "Positive" deception would mean God actively and intentionally creating a lie, rather than a mistake occurring due to the natural limitations of a physical system.</note>.

Indeed, it would be less troublesome to establish that perceptions of the body must be excited in the Mind not based on the identity or diversity of motions, but in a way that—whatever the motions might be—they are constantly corresponding to the state of the body as well or ill-disposed. This would be better than saying some operation of God is "positively deceptive." Yet the former does not happen; instead, the observations made by **Descartes** concerning the senses and the occasion by which they are excited are exactly how things are in reality. What, then, will you do regarding the difficulty proposed? I say that everything recounted about these sensations, supported as it is by experience, should not be rejected; but one must not conclude from this that there is an underlying fallacy in them, or that certain works of God are "positively" deceptive and erroneous in themselves.

**IV.** In order to see this more clearly, I will inquire: what can be called an "error" in these things? Surely nothing other than a deviation of sensations from the goal and use which God willed to assign to them. I observe that this goal, or use, concerns the connection of the mind with the body. I observe, furthermore, that it did not please God that this connection—at least in this state—should be indissoluble. I observe, finally, that the connection of the mind with the body is not merely forced and, so to speak, "brute" or <term>irrational</term> <note>original: *$\alpha\lambda o\gamma o\nu$* (alogon); meaning without reason or speech.</note>, but is in part rational, or a state in which reason has its own role, as is evident from the fact that the body can be ruled by will and reason. From these points, I conclude: those sensations should not be called "deceptive" which, due to uncertainty or obscurity, do not sometimes prevent the Mind from being dissolved from the body. For how could they "err," or deviate from their goal, if that bond of Mind and body was not decreed by its author to be indissoluble? Secondly, I infer that these same sensations are not to be considered deceptive if, when they alone are consulted, [they] destroy the union of the mind with the body...

But those who ought to use reason are unworthy of their humanity when they blindly follow their own impulses, such as those who are delicate, pleasure-seekers, and as many as are addicted to the senses in the governance of the body (whether healthy or sick); such people are deservedly regarded as beasts. Consult your intelligence; it will teach you that certain things must be accepted and others banished from the body—sometimes in agreement with sensations and appetite, sometimes without them, sometimes against them, and sometimes beside or beyond them—and it will teach you to form similar judgments about the state of the body. For if we ought not to follow spiritual impulses which propose a spiritual good to us without the use of reason (as was observed in the preceding chapter), much less should we follow the "brute" impulses which offer us bodily things. Therefore, the internal senses, whether they be Spiritual or bodily (the <term>faculties</term> <note>Lord Herbert of Cherbury (1583–1648) argued in *De Veritate* that humans possess innate "faculties" or natural instincts that lead directly to truth.</note> so celebrated by <term>Herbert</term>), are not safely brought forward on their own to prove anything. And more specifically regarding bodily sensations, one must not think these non-spontaneous perceptions were given so that we might be immediately impelled to act upon that toward which they seem obscurely to call us, or to judge according to them. Instead, they were given as warnings and signs, by whose arrival our **Reason** (and even the reason of others when we are weak) is called into counsel and warned that the state of the body must be attended to and properly provided for. This, then, is their use: to render the **Mind** solicitous for the body; and this goal they achieve. But as to whether the body should be cared for in that specific way and in that specific limb which are dimly indicated, or toward which those sensations call us—let a place be left for **Reason**, which has a right over the body for good cause. Even if Reason very frequently agrees with the senses, it sometimes calls us elsewhere than to the place where we would have rushed to ruin without it. In exactly the same way, although we seem to be called toward external objects by the perceptions of heat, colors, etc., through these sensations, Reason nevertheless does not call us there within, but teaches that such things are not in the external objects themselves, but within, in the **Mind**. ### §. D.
### 5. God suffers nothing in Himself. His sense is most perfect.

V. From those operations of God within me—which are not self-originating but also not deceptive—I move to the contemplation of God himself. But what I observe in Him on this occasion is free from difficulty: for in whatever way I look upon Him, I easily conceive Him to be absolutely **Impassible** <note>original: *Impassibilem*; the theological doctrine that God does not experience pain or changing emotions, and cannot be affected by any outside force.</note>, receiving nothing in actuality from another. He is such, firstly, in His **Knowledge** <note>original: *Notitia*</note> and His will, insofar as they are directed toward Himself. Secondly, He is such in His **Thought** <note>original: *Cogitatione*</note> about things and the determination of His will concerning them; for these do not come to God from the things themselves, as has been proven many times. Thirdly, He is such in his senses: for He has no senses similar to ours which proceed from an external source, since it is an imperfection to receive anything from elsewhere.

How He might be conscious of our sensations, however, is a rash thing to inquire. But a **Divine sense**—a sense of Himself with the most perfect joy—must not be denied to Him, even if it should not be called a "passion" <note>In philosophy, a "passion" is something one "undergoes" or is subjected to from the outside.</note>. This is because it does not flow from an external source, it is self-originating, it involves no imperfection, and it is inseparable from the Nature of the most perfect Being. For who could be called "most perfect" if they were claimed to possess all perfections, yet did not have in them complacency, delight, and supreme joy? Such joy does not differ from the consciousness of all perfections and of His own **Happiness**.

Meanwhile, any sense that implies an impression from something foreign, or inconstancy, or any other imperfection, does not properly belong to Him. The most serene Mind does not become angry, nor does He hate, nor is He moved by repentance toward anyone. Rather, the **Sacred Writers** <note>The authors of the Bible.</note> using those words are designating the changes in His operations—His presence or His absence toward sinners. This attribute, **Impassibility**, although a negative word, is nevertheless positive in its meaning; its difference from **Activity** has been explained elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XXI.
# (20) JUSTICE.

### §. A.

1. *Voluntary imperfections are unjust*. 2. *Justice in man*. 3. *Injustice, with several examples cited*. 4. *These affect man, but do not truly reach God*.

I. I notice in my **Freedom** <note>original: *Libertate*; referring to free will or the capacity for choice.</note> not only limits and imperfections insofar as all my thoughts are not stirred up within me according to that freedom (which is an involuntary impression); but I also detect other imperfections in it which are voluntary. This is because it is possible—and indeed happens all too often—that I voluntarily abuse my freedom and even disapprove of it. For instance, I might deny that I have committed certain things voluntarily in my thoughts, in my judgments, in the **governance of my body** <note>original: *corporis regimine*; how the mind directs the physical self.</note>, and in other matters, even though I truly perceive that I have committed them. Or, I might wish to govern my freedom differently than it ought to be governed. In doing so, both its true use and its governance are denied; this is indeed a great imperfection, and it is rightly called **injustice** <note>original: *injustitia*; in this context, it implies "unrighteousness" or being "out of order" with natural law.</note>. Before I take this opportunity to consider what ought to be understood by the **Justice** of God, I shall inquire more specifically into this injustice of mine, and the justice that ought to be in me as its opposite, so that these concepts and words may be rendered more distinct.

II. That which is **just** <note>original: *justum*</note> is that which is congruent, fitting, proper, and worthy of the nature and governance of some thing. Indeed, these terms—*just*, *proper*, and *fitting*—can be correctly used as synonyms. Therefore, since whatever reality exists in my nature, in the governance of my **Mind** <note>original: *Mentis*</note> and my body, in the rules of that governance—in a word, in everything that is or can be in me—since, I say, all of that is the operation of God, it follows that it is **just** for me (being an effect of God) to allow myself to be ruled by God. It is just to be disposed of according to His pleasure and rules; to let whatever He wills happen in me; and to be led by Him (who works all things) toward Him (the goal of all things). Nor should I hinder all those things He has joined to me—my body, external things, my neighbors—from being drawn toward Him through the connection they have with me. This is my justice in the state of nature, and it is rightly indispensable. This is how it is fitting for a true work of God to be ordered.

III. But if I resist this, then by resisting the **Divine operation** <note>original: *operationi Divinæ*; the way God acts upon and through creation.</note> I commit an injustice. The nature of this injustice—or rather, its absurdity—does not consist in the fact that something...
