->RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

...thence an incongruity <note>original: *incongrui*; something out of harmony or logically inconsistent.</note> in the **Nature of God** follows, whether in His pleasure or in His work insofar as it is from Him, but rather insofar as it must be admitted within me. If I ought to be a mere work of God, and yet I resist the work of God, then I harm and resist my very self, insofar as I ought to be that work; and this is absurd, incongruous, and ill-suited to that nature of mine which is and ought to be the work of God. This is **injustice** <note>original: *injustitia*; unrighteousness or being out of alignment with the divine order.</note>. 

If I attempt to act vainly out of myself, it is injustice; for in this way I wish to be a "non-work" of God, but a work of my own—that is, nothing. Yet it is incongruous for any being to positively strive toward nothingness. 

If I should desire that the **operations of God** <note>original: *operationes Dei*; the active ways God works within the soul or the world.</note> happen within me according to my own whim or pleasure, it is injustice: for the nature of God's work is the effect of God's pleasure alone, yet I wish it to be the effect of a "non-God" pleasure—that is, I wish for it not to be what it is, which is incongruous. 

If I should desire God's operations to happen in me, but not so in others, such as my neighbors whom I do not care for in the sight of God, it is injustice: for a true work of God represents God according to His pleasure, and is a channel through which the operations of God flow to others. But in this way, I do not represent the God who cares for all, and I refuse to be the one who carries out those things which belong to God’s work; the work wishes to be a "non-work." This is absurd. 

If I willfully govern my body such that my neighbor is not brought closer to God, but rather alienated from Him, it is injustice: I attempt to subtract God's works from Him in myself and in others, so that they become "non-works," and thus nothing. This does not befit the work of God. 

If, after I have committed an injustice, I deny having committed it; or if, after something just has been done in me, I deny it, both are a new injustice. The latter is a new injustice because God’s operation is denied directly; the former, because it is denied indirectly, and in its place is thrust forward something that is not God’s operation. Indeed, by denying that I have acted unjustly, I thereby affirm that God has always operated within me, and thus I boast of the injustice which is truly in me as if it were the work of God in me, or I take it upon myself insofar as I am the work of God. Yet it is indecent and incongruous for me, insofar as I am God’s work, to assert that I was made such by Him. On the contrary, it is just and fitting for one who is the work of God to manifest themselves insofar as and to the extent that they are (or are not) such a work: that is, one ought not to deny God's good things in themselves, nor their own evils.

### IV. These all serve to recognize the justice of God, and to distinguish it from that which ought to be in humans—provided that no one views these things from a corrupted principle, thinking (out of love for their own corruption) that justice consists in obtaining those things which they judge to suit themselves out of depravity. I have wished to see nothing else in these words except the justice of the nature of God, as well as the justice of God's pleasure; even though this pleasure is the rule for human justice, it is not yet human justice itself, nor the thing itself, nor the just work in...

# CONCERNING GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

Our righteousness or unrighteousness does not reach God, even though they are indirectly a useless attempt to make God not be God—namely, insofar as people wish to withdraw themselves from His **pleasure** <term>pleasure: (Latin: *placito*) God’s sovereign decree or what is pleasing to His nature.</term> and their dependence upon Him. It would imply that God does not have right and power over all things, and thus is not God. 

From this, it follows that the motive for **repentance** <note>original: *pœnitentiæ*; sorrow or a change of mind regarding past actions.</note> or sorrow for injustice should not be drawn from a consideration of ourselves, but of God. Or rather, if you like, from a consideration of ourselves insofar as we are not entirely our own, but His; and yet in many things—in our self-governance, in everything—we have willed to be "not-His." Otherwise, it would be absurd to grieve as if we had actually harmed the Nature of God or His pleasure, since that which we indirectly attempted is impossible.

->§. D.<-

*5. Justice exists in God's nature, pleasure, and work. 6. It must be extended beyond the punishment of evil. 7. V. In the **Supreme Thought** <note>original: *Cogitatione summa*; referring to the Divine Intellect or the Mind of God.</note>, those imperfections that I have already noticed in my own thought are not present. For whether that Thought contemplates and wills itself, or wills or works other things, indeed nothing **incongruous** <note>original: *incongrui*; something out of harmony or logically inconsistent with one's nature.</note> can be noticed anywhere. I perceive so clearly that a nature that is purely one, most perfect, and simple, is most congruent to itself, becoming, and thus just in itself, that I do not require a more laborious deduction of proof. 

Neither can I conceive of God decreeing or performing anything that is unworthy of Him, or by which He might testify either that He does not exist at all—that is, something that does not bear the mark of the existing God—or that He is not what He is; or that He does not want what He wants, or wants what He does not want. Therefore, no operation can proceed from Him that would show Him to be not independent, not wise, not powerful, not the Author of all good, not far removed from nothingness or self-hatred (that is, from evil), or not approving of His own work. In other words, one cannot conceive of anything unbecoming or any **injustice** in God or His actions.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS
<meta>catchword: or</meta>

VI. On the contrary, since it is fitting for God to portray Himself as He is through His own operations—if He wills to produce any—it is therefore just (for this **Justice** <note>original: *Justitia*; here referring to the cosmic order and rightness of God’s actions.</note> must be extended beyond the mere punishment of evil) that He should testify through these works that He is supreme, powerful, wise, good, the fountain of goodness, and the one who approves of what is good. (For this reason He preserves all things, and even those substances entangled in evil, because they are substances—that is, because they are His work—are sustained by Him and preserved from annihilation.) In the same way, as it is fitting for God to love and approve of Himself, it is fitting that He should be one who disapproves of that which does not love Him. If He allows any degree of reality or goodness to remain in such a thing, it is fitting that He also show by unmistakable and very serious signs that He does not thereby approve of evil or the neglect of Himself, but rather disapproves. This latter quality is called **Vindicative Justice** <term>Vindicative Justice: (Latin: *Justitia Vindicatrix*) In this context, it refers to justice that "vindicates" God's character. It is not petty revenge, but a necessary demonstration that God is holy and does not condone the rejection of His goodness.</term>, or **Simply Justice**. Yet Justice is improperly restricted to the punishment of evil alone; in truth, it is something much broader than is commonly thought. We see that it must be related to God’s Nature, to His every decree, and to His every work, so that nothing in them turns away from it, even though the ways of **Divine Wisdom** <note>original: *Sapientia Divina*.</note> are sometimes hidden in secret for a time.

VII. I shall attempt to derive a few points more specifically and clearly from these concerning God’s vindicative justice, since the chief fruit of these reflections is the illustration of sacred matters. When Vindicative Justice, which has evil creatures as its object, is said to be essential to God, we must not think that anything can be or has been taken away from God or the Divine Nature by creatures—something which would then need to be restored to Him so that the Divine Nature might remain consistent with itself. For if that were the case, something would be missing from the Nature or **Essence of God** <note>original: *Essentia Dei*.</note>. Rather, since God wills to depict Himself as He is through His works according to His pleasure, it is fitting that there be testimonies, marks, and serious, grand, and unmistakable signs in those works showing that God approves of Himself and the love of Himself, but does not approve of His opposite—the neglect of Himself. Therefore, this fitness, or Justice, should properly be called "essential" to the decree of God to represent Himself (as He is) through creatures (as He has now freely willed to establish them), rather than being directly essential to the Essence of God itself. If such testimonies are present, there is nothing further that the pleasure or will of God requires for its own fitness or justice, or for it to be conceived as worthy of God. By these testimonies, justice is satisfied; for in this way, it is vindicated from the insult and blasphemy with which it might be attacked—as if God approved of that which is contrary to Him, which would indeed be most unjust, or unbecoming to the will of God and to God Himself.

VIII. Now indeed, if I, who am a work of God, had allowed myself to be subject to God, then surely there would be nothing in me that would call into question the fitness of God’s decree to represent Himself in me. But after I willed to be **independent** <term>independent: (Latin: *mei juris*) Literally "of my own right." A legal term used here to describe the human desire to be one's own master, acting outside of God's authority.</term>,

# ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...if I have refused for God to be everything in me, but have instead denied Him and sinned, then although my essence and existence—or my **consciousness** <note>original: *τὸ conscium esse*; the author uses this to describe the basic state of being a self-aware creature.</note>—declare the sustaining power of God (and thus are not to be condemned or annihilated by God to that extent), nevertheless that denial of God cannot be conceived as pleasing, congruent, or fitting to the Divine will. It is fitting, therefore, for God to testify that the denial of Himself within me is not pleasing to Him. How shall He testify to this? What kind of testimony would that be? Would it be if God were to perform those good things in me in the future which He would have performed if I had not sinned, and if He were to sustain me in my rebellion in such a way that I might delight in my state, please myself, and be at rest? This is a foolish thought. Rather, it is if He ceases to work in me the good things He would have worked had I not sinned, and strikes unrighteous joys with restlessness; in this way, deprived of all goods, I would indeed be rendered utterly miserable in the future. Moreover, by persisting in the denial of God, I would continue to be eternally deprived of God’s best operations. Yet, in this way, my misery would vindicate Divine **Appropriateness** <note>original: *Decentiam*; the quality of what is "fitting" or "becoming" for God's character.</note> or **Justice**, crying out loudly that God utterly disapproves of the denial of Himself, and is completely alien and distant from it. Thus, the will that befits a Being who does not disapprove of Himself requires that a sinner be eternally miserable.

IX. However, I conceive that if I were not to persist in the denial of God and the embracing of myself over God—and furthermore, if I were to grieve greatly and most bitterly out of a displeasure for the sins committed and out of love for God, because I had wanted to be withdrawn from God’s authority and to be my own authority <note>original: *mei juris*; a legal term meaning "of one's own right" or independent.</note>—and if I were entirely restless in both mind and body, then I would be in that restored state in which the good will of God might most fittingly work in me again those things which had been interrupted. He would then bring to completion those things He would have done if sin had been absent, or perhaps even in a greater measure. Without this, it is impossible for me to think that God would communicate Himself happily with me. For whatever means I might think God could use, if the denial of God did not cease within me, if delight in the **not-God** <note>original: *non-Deo*; anything that is sought as an end in itself apart from God.</note> did not end, and if Divine love were not restored, then things would return to the point where God would be approving and embracing the neglect of Himself. Whatever "means" one might imagine would then have to be said to intervene only so that a constant denial of God, a **lack of love** <note>original: *non-amor*</note> for God, and a delight in the **not-God** could remain. Far be it from us to think such a thing.

X. But how could the cessation of the denial of God, this love, and the destruction of delight outside of God—how could a **holy sorrow** <note>original: *dolor sanctus*</note> arising from the love of God and the denial of myself (a thing good, perfect, and most real, which in itself is not evil or execrable, but if it is called such, it is only because it is a mark of an execrable thing, namely sin)—how, I say, could such good things be placed in me...

->### RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

...[continuation of the previous thought]... unless He who works all things also works these things? How indeed can I conceive of God working such great goods in me, a rejected sinner, in a fitting way, unless I first conceive that God has firmly testified that my evil is not pleasing to Him? The previous difficulty and the primary obstacle return. I cannot conceive that these greatest goods—and even that holy sorrow itself—can be placed by the Divine will into an unworthy subject <note>original: *subjecto improbo*; referring to the sinner as the "subject" or vessel of God's actions.</note> while still appropriately expressing His disapproval of the neglect of Himself. This cannot happen unless God has first testified to His supreme disapproval of that person. This obstacle returns like a circle, repeating continuously, until a specific kind of subject is provided: one who has nothing in himself worthy of God’s prior disapproval or displeasure, but who is most excellent and most precious. In this subject, there was no crooked will or denial of God; and yet, out of love for God and as a testimony of hatred toward sin, God fills this subject with the highest sorrows arising from the Supreme Love of God and a distaste for sin.

I maintain that both those holy sorrows must be the highest possible, and that subject must be the most precious and excellent. For since God is distant from sin beyond what can be imagined, the testimony that must be brought against sin ought to be more memorable and notable than can be said or thought. This could not be fully accomplished in me in this regard. And yet, since such a subject is not found in the natural state of men, it is the role of the wisdom of God to seek it elsewhere, and the role of His free grace to provide it.

But once such an innocent subject exists, and such a work of God has been performed in him, what shall afterward prevent the Goodness of God from fittingly wishing me so well that He works divine sorrows in me—and even in others, as it pleases Him—for the sake of His communion with me? What would prevent Him from bringing an end to my denial of God, and restoring those same operations which would have existed before sin, even if He does so gradually and in a different manner? 

Shall it now be said that there is still room for this insult—namely, that the Divine will, by working these goods in a sinner, acts as if it were not alienated from that which denies God (that is, from sin)? Certainly not, if God has most sufficiently purged and vindicated Himself from this insult by causing His beloved one—in whom there was previously nothing to be rejected—to grieve supremely for sins out of Divine love. 

Therefore, the Justice of God—or the **Appropriateness** <note>original: *decentia*; the quality of what is "fitting" or "becoming" for God's character.</note> of His will—will not prevent Him from subsequently placing those goods in me. Specifically: first, that I may grieve bitterly and out of love because I refused for God to be my everything and was the cause of the sorrows of the innocent one; second, that He may impose an end to the denial of Him that was in me; and finally, that He may restore His former operations in me. These things, in other words, you might express based on the outcome like this: Christ, by his death, vindicated the Justice of God and acquired for me **penitence** <note>original: *pœnitentiam*</note>, **repentance** <note>original: *resipiscentiam*</note>, and holiness; or, that I may bear his cross, denying...

### CHAPTER XXII.
# (21) TRUTHFULNESS.
### Section A.
#### 1. *The injustice of lying, fraud, treachery, etc.*

I. Among the preceding imperfections of Spontaneous Thoughts, this one must also be counted: that it can happen that I might deny those things about myself which I not only knew to be true, but which I myself willed, approved, and promised. This is a species of injustice, and it is called by the specific name *Lying*, or rather *treachery*. If I have promised something, yet do not perform it, injustice cannot help but lurk there, either in the promise itself or in its denial. For if I have testified that I desire and will that God, in certain circumstances, work something in me that is directed toward others (for that is what it means to "promise" in a sound sense), and if that which I willed to be done through me does not please God, then indeed the promise is rightly broken; but what was unjust in that promise was that God's displeasure was mistaken for a work to be done by God through me. But if the promise was concerning something good and pleasing to God, and yet it is not performed, it is an injustice: for if He does not perform through me that thing approved by Him and by me, it is because [to] His operation...

### §. D.

#### *2. God’s Truthfulness in His promises. 3. Verbal and natural promises.*

II. It is also clear enough from what has been said about the Justice of God that this Injustice must be removed from Him. For it cannot be imagined as fitting for the Highest Being <note>original: *Ens summum*</note> to disapprove of what He approves, or indeed to be changed. On the contrary, it is fitting for a constant God, who does not stray from His own decree, to show Himself as the fulfiller of His promise through its eventual outcome. This justice or "fittingness" is called *Truthfulness* <note>original: *Veracitas*; the quality of being habitually truthful or the impossibility of God deceiving others.</note>. Therefore, if He has promised that—even though I once refused to be ruled by Him—He will nevertheless rule all my thoughts in a singular way, or if He has promised me His grace notwithstanding my sin, I am able to demand it from Him through His Justice; that is, His truthfulness. This is because it is fitting and just that He does not deny, but rather establishes, His own promise.

III. It should be noted that among the promises of God—which are the objects of this truthfulness—one should not only include those things which God has signified He would do through certain words or writings. One must also include whatever He has presented to the mind as certain through any signs, ideas, or testimonies, whether through physical bodies or immediately through His own thoughts. Indeed, whatever God shows to the mind through ideas regarding the state of things—not only the future but also the present—He holds out as a kind of promise. For He effects all things; He outwardly brings to pass and fulfills those things which it is clearly established He inwardly marks out and, as it were, promises or sends beforehand. This knowledge—*Truth meets the one who uses the intellect correctly* <note>original: *Recte utenti intellectu veritas occurrit*</note>—which God has worked in our minds in such a way that it cannot be doubted, is like a primary promise. All other truths which God has impressed upon the Mind—and from which, when correctly observed, the existence of certain things or modes is inferred—are strengthened by this prior promise. They should not be brought into suspicion of being false, because God is Truthful. That which He has willed, unconquerably and insuperably, to be known by the Mind as present or even future, must be thought of as His own will; He is not to be thought of as disapproving or rejecting that will through the eventual outcome. Such a thought regarding Him would be an insult.

# (22) H O L I N E S S.
## C H A P T E R  XXIII.

->§. A.<-

**1. The Impurity and Holiness of the Soul.**

<margin>I.</margin>This too is one of the many imperfections just noted, which arise from the abuse of my freedom: namely, that I can willingly suppress my thoughts and all my spontaneous affections so that I cling to and am fixed upon things viler than I am. These things are less than the operations of God within me, which are most fitting and suitable to my state. This happens if I cast myself down toward things of an inferior nature, or try to drag them up to myself, or if, for their sake, I hinder the more divine operations of God in the mind. It occurs if I renounce these divine operations and grant their place to inferior things, as if they were superior. For example, this happens if I surrender my mind and affections to riches and metals <note>referring to gold and silver currency</note>; if I give myself to the care of the physical, sensual mass that is soon to perish; if I yield to vain rumors or to empty and ineffective thoughts about myself. Finally, it happens if the Mind <note>original: *Mens*</note>—which is placed for a moment among muddy things <note>original: *inter lutosa*; refers to the physical world/flesh</note> to be tested whether it prefers to cling to God rather than these, and thus to be separated from them (except insofar as certain things must necessarily be used and can and should be directed back to God)—if the Mind, I say, nevertheless entangles itself in those things while the divine work in the mind is neglected. In these matters, how great is the imperfection and how much is it to be blamed! For in this way, those things which God has perfectly separated and even distinguished by nature are most poorly confounded. It would be more orderly for heaven to be mixed with earth, water with fire, or precious things with filth, and for all things dissolved from their bonds to be mixed together, than for the thoughts of the Mind to be subjected to mud, and to desire to be occupied, penetrated, and filled by it. Therefore, when this occurs, these states are not undeservedly named after impurity, dissolution, and filth—being called "filthy," "impure," and "dissolute." Conversely, the acts by which each thing is set apart with those of the same status, and are rightly arranged and established <note>original: *sanciri*; the author is linking the word for 'establishing/consecrating' to 'holiness'</note> in their own degree and use, are rightly given names from purity and holiness. For the words *Holiness*, *holy*, and similar terms, designate a state or a commerce <note>social or spiritual interaction</note> of a thing with those things that are not unworthy of it.

RATIONAL THOUGHTS

# §. D.

*2. 3. 4. What is the Holiness of God? It is demonstrated. It is declared in Creatures through opposite ways. It must be referred to Justice.*

<margin>II.</margin> These things help me to conceive what should be understood as signified by the Attribute of Holiness as it relates to God. Indeed, I easily perceive that nothing else can be meant by it, except that God is separated from everything that is vile, or unworthy of His Nature, or His pleasure, or His work: indeed, from everything that does not clearly resolve back into Him. For everything that is non-God is unworthy of God. And although the work of God is not God himself, God nevertheless returns to himself in that work, and is everything there: it is the work of God for this reason, because God sees there Himself willing, working, and being all things. God is never absent from Himself—whether in reality, in pleasure, or in any work; all things are from Him, through Him, and to Him <note>original: "a quo, per quem, ad quem"; a standard theological formula describing God as the source, means, and end of all things</note>; He is foreign to any other principle, motive, purpose, action, or thing; He needs nothing; He excludes everything that is plainly foreign to Him, and whose entirety does not resolve into the one God. Therefore, if He wills anything, He wills Himself, He wills His own pleasure, and the representation of Himself in that thing: He wills to meet Himself. He seeks Himself within Himself through the adorable generation <note>Likely referring to the internal life of the Trinity or the eternal production of Divine ideas</note> and His communion with Himself; and He likewise seeks Himself outside of Himself in the shadowy production of things <note>A philosophical way of saying the created world is a faint reflection or "shadow" of God's reality</note> and His communion with them—or rather, He seeks that which, by reflecting Him in its beginning, middle, end, and all things, may finally be resolved, in its entirety, back into Him alone, whom He solely intends. Otherwise, nothing worthy of God with which He might communicate could be found.

<margin>III.</margin> And this is the Holiness of God, essential to Him and to be conceived in Him—most easily indeed if we suppose no creatures exist, but also evidently so once creatures are posited. For whatever happens, the <term>Concept of Being: *Conceptus Entis*, a fundamental philosophical category used to define the nature of existence</term> of the most perfect and most sufficient Being, which is everything to itself, is the concept of a being unable to seek or find anything outside of itself that is not either itself or of itself. Therefore, when evil exists (so to speak)—which is not from God, nor reflects God, but rather denies Him as much as it can—God shows that He is as far removed from it and from all impurity as possible. He does this both by preserving from evil those whom He loves (that is, those in whom He loves the representation of His own love, or even Himself), and by abandoning and punishing those who have willed and possessed it. And thus, in both cases, He shall be declared Holy through opposite ways.

<margin>IV.</margin> From these things it is clear that the Holiness of God must be referred to His Justice: nor [can] the concept we have of Holiness [be separated] from the concept of Justice...

# CHAPTER XXIV.
## (23) INFINITY.

### §. A.

->*1. The Mind, being capable of growth, is limited, without respect to spaces.*<-

<margin>I.</margin>Recalling the observations I have had so far concerning my Thought, however specific they may be, I return to more general ones with which I shall conclude these remarks. The first of these was reviewed in number twenty-two: that there are no perfections in me which cannot receive new degrees of increase—and these indefinite—that is, which cannot become more and more perfect. I do not, of course, conceive them as being closer to the essence of God than they are, or, speaking absolutely, closer than even "nothing" itself might be; for all things are infinitely distant from this essence. But they can nonetheless overshadow or represent it more or less, according to the pleasure of God. Therefore, I conclude from this that the perfections of my Thought are circumscribed by certain limits, since increase is nothing other than the further extension of a limited thing, or of its limits. Nor am I speaking here of spatial extension <note>The author is careful to distinguish between "growing in perfection" and "growing in size," as the mind has no physical dimensions</note>, or the limits of spaces; it would be foolish to attribute those to the mind, and to its cognition, judgments, love, and so on. Rather, as stated, I speak of the limits of perfections or realities suitable to the nature of my thought. I observe nothing here that I have not previously seen with evidence everywhere.

RATIONAL THOUGHTS

not only are their limits known, but we are convinced by positive reasons that they have none, nor indeed can they have any, but rather possess the fullest abundance that can be conceived by men and by God, which leaves no room for any further intelligible addition. And this very thing is held immediately, without reasoning, in the concept of the Supreme Being, the most perfect, of Pure Thought.

III. And this is what is to be understood by Divine Infinity—not some coarse phantom <note>original: "crassum aliquod phantasma"; the author is criticizing a physical or materialistic imagination of God's nature</note> such as they have often imagined in the schools <note>Referring to Scholasticism, the medieval system of philosophy and theology taught in European universities</note>, namely, an Infinity of spacious extension. They absurdly pushed this forward as a way to explain the Divine presence; they brought it into the open as if it were an unshakeable truth, merely to repel something that seemed to stand in the way of their own fiction. Namely, when it had been said by some that the extension of the world should be conceived such that no limits are prescribed for it, they objected that Infinity was thus attributed to the world—an Infinity which, however, belongs to God alone. They argued it was absurd to posit that the world is infinite, since God alone is such, and to say another is infinite is to deny Him. Behold thoughts truly worthy of the Infinity of God! For what? Is Divine Immensity the same as the Infinity of spacious extension, which they complain is being attributed to the world (even if it is called "indefinite" rather than "infinite" by others)? <note>This likely refers to René Descartes, who distinguished between the "infinite" (God) and the "indefinite" (the universe) to avoid theological controversy.</note> They certainly think so, if they complain that what is proper to God alone is being attributed to the world when they think the world is being established as infinitely extended. These absurd fictions about God have been defeated elsewhere. It is false that the Infinity of God is attributed to the world, even if it were called infinite in extension (which it is not called, nor can a determinate judgment be made on this matter). The Infinity of the world, if there were any, would be of a nature very different from Divine Infinity, for it would involve many imperfections—such as no one is ignorant can be found in all extension <note>The author assumes the reader knows that physical matter/extension is inherently imperfect because it is divisible and changeable.</note>—and thus it would be an infinity not absolute, but in a certain respect, and therefore of finite perfection: namely, that of extension. On the contrary, Divine Infinity is absolute and excludes all imperfections, for it is an Infinity of Thought, an Infinity of Intelligence, an Infinity of Dominion, Goodness, Power, Wisdom, Constancy, and in one word, of Each and Every Attribute. Any of these is called infinite because no reality or perfection is absent from it, but each and all are one and the same greatest and most perfect reality. This is how we are brought back to Simplicity <note>original: "Simplicitatem"; the theological concept that God is not "made of parts" but is a single, unified essence.</note>. This, therefore, is the true Infinity, proper to God alone. On this matter, there exist, among others, the memorable words of Augustine in the *Confessions* (a), which I cannot help but record here.

...had placed [the idol] in his heart, and it had become again a temple for his idol, a thing abominable to You. But after You caressed the head of one who knew it not, and closed my eyes so that they would not see vanity, I withdrew from myself for a little while, and my madness was put to sleep. This is a quotation from Book VII of St. Augustine’s *Confessions*, where he describes moving past his earlier, materialistic Manichaean views of God toward a spiritual understanding.</note>

IV. Some have attempted to raise difficulties here, where nevertheless there are none, since nothing is easier to conceive than the infinite. It is a concept that places us beyond the danger and fear of attributing more to it than it actually possesses, because it is obscured by no limits and is not rendered difficult to perceive; finally, it fills all our thoughts more simply and with more quiet satisfaction than any other thing. Nevertheless, some say it is absurd to speak of the infinite, because it cannot be grasped by our intellect, and therefore such talk consists of "words without a mind" <note>i.e., meaningless sounds</note>; or indeed, if it is said to be grasped, they argue it is against the very notion of the Infinite to be grasped by something finite. 

I respond: although it cannot be "grasped" <note>term: *capiatur* (grasped/contained); the author distinguishes between understanding that something exists and fully containing it within the mind</note>, it does not follow from this that no discourse at all should be held regarding it. It only means that we should not speak of it as if it were a thing that is or could be fully contained. Next, it must be noted that it is one thing to **comprehend** the Infinite with adequate knowledge, but quite another to **conceive** of the Infinite—even if inadequately and obscurely compared to the knowledge the Infinite has of itself—yet clearly and sufficiently enough for us to be certain that in Him lies the fulfillment of all perfections. By the first assertion, the Infinite would be enclosed by limits—namely, if it were claimed that a created Mind could have a concept of it so exact and full (that is, a concept of infinite Power, infinite Wisdom, and so on) in the same way the Infinite knows itself. 

But this absurdity is avoided when, in the latter sense, it is affirmed that the human Mind knows Divine Thought well enough to judge that it lacks all imperfection—or rather, that it is endowed with every perfection—which is to say, it is infinite. We sufficiently conceive His Power so that, even if the Mind can determine nothing about its specific objects, it nonetheless acknowledges that nothing can resist it. The same applies to the other attributes that can be observed in God; our knowledge of them is clear enough for us to judge them to be most real, most simple, and therefore Infinite in God. 

What deceived those men was a double phantom: first, they focused on the infinity of space; second, they used their **imagination** in this matter rather than their **intellect**. And since they could not imagine (as indeed one truly cannot) an infinity of extension, they wrongly applied this failure to the concept of God. Will they then profess that they do not know God to be without defects? To know this is precisely what it means to conceive of an Infinite God.

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...the whole infinite? I respond that the infinite <note>original Greek: τὸ infinitum</note>, in the sense provided, just as it is most simple, denies any parts whatsoever. Thus, it is asked absurdly: "Do I conceive of a part of the infinite?" How can I conceive of a part where it is the very essence of such a concept to conceive of no parts? "But then," you will say, "do you conceive of the whole infinite? Is the infinite—its essence and form, infinity itself—in your intellect, in your concept, in your thought?" I say that neither the infinite itself nor infinity are in my thought and knowledge, for if they were, my thought or knowledge would be God. Rather, in the mind there are certain outlines, such sketches, and shadowy designations from which I perceive that God, the infinite, exists. Nor is it necessary that these outlines possess within themselves the same perfections as that which they represent; otherwise, they would no longer be sketches, but the original itself. Nor is it unfitting for Divine infinity to be represented in a way that is not most perfect. On the contrary, it would be unfitting for it to be represented most perfectly by something different from itself; if something most perfect were placed outside of God, it would be a denial of God, since two most perfect things cancel each other out, as was seen in the section on Unity. Nor should you say that the question here is about representing the infinite most perfectly in an *objective* way <note>term: objective vs. subjective reality; in early modern philosophy, "objective" refers to the content of a thought (the thing as it exists in the mind), while "subjective" refers to the actual being or nature of the thing itself.</note>, rather than a *subjective* way, as if these two do not cancel each other out in different things. For this last point is false. Indeed, when dealing with thinking things, if I say, "this thought represents most perfectly this most perfect and infinite thought," it is the same as if I said, "this thought possesses a most perfect and infinite thought most perfectly," or "it thinks that thing most perfectly," or "it is most perfectly thinking"—which is to say, it is itself an infinite and most perfect thought. Thus, a perfectly objective representation or image of the infinite cannot be given except in an infinite subject. This is why the Son of God, the objective image or representation of God, must be acknowledged as God subjectively, because He is His most perfect image. It is not so with our mind, in which, besides shadows—though wonderful ones—nothing absolutely perfect exists.

VI. I say wonderful, for certainly it must be confessed that there is something wonderful here, and indeed, however it is explained, something astounding: namely, that the infinite is represented by a tiny thing—almost nothing—in whatever way that happens, yet in a way not unfitting for the infinite. How can any thing (my thought) exceed itself and the condition of its own nature? How can it have representations, or variations and modes of thought, more excellent than its own nature is? Can any modification exceed the nature of its substance? Can iron, remaining as it is, [have] modifications...

...I only perceive that if it had pleased God to create [the soul] with this condition, that it should exist for a certain time and afterwards cease to exist, that is what would have happened. Indeed, since I am not my own work, it does not depend on me that there should be more or less existence in me than I might wish; rather, I must expect whatever my Maker <note>original: *Fictori*; a term for a creator or fashioner, often implying a craftsman like a potter.</note> has seen fit to decree regarding this. II. Perhaps the effort will not be in vain if I attempt to inquire here and briefly set forth the reasons by which the **Immortality of the human Mind** is proved. These reasons are to be deduced from a consideration of the nature of the Mind—which is **Thought** itself—and from certain attributes of God. Truly, account must also be taken of the word *Death* or *mortal*, which admits of several meanings. In this way, whatever must be concluded on this matter will be clearly held.

III. **Death** in general, in its simplest sense, is understood as a certain cessation and a lessening of existence; and it can be referred either to a **substance** or to its **modes** <note>term: 'modes' (*modi*) refers to the specific qualities, shapes, or states that a substance can take on—for example, 'roundness' or 'motion' are modes of a physical body, while a 'specific idea' is a mode of the mind.</note>. These produce a fourfold meaning of death, any of which could be multiplied by many subdivisions, which I omit. (There is no need to treat here the composite made of several substances—the separation of which is also called death.) Now, since extended substance with its modes is really distinct from the Mind and its modes of thinking, who does not see that no room remains for this doubt or question: *Is the mind mortal in the sense that the body is mortal?* Indeed, it is well known that no substance or extension of any tiny body is ever annihilated. But even if it were supposed that every body is mortal regarding its substance—that is, that every extended thing would eventually cease—what has this to do with the mind? Would the mind also die in that same sense, that is, cease to be extended? **Absurd.** How shall the mind cease to be that which was always foreign to it? We must judge similarly regarding the death that causes certain modes of the body, which were present before, to cease. When those bodies, which are properly said to be "generated," are resolved into particles—which have other shapes, other motions, and a different structure than before—when their organs collapse, their parts (whether sensible or insensible) are separated, scattered into thin airs, mixed with earth, with waters, with which other [vapors]...

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...compose vapors, mud, grass, insects, and so forth; then they are said to die, because the former modes <note>term: 'modes' (*modi*) refers to the specific qualities, shapes, or states that a substance can take on—for example, 'roundness' is a mode of a wax ball.</note> by which all these things were joined and sustained in one **System**, cease to exist. Is the **Mind** to be called mortal for this very reason and in this sense? Or is it to lay aside the former shapes, motions, the joining of particles, and the position it once had, and—through parts shaped, moved, and arranged in other ways—be mixed with air or water or earth to compose certain bodies? How absurdly it would be asked whether the Mind is going to lay aside modes which it never had, nor can have by its own nature! Is it necessary to say explicitly that the Mind is not mortal in the sense that the body is called mortal; and to recommend this argument as if it were some excellent and highly memorable discovery? Indeed, this kind of argument has been made necessary by the very crude prejudices of those who have imagined Minds to be like bodies, or like a thin portion of air, or fire. But it would have sufficed for them if the **real difference** between the mind and the body were shown; once this is established, it seems unnecessary to point out that one cannot lay aside the modes of the other—that is, to die in that sense.

IV. But if we come to that meaning of **death** which, when applied to the mind, asks whether some or all of its modes of thinking—or **Thought** itself, the very substance <note>term: 'substance' (*substantia*) refers to the fundamental essence of a thing that remains the same even as its 'modes' change.</note> of the Mind—are going to cease to exist, we then approach the heart of the difficulty, although the difficulty is not equal in all these cases. For as far as certain modes of the mind are concerned, since there is no doubt that some are destined to cease in the mind—and they cease daily for a very long time, or even sometimes forever—there is no doubt that the mind can be called mortal to that extent, with respect to those specific modes. Therefore, the Mind can be called mortal, or even dead, insofar as (for example) it has laid aside all modes of thinking about earthly, vile, and base things; this is the **death of the saints** <note>original: *mors sanctorum*; a theological concept of 'dying to the world' or letting go of worldly desires.</note> and is truly pleasing to God. Likewise, death can be attributed to every mind separated from the body, insofar as it is stripped of the modes of thinking that occur through the external senses—hunger, thirst, bodily pain, and pleasure—which it perceived on account of the body. Furthermore, nothing prevents us from calling the mind "dead" when it is deprived of its most noble and excellent modes of thinking—its greatest gifts and perfections, such as the contemplation and love of God. Indeed, it can be called dead with greater right than a body is called dead when deprived of its own remarkable modes, having become an awkward and useless mass, a stinking corpse. This is called **spiritual and moral death**, which the sacred Authors often discuss. Now, the author addresses whether the Mind can die in a psychological or spiritual sense, and critiques René Descartes' view on the immortality of the soul.</meta>

->### RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

...is entirely that state in which black, dreadful, and enduring things, mixed with no leniency or hope, follow; it is even said to undergo death. But let there not be a primary question about all these things now.

V. The question is asked: will all **modes of thinking** cease in a created mind, so that nothing in any way—whatever it may be or could be—thinks or perceives anymore? This is the opinion of certain "sleepers" <note>This refers to *Psychopannychism*, the belief that the soul "sleeps" or loses all consciousness between death and the final resurrection.</note> who assert that the Mind is stripped of all thoughts upon separation from the body, and is thus dead until a certain fixed time. I respond: as long as the **substance of the Mind** itself is supposed to remain in actuality, it must be concluded that it also thinks in actuality, or is conscious. For this is the very nature and substance of the mind, as has been demonstrated elsewhere. And just as a body existing in actuality cannot be stripped of all bodily **modes** <note>term: 'modes' (*modi*) are the specific states or configurations of a substance—like 'warmth' is a mode of water.</note> at once, but must necessarily be endowed with some; so a Mind or a thought cannot exist without being in some state, or thinking in some way, whatever that may be. But if it is supposed that the **substance of the Mind**, or **radical thought** <note>original: *Cogitatio radicalis*; the fundamental essence of the mind that makes thinking possible.</note>, ceases, then by this very fact it is clearly inferred that all modes of thinking also end. Thus, the difficulty of this matter, and indeed the whole thing, is resolved into this question: **Is the thinking substance, or the Mind itself, going to cease to exist?** Regarding the **Absolute Power of God** <note>A theological concept (*Potentia Dei absoluta*) referring to what God could do by His sheer power, regardless of the laws of nature He established.</note>, there is no question of whether God *could* do this, speaking absolutely. Rather, the question concerns what will happen according to God's good pleasure: namely, has it pleased God that the Mind, which is joined with the body, should last only until the body is dissolved—after which it would cease to exist?

<margin>(a) Descartes, *Meditations*, in the **Second Replies**, number 7.</margin>VI. Many people believe that this question cannot be solved without the **verbal revelation** of God. Among these is **Descartes** (a), who says:
> *Regarding what you add—that the immortality of the soul does not follow from its distinction from the body, because it can nonetheless be said that God made it of such a nature that its duration ends with the duration of the body’s life—I confess I cannot refute this,* etc.
And later,
> *It is for God alone to answer;*
and he immediately recurs to revelation. His reason is that these things depend on God's free will and decree. But that reason carries no weight in this matter; for even the essences of things, ideas, and truths depend on God's free will (as he himself acknowledges), and yet we determine many things about them—even future things, as in physics—without revelation. Or rather, we acknowledge and announce them as determined by God. Why should we not also attempt the same regarding the **perpetual existence of the Mind**? Indeed, it is not believable that God, who has revealed to us so many things in nature—and quite minute ones at that—would have hidden from us in nature a matter of the greatest importance of all: namely, whether we, he, and all things are to become, respectively, nothing or everything to ourselves.

->### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.<-

Indeed, revelation itself—which rebukes for ingratitude those who did not give due thanks to God after inspecting His works—convinces us by that very fact that there are testimonies in nature concerning the praises due to God, who acts both well and powerfully within nature. This applies even more to the immortality of the soul, for which the greatest praises are due to Him, since the soul is a Divine work of His Power intended to continue within the nature of all things, and serves as the basis for many of His other operations. Therefore, we shall seek those testimonies by which God shows that the existence of Minds <note>original: *Mentium*; the author uses "Mind" and "Soul" almost interchangeably here to refer to the thinking, immortal part of a human.</note> will by no means cease, even if the body is dissolved.

VII. These testimonies arise either from the contemplation of God himself or from His works. To these latter works, we refer to the fact that God has so arranged things that, although all things to which a Mind can be joined might be conceived as destroyed, the concept of the destruction of the mind does not necessarily follow. Among created things, it is clear that nothing acts more upon the mind—and the Mind in turn suffers more from nothing—than the body proper to each Mind. It is so much so that if ruin were to be feared from the destruction of anything, setting aside all other things, it would be feared from nothing more than from the ruin of the very home which each Mind inhabits, by whose fall <note>The author uses the metaphor of a house collapsing to describe the death of the physical body.</note> it might perhaps be crushed. But this doubt lacks reason: for,

1. The Body (an ignoble <note>term: 'ignoble' (*ignobilis*) in this philosophical context means "lower in the hierarchy of being" or "lesser," rather than "shameful."</note> and less perfect substance) is not annihilated when the mind is separated from it; why then should the mind (a nobler and more perfect thing) be thought to be annihilated when the body is separated from it? No reason can be alleged for the continued duration of bodily substance when released from the soul that does not, by greater right, apply to the Mind. But if I should say that it is evident to the senses that the body remains after the soul has left it, but not so for the soul; that is neither true of all parts of the body which are dissolved, nor is the perception of the senses as firm a means of proving the existence of bodies as the reasons soon to be alleged for the immortality of Minds from the perception of God's attributes.

2. The body dies, or rather changes its modes <note>original: *mutat modos*; the author argues that "death" for a body is just a change in its state or configuration, not its total destruction.</note>; therefore, to say the mind must be annihilated would be absurd reasoning. For such logic does not only pass from one subject to another of a different nature (as if I were to say: water evaporates, therefore also the diamond which is in it—even though a diamond is more similar to the nature of water than the Mind is to the nature of a body); but it also concludes wrongly, since at most it could have been concluded that changes in the *modes of thinking* also occur in the mind when something similar happens in the *modes of the body*.

3. Since the Mind's most intimate and noble thoughts do not depend on the body, nor does the body contribute to understanding, to reasoning, to contemplation, to the love of spiritual things, and other acts—except in the same way that shackles contribute to a walking prisoner <note>A classic Platonic metaphor: the body does not help the mind think; it merely limits and directs its movement while the mind is "imprisoned" in the physical world.</note>, as was seen in the first Book—it follows

->## RATIONAL REFLECTIONS<-

it might be concluded that when the body is removed, these faculties—and thus the mind itself—are by no means abolished, just as a prisoner is not annihilated when his chains are loosened, nor is he deprived of the ability to walk. Rather, these faculties are increased and perfected, and it is then that the mind is most active and vivid. Granted, the *exercise* of those faculties that required a bodily medium may perish—such as those concerning the external senses or the heavy sequence of physical pains and pleasures—and perhaps even, if it pleases the Almighty, those very faculties themselves, or the power of perceiving in these ways in the future. Yet, should the Mind, thus liberated from its heavy burdens and tormentors <note>original: *crassamentis tortoribusque*; the author views the physical body's limitations and sensory pains as weights or "torturers" that restrict the soul.</note>, be said to perish for that reason? Certainly, it would be more just to say that a body which was made invulnerable and unalterable, and freed from those things that could harm it, had "perished" or "died" because of that liberation.

Perhaps, indeed, you will suspect that the more noble faculties of the Mind and their exercise depend on the proper state of the body, because in sleep the Mind seems absorbed, losing all the vigor of its faculties. This, however, ought not to happen if the mind, when removed from the body, were to possess vivid faculties. For since the mind is freed from many bodily objects during sleep, should it not be freer then, when it is more restored to itself, if it were truly independent of the body? 

I respond that in sleep the Mind is not free from the body, but remains closely joined to it. However, the Body—or rather the animal spirits <term>animal spirits: In early modern science, these were thought to be very fine, subtle fluids that transmitted movement and sensation through the nerves.</term> and their instruments, by which the Mind is directed—are not then in such a state that the Mind can spontaneously direct their movements, as they are languid, inconstant, interrupted, and fading outside of wakefulness. Hence, during sleep, by the force of the union still enduring, languid, interrupted, involuntary, and fleeting thoughts are excited in the mind, which seem either to be almost non-existent or entirely absorbed. The Mind is more heavily burdened in sleep than in wakefulness. The chains then grow so heavy that they do not allow the prisoner to walk freely, but instead cast him down. 

But if the mind, whether in sleep or in any other state, were less bound to the body than it usually is, there is no doubt that it would possess a nobler and more spontaneous exercise of its intellectual faculties. Hence, in diseases that loosen the bond between the Mind and the body, there are sometimes noble ecstasies, sublime thoughts, and the discovery of things previously hidden. And

He himself—and truly so, as the outcome proved—regarded these as signs of the dissolution of his Mind from its partnership with the body. Is it not also true that those who withdraw the Mind from its partnership with the body to such an extent that they become accustomed to using the pure intellect without the imagination, do they not have...

Finally, I cannot suspect that the body itself, or any creature, can properly be the cause of the death or annihilation of the soul: for since the life opposed to that death is nothing other than the sustaining of the mind’s existence, and death is indeed the cessation of that sustaining; that which does not sustain the Mind cannot cease to sustain it, or bring death upon it. As the body did not create the mind in the past, so it does not sustain the mind now, nor, for the same reason, does any other creature; Therefore, it cannot be the cause of its annihilation—nor can any creature, or any creature’s will, power, or action. God, therefore, the Creator and Sustainer <note>original: *Creator & Conservator*; a standard theological pairing emphasizing that God not only makes things but actively keeps them in being.</note>, has so disposed all things that no just suspicion concerning the immortality of the mind can be held. This ought rightly to be taken as an argument in favor of it in matters of the greatest necessity.

->### VIII.<-

Perhaps someone might think of it this way: Although the body is not the cause producing and sustaining the Mind—nay, although it has no necessary connection with the mind, nor is it absolutely necessary to conceive of the mind just because the body is conceived, nor the destruction of the mind upon the perceived dissolution of the body, just as one does not conceive of the mind's presence simply by the body's presence: yet, just as God was pleased for the mind to begin to exist once the generation <note>meaning: the biological creation or birth</note> of the body occurred; so who knows, setting aside revelation, whether God has pleased that the Mind should no longer exist once the corruption <note>meaning: the physical decay or death</note> of the body occurs? This is so even though, as was said, the concept of the Mind's existence and destruction is not precisely involved in the concept of the body's generation and destruction, as is clear to one who pays attention. And this is indeed the ultimate boundary of doubt <note>original: *ultima dubitationis meta*; the furthest point one can reach using logic alone before needing divine revelation.</note>, beyond which it is not possible to go. To this it would suffice to respond, by the example and comparison already cited, that however adverse it may seem, the force of our assertion is by no means weakened, but rather strengthened: for, just as we do not conceive of the Mind (which did not previously exist) existing simply because the body's generation has occurred—nor do we affirm it for that reason, but rather, having been taught by experience and the most certain signs, we judge it to be present—so, upon the destruction of the body (which does not involve the concept of the annihilation of the previously existing Mind), it should not be thought that the Mind ceases to be, unless this is established by the most certain experiences and reasons. Since these are lacking, we must judge that the Mind's prior existence continues. ...once the body is removed, those faculties—and therefore the mind itself—are by no means destroyed, just as a prisoner is not annihilated when his chains are loosened, nor is he deprived of the ability to walk. It may be that the exercise of those faculties which required a physical medium perishes—such as those concerning the external senses, or the coarse series of bodily pains and pleasures; indeed, if it pleases the Supreme Being, those very faculties themselves, or the power of perceiving in these physical ways, may cease in the future. But should the Mind, thus liberated from these dregs and torturers <note>original: *crassamentis tortoribusque*; the author uses "torturers" to describe how physical sensations and pains can constrain and afflict the soul.</note>, be said to perish for that reason? Certainly, one might say with greater justice that if a body were rendered invulnerable and unchangeable, and were freed from all those things that could harm it, that body itself should be said to perish and die.

Perhaps, however, you might suspect that the nobler faculties of the Mind and their exercise depend on the body being in a proper state, because in sleep the Mind seems to be absorbed along with all the vigor of its faculties. This, you might argue, ought not to happen if the Mind possessed vivid faculties when removed from the body. For since in sleep the Mind is freed from many physical objects, should it not be freer then—when it is more restored to itself—if it were truly independent of the body?

These motions, outside of waking hours, are languid, inconstant, interrupted, and vanishing. Hence, while sleeping, through the force of the bond that still lasts, there are excited in the mind languid, interrupted, non-spontaneous, and vanishing thoughts, which seem to have been either almost nothing or entirely absorbed. 

The Mind is more burdened in sleep than in waking. The chains then become so heavy that they do not allow the prisoner to walk freely, but rather cast him down. But if the mind, whether in sleep or in any other state, were less bound to the body than it usually is, there is no doubt that it would possess a nobler and more spontaneous exercise of its intellectual faculties than usual. 

Hence, in illnesses that relax the bond between the Mind and the body, we sometimes see noble raptures, sublime thoughts, and the uncovering of things previously hidden.

### RATIONAL THOUGHTS

...we are convinced by reasons, without which we rightly judge that it <note>Referring to the soul or a created substance.</note> remains in its first state, that is, in nothingness; we also bring forward these same reasons so that we do not suppose whatever we please to be defined as existing, unless a certain reason and valid cause is held for this very annihilation of the thing. Without such a cause, the thing must be judged to remain in its prior state—that is, in the existence which it previously enjoyed—unless we wish to judge a matter, without any cause, contrary to what is clearly known to have just been the case; which is to say, unless we choose to err knowingly.

IX. But so that there may be an end to all dispute and conflict, I will now state how it is affirmatively established that God wills that no mind should cease to exist. This, as has been said, depends on the <term>good pleasure of God</term><note>original: *placito Dei*; this refers to God's sovereign and rational decree, rather than a whim.</note>. Now, the good pleasure of God—besides extraordinary revelation (which is prophetic)—is chiefly evident from those things which are described in the internal notions of the Mind, or are founded upon them. Since nothing among these is clearer or more evident than the knowledge of the Divine attributes, as is clear from all that has been said, we conclude most firmly that God wills to be acknowledged by us in this way. Thus, if a concept of some attribute concerning my own Mind (for example, that I ought to be carried toward God by love) is clearly joined to the knowledge of some divine attribute, I cannot deny it without obscuring that divine attribute and ascribing to it things that are unbecoming and insulting. It is plain, therefore, that such a concept of my mind—or that attribute of my mind—must be held as most true, pleasing to God, and established and decreed by Him.

Certainly, I know of no firmer means of proof in the whole universe of things than that which is so founded in the knowledge of the Divine attributes that it cannot be denied without these being—I will not say destroyed—but insultingly misrepresented. This is not because there is any danger to the attributes of God themselves; whatever humans may decide, those attributes are secure in themselves. But if there is any danger, it lies in our knowledge of them, which could be defiled and obscured by those falsehoods by which the light of the knowledge of God would be cut off from us. 

That is exactly what happens in this case. For if the *mortality of the Soul* is asserted, then *God's Justice*, *Constancy*, *Wisdom*, *Retributive or Vindicative Justice*, *Holiness*, *Truthfulness*, *Goodness*, and *Gloria* are by that very fact misrepresented. They are presented to our perception with such disgrace that they could not even be thought of, let alone attributed to Him, without horror. Conversely, when we contemplate their ideas in their proper beauty—which we hold to be God's good pleasure—the Immortality of the soul is inferred from them, which in turn illuminates the knowledge of those attributes as much as possible. And these things are thus evident.

X. (1) *From the Justice of God*. God, by His good pleasure, created the mind so that it might, in its very substance, to some extent foreshadow the perfections of God. It is a work worthy of His pleasure and His Power, and therefore, it is not to be annihilated. For...

### ->ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL<-

...convinced that God, in establishing and working, approves of Himself, and therefore does not disapprove of His own true work. For I would be affirming without cause that God does not approve of Himself as the one establishing and working, if I thought He destroyed His own work and rebuked Himself as if He had not acted or consulted well. Would not the propriety or **Justice of God** <note>original: *Justitia Dei*</note> be attacked by my thinking in such a way? But, you say, evil is found in the mind, and evil is *not* the work of God. What of it? It will soon be seen that the Mind ought not to be annihilated for that reason. But for now, it shall suffice to note that the substance of the mind itself is not evil. The radical perception itself, or consciousness, is good; it is the work of God, and it remains. Why would you suggest that God disapproves of it? Conceive of Him disapproving of the "alien work"—sin—while His own work continues to exist.

XI. (2) **From Constancy joined with Justice.** I am bound to think of the **Most Perfect Being** <note>original: *Ente Perfectissimo*</note> that it is fitting for His works to bear the most real image of His own constancy, so long as experience does not scream otherwise and reason does not prove the contrary. To conceive of the **Constancy of God** in the most worthy manner, and in a way consistent with His propriety or Justice, we must hold that God approves of this constancy in Himself, in His own decree, and in His works—that is, in His own records and sketches. And therefore, that which is good in His works, and which can never become evil regardless of what happens (namely, the **Substance of things** <note>original: *Substantia rerum*</note>, and specifically of Minds—setting aside their temporary state, of which I do not speak—the substance, I say, of things is always the work of God), must be judged to remain constantly. The contrary cannot be established except by someone who—changing and entirely removing those things which could be the images of Divine Constancy according to his own whim—would not fear to boast that his own concepts are most worthy of a perfectly constant God.

XII. (3) **From the knowledge of Wisdom, the same Immortality is proven.** Who would say that I correctly and properly conceive of the **Wisdom of God** in establishing and placing those things which are outside Himself, if I were to state that God had given to some simple substance a noble and most remarkable faculty—the very foundation of all things—which almost continually tends toward something, and yet this "something" or its object was never to be given? Would it not then be a frustrated and useless faculty, created by God along with its inclination? Who would dare attribute to the Wisdom of God that He gave men the faculties of seeing, hungering, thirsting, and loving, and placed in them inclinations toward objects, but yet willed to provide nothing visible, nothing edible, nothing drinkable, and nothing lovable which they might ever enjoy, no matter what they did? Who would not blush to slander Divine Wisdom by suggesting He acts in such a way? And yet He gave a most real and noble faculty...

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

The **Desire for Immortality** <note>original: *Desiderium Immortalitatis*</note> is inclined toward its object with intensity, fervor, and constancy in all people. This is true for both the virtuous and the wicked—even though the latter wander in their methods, wishing only to live perpetually in a coarse and pleasure-seeking way—yet all deeply desire immortality. If God had proposed that the possession of this object, immortality itself, could in no way be acquired, and if He were going to reduce Minds to nothingness, this would be a foolish impiety. 

Lest any room be left for a false objection—by arguing that many people have the capacity for ruling, teaching, or other skills, yet lack the objects for them (such as a kingdom or students)—let it be noted that the question here concerns a thing, a faculty, and its inclination, which are the most simple and common traits among all created things. We are discussing an object that is not a "particular" thing (the kind that cannot be possessed by many people at once), nor is it an object of a different nature than the one desiring it, nor something external, fictitious, or impossible. On the contrary, we are dealing with a **common object** <note>original: *objecto communi*</note> that belongs to the very nature of a **thinking thing** <term>thinking thing: *res cogitans*, a philosophical term for the mind or soul</term>, since it is itself the continuation of thought. Thus, it is an internal, true object, already materially existing (for it is existence itself), for whose duration the Mind pants with full desire.

(4) Furthermore, who could conceive without horror of that same **Wisdom** <note>original: *Sapientia*</note> according to which all things are arranged, if it were conceived in such a way that it arranged for virtuous Minds to be so afflicted by harms and "crosses" from the wicked (as often happens) that they are reduced to nothing by a horrific end through the destruction of the body? And this at the hands of those wicked men who, after living peacefully for a long time, finally undergo the absolute end of a long and wealthy life alongside the virtuous, and fall into the same state of nothingness as them?

XIII. (5). **Vindicative Justice** <term>vindicative justice: *justitia vindex*, the aspect of justice concerned with punishing wrongdoing</term> against evil minds does not demand that their substance be annihilated, as was stated in its proper place. In fact, the true concept of this Justice is denied if one supposes that God, once a sin is committed, reduces the sinful minds to nothing or ceases to sustain them. For by doing so, it would be established that God is silent and behaves, once sin is admitted, as if nothing at all had been done or admitted. To **annihilate** <note>original: *annihilare*</note> is to behave as if nothing had happened. In this view, God would be considered no more distant from evil than He is from nothingness. To Him, a mind sinning would be the same as a stone lacking the power of sight; it would be as if He were testifying that He disapproves of His own hatred for sin, leaving the matter in nothingness. All of these ideas strike against the knowledge we have of God.

XIV. (6) **Divine Holiness** <note>original: *Sanctitas Divina*</note> cannot be rightly conceived by me unless I confess the immortality of Holy and virtuous Minds. For how could I assert that Holy Minds—who love God, are His friends, and represent God in all things—are to be destroyed by that God who [loves] Himself, His own pleasure,

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL

...seeks and approves His own image in all things? To whom, if not to a hater and enemy of holiness and Divine love, should we attribute the will to destroy—along with pure minds—that very holiness and love of God which those minds embrace and cherish? This is a thought too atrocious to be considered applicable to God.

XV. (7) I also conclude the immortality of the soul from the **Veracity of God** <note>original: *veracitate Dei*; the philosophical principle that God, being perfect, cannot deceive His creatures</note>. God has impressed upon my mind the most evident idea of immortality: He has proposed it as a goal possible to be acquired; He positively inclines the Mind toward it; and when all things are surveyed as diligently as possible, new testimonies regarding the certainty of immortality are discovered in the works of God (which have preceded us). Those who make the best use of their faculties, having examined all things, cannot help but be led spontaneously and without indifference to be persuaded of the immortality of souls. Indeed, even the impious themselves, when they bid farewell to coarse objects in whatever way and contemplate spiritual things, having searched through all their hiding places, are so conscious of a **future state** <note>original: *futuri status*</note> that they can set aside that consciousness by no clever arguments or considerations. Unless all these things be from God, unless they be testimonies of His pleasure and promises of a future state engraved within us, tell me, I pray, what signs would be fit for testifying to the will of God? And who would deny that an outcome corresponds to those things by which we are positively, powerfully, and inevitably led to affirm something—the operations of God in our mind being most clearly perceived? Who, I say, would deny this, except a wicked slanderer of Divine Veracity and a destroyer of that knowledge in the Mind? Therefore, just as it is true that men ought to abstain from insolence toward God, it is equally true that they are convinced that created Minds are, by the Divine pleasure clearly engraved on those minds, **Immortal**. This was never denied or called into doubt by any probable argument, but only for vain, foolish, and impious reasons. If anyone truly wishes to be securely persuaded of this truth without many complex reasonings, let him only guard himself against that **spiritual death** <term>spiritual death: *mors spiritualis*; usually referring to the soul's separation from God through sin or lack of awareness</term> which was spoken of at the beginning. Otherwise, it is not so surprising if the wicked, in order to escape eternal death, greatly desire to fall back into nothingness; and some, blinded by the habit and the just judgment of God, may persuade themselves that this will be the case.

XVI. We pass over several other demonstrations, such as those which can be solidly deduced from the **Goodness and Glory of God** (concerning the latter, as a specific point, nothing has yet been said); for from what has been stated, the truth of this Proposition is sufficiently clear: **The human mind will never cease to exist.** This assertion is not opposed to the one I brought forward at the beginning—namely, that if God had absolutely willed to arrange things otherwise, and to overshadow His attributes in me in another way...

<margin>
(a) *The Art of Thinking* <note>original: *Ars cogitandi*; this refers to the famous "Port-Royal Logic" by Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole, a seminal 17th-century text on logic and philosophy</note>, Part I, Chapter VIII.

XVII. Concerning the **state of the Mind released from the body** <note>original: *statu Mentis à corpore solutæ*</note> (to say something of it here), nothing can be precisely or specifically determined, because this depends on the pleasure of God, which has not been entirely revealed. Meanwhile, a general idea of it can be held, if it is assumed that no other sudden and violent change occurs beyond what is known to change; that is, no such change that passes from one contrary state to its opposite. Instead, all things should be thought to remain in their primary state, as far as can be conceived, and to become more and more rooted in it through the habits of the intellect and the will. Furthermore, according to the rule governing the state of minds, they should be thought to increase indefinitely in the strength of their morals and customs. In conceiving the state of the immortal Mind released from the body, there is no reason to depart from these two rules, which are established as true here, and which would be asserted elsewhere to change without cause, or even falsely. Therefore, **First**, it must be thought that Minds released from bodies—provided they are indeed released and have no further connection with them—also no longer have any perceptions of those things that are immediately or directly excited in us through the bodily organs, without which they would never be perceived. Thus, as long as Minds do not take up a body again, they are entirely deprived of the perceptions of the external senses—sight, hearing, and others—and of their objects, as well as of bodily pleasures or pains. For this reason, it cannot properly be said that **Souls separated from the body** <note>original: *Animas à corpore separatas*</note> are tortured by some unknown fire. For although pain, even bodily pain, exists only in the Mind, and bodily fire (as God has arranged it) can provide the occasion for a painful perception—as the author of *The Art of Thinking* <note>see margin note (a)</note> rightly observed—this cannot be supposed to happen in Minds released from the body (a) from such a fire, unless the very hypothesis that those Minds are released from the body is destroyed. If they are judged to be separated by death from the body that subjects the mind to the senses, they cannot be judged to be tortured by **hellfire** <note>original: *igne tartareo*; literally "fire of Tartarus," referring to the classical or biblical concept of hell</note> or any other physical fire; for to suppose this, it must be assumed that they remain united to some body, or are united anew (at least to the fire itself). Since this is not evident from nature, it must not be affirmed without a revelation of the divine pleasure.
