### Hh 2

...real things were applied, it was a spontaneous thought by which they willingly, beyond necessity, excited themselves to think about, seek, embrace, and accumulate earthly things, so that they might take pleasure there. They became accustomed to being struck and carried away by love, hope, hatred, anger, and anguish due to the presence or absence of these things. There is, I say, reason for us to think that those minds will retain these habits, notwithstanding the dissolution of their connection with corporeal things, since these habits did not arise from the necessity of that connection, but were born spontaneously from the mind itself, and were spontaneously rooted there. And since these Minds are usually habitually ignorant, and so will remain; and since they are to be endlessly vexed with their firmly fixed phantasms <note>original: *phantasmatibus*; in this context, it refers to mental images or sensory impressions of physical things that the soul can no longer touch</note>, the objects of which they will no longer be allowed to enjoy; and since they are to be struck and torn apart by those passions with which they were accustomed to torture themselves due to the lack of what they desired—how great must the misery of this immortal state be considered!

XIX. Thirdly, we have from these same principles that those Minds which, in this life, applied their intellect and affection to sciences and Knowledge of corporeal and earthly things—such as in Physics, Mathematics, many Histories, and other such fields; or even of Divine things, such as in Theological matters, in those things concerning Religion, in the literal study of scripture, etc.—and which are occupied in these with self-love, delight, satisfaction, pride, and self-estimation, seeking, rejoicing, and delighting that they are, and are held to be, so great, so learned, subtle, and spiritual; or if they are not held as such by others, or even by themselves, and do not find a way to rest in the idea of their own science and excellence as they would like, suffering instead as they are suffocated by anger, anguish, and hatred: we understand that such minds, after their separation from the body, turn into **Diabolical Minds** <note>original: *Mentes Diabolicas*; the author is describing a state of high intelligence coupled with absolute egoism, mirroring the fallen state of demons in classical theology</note>, or similar to Diabolical ones. For a pure Mind—that is, one released from the body—which is understanding, learned, and proud, disposing of its acts and passions according to its own spiritual self-estimation, is a Diabolical Mind. This is the most certain outcome of the sciences, even those which treat of the most Divine and most Spiritual things, where they are possessed by anyone without humility and self-denial. **Do not therefore be lifted up with pride, but fear.** <note>A reference to the Latin Vulgate, Romans 11:20: *Noli altum sapere, sed time*</note> Nothing else will follow from a more evident knowledge except the troublesome reminder of the Magnitude of the absent Good, and the clear and undeniable conviction of a huge fall and evil, reverberating perpetual tortures of thought from the habit of self-love (the worst principle and one not pleasing to God).

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS

For them, after leaving the corpse behind <note>The author uses the stark term *cadaver* to emphasize the physical body as a discarded shell after death.</note>, they will no longer be disturbed by vain and evil things, but will be habitually and constantly absorbed by the knowledge and love of God. 

For just as the fundamental state of being remains constant as something evil in others, so it persists as something good in these people. And although the labor—which the Mind performed in sweating to eliminate and delete the smallest folds and final marks of evil inclinations, and in acquiring the perfection of most holy habits in the total surrender of oneself to God—may not have been fully completed when the Mind was released from the body, nevertheless, a constant principle remains. This principle of turning away from vanity and applying oneself to the one God remains "stored deep in the mind" <note>original: *alta mente repostum*; a classical allusion to Virgil's *Aeneid*, referring here to a principle rooted in the very depths of the soul.</note>, fixed and penetrating the foundation of the soul, always offering itself and always welcome. Once the release [of death] has occurred and the obstacles of temptation that fostered involuntary imperfections are removed, whatever "traces of ancient deceit" <note>original: *priscæ vestigia fraudis*; a reference to Virgil's *Eclogues*, used here to describe the lingering remnants of original sin or past bad habits.</note> remain will be deleted quickly and easily, and the goal which was solely aimed for will be obtained. Regarding those things which will happen when bodies are resumed [at the Resurrection], Divine revelation must be consulted as the sole source of knowledge. But that revelation says this of the principal goods: *What we shall be has not yet been revealed* <note>original: *Quod erimus nondum patefactum est*; a quote from 1 John 3:2.</note>.

### §. D.

->*21. God is Immortal in a more noble sense than the Soul, and in a way unique to Himself alone.*<-

XXI. Whatever must be said hereafter about the *Immortality of God*, since it is evident in itself, it will suffice to note in a word. Truly, I conceive not only that God is not mortal, but that He is not even immortal in the same sense that I said the Mind is immortal. No perfections of God will be diminished in any way, much less in a way that would reduce them to absolute nothingness. ### CHAPTER XXVI.
# (25) GLORY.

->§. A.<-

*> 1. There is no occasion for the Mind's glory regarding itself. 2. This is proved from the Mind's vain phantom of itself. 3. From the consideration of God as the worker. 4. From the consideration of His work in general. 5. From the consideration of the work insofar as it is a thinking thing.*

I. I come now to the final consideration with which I closed the number of my previous observations about my Mind: namely, that having seen all these various imperfections of my mind, and the total dependence of its perfections upon the will of another, there is no reason why I should think so highly of myself, or present myself to be stared at and admired.

II. I would not wish to say that the gifts and works of God within us should be passed over in silence or thought, or even despised; nor should they be denied or hidden by a false affectation of humility. There is no place for a lie, nor should the operations and images of God be disapproved of wherever they may be, by anyone who loves justice. But it happens most often that men, when considering their own good qualities (which are from God)—for I am not speaking here of those who are puffed up by their own evils—it happens, I say, that when reflecting on the works of God within themselves, they look at themselves as if they were distinct and separate from those works. In this act of reflection, they consider themselves as something apart from the works of God within them. Thus, they contemplate a <term>phantom idea</term> <note>original: *ideam phantasticam*; here meaning a mental fiction or a "false image" the mind creates of its own ego.</note> of themselves as distinct from God’s work. This phantom is actually nothing, since everything that is not the work of God is non-existence. Yet, they attribute those good things to this phantom self, as if this "self" were more worthy than the phantom ideas others form of themselves, and as if they were more suited to receive those gifts than others are. In this way, each person evaluates, praises, and inflates a vain specter of themselves based on God's gifts; they take joy in contemplating <note>original: *contemplatur*; the text ends mid-word with the catchword "pla-" pointing to the next page.</note> that idea of self as something distinct from God's gifts...

III. Certainly, if there are many things in me—and indeed however excellent these gifts and works of God may be—upon which I might wish to reflect by contemplating them and considering them as being placed within me, I am convinced of one thing. Whatever I could suppose for myself, or for that subject <note>In philosophy, the "subject" is the underlying "thing" that possesses qualities or undergoes experiences.</note> in which those works exist, it can be nothing other than one of those very works of God. It is something that He Himself first established, placed, and sustained out of the mere liberality of His most free pleasure <term>placitum</term> <note>The term "placitum" refers to God's sovereign choice or "good pleasure," suggesting that creation exists because God simply willed it so, not because of any external necessity.</note>. Upon this, as a base, He has likewise imposed other gifts out of the mere freedom of His will, as many and as great as He pleased. So much so that if it is asked: "Why was this placed here, and why was that or another thing added to it?" nothing can truly be assigned as a reason except the pleasure and operation of God. Namely, it pleased God by His own choice to work this first, to establish the connection of this first thing with another, and to work this second thing out of freedom, and so on, adding work to work solely for His own pleasure. Therefore, if a cause for the reality of any position must be assigned, proved, or if it is to be rejoiced and gloried in, nothing at all occurs to me to bring forward except the voluntary pleasure of God, and His good will toward me and others. For this reason, one must glory and rejoice in this alone: that His will is the "all in all" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:28, implying God is the ultimate reality in everything.</note> within all things, besides which there is nothing. Thus, in all reflections, one must tend toward God.

IV. A work—a shadowy work, a non-necessary work—is not something absolute but relative. It is relative to the worker, to the substantial worker, and to the free pleasure of that most substantial worker. Whatever reality I am, and whatever is in me, is continually such a shadowy and non-necessary work. Therefore, in the consideration of oneself, not even in the slightest thought should the "end point" <note>original: "terminus"</note> be fixed upon the self, or upon some phantom that does not work all things by its own pleasure—a non-God. One should not adhere to the self as if it were something substantial, nor approve of it with an approval that ends in that thing itself, nor wish it to be approved by others. To do otherwise is to take away and deny God—the origin, exemplar, and end of all things—and substitute an absurd nothingness for Him. Nor is it fitting for me to think of others differently than I think of myself in the manner just demonstrated. For they, and all things, are nothing but occasions for praising and approving God alone, who works all things out of goodness. Apart from Him, they are from themselves, to themselves, and through themselves not a work, not a shadow, not even something accidental; they are absolute nothingness.

...simply <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with "pliciter," likely completing "simpliciter" (simply/purely) from the previous page.</note> as a thinking being—not for the sake of that operation itself (that is, just so the operation could exist), for the same could be said of the most unreasoning beasts, and the creature would then be its own goal. And as for the fact that—beyond the consciousness of God working within me—this same God has made me somehow aware of certain other things (since He has given me ideas of others, or made known to me that He works in others and brings it about that they glory in Him once He is recognized): He has shown this to me not so that I would merely be aware of others (which is a form of empty knowledge) or praise them, but so that I might be conscious, and rejoice, and glory in the fact that God exists and is held by others to be the one who is **all in all** <note>original: "omnia in omnibus"; a common theological phrase suggesting God is the ultimate reality within every part of creation.</note>.

### §. D.

->*6. The essential glory of God. 7. The relative glory of God in creatures. How glory is given to God. Why God is to be glorified and praised.*<-

VI. But when God reflects upon Himself and—insofar as He can be conceived as differing from Himself—contemplates Himself, He is that one who meets Himself alone. To Himself, He is all things; to Himself, all His perfections belong indivisibly. And since He exists as the one who approves of those things which are in Him, He cannot but rightly refer that most perfect approval and estimation back to Himself, and let it begin and end with Him. And this is the true **Glory of God**, which is **essential** <note>original: "essentialis"</note> to God: that from Himself, toward Himself, and through Himself, He considers and approves His own perfections and Himself, and that He holds a good testimony of Himself to Himself, and a good consciousness of His own being.

VII. We also conceive of a glory in God that regards Him only through the mediation of His good pleasure <term>placitum</term> <note>As noted previously, "placitum" refers to God’s sovereign and free will.</note> and His effects. Specifically, we perceive that God approves and values every one of His choices and works, and refers them back to Himself as their model, author, and goal. In this sense, God is said to have established all things for His own glory—namely, so that they might be **shadows and images** by which God is represented as approving of Himself and as being the one who is all things. For this reason, this glory is also said to exist **objectively** in creatures, and even the most unreasoning beasts are said to give glory to God. However, a certain more special glory from minds...

...[by the] Holy ones <note>original: "Sanctis"; refers to the "others" mentioned on the previous page who recognize God's work.</note> is said to be attributed to God, it comes back to the same thing; for this glory is the work of God within those minds, nor should it be thought that any glory of God can proceed from a Creature as if from the creature itself. God Himself effects that glory of His in them and through them—or rather, He renders Himself glorious in them, and creates them (by a singular benefit) for His own glory. He Himself places more excellent outlines <note>original: "delineationes"; an artistic metaphor suggesting God "sketches" His image into the soul.</note> of Himself within them, and brings it about that their Minds are both spontaneously directed toward understanding and loving the glorious nature of God, and that they allow the work of the Divine pleasure to be done in themselves, considering it as a painting and a result of the most glorious God. In this way, truly all things are done through the holy ones for the glory of God.

But meanwhile, let it be noticed (as has been said) that this Glory is not essential to the Nature of God; for if God had willed to will nothing different from Himself, this glory would not have existed. Nothing can be conceived that could be added by anyone—not even by God—to the Divine Nature as something essential to it. He is not rendered more magnificent or more adorned in Himself. All of this must be traced back to the pleasure of God in such a way that, if He has produced images of His glory in minds, and if those minds praise God, one must not think this is because He has need of it, or because it is necessary for Him. Rather, He wills to be shadowed forth as glorious in His own [creatures], and they ought to be carried along in this highest fervor, because it graciously pleased Him to will it to be so. **Verbal glory**—speaking, singing, etc.—which many so stupidly embrace as the true glory of God (and indeed of themselves), has no place here, where we are dealing with thought alone; and when it stands alone, it deserves to be called smoke and a lie.

...for perhaps hardly anything regarding these matters can be shown that cannot be sufficiently and conveniently illustrated through these principles. For this reason, all the opinions, difficulties, and controversies held by others concerning these things have not been reviewed, since the single presence of truth is itself sufficient to dispel any clouds without further preparation.

II. Now if, for the sake of custom, a classification of Divine attributes is requested, it is sufficiently clear from what has been said that the first and most useful division is that of attributes by reason of Nature or Essence—such as *Intelligence*, *Height* <note>original: "Altitudo"; refers to God's exalted state or transcendence.</note>, *Infinity*, etc.—and attributes by reason of God's Pleasure <note>original: "Placiti"; referring to God's sovereign will or choice.</note>, such as *cognition*, *Indifference* <note>original: "Indifferentia"; in this context, it refers to God's absolute freedom of choice, not a lack of concern.</note>, etc. Indeed, under almost every attribute, or rather the name of an attribute, this classification lies hidden, as has very often been noted in its proper place; but because this is commonly neglected, confused, or overlooked, it has hindered the clarity and ease of concepts regarding these matters in no small way.

III. But if, for the sake of memory, more specific classifications are sought so that the Divine attributes may be recounted in a certain order, hardly any others can be given than those taken from the occasion of things distinct from God. Among these—besides that which anyone is able to take from the occasion of their own thought, as has been observed—the following may be employed. Divine attributes can be conceived either from the occasion of the universe of things in general—which universe, since it is one, varied, whose members communicate with one another, and is large (yet something can be added to it, nor is it totally grasped)—here we are permitted to think of God’s *Unity*, *Simplicity*, *Goodness*, *Height*, *Infinity*, and *Incomprehensibility*. 

Or they may be conceived from a more specific consideration of things: if you look at existence regarding its principle, from there we conceive *Sufficiency* and *Power*; regarding its duration, *Eternity* and *Constancy*; regarding its end, *Immortality*. If you look at the essence of things, and indeed in general—whether things are thinking beings or otherwise, whether they are future or not—you conceive *Dominion*. If you place before your eyes the Essence of thinking things and their nature specifically, there occur to you regarding God: *Life*, *Spirituality*, *Activity*, *Intelligence*, and *Liberty*. If you consider the state of their nature or degrees of perfection: *Knowledge*, *Impassibility* <note>original: "Impassibilitas"; the theological concept that God does not experience pain or changing emotions from external causes.</note>, and *Happiness*. If you consider governance: *Wisdom*, *Justice*, *Truthfulness*, *Holiness*, and *Glory*. All of these are indeed what have been proposed in the preceding chapters so far, though in a different order. The manner in which these attributes occur from those considerations was noted in the first six chapters, but in the others, because it is very easy, it was omitted. However, lest anyone be disturbed that *Intelligence*—which many conceive as a hypostasis <note>original: "hypostasin"; a technical term for a distinct person or substance, often used in Trinity doctrines.</note>—is called an attribute here, let it be known that the intention here is not to dispute such matters; and therefore, by "attribute" nothing else is meant here...

# RATIONAL REFLECTIONS

...to be signified here than whatever can be thought about God. This is what had to be pointed out first.

IV. I would place this last method of describing and knowing the Divine attributes after that one which was proposed from the beginning—derived from the inspection of Thought alone—and employed afterward. For this last method, being drawn from foreign and unknown matters and partly from scholastic terms <note>original: "terminis scholasticis"; refers to the specialized, technical vocabulary used in medieval university philosophy, which the author finds needlessly complex.</note> not understood by everyone, gathers no small amount of obscurity. But the former method, which I have followed, is so natural and so easy that nothing more evident or easier could be found in a natural and discursive state. It is natural because, without the help of laborious art, thoughts can present themselves to anyone—almost in the same order as above—just as those concerning myself occurred to me, from which I returned to God. It is also extremely easy, since it is founded both on certain perfections that are within us (or rather, which do not differ from our very selves) and, for the most part, on the uncovering of many imperfections so well-known to us that it is impossible for anyone not to feel them within themselves. One is convinced that these are truly imperfections, and thus immediately possesses an actual idea of the absolute perfections opposed to them—that is, of God Himself. For it seems impossible to recognize something as imperfect without comparing it to the knowledge of the opposite perfection, known by that very act, as demonstrated before. Therefore, since the very imperfections of Thought are used to serve that degree of knowledge concerning God which was explained in the preceding pages, there does not seem to be any Mind, however imperfect it may be, which—using reason—cannot reach that point. Once this is acquired, it may aspire to further things; for this is not the final step, indeed, it is scarcely even the beginning.

V. Therefore, lest a destructive confusion arise here, I would wish to warn again and again that the knowledge of God, along with the method of acquiring it as it has been treated so far, is proposed only as *natural*. It is that which can occur to anyone from innate principles, through right reason, and according to the truer laws of reasoning. This is so that the ineffable and far more perfect knowledge of God remains untainted and untouched—that knowledge which the Spirit of God (its sole Teacher and distributor) pours in during a state of self-denial and rebirth <term>Regeneration: the spiritual process of being "born again" or renewed by divine grace.</term>. It is this which truly deserves to be called the Theological and Christian knowledge of God; it does not contradict the former natural knowledge, but rather fulfills or, more accurately, absorbs it. But today, it is not uncommon for a "Theological Knowledge of God" to be passed off which is acquired and obscured by devious arts, and—if the Scripture is occasionally used—is encrusted with words perceived without Spirit or reason. Such knowledge becomes worse than natural knowledge, and indeed, in many ways, worse than even pagan knowledge <note>original: "Ethnica"; referring to the beliefs of non-Christians or "heathens."</note>.

# ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

VI. Do not, therefore, linger or stop here. Why should you settle for that knowledge of God which minds—perpetually impure, unhappy, and hateful to God—are able to acquire, and may even now and in the future possess? It is a small thing to acquire thoughts and reasonings about God from any kind of superficial consideration of your Thinking and your more general faculties. You can be led to such thoughts even through imperfections—indeed, even from those things that are to be blamed—as has mostly happened so far from the consideration of the Mind according to its first definition, by which it was asserted to be variable and limited (*Book II, chapter vi*). You will know God more worthily through the denial of yourself in all things. From this, a nobler Knowledge will follow, produced by God in a special way; for when God performs His wonderful works within us, we will be permitted to gaze upon the beauty of the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original pattern or model—in this case, God—of which human perfections are merely "paintings" or "images."</note> and Author through those perfections, as if through images and tablets. 

You will arrive there if you proceed according to the second definition of the Mind: that it tends toward God through the love of understanding, with a contempt for oneself. And these are matters of practice <note>original: "praxeos"; referring to lived spiritual exercise rather than theoretical study.</note>, not of reasoning. 

But (which is the third way of knowing God, according to the third description of the Mind) where self-denial and—if I may put it this way—the forgetting of ourselves, along with the operation of God, are to be made perfect, then the knowledge of God will be perfect. The multiplicity of fleeting concepts will be absorbed and, as it were, lost into one solid "something, I know not what," like a tiny drop to which a torrent, a river, or a sea is added, by which it is swallowed up. And this third way belongs to the class of things in which man, possessing nothing of an active role in himself, has no faculty for speaking or reasoning about them. These things are properly ineffable <note>original: "ineffabilia"; things that are impossible to express or describe in words.</note> and can be called the **hidden manna** <note>original: "manna absconditum"; a reference to Revelation 2:17, signifying secret spiritual nourishment known only to the recipient.</note>, which only the Saints sometimes taste here; a name known to no one except the possessor. These things are not to be expected by the inexperienced; they are blind, even if they seem to themselves to see. If you wish to hear anything spoken about these matters, consult the Divine and experienced **Tauler** <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361) was a famous German Dominican mystic whose writings emphasized the soul's "ground" and the process of total surrender to God.</note> in all his works.

VII. Since, however, an obstacle exists in all of us that is so opposed to this most Divine Knowledge of God that God will not grant it unless the obstacle is removed, we must take care to do this. We must strive so that this obstacle (which is called evil and sin) is rightly and clearly recognized as soon as possible, so that no further entrance for it lies open in the Mind. And this is what will be treated in the following Book. Once this is recognized, if the Mind constantly and sincerely desires to be purged of it, there is no doubt that God will come to help and to work, nor that He will give whatever pertains to the most Divine Knowledge and enjoyment of Himself.

# BOOK FOUR
### IN WHICH
## EVIL or SIN IS DISCUSSED.
### CHAPTER I.
->*Concerning those things which are to be noted beforehand for what follows.*<-

<margin>I.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'D' containing floral patterns and scrollwork.</image-desc>We have spoken thus far of the Supreme Reality <note>original: "Realitate Summa"; referring to God as the ultimate source of all existence.</note> and of intermediate things—especially thinking beings—or rather of God and His creatures, particularly spiritual ones. But since these latter types of beings are subject to evil, and because some of them—specifically all human minds—are occasionally contaminated by it, it is necessary to meditate on certain aspects of evil so that we may have a fundamental understanding of all things in general. Therefore, from now on, this subject will be treated with God’s help; but first, let these warnings be observed.

<margin>II.</margin>
II. First, so that the "evil of fault" <note>original: "malum culpæ"; referring to the act of sinning or moral wrongdoing.</note>—whose nature is to be presented here, rather than its consequences—is not confused with the "evil of punishment" <note>original: "malum pœnæ"; referring to the suffering or penalties that follow sin.</note>, it will very often be designated here by the name of **sin**.

<margin>III.</margin>
III. Second, the goal here is not to satisfy anyone's greed or curious questions <note>original: "curiosis quæstionibus"; in this context, "curiosity" refers to an unhealthy or prideful intellectual prying into divine mysteries.</note>, which would itself be a kind of sin. Instead, the aim is only that whoever seriously wishes to inquire into their own sins may be led to give glory to God alone by acknowledging that all real things come from Him. Meanwhile, they should humble themselves—since nothing real originates from themselves—even to the point of nothingness. Indeed, they should not only lower themselves to nothingness, but also, because of the evil they have committed, see and feel themselves cast down *below nothingness* <note>original: "infra nihil"; a mystical expression suggesting that a sinner is in a worse state than if they did not exist at all.</note>, regarding themselves as hateful and likewise without excuse. These three things are certainly sufficient to satisfy the conscience of anyone, as much as can be required in this matter. However, if anyone inquires more specifically about the sins of others—such as those of infants—because such a question is asked not so much for the good of those infants (who are incapable of receiving instruction) but rather to satisfy the curiosity of the questioner, let them look elsewhere for answers. Regarding adults, anyone who is wise in these matters will easily judge from their own self and their own experience—not necessarily concerning the specific types, degrees, or duration of sin, but concerning its root, foundation, and reason, or rather its absurdity—and will...

...will investigate. For once one wicked thing is recognized, all others of the same cloth <note>original: "ejusdem farinæ"; literally "of the same flour," a common idiom meaning things of the same kind.</note> can be known without effort.

IV. Third, since it is not the intention here to present a standard theological topic <note>original: "locum communem"; a "commonplace" or standard category of study in Scholastic education.</note> on sin in the scholastic manner, but only to show those things which can be demonstrated from principles innate to the Mind—as has been done thus far—according to the norm of right reason concerning sins committed in an actual manner; there is no reason for anyone to be disturbed if the principles, method, or names commonly found in their writings are not used here. Nor should they be troubled if we pass over in silence the common definitions of sins (whether true or false) or the divisions into original sin, imputed sin, propagated sin, habitual sin, and the like. What has been written about these or similar things by others is left in its proper place; nothing is denied here, nor is any judgment passed upon them. If anyone misses their own specific dogmas in the following pages, I would not want them to be more indignant than when they do not find talk of the mystery of the **Incarnation** or **Resurrection** in philosophical writings. For philosophers omit such things because they do not see them flowing from the principles they use, yet they do not thereby deny that those same things can be discovered and demonstrated from other principles. Here, however, we use only natural principles; although from these, those things can be deduced by which the other types of sin may be illustrated more than many might believe possible. But these we shall pass over.

V. Fourth, so that a more certain persuasion of the value of these principles we use here may be given in advance, I would like it to be noted that they are such that they can not only be referred to **syntheresis** <term>syntheresis: the innate spark of conscience or the natural capacity of the human mind to grasp the first principles of morality without being taught</term>, and thus impress their own certainty upon the attentive mind, but are also commended by the sacred scriptures. For these scriptures assert that a law is given, inscribed on the mind, as a principle for discerning good and evil, and that humans are to be judged according to its tenor.

VI. Indeed, all the principles for the following sections are contained and proven in those discussions; and truly in such a way that all the remaining work consists in arranging them, deducing conclusions from them, and applying them to this matter.

### CHAPTER II.

*1. The most general concept of sin. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Those things which do not belong to sin are generally excluded from it: God, God’s pleasure, God’s work insofar as it is from God, absolute nothingness, the absence of existence, and the nothingness mixed with reality insofar as it is from God. 7. But not insofar as it is from man.*

I. But for the sake of greater clarity, the matter must be explained "from the egg," <note>original: "ab ovo"; a Latin idiom meaning from the very beginning.</note> as the saying goes. To begin with, we must hold a general concept of <term>sin</term> <note>original: "peccatum"; in this philosophical context, it refers to a moral or logical "missing of the mark" or "error."</note>, even if it is a somewhat blurry one, so that we at least know what we are looking for. It is not unreasonable to seek a general knowledge of something beforehand when its specific nature is still being investigated. We can correctly derive this from the concept of **Justice**, by perceiving its opposite in the mind—namely, indecency, incongruity, or a thing being in conflict with itself or with its own state. What that "thing" is, and what the "conflict" within it entails, must be uncovered more specifically.

II. So that nothing foreign is assumed here, and no phantom is allowed to lead us into error, I am removing as much as possible, and I will resume with as little as I can.

III. First, therefore, I suppose that everything which could possibly not exist, does not exist, thinking to myself: If God were so alone that besides Him—besides His **Essence**, the truths of His Nature—there was absolutely nothing; not only no existing thing, but no essence, no idea, no established truth, but an absolute **Nothing** of all things, essences, truths, and ideas (which has been demonstrated as possible based on what was said regarding the <term>Dominion of God</term> <note>The concept of God's absolute power and ownership over all possibilities and existence.</note>); then there could be no sin. This is self-evident enough, since the Nature of God is most perfect, most consistent with itself, most harmonious, and—if I may put it this way—most unified. Nor would it be incongruous or ill-fitting for Him, nor would it contradict Him, to be One and Alone while everything else is absolutely excluded (based on His Dominion). Therefore, I conclude that the Divine Essence or Nature is incapable of sin; and furthermore, that the absolute nothingness of all things is not sin.

IV. Second, if we consider God (whom I now consider along with His <term>Pleasure</term> <note>original: "placito"; refers to God's sovereign will or decree regarding what He chooses to bring into existence.</note>) in such a way that He were alone, so that besides His pleasure regarding the establishing, placing, and governing of things, there was nothing; or, if those things did not yet exist but were still "to be" (as before creation); then I easily perceive that there would not yet be sin. Therefore, sin is not to be sought in the pleasure or the concept of God

<summary>The author begins a logical "process of elimination" to define sin, arguing that sin cannot exist in God's nature, in absolute nothingness, or in God's sovereign will prior to creation.</summary>
<keywords>nature of sin, Justice, Essence of God, Divine Pleasure, Dominion of God, absolute nothingness, logical consistency</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the rationalist inquiry into the origin of sin, specifically arguing that while God is the cause of all existence, He is not the cause of the "form" or "essence" of sin, which arises from the inherent limitation of created beings.</meta>

<page-num>256</page-num>
<header>RATIONAL THOUGHTS</header>

ought: for whatever that <term>good pleasure</term> <note>original: "placitum"; refers to God's sovereign will or decree.</note> of God might be or could be, it would nevertheless be worthy of God (out of **Justice**) and good (out of **Goodness**), and God would seek Himself in it (out of **Holiness**). Thus, that decree would be a representation and image of God, and would have God as its beginning, middle, and end—all of which are the best things and most consistent with God Himself, and therefore do not bring about <term>sin</term>. Indeed, the good pleasure of God does not even give rise to the possibility of sin when considered in itself without an external work; as long as it remains so, sin cannot even exist or be conceived as existing. 

You might say, however, that the fact that sin is possible is derived or conceived from this, and therefore the concept, notion, or idea of sin must be taken from the decree of God, without which sin would plainly not exist, not even in potential or in concept. 

I respond, first, that neither the possibility of sin, nor the concept or notion of it, is sin itself. Furthermore, the notion and possibility of sin are indeed "from the decree of God" only insofar as if it had not pleased God to decree that any thing should be made, sin could neither exist nor be known—just as if He had not decreed that I should exist, no sin could have been committed or known by me. But this is nothing other than saying that the possibility of the **subject** (the person or being) in whom sin can exist and be known is derived from God's decree. 

But in truth, the notion, idea, and nature of the possibility of sin is *not* from the decree of God, nor is it because things were decreed; rather, it arises from the fact that things—if any are decreed—are of themselves, and without the intervention of God's decree, nothing solid, nothing self-subsisting, nothing self-preserving; they are "non-God." Therefore, so that they might be capable of falling short, there is no need for the decree of God to intervene positively. For this reason and in this sense, sin is possible without the decree of God; that is, the concept of its possibility is given, the reason and cause of which is not God’s decree.

From these points, it clearly shines forth that while God is said to be the cause of **Essences**, natures, forms, and truths when He decrees them (out of His **Sovereignty**), it cannot be said that He decreed the form and essence of sin (whatever that may be), much less that He is the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>original: "causa efficiens"; the primary agent that brings something into being.</note> of its existence. For since "to effect" something is to testify to the power and likeness of one's decree through an external work, how shall He work that which He did not even decree? Moreover, He does not decree that which is unbecoming to Himself and His work. The object of His decree is reality and decency. Whatever is decreed is, by that very fact, decent and good. That which has no perfection requires no decreeing cause, nor is it decreed; but it is left, so to speak, untouched. It is therefore said <term>improperly</term> <note>meaning "metaphorically" or "inaccurately."</note> that God decrees that sins should happen, just as it is also improperly said that sins are "against" the decree of God. For just as God and His decree, although every reality in the subject of sin depends upon Him, nevertheless does not touch those things which are in the sin, so neither is He touched by...

is not touched by those things, nor is His <term>good pleasure</term> <note>original: "placitum"; refers to God's sovereign will or the specific choice He makes to create something.</note> positively burdened by their opposite, by which it might be voided. To think this of God is not unworthy of Him. If any concept of guilt is involved in this, we shall see later that the reason for it must be drawn from the subject of the sin <note>The "subject" refers to the person or creature committing the act.</note> and rightly attributed to that subject.

From this, it is also proved that if something has been decreed but does not yet exist, it is not sin—just as nothingness itself is not sin.

### **V.**
To these considerations—first regarding God alone, and then regarding God together with His good pleasure—I add a third, which involves the actual existence of the things He decreed. Specifically, if the things God pleased to establish were produced and existed in such a way that nothing was considered in them except that they are the work of the Divine good pleasure, even then I find no sin. For it is not unfitting, but on the contrary very appropriate as something worthy of God and His good pleasure, that it should receive its completion from God (out of **Power**). And a thing produced cannot help but be perfect to that extent, since it is an effect representing a **Most Wise Cause**. Therefore, I conclude that no work of God, and no things existing and enduring, are sin; whether all things are equally perfect or not; whether they are placed together or one after another; indeed, even if they do not all reach their perfections at once, but gradually—for example, if organs, mass, and strength are given and increased gradually in bodies, or knowledge, science, and prudence in minds—or even if everything were given all at once. It is not unfitting, nor does it violate any sense of propriety, that those things receive their <term>realities</term> <note>original: "realitates"; in a philosophical sense, this refers to the positive qualities or "thing-ness" of a creature.</note> either all at once or in stages, since they proceed from the pure generosity of the Creator, who owes nothing to anyone. Therefore, reality mixed with nothingness—that is, a being that has not yet attained the perfections it is to attain in the future—does not in itself imply sin.

### **VI.**
Thus I observe that it belongs to God to please, to establish, to will, to decree, and to effect, and these clearly do not touch upon sins. God has nothing positive in Himself, in His decree, or in His work that in any way reaches toward or tends toward sin. To assert the contrary would be blasphemous. Sin is something entirely abandoned by God, who has no commerce in being, in decreeing, or in acting, except with reality and perfection. Therefore, whether I look at the nature of God alone, or His nature with His good pleasure, or His nature with His works, I find no sin therein, nor any cause of sin. And yet sin exists, and it exists in me; it is not a mere nothing, but whatever it becomes, it has something within it that acts as a form and essence. It is not something...

It is not the <term>good pleasure</term> <note>original: "placitum"; refers to God's sovereign will or the specific choice He makes to create something.</note> or the work of God; I am the work of God's pleasure, and nevertheless I possess sin. How shall we bring these incompatible things into a fitting order? But how could they ever fit together, since it is the very nature of sin to be absurd and disordered? Meanwhile, since the concept of sin is not itself sin, and since one can have a correct knowledge of the absurd—even if it is perhaps not perfectly clear in every respect, as every absurdity involves something obscure—I will try to grasp it in whatever way I can. Therefore, I will look around myself more carefully. For although I have gathered from what was already said that sin is a kind of nothingness which wickedly, improperly, and unsuitably imitates the form of reality; that it is not the pleasure nor the work of God; and that it is the absence of God's pleasure and operation in that <term>subject</term> <note>The "subject" is the person or being who commits the sin.</note> whose entire reality is the effect of God's pleasure—nevertheless, with these or similar definitions, I will not have sufficiently achieved a perception (setting aside other questions) of where, from where, what, and in what way sin exists as clearly as possible.

### VII.
Perhaps I will accomplish this more clearly if, noticing that sin is not a <term>Being</term> <note>original: "Ens"; a philosophical term for something that has actual existence.</note> considered on its own, nor is it <term>nothingness</term> <note>original: "nihil"; the total absence of being.</note> viewed on its own, I suspect it is to be found in a mixture of both. For what, where, and from where else would it be? Yet I saw just now that reality mixed with nothingness does not necessarily involve sin <note>This refers to the inherent limitation of created beings, who are "something" but not "everything."</note>. But so be it. That mixture, insofar as it is made by God, is truly and rightly made, since the most powerful Being can indeed place reality within nothingness if He so wills. However, if that mixture is made improperly—namely, by a powerless being, by me who am nothing of myself—if, that is, I attempt to interpose reality, or a certain "Entity," into nothingness, must this not be regarded as something absurd and evil? Certainly, something of what we seek lies here. But because these things are so very abstract in this way, and the terms are not commonly used, it is better to consider them as they are in a subject consisting of body and Mind, and to express them in words as common as possible, rather than pursuing them in a manner that is neither sufficiently intelligible nor, due to abstraction, sufficiently fixed. Therefore, I set aside these more general considerations of Being and nothingness to take up something more specific.

1. 2. 3. 4. *What specifically must be excluded from the category of sin (1) in the Body. 5. (2) In the senses and passions. 6. 7. 8. (3) In the Mind. I. I conceive of God and of nothingness, and myself as being placed, as it were, between the two: insofar as I come from myself, I am clearly nothing; but insofar as I come from God’s <term>good pleasure</term> <note>original: "placitum"; referring to God's sovereign will or the specific choice He makes to create something.</note>, I am something that neither is everything, nor possesses everything. I will therefore examine both certain realities that I possess, and the absence of others that I lack, so that I may know what in these is not only the proper <term>subject</term> <note>The underlying entity (the person) in which a quality exists.</note> of sin, but also its formal <term>essence</term> <note>original: "formale"; the defining characteristic or nature that makes sin what it is.</note>. This could indeed be resolved by a shorter route by contemplating the Mind alone—as has been done until now—which would drive away error through the presence of truth. However, many people are hindered by numerous and common <term>obscurities</term> <note>original: "ambagibus"; literally "windings" or "digressions," referring here to confusing mental habits or circular reasoning.</note> into which they fall back out of habit, not noticing that these conflict with true principles unless they are expressly warned about it. Furthermore, nothing is more common than that principle of superstition by which righteousness or sin is sought and primarily located in physical and bodily things—in mass and in motions. Therefore, I will resume my inspection of the body alongside the mind, since I consist of both.

II. Concerning the nature of my body, I cannot bring it under the suspicion of sin if I consider it in general, insofar as it shares traits with other bodies: being extended in space, divisible, movable, in motion, or at rest, etc. To that extent, it is purely the work of God—and a <term>brute work</term> <note>original: "brutum opus"; an inanimate or unthinking creation.</note> at that—which beyond doubt cannot even be a subject of sin. Likewise, the absence of certain realities ought not to be counted as sin: for instance, that it does not have every possible part, every bit of mass, or every possible motion; the absence of these is "mere nothing." This must be extended to all bodies, for a safe <term>induction</term> <note>A logical conclusion drawn from a specific example and applied to a general rule.</note> can be made from this one instance.

Furthermore, these same motions are common to the righteous and the wicked; therefore, if sin were in them, it would be in both, since there would be no difference in the motion: one killing a beast and one killing a man, one taking his own things and one grasping what belongs to another, and so with the rest; insofar as they are moved similarly in the body, they would sin similarly. Finally, as many as do not possess the use of reason, whether because of sleep, or disease, or another natural cause, are not usually blamed for irregular motions. Whatever can be said of the body or its motions in relation to sin is this: namely, that those things can be either the occasions, or the instruments, or the marks and signs of sin, as Scripture itself testifies. Thus, the body and all things which concern it, and which strike against the organs of its senses, are "subjected to vanity" and sin—not by their own fault, but by the fault of the one subjecting them. Therefore, the fault, or the evil itself, must be sought in the one subjecting them, who is certainly not the body.

It is absurd to establish evil in the object which is the occasion of evil, for even a good law is sometimes the occasion of evil; it is absurd to place it in the instruments, and absurd in the signs. You would ridiculously ascribe the shame of intemperance, for example, to the wine, or the cups, or the barrels, or the <term>hanging ivy</term> <note>original: "suspensæ... hederæ"; in the early modern period, an ivy bush or branch was commonly hung outside a building to signal that it was a tavern where wine was sold.</note>; of murder, to the sword; of falsehood, to words:

VI. It remains, therefore, for me to consider my **Mind** in itself, without respect to the body, or insofar as I am **Spontaneous Thought** <term>Spontaneous Thought: The capacity of the mind to initiate its own actions or thoughts from within, rather than being merely pushed by external physical forces.</term>. Certainly, when attending to that which I have elsewhere called the *material of Thought*—namely, the act of being Conscious or perceiving what is within me—I cannot find any evil therein. For this is the work of God; nor are the wicked said to sin simply because they are conscious of what is within them, as that capacity is common to even the best of minds. Among the *forms of Thought* or of the Mind which I observed above (a), some of which I noticed were more principal and others less so: if I were to fail in the contemplation of these things out of ignorance or even error (such as thinking about merely earthly things, or speculating on the nature of material objects and human sciences), and if a defect or lack of some reality in my mind resulted from this, I should not therefore be said to have committed a sin, but an error. 

Therefore, we may now define **Sin** more specifically than before: it is not just any improper representation of reality, nor a mere lack of God’s pleasure or work (since these are present in any error). Instead, we must return to the principal and most proper forms of the mind. Sin consists in either an improper imitation of these forms, their disorder, or some other defect concerning them. These forms of the mind mentioned above relate to: 
1. Limitation combined with variation; 
2. The tendency toward a Being other than the Mind itself—namely, toward the **Supreme Being** <note>God.</note>, or what is the same, toward the representation of another; 
3. And dependency upon Him. 
All of these are permeated by **Spontaneity**.

...those things which I do not yet perceive. But although those things involve an absence of action, they do not therefore encompass evil, since it is not necessary for all things to be present in the mind at once; nor is even the capacity for sinning itself—I would not wish to say the *faculty* <note>The author distinguishes between a "capacity" (a potentiality) and a "faculty" (a power or tool), arguing that having the potential to do wrong is not the same as being inherently sinful.</note>—sinful, as it is not a positive thing <term>positive thing: In scholastic philosophy, a "positive" reality is something that has actual being or substance, whereas evil was often defined as a "privation" or a lack of something that should be there.</term>, as was noted just now.

Ignorance, therefore, is rightly said on this basis not to be a sin; nor is it reckoned as sin in little children in whom it prevails, just as its opposite—namely, knowledge—does not constitute righteousness. As for the fact that they make an exception for ignorance of the law <note>original: "ignorantiam juris"</note> here, because it happens for the reason that the opportunity for learning was voluntarily neglected out of a free principle, this implies nothing else than that the sin must be attributed to spontaneity <term>spontaneity: The mind's power to act from its own internal determination.</term> rather than to ignorance, which is a consequence of sin and an occasion for it in the future.

Regarding habits, there is nothing evil if, by the repetition of past acts, the mind is disposed toward repeating the same in the future: this, viewed in itself, is good and an effect of the Divine pleasure. What "specifies" a habit, so to speak—or what renders and labels it good or evil—is the **action**; therefore, it is the action, not the habit, that must be considered here. But if, through past sinful actions (where evil is properly found), I have acquired bad habits, yet in the present and future I resist them entirely with my will, I do not think I shall be reckoned as one who is still currently committing a sin; however, if I actually consent and give myself over to them, then the actions themselves must be condemned.

Therefore, it remains for me to seek sin in the acts of limited thought. If sin does not consist in ignorance or in the limits of thought itself, much less does it consist in **Knowledge**, or the reality that exists within those very limits—not only in the knowledge of the true or the good (the knowledge of God and His pleasure according to a certain measure), but not even in the knowledge of what is false and evil. For even if I should know errors, vices, enormities, blasphemies, and monsters of that kind—even if Diabolical and horrific thoughts were presented to the Mind—provided I do not voluntarily consent to them, but resist, I do not sin. Indeed, this is often useful for the refutation of evil and the confirmation of virtue; and it sometimes happens that it would be an evil thing not to have experience or knowledge of some of these things. This proposition, "Satan is to be worshiped" <note>original: "Satanas est adorandus"</note>, is abominable; nevertheless, it entered the knowledge of Christ at the suggestion of Satan himself—with horror, certainly, and rejection, but it entered nonetheless. Hence, intellectual Diabolical temptations do not harm when they voluntarily displease, nor do they bring evil upon the tempted mind.

### RATIONAL THOUGHTS.

...imperfect and limited, it should tend toward God, and find its rest in Him as He is represented within it. Then finally, that it is from Him in every way and most absolutely in its becoming, its being, its acting, and its governance—and in a word, dependent in its every reality. All of these things are excellent and most noble. This permeating spontaneity <term>spontaneity: The mind’s ability to initiate action from its own internal nature.</term> also, as a work of God presently in act, is good in itself, and especially good when it is determined to be applied to these higher things. 

Behold, therefore, when I gaze upon all things that are in me before God—the matter of my thought, the forms, the faculties, the habits, the acts, the spontaneous determination—none are evil. And the fact that many realities are missing from these (as I have seen), and to that extent they participate in "nothingness" <note>In this philosophical tradition, "nothingness" or "non-being" is not a thing itself, but the boundary or limit of a created thing's existence.</note>, is not an evil. All these things are well-ordered, and yet I abound in sins. From where does this come? Is it because I determinately deny and reject the form of the Mind insofar as it directly regards God, as if I were explicitly saying: "I do not wish to be limited by God, I do not wish to tend toward Him, to represent Him, or to be and be governed by Him"? This indeed would be a sin, and perhaps not far removed from that which is called "unpardonable" <note>original: "irremiſſibile" — a reference to the "unforgivable sin" mentioned in Christian scripture.</note>. But I will not examine that now, nor will I attempt to resolve it into clearer ideas, since it is not found in common sins. But I would merely wish to caution against many flattering themselves, as if they were not sinning when they do not expressly reject God. For sin—I do not mean in some specific kind or in degrees, but in its general nature—is not an explicit rejection of God represented in thought.

IX. That form of my Mind which presents God to me on all sides as limiting, representing, and working, also presents to me the idea of myself as I am alone without God—namely, as one who is nothing, possessing not even the slightest degree of reality in myself, nothing that ought to be represented by anyone, or be the aim or original of another, and finally, nothing that works anything by itself. And just as I do not have this from God—namely, that I am nothing, since that which is nothing does not have a cause for its work—but rather from myself insofar as I am from myself, or insofar as I am nothing; so there is no need for a determination to be placed in me by God that is spontaneous from me, toward me, and through me. This would be contradictory and absurd. In this way, I would embrace myself as a "Being from myself" <term>Being from myself: translated from "Ens à me," a technical term usually reserved for God, meaning a being that exists by its own power and has no cause.</term>, as something through myself, my own aim, etc., which is an imperfection and tends toward non-being. God neither establishes nor effects this, nor has He offered a positive occasion for such a determination to be in me, since all things inside me and outside me present the opposite to me and cry out that God is everything and I am nothing. Therefore, I am left here by God to this "un-determined" state. And because I am variable by my very self, insofar as by my nature I am not the Supreme and most constant Being <note>original: "Ens Summum & conſtantiſſimum"</note>, it can happen that I fall away from this...

...state of non-determination in which I am not determined by myself, toward myself, or through myself, toward some empty specter worse than nothing. And this is what happens when there is sin; indeed, this is the very root and innermost foundation of sin from which all else flows. Because I was truly indifferent <term>indifference: The capacity of the will to choose between different options, or to act or not act.</term> to this, the fault is inseparable from the sin. But so that these matters may be perceived more clearly, some things must be expressly explained regarding liberty—and especially regarding indifference—and it must be shown how much this contributes to sin. X. But this must still be noted: the nature and actual commission of sin does not require the Mind to behave toward it in a reflexive way <term>reflexive way: A conscious, self-aware turning of the mind back upon its own thoughts.</term>, as if it had to say to itself: "I wish to be determined by myself; I wish to be governed, considered, and held as something by myself, for myself, and through myself; I wish to represent myself; I wish not to be limited in this or that way," and such things. If these are indeed present, they make the sin more grievous—namely, a proud sin committed against conscience. But for it to be a sin, it is sufficient that the thought, even without reflection, behaves *as if* it were such as has just been described. For in this way the "I," insofar as I am nothing from myself; the "I," insofar as I am something through God; God Himself, insofar as He established and made me; He also, insofar as He represented Himself; and even He Himself, insofar as He is who He is—all are consequently denied.

### RATIONAL THOUGHTS

I. ...from which these conclusions will be drawn. **I conceive:** <note>original: *Concipio*</note> they refer this to the Intellect as its specific act, but we call it simply a perception of thought or of the Mind. ***I conceive spontaneously:*** <note>original: *Sponte concipio*</note> this, which they ascribe to the Will as its act—and for which reason they also attribute Freedom to it—we call <term>delight: translated from *allubescentiam*, referring to the mind's natural attraction or "liking" toward a thought.</term>, or pleasure, or rather **Spontaneity**. ***I spontaneously conceive my God:*** they refer this to what they call the Freedom of Spontaneity. But for the sake of avoiding obscurity, as I have said, I prefer to say that the act by which the mind spontaneously perceives an object suited to itself belongs to **determined spontaneity**, or is a **spontaneous determination**. There is no obscurity in the analysis of this proposition regarding its form, and it is clear from this what should be understood by Intellect, Will, Liberty, and the Liberty of Spontaneity. You will grasp and express these more clearly as: "The Mind perceives by a **determined Spontaneity**," rather than if you said with the <note>The "schools" refers to the Scholastic philosophers, the traditional academic authorities of the time who relied heavily on Aristotelian logic.</note> schoolmen, "The Soul possesses an Intellect and a Will which is free with the liberty of Spontaneity."

II. It has been expressly demonstrated, where we dealt with Divine Power and Liberty, that all these things—and specifically **determined Spontaneity** occurring through the intervention of perception—come from God. Therefore, all the difficulty that remains concerns ***Indifference***, which can be seen, as if at its birth and root, from this consideration. Namely, if that which my Mind spontaneously perceives is not seen—either because something is lacking in the reality of the perception, or in the object itself—to agree with what God has manifested in the form of the Mind concerning Himself, His pleasure, or His work, then I remain **undetermined**. That is, I hesitate: should I make this my own through my mind? In other words, should I be carried toward it by spontaneous thought and remain in it as if it were something that fits God’s idea, pleasure, or work? I would prefer to call this **undetermined spontaneity**, or the **non-determination of spontaneity**, rather than the "liberty of indifference"; for regarding this undetermined spontaneity, the question is finally asked: is it "indifferent" or not?

III. From this, one should note that the suspicion of indifference in the created Mind—and the foundation of it, if any is granted there—is a negation, or rather, a "non-position" of determination. This arises because the Mind does not find or uncover an object suited to its perception and delight. From this, it is easy to decide what must be judged concerning the indifference founded there—whether it be a perfection or otherwise. But this will be sufficiently clear from what follows. First, we must see what indifference is.

IV. If one had to speak in the manner of the schoolmen, I would say that the question here is not about indifference in a moral or physical sense, but in a **Metaphysical** sense; yet...

### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL
<page-num>267</page-num>

I would prefer to say that we are not dealing here with the reasoning by which certain things are called neither good nor evil, but <term>morally neutral: from the Greek *adiaphoræ*, referring to actions or things that are neither commanded nor forbidden by moral law.</term>; nor are we dealing with that which is a passive aptitude of a subject for receiving various forms from an agent, just as it pleases the agent: in which sense a human is "indifferent" to whether God works this or 그that amount of **reality**, or nothing at all, within him. The **Indifference** being discussed here is to be conceived as a principle in which the reason and cause of the nature and existence of things (to which indifference is said to be given) is sought and fully found without further appeal. It has often been said that such an indifference is granted to God regarding all things that are not of His own nature: hence He was able to establish and bring about their natures, existences, and truths in this or another way, and of all these things, in whatever way they might have existed, no principle is given beyond His own pleasure. It was expressly demonstrated in the third book, where we discussed liberty, that sin must proceed from a similar principle—that is, an indifferent one. And certainly, sin comes either from no principle at all (or something that acts as a principle), in which case sin would not exist; or from a necessary principle—whether absolute or hypothetical—but outside of God, His pleasure, and His work (which in themselves are entirely without fault), no such principle is held; or, it comes from an **indifferent** principle. Can it even be doubted that the reason for a sin—whether committed or negatively not committed (I am not speaking of the positioning of the good)—is given in the created mind, considered in a certain respect, without further appeal? This is the very definition of indifference.

V. It appears from the examples provided that Indifference—whether it exists in a firm or weak **Thought**, or whether its boundaries are positive or negative—must be recognized as being itself either positive or negative. For when a thing has the power to establish this, that, or some other good, its indifference is purely **positive**; but if its indifference is toward establishing a good or omitting it, it is positive on one side; but if it is indifferent to the point where it either does nothing at all by itself or commits an evil, then its indifference is **negative**. It is demonstrated by the **Divine Power** <note>original: *Potentia Divina*</note> that the first two types of indifference belong exclusively to God alone, to the exclusion of every creature: therefore, if any indifference is to be attributed to the creature—as I have shown it must be—only the last remains, which is **negative**.

VI. But this does not please everyone who wishes to believe that they are "something" by their own power. Hence, they assert that they are **positively** indifferent, either in choosing between two goods, or at least between the positioning or the omission of a good. For this reason, many derive the origin and reason for evil from this: that since they are indifferent (or at least were before evil was admitted), if from

VII. As for these two objections brought forward, it will hereafter become manifest that the matter is not as it appears at first glance. Regarding **Indifference**—whether partially or totally "positive"—the proof deduced from the **Power of God** remains invincible: that such indifference belongs to no <term>Creature: Any being created by God, including humans and angels.</term> in any state whatsoever, not even to the Angels, nor even to man in his state of innocence. Nothing has ever been able, nor is anything else besides God able, to establish anything real by its own force; who, then, could have been "indifferent" to establishing a thing or otherwise? Just as it is true that nothing can be added to God’s Power by another, and that no thing exists as a limit to exclude it—that God alone is independent, that nothing exists without the force of His will, and nothing exists of itself; in short, that God is God—so it is true that no one besides Him establishes anything real, or is <term>positively indifferent: The supposed ability of a creature to act entirely on its own power without being determined by God.</term> toward it. Either God and the most self-evident and Holy truths must be denied here, or that blasphemous idol of "positive indifference" must be exterminated. For it is contrary to common knowledge regarding God’s power and the creature's dependence; indeed, it is harmful, useless, and lacks any foundation. For the fact that some embrace it lest they become too vile in their own eyes, or lest (as someone alleges) it follows that everything must be attributed to God and nothing to creatures, is an abomination. It comes from nothing other than a mind following in <note>original: "Diabolicis insistens vestigiis"</note> diabolical footsteps, seeking to glory in itself.

VIII. But perhaps some of those who have championed this "indifference" acted from another, less wicked motive. Perhaps they did not notice all the consequences that arise from comparing it with Divine Power, but resorted to positive indifference for other reasons: some to show that sin is inexcusable and blameworthy; others because they seem convinced of it within themselves by their own sense and conscience—that they are indifferent. I do not see what else could be used as a pretext.

IX. But these arguments have no strength to prove what is assumed. For, to begin with the first point, the consideration of **negative indifference** in the mind is sufficient for recognizing the guilt of sin. The mind was able either to remain in a state becoming of its own <note>original: "nihilum suum"</note> "nothingness" <note>This refers to the creature's natural state of total dependence on God, without whom it is nothing.</note>, performing nothing from itself, or to fall away from that into a privative, unbecoming, and sinful state. Therefore, this "positive indifference" is alleged without necessity. Furthermore, it is both useless and harmful. To see this, it must be understood that for something to be blameworthy and inexcusable, its opposite—which ought to have been done—must be...

### X.
What was secondly alleged is also hollow. For many appeal to the senses. "Look," they say, "we experience ourselves to be indifferent toward the establishing of things; we perceive it, we feel it." They argue that what is established by "inner sense" <note>The personal, subjective feeling of making a free choice.</note> ought not be denied just because it cannot be reconciled by us with something incomprehensible—namely, the Power and <term>concurrence: The theological concept of God acting alongside or through the actions of His creatures.</term> of God. They say that what is clearly perceived should not be denied on account of that which is by its nature incomprehensible. 

I invert these arguments thus: This thing is clear and evident: that God is the Author and Producer of all real things; that no thing has being or acts from itself apart from Him; and that "positive indifference" in a <term>Creature: Any being created by God.</term> not only cannot be reconciled with Divine Power, but is diametrically opposed to it, denies it, and removes it. 

Moreover, what is—or at least at first glance seems to be—incomprehensible is this: that something within us exists or is established by another (namely, whatever real thing is spontaneously within us), yet we do not feel it as if it depends on another, but rather perceive it as if coming from ourselves. Therefore, if what is evident ought not be denied because of something incomprehensible, it must be concluded that the first point—being most evident, namely that God alone does all things and the Creature is indifferent to nothing in a "positive" sense—ought not be denied just because we do not immediately comprehend how that which we seem to feel as if coming spontaneously from ourselves is, nevertheless, not established by us. 

What is surprising or inconsistent if the manner in which God acts in Minds is not entirely understood? But it would finally be inconsistent if the principles of Divine Power and the impotence of the creature had not been made manifest, or were presented as distorted. For God is properly acknowledged and, so to speak, treated when these things are made manifest in that way...

...namely the power of acting remains hidden; but not the reverse. When the latter <note>The human act of willing.</note> is said to be evidently perceived, while the former <note>God's underlying action.</note> are either disguised or ignored, God’s honor remains intact within the Mind.

### XI.
But furthermore, I say it is false that anyone feels themselves to be <term>positively indifferent: Having an active, independent power to choose between two options without being determined by any prior cause.</term>. For everything they claim to feel can be attributed either to the **indifference of the subject**—when, out of many operations that God could place within them, the person does not know which ones they are about to experience—or to **negative indifference**, or to a **positively determined spontaneity**. This spontaneity, because it is not felt as coming from an outsider, is thought for that reason to come from oneself.

If that were the case, every spontaneous **Thought** would be by its very nature removed from God’s **Power** and independent; and God would not even be able to work within it—a notion that has been thoroughly refuted. Truly, there are other reasons why an action is not felt as coming from something foreign and external. To resolve this knot, there is no need to transform the **Creature** into the **Creator**, or vice versa. 

Our very continuous preservation of ourselves is spontaneous, and it is not perceived by our senses as proceeding from another; yet the intellect proves that it does not come from us. The reason why this preservation, along with other operations of this kind, is not perceived as coming from an outsider is that it is **intimate** to us. There is nothing more intimate within us against which it could be compared and thus felt as "foreign." Anyone who directly perceives something as diverse from themselves and coming from an outsider is, to that extent, distinct from the thing so perceived; this is why even from crude and bodily sense we conclude that there exists something different from us. 

But the work of God, which effects spontaneous thought within us, is intimate to us—or rather, it is our very "innermost." At our depths, we *are* that work. What remains in us, besides that, which could receive a direct sensation of that work as something different from us, and by whose comparison it could be felt as extraneous? This remains true even though, through the reflection of the intellect, we perceive that everything real—however intimate it is to us, and even if it is our entire spontaneity—is placed there by God.

Had he attended to what he proposes as a "common notion"—that God is the end, principle, and middle of all things—he would not say, as he does, that in this way Liberty is only harassed and limited by foolish discourse.

...that one is absolutely always able to do so, and that in this, a greater use of this positive power is made than if it were otherwise. These views are either false or poorly expressed. He <note>René Descartes</note> himself in his *Meditation IV* states that no positive faculty is required for making mistakes; is such a faculty, then, required for sinning? We should not speak of a **positive power** to follow the worse path, but rather of an imperfection, or a **negative lack of power** <term>impotentia negativa: a lack of ability or strength, rather than a deliberate force.</term> from which it is possible to fall into <term>privation: the absence or loss of a quality that should normally be present.</term>. Nor should we say so much that **we are absolutely able** to do this, but rather that we are always sufficiently imperfect in ourselves to be liable to this defect.

### XIII.
Thus, only the **indifference of negation** <note>The state of being undecided because of a lack of determining factors.</note> remains to be attributed to the creature. It is not a new idea that within a positive subject—and even within an act or an object—something negative must be considered. But how can there be "indifference" in respect to "nothing," seeing as indifference requires at least two terms <note>options or boundaries</note> to exist? 

In truth, there is a well-known difference between "merely negative nothingness" and what is called "privative nothingness." To speak more clearly (since this is perhaps ignored or obscured by some who do not use the terms in their proper and convenient sense): sometimes **the "nothing"** <note>original: "τὸ nihil"</note> is present, so to speak, where it ought to be. It ought to be present in that which is plainly nothing of itself in respect to its essence, existence, preservation, and all things. In such a thing, there should be nothing of its own determination, no purpose centered on itself, no principle originating from itself, and no representation of itself as if it were something. In this sense, it is called **merely negative nothingness**. 

At other times, however, **the "nothing"** is missing from where it ought to be, and in its place stands an empty phantom of reality and a hollow imitation; this is called **privative nothingness**. In respect to these two, there is an "indifference" in the Mind—or at least it existed before the Mind sinned and became corrupted by the habit of failing wickedly. 

For it cannot be denied that God left the mind undetermined by itself and toward itself (which is one of the terms of indifference); and it is clear from the outcome that the other term (**privative nothingness**), which is opposed to the first, now actually exists and was once a potentiality. In whichever of these states the Mind might have remained, the reason and—if it must be so called—the cause for it (precisely as it is considered without reality) would have to be sought in the Mind. (This is the reason for indifference.) <note>The original text contains a typo "indifferntiæ" for "indifferentiæ".</note> Since the form of both states viewed this way is "nothing"—indeed, the latter is worse than nothing—no positive cause is required. This should be beyond doubt regarding the latter state <note>sin</note>. But there is no reason for difficulty in the former either: for although God, by working the most positive things in the mind, could have rescued the Mind from indifference so that it remained constantly in "nothingness" with respect to itself (as was done in the case of the **holy Angels**), yet it cannot be said that the state of the mind—which is nothing by itself—was insufficient before sin for the mind to remain, by its own nature, as it is fitting for that which is nothing of itself to remain.
