<margin>XIV.</margin> Therefore, if I—who am a **Spontaneous Thought** through God—remain in that "nothing" which is a state of non-determination <note>A state of being a "blank slate" or having no self-willed direction.</note> from myself, toward myself, through myself, and for myself; and if I remain to myself as one who is nothing from, toward, or through myself—even while I will, desire, choose, or work—then I do not sin. But if that *nothing* is absent—that is, if I, a spontaneously thinking thing, fail to maintain that "nothingness" or non-determination from myself—and if some empty **phantom of reality** <note>original: "realitatis larva inanis"</note> is present, by which I (who am nothing) seem to myself to be someone who is something by my own power, or who knows, desires well, wills, or works from myself: then by that very act, I sin. From this it is clear that sin is not **Spontaneous Thought** itself, nor is it the actual position of that thought; rather, sin is the absence of the "nothing" that is owed in the mind. It is a <term>privation of nothing</term> <note>The loss of the humble state of being "nothing" before God.</note>, a state far more imperfect and worse than "nothing" itself, even if it sometimes appears to be a close imitation of God.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>1.</margin> *Notable difficulties arising from the preceding seven points. 2. 3. Whether a human being ought to perform anything positive from themselves? 4. Whether the negative state favors negligence. 5. 6. 7. Whether the Mind can remain in that state; how many perfections follow from it. 8. Whether the Mind finds occasion for boasting therein. 8. 9. 10. Once sin is admitted, does indifference remain? What is the cause for the removal of sin. The three primary types of sin. 11. 12. Concerning the foreknowledge and Governance of God regarding sins. 13. Whether God could have removed indifference, and why He did not?*

<margin>I.</margin> In this way, I say, all positive things are asserted to belong solely to God, the **Author** of all things, while nothing is attributed to the **Mind** that must be referred back to God as the efficient cause. For if the mind—which is nothing of itself, does not exist for itself, and is not to be ruled by itself—becomes and remains not from itself, not for itself, and not through itself, then it "posits" <note>brings into being or asserts</note> nothing. It carries itself as nothing, and to that extent, it bears the image of "nothing"—or rather the image of itself, insofar as it is absolutely nothing of itself. This is what befits "nothing." To that extent, no perfection is present in it. But if the mind sins by not admitting (or rather, not permitting) these things, then it perpetrates something even less real, for which it must be blamed. But here several difficulties arise, which we shall propose in the form of questions and attempt to resolve.

II. (1) The first mention of this was already made above where **positive indifference** <note>original: "indifferentia positiva"; the idea that a human has an equal, independent power to choose between two paths without divine influence</note> was rejected, and it was asserted that the creature puts forth <note>original: "ponere"; to posit or establish as real</note> nothing from itself; therefore, sin is not properly the "ceasing" of the creature from working well. It might be asked: should a man not work? Is he not bound to produce works, and indeed good ones? Does God not often demand this of man? Why, then, was this denied above, even regarding a holy and innocent man—indeed, regarding all creatures? I respond: the reasons for this assertion were alleged in their proper place in such a way that (if I may speak confidently) I do not think they can ever be weakened by anyone. Regarding **Scripture**, I say that although it uses words that properly signify the "positing" <note>the actual bringing into existence</note> of things, and says that men "work" good things—and even that some "save" their neighbors—it does not, however, overturn itself; for everywhere it cries out that all things are made by God, and without Him, nothing; all things are from Him, through Him, and to Him, and many other things of this kind. Therefore, we say those phrases are **improper** <note>figurative or metaphorical</note> and are to be understood according to that manner of speaking by which an effect is attributed to an **instrument**, even though the effect must be referred to the **efficient cause** <note>The actual agent that brings something about; here, God.</note>. God conceived the ideas of things as He willed, He established them, and He expressed them outside of Himself through their existence, production, and governance. To man, who is made from these, God granted that he might conceive some of these ideas imperfectly, and He wills to use man as an instrument which it pleases Him to have intervene in the positing of certain things. Thus, man is, in respect to God, like a certain infant looking at characters <note>letters or written signs</note> he neither invented nor painted; his hand is taken up by a teacher as an instrument—which on its own is motionless and unfit for this—and is directed toward the correct writing of similar letters, yet he contributes nothing to this from himself, unless perhaps, so far as it is in him, he might inject a **hindrance** <note>original: "remoram"</note> while wishing to scribble fanciful lines from his own impulse (which is like a **privative nothing** <note>original: "nihili privativi"; a lack of something that should be there</note>). Just as it would be foolish to conclude that the writing belongs to the infant because the word "writing" was applied to him, it is likewise a poor conclusion from the words of Scripture to say that man works **positively**, as an efficient cause in his own right. Similar expressions are therefore to be returned to God, insofar as He works through man, who is himself God's work.

III. The reason why these formulas of speech were not used by me here is that simpler and more proper terms seem to agree better with **philosophical discourse**, from which all ambiguity, or the occasion for introducing foreign concepts through figurative formulas, ought to be banished. Therefore, for this reason, it was said of God alone that He "works" and "posits" something real. Of man, however, it was said that he is nothing from himself in his beginning, his being, his working, his being ruled, in his start, his middle, or his end; or, if he becomes a sinner, he is less

...still exist. The **positive** is attributed to God, the **negative** to the human, and the **privative** <note>original: "privativum"; in traditional philosophy, a "privation" is not just the absence of something, but the lack of a good that ought to be there, such as blindness being a privation of sight</note> to the sinner. These are plain and proper expressions, for the matters themselves are just that genuine and simple. Whatever is real—or has been, or ever will be—in a human being is either the work of God, or it is nothing. Whatever can be asked or demanded of a human in respect to their **efficient cause** <note>the actual agent that brings something into being</note>, their principle, or their goal—insofar as it is not the operation of God but is considered the work of man—is nothing. And that this "nothing" should be merely **negative** is the duty of the human. Nothing more noble can be demanded or expected from a creature than **nothing**: that is, the negation of its own operation, its own goal, its own principle, and the like.

For this reason (though it might seem strangely false if viewed in isolation), it is most true that the human is not obligated by God to perform a **positive work**, or to work "positively." Nor are the commands of God the kind of obligations that require something real to be **posited** <note>original: "ponatur"; established as an objective reality</note> by creatures. For it is inconceivable that a human could work anything positive from themselves, distinct from God, without attributing to themselves what belongs to God alone—whose Power (and consequently His Nature) would thus be denied. It is much less possible to conceive that God would obligate a human to such an absurdity, which is contrary to the Divine Nature. 

Hence, all the commands of God to humans must ultimately be resolved into the **negative**, so they may be perceived as they truly are. Let humans hold themselves as a mere nothing; the rest is God’s to work. Indeed, from an inspection of the **Decalogue** <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, it appears that almost all the commands are negative; and that which seems affirmative—enjoining rest—actually commands a cessation and negation of one’s own operation.

As for what theologians say regarding the **Covenant of Works** <note>original: "fœdere operum"; a theological concept suggesting that before the Fall, humanity could earn eternal life through perfect obedience</note>—when the human had not yet sinned, in which merit was supposedly possible and which did not exclude "boasting"—it is clear these can only be understood in a **negative sense**. Namely:
*   **To work**, when applied to a human, means to conduct oneself from oneself as **nothing**—which is required of the creature as its own "work."
*   **To merit** means to be, from oneself through a certain devotion, in such a **negative state** which is followed by rewards or certain gifts according to God’s promise.
*   **To boast** <note>original: "gloriari"; to take pride or glory in one's status</note> means to think truly that one has not turned aside from that state of "nothingness" to which the reward is attached, but has remained in it, and has not rendered oneself unworthy of the promised effect through sin.

Otherwise, in a positive sense, the human can neither be obligated to work from themselves (as just stated), nor can they positively "merit" (as was proved regarding the power of God), nor finally could they have any basis to boast of any reality established by themselves. This was noted in the chapter on the **Glory of God**, and will soon be shown in Question 4: that boasting in a state of nothingness would have been **improper** <note>technically or figuratively incorrect</note>. Meanwhile, however, the human—swelling with a haughty phantom of their own Power—can be provoked by words...

**IV. (2)** Secondly, it can be asked: Does this not favor human sloth and neglect? For it seems an occasion could be taken from this to care for nothing, love nothing, do nothing, apply oneself to nothing, and express no effort, but rather to leave all things to God in such a way that people watch idly as things go as they go, with their hands tucked into their robes <note>original: "manibus suis in sinum reconditis"; a classical idiom for idleness or "sitting on one's hands"</note>. I respond: the form of this idle state which is being criticized is not merely a "nothing" in the negative sense. Instead, it is the absence of that "nothing," or rather the presence of a **fantastic specter of the self** <note>The author argues that true "nothingness" is humble, whereas "sloth" is actually a form of self-centeredness where one's own comfort becomes the goal</note>, of one's own pleasure, and one's own delight; it is a vain return to oneself, as if each person’s charming leisure were their own ultimate goal. This, however, is not conducting oneself before God as a "mere nothing." Furthermore, among the operations by which God drives out the **privative state** <note>the state of being deprived of good or grace</note> from humans—and which He brings about in them after this expulsion, but in a fuller and more divine way than before—are these very cares, diligence, effort, love, actions, and labors, and the most effective ones at that. All of these are so far from being removed by the "negative nothing" that exists in a human, that instead, a most ample and fit place is granted to them through it, as shall now be further discussed.

**V. (3)** Thirdly, it is asked: Can the **Mind** <note>original: "Mens"; the intellectual or rational part of the soul</note> be or remain in that "nothingness," in that **non-determination**? The reason for doubting this is that since the Mind is **spontaneous Thought** <note>original: "Cogitatio spontanea"</note> placed in continuous act, it does not seem possible for it to exist without an object toward which it is carried and determined in some way—just as matter cannot exist without some positive shape and mode. The form of an actual Thought cannot be and remain "nothing," especially that Thought which is made in the image of God or is representative of Him. How, then, is this constantly demanded of the Mind? The answer is that the Mind indeed cannot be in that state absolutely and simply, such that it exists and remains without **determination** <note>the act of being directed toward a specific goal or thought</note> toward some object to which it is applied—as if it willed nothing or tended toward nothing. Nor has that been asserted. But the Mind can, in respect to itself (insofar as it is nothing of its own accord), pass itself over, not determine itself, not look at itself, and not conduct itself as the **principle from which, according to which, and for the sake of which** <note>original: "principium à quo, & secundum quod, & ob quod"</note> it ought to be ruled. If these self-negations are present, in this very moment God will work within the Mind a **Divine determination**, a Divine goal, Divine motives, and Divine principles. These are the most worthy of all God’s operations, provided they are not subjected to other things as mere means, but instead hold dominion in the heart. Finally, the means, the modes, and everything pleasing to God will not be lacking. The negation or passing over...

-># RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

The dismissal <note>original: "dimissionem"; completing the word from the previous page's catchword</note> of oneself is immediately followed by the placement of God, and with more certainty than when a space in nature, deserted by one body, is immediately occupied by another; for even here, an absolute vacuum cannot exist. The **Mind** <note>original: "Mens"</note> cannot be duly empty of itself and simultaneously empty of Divine operations.

**VI.** Those who have experienced this testify that it is so. But even in those without such experience, God has left enough light or manifestations of His operations (which He never fully withdraws, even from the worst of people) by which they may be convinced of this truth. Let each person ask themselves: What if I willed, chose, desired, or turned away from nothing—whether within myself (such as my thoughts, will, emotions, and the like) or in the external universe—for my own sake and because of my own self-interest? What, I ask, would happen if I abandoned this self-regard? Undoubtedly, since God preserves the thinking being by His own will, and as previously stated, my thought cannot lack every object and determination, and yet I would not be determined toward anything by my own self, it would remain for God to work this within me.

What indeed, and in what way? Certainly nothing against Himself or His own pleasure, but surely according to Himself. Therefore, since He is not estranged from Himself but is directed toward Himself, loves Himself, and approves of Himself and His own pleasure and work for His own sake, He would also work in me a determination of myself toward Him, and a love and approval of Himself and all His things for His sake. And since He alone is the **beginning, end, and goal** <note>original: "principium, finis scopusque"</note> of all things, He would also refer all things in me to Himself, and would begin from His own motivation. In this way, He would not leave in me a solitary image of my own "nothingness," but would use it like a space which He would fill with His operations, which represent Him perfectly. 

To put it graphically, He would be the one in me contemplating, loving, and willing Himself, His own pleasure, and His own work; He would be the one praying to Himself, choosing, rejecting, arranging, acting—in short, He would be everything. I would not want this to be understood regarding His **essence** <note>original: "essentiæ"</note>, as if His Nature were a "subject" in me that admitted these modes into itself; rather, He would be these things through His operation; He would be the doer. Or, to speak with the **Schools** <note>the Scholastic philosophers of the universities</note>, He would be these things **causally and efficiently** <term>causaliter & efficienter: acting as the source and producer of the effect</term>, but not **subjectively and essentially** <term>subjective & essentialiter: being the actual substance or underlying nature of the person</term>.

**VII.** And then, in truth, far from being deprived of the Divine image because of the state of my "nothingness," that image would be most conspicuous in me in this way, where divine operations are joined. For if He works diligence, cares, and holy labors in me, does He not thereby present a sketch of His own **Activity** <note>original: "Activitatis"</note>? If He effects patience—for example, endurance and cheerful acquiescence in adversity—does He not show Himself as if in an image, happy and sufficient, since He thus appears...

This is that *Nothing* <note>original: "Nihil"</note> which has been so greatly commended by Holy Men in their mystical and Divine contemplations.

This can be seen from the Dominion of God, who distributes these goods freely, moved by no external motive, giving what and as much as He pleases. Thus, even if all minds, like the Holy Angels, had remained in such a state with respect to themselves, they would never have had cause to boast about the establishment of even the smallest reality. This is eternally far from every creature. To say that the Mind of itself does not sin is nothing other than saying that the Mind, insofar as it is the work of God, is not to be accused of sin, as was also advised at the beginning; and that the same Mind, insofar as it is nothing from itself, is also not guilty of sin. Finally, it is absurd, contradictory, and impossible that the Mind in a state of nothingness could boast in itself, properly and in a positive sense; for "not-boasting-in-itself" is the very state of nothingness, and whoever seeks to boast in themselves by that very act falls away from that state and determines themselves toward themselves. However, whoever remains in that state, by that very fact, does not look at themselves, but passes over and leaves themselves behind. But I ask you, what occasion is there for boasting: "I boast in myself because I am, or because I have been until now, in a state of nothingness!" That is: because I am nothing in respect to myself—not only in substance but also in governance—and until now I have been as is fitting <unclear>for</unclear> nothing to be in respect to itself, therefore I shall conduct myself as is unfitting <unclear>for</unclear> nothing to conduct itself: which is the same as saying, "I shall boast in myself." These things certainly do not spring from remaining in a negative state.

IX. (5) Fifthly, on the occasion of the second part of the previous response, one may ask: are the things said about the indifference of the mind between the nothingness of negation and of privation <note>The author distinguishes between "negation" (the simple absence of a quality) and "privation" (the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, i.e., sin).</note> such that the Mind is just as indifferent after sin has been committed as it was before? X. But now perhaps someone will ask, what cause is required? A negative one, perhaps another will say, and therefore one that comes from the creature. What then is that? *A state of mere nothingness?* That has indeed been expelled from the sinning creature through sin. *Indifference?* That too has been expelled, and there is a falling away from nothingness toward its privation; there is a turning away from one extreme and a leaning toward the other: which does not settle the matter, but rather the opposite. What cause, then, is to be assigned, since besides those things reviewed there is nothing in the creature that can be suspected to come from itself? Certainly it is clear from this that for the removal of <term>privation</term> in a subject that remains, a most real, operating cause is required. But what kind of operating? *Must one work positively so that "nothing" may return?* Indeed, so that all vain <term>phantasms</term> <note>original: "phantasmata"; these are illusory mental images or delusions that fill the mind when it is turned away from divine truth.</note> may be cast out, there is need for many internal and external particular acts, exercises, and various incomplete modes and forms: for by these both the privation and the manner in which it flourished in the mind are emptied out. And the empty mind is thus led back to the state of nothingness, which—as was said regarding the third question—is followed by new operations, simpler, purer, more immediate, direct, complete, solid, and uniform. Therefore, the removal of privation can be compared with the removal of nothingness (which happens through <term>position</term> <note>original: "positionem"; the act of establishing or placing something into existence.</note>), and it demands a similar cause. Let us take the matter from the beginning. A cause is given for the removal of the state of mere nothingness: therefore, also for the removal of the privative state. The state of nothingness is removed in two ways: one good, the other bad; hence there are two kinds of causes: perhaps we shall see the same concerning the privative state. The state of nothingness is removed—but badly—by man, through his own perverse positioning, which is a cause that (except in false appearance) is no more powerful than <note>original: "τῷ nihilo"; the author uses the Greek article for "the" with the Latin word for "nothing."</note> *nothing itself*; in fact, it is truly more imperfect, and is rightly reduced to a "privation of nothingness," or to "less than nothing." Since evil is a condition worse than nothingness, this cause becomes—if one may speak this way—something more than most real. Is it not possible to find testimony of these things from God’s grace within the mind? 

But as for whether all others—those in whom God does not work all these things in this way—are nevertheless led back by God to that state of indifference, so that for some period of time it is left entirely to them anew to embrace themselves or not? It is not the place here to inquire. But even asserting that does not bring any absurdity, for in that case, nothing is attributed to man, and nothing is taken from God, to whom every lessening and suppression of evil is ascribed; rather, such an idea is fit to commend God's mercy. 

Hence, there is no reason for anyone to be offended by certain formulas of speech which some truly upright men, zealous for the glory of God (to whom they refer all things), sometimes use. For example, the claim that men still have **free will**, the freedom of choosing life or death, God or the Devil, salvation or damnation, or even the power of doing good or evil. Regarding these phrases (though the proud may abuse them), they are to be correctly understood to mean that man is not only always uncoerced in these matters, but also that God preserves for man that state in which he is permitted to behave either in a **privative way** (which is to embrace death, etc.) or in a **negative way**, which is followed by the vital and saving operation of God. And in this respect, man should be thought of as "indifferent" or called "free" to work good—not immediately, of course, as if good could be established by man himself; but rather indifferent toward that "negative state" whose presence is followed by the operation of good, which comes from God and is done by Him. ### XI.
(6) But a further difficulty, which we place in the sixth position, can be proposed for resolution. If before sin—indeed, before any of the three types of sinful states—the **creature** <note>In this context, "creature" refers to any created being, specifically a human soul.</note> is made **indifferent** <note>Latin: *indifferens*. Here, it means a state of neutrality or "free choice," where the soul has not yet tipped toward good or evil.</note> in the manner already described, so that the reason and cause for whichever state it later enters lies in the creature and not in God; how then shall God certainly foresee sin? Would His knowledge not then depend on the uncertain habit of an "indifferent" mind? Or indeed, would the operations He would have performed, had sin not existed, not depend on the creature to such an extent that they could be hindered by it? Finally, how can a certain governance belong to God regarding these matters?

I respond: *Let created thought beware lest it attempt to raise itself beyond its own sphere in these matters, and thus fall into sin.* Let us stick to what has been demonstrated so far. If certain things arise that we do not grasp, let us be mindful of the limited lot of our own cognition. The difficulty arises chiefly from this: that people wish to consider the knowledge of sin as being just like the knowledge of **real entities**. <note>The author is distinguishing between "real things" created by God and "sin," which he views not as a "thing" but as a lack or "nothingness."</note>

However, let these conclusions be held firmly:
1. Since all things were **absolutely nothing** in respect to essence, substance, and existence, it depends solely on the indifferent pleasure of God that they should exist and be made what and as many as He willed and has willed.
2. When all things, or some things, are in a **nothingness of determination**, <note>Latin: *nihilo determinationis*. A state where a choice has not yet been made.</note> it depends solely on God’s pleasure as to what, how much, and in what manner He works within them. 
3. When all things are in a state of **privative nothingness** <note>Latin: *nihili privativi*. Philosophically, evil is often defined as a "privation" or a lack of the good that should be present, rather than a positive substance created by God.</note> (that is, sin), it depends solely on God’s pleasure as to which ones He works in, and what, how much, and in what manner He works.

Therefore, the knowledge that God has concerning the essence, existence, and modes of these realities comes from Him alone, and that independently of every creature. 

Furthermore: The **Divine Operation** opposed to sin—viewed generally without determining specific degrees, etc.—depends on me only to this extent: *that if it does not happen within me, I am the cause of its absence.* This is not properly a **dependence of the operation** itself, just as the **light of the Sun** does not depend on me, even though by closing my eyes I cause myself to be deprived of it.

Let us proceed. God is by no means the cause of the idea, notion, or existence of sin. In whatever way God knows sin, He does not depend on anyone—nor even on time—for the slightest reality of His cognition. Privations or sins are foreseen by God (in whatever way that happens) such that this foresight is not the cause of why sins exist or are; or rather, it does not "bring them about," since they do not require a positive cause. All these things have been demonstrated in their proper places and are sufficient.

...firstly, regarding those three types of sin already reviewed, I am not speaking of those sins that follow once the first has been committed—for those are easily understood and foreseen once the first acts are presupposed. But what of the *first* sins? I say, after having thought long upon it and cast my eyes here and there, that we must return to this honest confession: I do not know, nor can I know, nor ought I to know, nor do I even desire to know any further. (a) *Your wonderful knowledge is too great for me, and so high that I cannot reach it,* says the divine Man <note>Refers to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>. Is it necessary for the peace of my soul that I know exactly how knowledge exists within God? Therefore, we leave aside these rash inquiries, content with what is clearly recognized.

### XII.
Regarding the Divine governance and providence concerning those more specific sins that follow once one of the primary sins has been committed—or rather, concerning the various appearances and "faces" of sin—the matter is easily understood. I call these the "appearances," or "faces," or "garments," or "signs" of sin: the particular ways, usually showing themselves outwardly, by which it is made manifest that the **Mind** has turned away from its own state of **nothingness** <note>The author uses "nothingness" (*nihili sui*) to describe the soul's proper state of humble dependence on God; to leave this state is to claim a false self-sufficiency.</note> toward an **empty idol**. One person reveals this by absurdly focusing on metals or wealth, another on carnal things, or other matters which are sometimes thought to be very great, or even highly spiritual. I would prefer to call these the different "garments" and "appearances" of a single internal and enduring sin—a single state of privation within the Mind—rather than different species or natures of sin. 

Now, as far as the sin itself is concerned, if we are to speak accurately, God does not "govern" it; for there is nothing positive in God that could properly terminate in sin, which is a **non-entity** <note>Latin: *non-ens*. In scholastic philosophy, evil is not a "thing" created by God, but a lack or "privation" of good.</note>. Instead, God establishes and governs the *subject* of the sin—that is, the **Spontaneous Thought** <note>The active power of the soul to generate its own ideas and choices.</note>, as well as the body, its modes, its movements, and the objects surrounding it in this or that way and time. These things are not sins in themselves; they are realities. As has been demonstrated, all reality is established and governed by God according to His most free will. Consequently, when the sinful Mind is joined to and entangled with these realities, it causes its own sin (conceived and already committed within itself) to appear in various ways, according to the countless diversity of surrounding circumstances. From this, the sin acquires different names: for example, murder, theft, greed, lust, and so on, depending on the different means through which it appears that the mind has deflected from its proper "nothingness" and has absurdly wished to view and rule itself as its own Master, principle, and goal. 

However, we set aside these particularities. Let it suffice here to have noticed how certainly God—who knows His own will most certainly—foresees even this accidental diversity according to His own real operations; and how holily He presides as **Ruler** over that diversity.

To Him, *darkness is light* <note>original: "Tenebræ sunt ipsi Lux"</note>, or rather, the darkness commends the beauty of His light. It is easy for an attentive person to illuminate all the divine attributes by inspecting sin in its own truly admirable way.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *Several properties or denominations of sin are explained.*

*1. That it is unjust. 2. Negation of God. 3. Privation. 4. Adherence to oneself, appropriation, one's own will, etc. 5. Pride. 6. How the sinner is to be regarded.*

<margin>I.</margin>
It is clear from what has been said, First, why sin is called *unjust* and indecent. For whether I look at myself insofar as I am the work of God, it is absurd for me to conduct myself as if I were not-the-work of God, or as the work of myself—which nevertheless happens whenever I wish to be "something" from myself and to be ruled by myself. Or, if I look at myself insofar as I am the work of my own self—that is, insofar as I am nothing at all—it is likewise unjust for me not to conduct myself toward myself as nothing.

<margin>II.</margin>
Second, it is clear how sin is a *negation of God*. God, the Ruler, Goal, and Principle of all things, is alone something from Himself, and is one and the same; and He is represented thus through the form of my Mind <term>Mind: The author uses the Latin *Mens* to refer to the higher rational faculty which, when healthy, reflects the divine order.</term>, insofar as the Mind is limited by Him, tends toward Him, and is established by Him. But when I do not remain in a fitting nothingness <note>The author argues that creatures have no independent existence; to claim independence is to ignore the "nothingness" from which we were created.</note>, but instead I attempt to limit or not limit myself through my own power—as it seems best to me, who am nothing—then I do away with God as Ruler. And when I held myself (who am nothing) as the goal, I do away with God as the Goal. Finally, when I pretend to act as if from myself, I deny within me God as the Principle: that is, I wickedly deny God. From this, one may observe how many things in us are infected by sin. Every act of body or mind regarding this or the future life, from which God as Ruler, End, and Principle is absent, is stained by sin. The faculty of either the body or the Mind is good, the object is good, and the act is good; but the negation of God—the failure to relate back to Him through the absurd positioning of "myself" (who am nothing)—is evil. For example: the faculty and action of rejoicing are good; knowledge or material riches are also good; but if I rejoice in them without God, that is, for my own sake, because...

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, one can see how Sin is a privation <term>privatio: the absence of a quality or state that is normally or naturally present</term>. It is a privation or an undue absence of that state of nothingness in which I ought to have remained. It is also a privation or undue absence of God's operation within me. Not that God was required to work in me or was obligated to do so; but since His operation is absent through my own fault—even though it comes from His generosity—this absence is called "undue" or "wrongful." The "form" which the Mind received from God is, as I have seen: (1) To be limited or even increased and varied according to God's pleasure, or to be placed and exercised by Him in different states, sometimes having more and sometimes less reality. (2) To tend toward Him. (3) To depend entirely upon Him. But when I sin, I resist Him, behaving as if I were not through God, not toward Him, and not from Him. Therefore, in me as a sinner, there is a privation of my own self (insofar as I am God’s work), of my own form, or at least of its more worthy completion. Hence, the sinning Mind is truly a formless monster, or a thing without form.

Specifically, when the Mind sins, it does not overlook itself; it does not hold and maintain itself as is fitting for something that is "nothing" of itself. Instead, it positions itself as if it were something *from* itself, *toward* itself, and *through* itself. Continuing in this vein, it infects whatever faculties and acts it has with this mask <note>original: "larva"</note> of itself. This is properly what it means to adhere to oneself in act and habit. -># ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL<-

I turn toward myself, I stand as the Judge and director of my own existence, and I ask of myself (as I did at the beginning) what is the best and most pleasing way of living? I choose that which soothes the mind and body with honor, abundance, and pleasant sensations, and which removes me from disgrace, poverty, and pain. I establish the objects of science or knowledge, of love, hatred, sadness, joy, and other faculties and passions as they appear to *me*, rather than as they appear to God, to His pleasure, and to His dispensing providence. Then my Mind <gloss>Mens</gloss> clings to itself, and claims itself for itself; it acts as if it were its own work, to be cared for and governed by itself and for itself, through means which it usurps as its own. It considers itself private, its own master <term>sui juris: a legal term meaning "of one's own right," or not under the power of another</term>, and belonging to itself; and in doing so, it commits a theft. And this comes from sin as it has been explained: namely, the Mind absurdly positions itself as the director, the end <term>finis: the ultimate goal or purpose</term>, and the principle <term>principium: the source or starting point</term>, when in fact it is none of these things.

But it also happens sometimes that we seem to ourselves to cling to God, when in truth we are most miserably slaves to ourselves. For if I give myself to spiritual goods, knowledge, meditations, prayers, and to the love and pleasure of God itself in such a way that I intend my own benefit in this and the future life—enticed by the pleasant feeling of these things, or struck by the fear of the opposite discomforts—then I cling not so much to God as to myself. I am attached to Him only as a means <term>medium: the instrument or way to get something</term>, but to myself as the "end" for whose sake the means is tended and sought. That is, I wish to cling to God because I first cling to myself and desire to cling to myself even more; I hold myself as the one for whose sake God and all other things exist. Thus, God is used as a ladder and a set of steps placed underneath so that one might ascend to the summit of one's own advantage. 

In this way, the sinner—who, in relation to the whole of reality, is no more than a single hair is to the human body—acts more absurdly than if the entire body were measured by the convenience of one hair, as if the body had been made just so that one hair might be nourished, or as if the mind were joined to that body simply to ensure that hair was well-tended and governed. One must be careful, however, not to cling to oneself now as the source, now as the means, now as the end—whether in all three ways or in just one, while relating the others to God. If I should desire certain goods for the sake of God and for Him alone, yet I still look upon myself, my resolutions, my promises, my industry, and my habits as the "acting principle," then while embracing God as the *end*, I am still clinging to myself as the *source*. If I cling to God as the source, wanting Him to use His power to do those things that delight me, then while holding God as the *source*, I cling to myself as the *goal* <note>original: "scopo"</note>. Finally, if I look upon God as both the end and the source, but I want those things which He is to do in me for His own sake to be done according to my own reasoning, my imagination, and my ways; then I cling to myself as the *means*. By doing so, I displace God—as I have just said—now as the end, now as the source, now as the means, through this self-clinging and self-embrace...

<summary>The author argues that the root of sin is "self-adherence," where the individual treats themselves as the source, means, or end of their existence. This displacement of God is portrayed as an absurd inversion of reality, likened to an entire body serving a single hair.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's psychological deconstruction of sin. On the previous page, the author explored how the "I" (the Ego) usurps God’s role as the center of existence. Here, the focus shifts to how even reliance on others can be a form of self-idolatry, the definition of pride as a departure from truth, and the necessity of radical self-loathing as a response to the "nothingness" of the sinner.</meta>

-># RATIONAL REFLECTIONS<-

...of my most vain idol, myself. Although sin also seems to consist in clinging to other things—as when a person, not trusting themselves, thinks they cannot obtain goods (whether apparent or real) without the effort, industry, work, or favor of others, as if God were powerless without them—nevertheless, because these things borrow their force from each person's own imagination, they are poured back into each person's adherence to themselves. Everything in the state of a Creature—its preservation, action, and governance—for which the reason given by the creature is *I* <note>original: "Ego"</note>, "I will," "it pleases me," and the like, and which is not truly God's pleasure, is sinful. That *I* <note>original: "Ego"</note> to which one clings is the worst position of the Idol of Jealousy <note>original: "Idoli Zelotypiæ." This is likely a reference to the "image of jealousy" mentioned in the Book of Ezekiel (8:3), signifying something that provokes God's righteous anger by taking His place.</note>.

V. Fifth, it is clear from these points that sin is rightly designated by the name of *Pride* <note>original: "Superbiæ"</note>, since pride is nothing other than thinking more of oneself than is just, and exceeding the truth in the opinion or governance of oneself. This happens when the sinner, abandoning his own nothingness, seems to himself to be "something" from himself—either by inspecting himself or by comparison with others—and when he behaves as if he were something great. In this way, as has been seen, God is denied and driven out so that the sinner may occupy His place as if he were more worthy. The Mind's recourse to God as a "means" toward an "end" <note>The author is criticizing the use of religion as a tool for personal gain.</note>, which the sinning Mind establishes as its own benefit, must rightly be held as detestable pride, since it places God below the Mind. Reflect from this on what true humility is, how necessary it is, and how truly it is said to include every virtue.

VI. Finally, from this we know that the sinner must not only regard himself as nothing, omit himself, pass himself over, and deny himself: but he must even hate himself, be indignant with himself, detest himself, shudder at himself, oppose himself, and be his own enemy with mourning and grief. For if he had remained in an unblemished state, he would then simply have had to regard himself as nothing; and there is no doubt that the pure Minds of the Angels <note>original: "Angelorum Mentes"</note> conduct themselves in this first way. Since they are by themselves mere nothingness and have absolutely nothing from themselves, they regard themselves as nothing and claim nothing for themselves at all. But indeed, that which is worse than nothing—namely, the sinner—from whom not only can nothing good proceed to show himself pleasing to God, but also from whom everything that exists is more rejectable than nothingness; who, as such, has nothing of his own except what is worse than nothing, more injurious to God, and more hostile; such a one, I say, it is fitting to treat as "less than nothing." That is, one must pursue him with the greatest aversion and with the greatest complaints, and he must be judged as abominable as his opposite—namely, God and His pleasure—ought to be loved and desired.

-># ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL<-

## THE FINAL CHAPTER

*1. 2. 3. 4. A few words on the extension or repression of sin in actions and at the root. 5. 6. On the distinction between the sins of the righteous and the unrighteous. 7. On the certainty of one's own state. 8. The conclusion of all things.*

I. It can be seen, both from what has been deduced so far and from other points that could be—though need not be—brought forward, that the idea of sin, as it has been set forth, serves primarily to allow one to judge it rightly. It allows everyone to know the extent to which they are either free from sin or enslaved to it. The common people <note>original: "vulgus"</note> are deceived about sin by judging according to externals, appearances, and indeed those more "shining" actions which strike and move anyone, even the most dull-witted. They compose their judgments as if the nature of sin consisted in these outer husks <note>original: "corticibus," literally "barks" or "shells." The author suggests that external behavior is merely the surface of the true spiritual reality.</note>. That life is praised as upright which displays nothing offensive to human eyes—that is, to their customs and their judgments of what is good (which are often the worst). But as a life produces more or less of those things externally which deviate from those standards, it is likewise judged as more or less evil. Not only does one person judge another this way, but, what is worse, each person judges themselves. What else is this than to basely deceive oneself? One must descend to the very innermost roots of thoughts and the principles of *Being and nothingness* <note>original: "Entis et nihili." This refers to the metaphysical status of the creature: God is "Being" itself, while the creature, on its own, is "nothingness."</note> in the sight of the Supreme Being; only then will the difference between the righteous and the unrighteous, and between greater and lesser sin, become clear. Then, perhaps, some who are most just and upright in their own opinion and that of others might recognize themselves as constantly sinning in this way. But how few are those who strive to ensure that their own foulness is known and understood by themselves?

II. There are those whose sin is something intermittently lasting and permanent; from whom their "due nothingness" <note>original: "debitum suum nihil." A technical term in this context meaning the humble acknowledgment that the creature is nothing without God.</note> is continually absent. Absent too is the surrender of oneself as an existing being, as a non-goal, a non-principle, and a non-Lord. Consequently, God as the All, God as the Goal, God as the Principle and the Lord is absent. Instead, there is present the self of each person as if it were "something"—though it is an empty shadow <note>original: "cassa umbra"</note>—and this is present in all actions, purposes, prayers, love, choice, and other such things. If these people occasionally allow their "nothingness" to intervene—by admitting that they are nothing, can do nothing of themselves, or deserve nothing, and similar things—they do so with the intent of acquiring something for their idol <note>the self</note> from God or from men, so that they might render that idol more conspicuous by this "shadow of humility." They might even permit God, who surrounds them on all sides and is ready to enter, to take part, but...

-># RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

->290<-

...Him as a means, as a servant, and as an executor of their own lust, and not as the Beginning, Director, and sole End of all things (a privilege they instead reserve for their own fantasy). The sins of such people are not to be counted as if they were interrupted acts, scattered here and there and sown intermittently throughout their lives—in the way they occasionally commit certain external irregularities. Rather, their whole life is one single, continuous sin, or involves it, since the absence of what is owed <note>That is, the honor and orientation of the soul owed to God.</note> and the presence of what is not owed <note>The elevation of the self-ego.</note> endure without interruption. Therefore, whatever such minds do or omit, whether they appear upright or appear wicked (for it is all the same in this investigation), they sin. 

Their ignorance, their knowledge, their love, their senses, their passions, and their intentions are not indeed evil in their substance <note>original: "materialiter," meaning the raw matter or faculty of the thought is not inherently evil, but its orientation is.</note>, but they are contaminated by evil. This is because they exist outside of any regard for God, springing instead from alien reasons and motives—various ones, just as each person has fashioned them differently on various occasions. Yet all of these can easily be resolved into a single idea of sin. 

And so, if such people are ignorant of God, they sin by clinging to their own negligence; or if they do know Him, they sin by acquiring and holding that knowledge unjustly—either because they are curious, or because they wish to be considered learned, or holy, or close to God, or as if they were His private secretaries <note>original: "quasi à secretis." This refers to those who claim a special, privileged intimacy with the divine to bolster their own status.</note> by themselves or by others. They sin when they do not pray, for then God is deserted; they sin when they pray—that is, when they pour out their lusts <note>original: "concupiscentias"</note> before God so that He might agree with them and fulfill them. They sin by practicing temperance and sobriety, specifically so that the idol of themselves, to which they refer everything, might last longer, or so they may be celebrated as sober men; but they also sin by intemperance, choosing pleasure as the Counselor and Ruler of the life they lead. 

They sin in giving alms, for looking only to themselves, they think they can thus bend God to their own advantages, or they attempt to corrupt His rightful judgments against them with gifts. That they also sin through greed and hardness of heart is neither doubtful nor obscure. Whether they work or are idle, they sin; they are far from that state of "nothingness of self and everything of God" <note>original: "nihilum sui, totumque Dei." A common theme in mystical theology involving the total surrender of the ego to the divine will.</note>; in its place is the positioning of their own self-indulgence. 

Do they punish the guilty—thieves, murderers, atheists, or blasphemers? They sin no less. A love of themselves and their own conveniences rules them, lest they themselves be harmed; likewise a desire that they might appear to themselves and others as glowing with Divine Zeal. But if they let the guilty go unpunished, they become accomplices to the crime and thus also sin. 

What more shall I say, except to agree with the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "cum Sacris"</note>, that no good dwells in them, that a bad tree cannot bear good fruit, that they are unfit for every good work, and that nothing is pure among the impure? Wherever they turn, with whatever garment or appearance—even the most holy and angelic—they may be covered, they carry a fountain of sin within them, branching out into streams in every direction, by which everything, everything...

...completely; those things within them are infected not by an interrupted act, but by one single continuous stretch. The entire course of such a life, which is not referred to God as is fitting, abolishes God as far as it is able. It confesses nothing to God as is owed, except perhaps indirectly—as a state of deserved nothingness—or directly, in the sense that every real thing within a creature should confess in the thing itself that God alone is all things, operating from Himself, toward Himself, and through Himself. To continually employ a good and a work belonging to another <note>The "another" here refers to God, the true owner of all things.</note> without acknowledging its Author and possessor, without consulting Him, and even for the purpose of removing Him as much as possible, is a continuous act of hostility. This is what the sinner does: using mind, body, time, and many other creatures, even if he does so in a way that does not outwardly offend other men. Nor is it possible to be liberated from this state and return to friendship with the Supreme Being except through a hatred of one's own self (as a sinner), a displeasure rooted in sorrow, and the restoration of that state of "nothingness" <note>A theological term for humility, recognizing that the creature has no independent existence or goodness apart from God.</note> which lasts forever and in which it is fitting for us to be before God. Indeed, the undue absence of these things provides the principles, fuel, and growth of sin; while their presence is the very field of God’s operations.

III. However, I would not want it concluded that the only people to be considered truly sorrowful and self-denying are those who no longer sin at all, or that no one who remains liable to sin to some degree can be outside the state of sin. But, you might ask, why should this not be so? Why is it that from a single act of the Mind, by which it first applied itself to sin, there followed such a continuation and habit of sinning that the mind was rendered unfit for the opposite and was established as purely sinful, without any mixture of justice? And why, in the same way, is the mind not rendered so unfit for sinning by a single act of self-hatred, self-denial, and divine operation (if it is truly present) that sin is clearly no longer mixed in, but only pure justice? Unless this is the case, does it not seem that good is more powerless and imperfect than evil? Furthermore, if sin were to return while in a state of self-denial, would not that habitual state of pure iniquity return by that very fact, just as happened after the first sin? 

It certainly would return—to answer this beforehand—unless God, by His powerful grace, prevented it. But regarding all these matters, I say that one must not judge evil in the same way as the eradication of evil and the establishment of good. For evil does not need to be positively sustained in order to last; once admitted, it endures purely and constantly through itself, without any positive cause and without God, provided it is simply left to itself (which is not a perfection in it, but a massive imperfection). But it is not so with the eradication of evil and the positioning of good, which require a cause that is positive in the highest degree. For these things, once begun by a most powerful cause, cease if they are not continued by it; and once established, they do not sustain themselves, but must be continually reproduced by another—namely, by God, who according to His pleasure...

# RATIONAL THOUGHTS.
<meta>catchword: suffi- (likely "sufficit," meaning "is sufficient")</meta>

...the agent <note>Referring to God as the primary actor in the soul's restoration.</note> establishes rules, a method, and a measure for His operations at their beginning and in their continuation. Thus, nothing prevents Him from choosing to begin and increase something incrementally and in stages. Nevertheless, He acts truly and constantly, eventually leading the work to completion. He does not immediately cast out "privation" <term>privatio: the theological concept that evil is not a substance but the absence or "lack" of a required good</term> in the first moment to perform sublime works. Instead, He begins—sometimes for a long time—through the lowest and coarsest things. These coarser elements attack, fight, and gradually overcome the sin that was within them. Then, He slowly introduces more sublime and stronger elements to battle against the more robust evils, until victory is finally obtained and the person enjoys that Divine peace which exists in the Mind on the Divine side. 

For this reason, pauses are left by God—for the wisest of reasons—during the first and even the middle periods of the restoration of minds. There are gaps to be filled later and weaknesses to be healed afterward. This is done to bring us to self-knowledge, to make us distrust ourselves more, to deny ourselves as nothing (or less than nothing), to provide a caution and a stimulus for prayer, to foster humility and compassion for others, and finally, for His glory. 

Therefore, a Mind touched by a hatred of evil and a love for God should not completely lose heart when it does not see such an abundance of God's operations within itself, but instead notices its own weaknesses. Much less should it grumble against God or argue with Him. Rather, it is fitting for us to grieve that evils are present and goods are lacking through our own fault—goods which would have been given to us had we not sinned. Yet, if we look to God, who justly disposes His grace (which is not owed to the sinner), we must revere His judgments concerning us with silence, acquiescence, and adoration. Indeed, in this very act lies the greatest **self-denial** <note>original: *sui abnegatio*</note> and **divine operation** <note>original: *Dei operatio*</note>.

IV. Certainly, whatever happens regarding the "remnants of sin" <note>original: *reliquiis peccati*</note> in those whom God takes up to be restored, He does not permit the innermost and ultimate depth of the Mind, so to speak, to be touched by evil. Nor does He allow the conscience and the intellect to be defiled, except in the most extraordinary cases (and even then, not directly). Nor does He allow the greater part of life or its habits to be bound and held by evil. Within the depths of the mind, a hatred of one's own sinful self presides—even if in a weak way, it is nonetheless sincere. There is a sense of one's own "nothingness" <note>original: *nihilum sui*</note> and a frequently repeated reflection upon these things, from which habits are born. There are also many other operations of God present: knowledge and love, through which God remains the Beginning, the middle, and the goal of all things in the mind. 

Yet, the nature of the Mind, as God has established it here, does not allow for a direct, actual, and express reflection upon a single object (such as God) at all times. For who would require this to be constantly present even in matters where sin is absent? After all, an intention or a habit of referring things to God—even when one is not actually thinking of God due to the limits of thought—

->### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.<-

...be sufficient? <note>Continuing from the previous page's question regarding whether God's initial actions in the soul are enough.</note> Since the body also necessarily holds back the thoughts of the Mind at times, and since God has willed not to banish all ignorance and every fold <term>plica: a metaphor for ingrained habits or "creases" in the soul's character</term> of evil habit from the mind all at once, nor to perform every good immediately, hence there arise in the mind occasional languors and defects. Yet the most good God uses these so admirably that they serve like a wall, so that sin may not penetrate incurably to the very bottom of the Mind. 

Consider, I pray, the Mind’s most vast and swift faculty of thinking, by which it could reflect on God either always or often; its freedom, by which it is held back by no body against its will; its knowledge, by which ignorance would not be clouded; its full spontaneity, which would not be enticed by the preceding "folds" of wicked habits and various, almost involuntary impulses. If sin were to happen where these perfections were present, what would they have profited those who possessed them? They would only have made the soul incurable by rendering everything totally and profoundly devastated. This is evident in the Angelic Minds <note>Referring to the fallen angels, whose sin is traditionally considered "incurable" because it was committed with perfect knowledge and will</note>; for since they were endowed with these high prerogatives, they admitted sin, but a sin that cannot be erased. 

But if sin happens where the limits of thinking are narrow—where the body necessarily holds back thought so that at that time one cannot think of God—then a person is prevented by these very limitations from forgetting God out of the Mind’s innermost insolence. He is prevented from choosing earthly lusts over God out of a totally free and malicious choice. If, while ignorance remains, it is ensured in this way that the intelligence and conscience are not fundamentally penetrated by evil (which would happen if clear knowledge were always present); and finally, if sin is committed where the "folds" of past evils and habits create an impulse in the mind against the person's will—often with the mind enduring this with a groan—then the pure and innermost consent of the will is protected from being violated by a purely spontaneous desire to embrace evil. 

And thus the innermost parts of the Intelligence, the Will, and the Mind are preserved, so that sin, when it occurs, strikes against those things which are more external. It exerts its force—much like the Serpent striking the heel <note>original: "ut Serpens in calcem"; a reference to the curse in Genesis 3:15</note>—and indeed expires there, while the inner parts remain more secretly hidden. Thus the admirable God disposes darkness around His tabernacle <note>The "tabernacle" here is the soul where God dwells</note>, the Mind in which He remains, and uses those darknesses for its protection. Thus His ways are so admirably kind that where we often think there is a rightful place for complaint, such great thanks must be given to Him that they exceed our understanding. 

Meanwhile, I would not want this to be taken as if these things were said to cloak sin or to patronize it. Everyone knows that Diabolical sins are more atrocious than merely human ones; and among human sins, those which are done knowingly, purely, spontaneously, and with no violent impulse, outweigh those which happen otherwise. The lapses of those with high perfections are more grave and almost incurable. To illustrate this in passing was my intent.

->### RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

**V.** There is no reason for the wicked to think they are joined with the righteous, simply because they are said to agree in some matters. The learned and the unlearned often agree to the extent that neither of them thinks of the sciences for a time; both are occupied with something similar and act in a similar way. Indeed, both may be infected by the same error—such as when both, looking at the Sun, admit the thought that it is no larger than it appears to be. <note>original: "non esset major quam apparet" — a common philosophical example illustrating how our senses can deceive both the wise and the ignorant alike.</note> But if one were to examine the innermost disposition of the mind, its habits, and its ordinary and principal actions, how great is the difference between the two!

In this way, and even more so, do the righteous differ from the wicked. The righteous are only sometimes in an **act** of sin, whereas the wicked are always in a **state** of sin; their sins also differ fundamentally from one another. The lapse of a righteous person occurs in the "subject"—in the external expression—while in the Mind, the innermost core, the principle, habits, purposes, and the primary way of conducting life remain good and Divine. Furthermore, he does not persevere in sin, but the mind immediately turns away from it toward God. He is much like a magnetic needle <note>original: "acus magnete tacta" — a popular 17th-century scientific metaphor for the soul's natural orientation toward God.</note> that has been twisted from its direction by a violent obstacle and held to the ground; even so, it retains the principle of its path within itself, and as soon as it is returned to the open air and set upright, it immediately looks toward its pole again. Finally, this sin is diminished day by day until it reaches that measure of perfection which is permitted here through divine grace.

A repenting sinner is like a child who, having seriously detested his own disobedience and desertion of his father’s will, is no longer prepared to follow his own whims. Out of a most tender love for the Father, he returns home and toils at the labor assigned by the Father. But because his limbs are less agile and less accustomed to work than if he had never left (and had allowed himself to be trained by his Father), he proceeds slowly at the start of resuming his work, pauses often, and makes many errors. Yet these errors are not made in destroying, but in building up the Father’s work; they are not done by design, but unwillingly or without thinking; they occur not always, but only at intervals. He corrects himself as much as he can, day by day, until at last he attains perfection in the Father’s work. The others <note>the wicked</note> run about the city streets, willfully ignorant and idle, or even devoted to those things which are hateful to the Lord.

**VI.** From these things, it is clear what should be thought regarding the sins of the righteous and how they appear. If the wicked—who neglect God but care only for themselves—misuse these appearances by flattering themselves, what is there that they could not misuse? ->### ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.<-

...to behold Divine thoughts and operations in such a holy mind, so that they may be led by them to God. God will cause the Holy Mind to make these operations appear to others through certain signs in the body, so arranging the tongue, all the limbs, external goods, and external life, that those who see nothing there which does not tend toward God alone—through the setting aside of all things that are not Himself—may be stirred to the pursuit of a similar life. The mode and form of this life, which is pleasing to God, is set forth in that humanity which God Himself most closely united to Himself, in the **God-Man** <note>original Greek: "Θεανθρώπῳ" (Theanthrōpō) — a theological term for Christ as both fully God and fully human.</note> Jesus Christ. He lived a life that was simple, humble, patient, and knowing no violence; it was neither soft nor grand. He trampled upon attachment to creatures, earthly things, the senses, pleasures, passions, the honor and glory of the world, the wisdom of the age, and the tricks and subtleties of worldly discourses and sciences. He crushed all low and earthly forms of thought and all similar things in which men usually seek themselves, and which remove the necessary state of self-denial. He did this so that man might learn to abandon himself in all things, to cling to nothing, and to not be his own goal or motive, so that the Divine form might be restored in him according to God's pleasure—even though that form often appears, in its outward shapes, to be low, bitter, and unpleasant. No way of living, or if you prefer, no Religion, is more truly and evidently rational than this.

**VII.** Meanwhile, such is our blindness that it must be admitted it is difficult not to be deceived—I do not mean in judging generally and abstractly, as we are doing here, about the state of sin, of "nothingness," <note>original: "nihili" — likely referring to the philosophical concept of the creature's inherent nothingness apart from God.</note> and of the operations of God—but in each person's subjective recognition of themselves and others. Some sometimes think they are doing poorly when they are doing well; sometimes they think they are doing well when they are in the worst possible state. Regarding others, envy, or the desire to please, or a mere similarity in habits perverts our judgment. How then shall I rightly and certainly know whether it is sin, or indeed the operation of God, that is occurring in me or in others? Many think they are dead to sin, that they are practitioners of self-denial, that they are reborn, and full of divine operations, and yet they are deceived. Beyond the particular experience of the Divine truth itself, nothing is certain. Even in natural matters, very many consider themselves most learned who possess nothing but trifles. Just as no one intimately knows what natural truth is, or what a clear and distinct perception is, except the one who actually possesses it—for he alone is most certain that what he possesses is the truth, and that others who are not so disposed are deprived of it (even though those in error are also most persuaded that their errors are the truth and their concepts are clear and distinct)—for truth affects the mind in a certain way that is inimitable to error. Truth touches the roots of thought where error cannot reach, even if the inexperienced do not notice it or even think they are experiencing it themselves. Thus, only he who has experienced and received the truth of the supernatural operations of God knows...

->### RATIONAL THOUGHTS<-

truly knows what that [Divine operation] is, and can testify with certainty that they are not deceived; they know their testimony is true, and that God is working within them in a unique way. However, for another person who has not experienced this, but who nevertheless thinks the same of themselves, their error cannot be demonstrated by any human through the perception of the opposing truth. For no one can move and affect another’s innermost depths in the way that person is affected by God. Furthermore, the most certain kind of God's operation is of such a nature that God affects the mind without any medium <note>original: "sine ullo medio" — this refers to 'immediate' grace or revelation, where God acts directly on the soul without the use of senses, images, or logic.</note> in the way most proper to Himself, and most different from all those operations where intermediaries intervene. Therefore, this cannot be shown, demonstrated, or even named by anyone to another—that is, its idea cannot be sparked by words—since it rejects every medium. If it were otherwise, it would not be an immediate operation of God, whose presence is established by God alone—purely, so to speak, and through Himself—without anything else.

Meanwhile, just as a person who possesses knowledge is sometimes not actively moved by that knowledge, so Divine operations often lie hidden without being directly felt. They are then thought to be absent—which leads to the lamentable complaints of even the holiest people—and yet they are present most closely and most truly. But in this latter case, it is best not to cling to the *feeling* of these operations, nor even to the operations of God themselves insofar as they relate to us. Instead, one should choose nothing, desire nothing, and will nothing—neither sweetness nor bitterness, greatness nor smallness, things visible nor things despised, knowledge nor ignorance. One should not care whether they are hidden or revealed, whether they perform miracles or not, or whether they see such things or not. Rather, one must offer oneself absolutely, without condition or regard for oneself, and indeterminately to the Divine pleasure. One should deeply desire that whatever seems good to God be done in us, concerning us, and by us—whether we feel we are consenting or not. For afterward, God will manifest His most divine operations along with that surrender, and they will be accepted and known with the greatest safety. Without this surrender, there is a danger that even the best of people might embrace and follow their own emotional impulses <note>original: "affectus" — often referring to passions or subjective feelings rather than divine guidance.</note> instead of God's operations.

If, however, it is a question of judging the spiritual state of others, this cannot be done correctly by those who are themselves in a state of evil. As long as the multitude remains carnal <note>meaning focused on physical desires and worldly logic rather than spiritual insight.</note>, it judges things to be the opposite of what they truly are. For even the Sophists <note>The author likely refers to scholastic philosophers or rhetoricians who use complex but empty logic to maintain their status.</note>, when the question concerns easier matters that do not oppose human desires, triumph before the crowd while proposing foolish nonsense for so many centuries, having driven everyone else out. What then will happen when they deal with matters of a deeper inquiry?

### VIII.

To say something regarding this state of affairs: the world has labored so that, even if the divine light cannot be recognized through its own people, its own darkness—which it offers to be felt by the hands of everyone—is not ignored. Thus, it can now be noticed without difficulty that the world, which is the work and inheritance of God, has been alienated from its God. Hardened in rebellion, it has become exceedingly Atheistic <note>In this context, "atheistic" refers to "practical atheism"—living as if God does not exist or has no authority, rather than a modern philosophical denial of His existence.</note> and lies submerged in evil. It is given over to vanity, which has now passed into established rules and is regarded as moral uprightness, honesty, and a matter for boasting...

Consider those who, joined as if by a divine bond of kinship, called themselves Christian brothers. They professed to be redeemed by Christ and should have been ready to pour out their bodies, minds, lives, and possessions—which were not their own, but at the Lord’s disposal—at His slightest nod and command, however harsh or absurd it might seem to them. Yet, instead—not to mention their other iniquities—one could see them (despite the prohibitions, commands, dogmas, parables, and sacraments of their Lord’s kingdom of patience, despite the banner of love, the formula of prayer, the final testament, and finally His own example) raging against one another over earthly trifles. They cry out to Him whom they called their common Father, asking that He provide them with the spirit, the swords, and the fury to courageously fill everything with the slaughter of their fellows. They sing even greater thanks to the Father the more people they have butchered, and the more perfectly and profoundly Divine Charity <note>original: "Charitas" — the highest form of Christian love, selfless and directed toward God and neighbor.</note> has been extinguished in their hearts. 

And this is how things have been until now, and how they still are, approved by everyone—even by those who are, if we are to believe it, the "lights of the world." But what is to be expected as long as (and this is the source of evil) everyone thinks they have the right to dispose of themselves and other things—either all or some—at their own pleasure? And many even imagine they have this right from God or from nature! For what else is it to make God the Author of sin, if not this? Namely, that God would have established and brought it about that man’s own Idol, his own worship and rules, should act and dispose of himself and others based on the principle of his own pleasure, for his own sake, and because it pleases him! And these things, mixed and translated in various ways, are taken as the legitimate foundations of human society (if one is permitted to follow a blind guide)! ### RATIONAL THOUGHTS ON GOD, THE SOUL, AND EVIL.

...they would possess those things which serve more and more to intoxicate them: so great is the calamity of this servitude that unless you come quickly, O God, the Restorer <note>original: "Reparator" — one who repairs or renews creation.</note> of all things, upon whom alone the eyes of your people are fixed, your works seem destined to suffer total ruin. And would that, as you have indeed promised, O truthful God, you might soon be present to act, so that our crimes might be blotted out and we might be led back, through a hatred of our [selfish] selves, to the state of nothingness <note>This refers to a mystical concept where the soul empties itself of ego to be filled by God.</note> that is our due. May you bring it about in us that, all other things being dismissed like mere rubbish, we have but one zeal: for You, just as You offered Yourself to be seen in Your **Holy humanity**; and may You take us up as little children—who wish henceforth to be ignorant of all things so that we may be committed to You alone—as disciples of Your Spirit, to be taught by Him those things which You have reserved for those who love You. Thus, once the vain phantom of our "self" is expelled, You alone may reign in all things, possess all things, fill all things, and through the perfection of Your works, be all in all.

Lord, may You also wish, according to Your good pleasure, to kindly accept whatever good is here (for if there is anything, it is entirely from You); and whatever evil has been committed in these pages, or if anything has been said that is not becoming of You, do not impute it to me; and employ all of it to promote the praise and glory of Your Name. This is not because I think You have any need for words composed with such art—according to the modern custom, and not without weariness—nor do You know that I intend for men to strive for an artificial science or knowledge of You from this work. But if any good can come from the study of **Philosophizing** (as it is called among men) when it is truer and more sincere, I intended to offer that to You, O God, as a **Sacrifice**. My hope was that if any of those who, while pretending to be wise in their studies, often become fools, should look upon these thoughts ascending toward You, they might leave behind the ashes, the skin, even the waste and the smoke of the words, appearances, and imperfections found here. Instead, by following whatever sense of the higher things is present, may they turn their strength, their eyes, and their hearts to You alone, O Lord. For You have willed to lead us to Yourself through mediums, however imperfect they may be; You did not refuse the metals, though mixed with impurities from their origin, nor those spoils which had been subject to vanity in Egypt, for the construction of Your tabernacle. <note>This is a common historical metaphor: just as the Israelites took Egyptian gold to build God's Tabernacle, the author argues that "pagan" or secular philosophy can be "purified" to serve Christian truth.</note>

# APPENDIX.

## Containing several **second thoughts** <note>original: *δευτέρας φροντίδας* — a Greek idiom for "afterthoughts" or more mature reflections.</note> concerning: I. The Soul. II. III. IV. Material things and brute creatures. V. The attributes of God. VI. Knowledge. VII. Simplicity. VIII. Power, concurrence, liberty, and the indifference of the created will, and sin. IX. Justice. X.
