<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop-cap 'H' initiates the text, featuring an intricate design of scrolling foliage and floral patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

You have before you, Reader, these free thoughts of mine, just as I wished to share them candidly two years ago—the best I had to offer then. Let your judgment of them be free. I have not sworn any oath to them <note>The author is saying he is not dogmatically wedded to these specific ideas.</note> except insofar as they commend to me a God who is All-Sufficient and Lovable. Indeed, since they are being published later than I expected, I had considered that some things in them ought to have been changed afterward. Yet, I leave them in their original state, not refusing to let it be known how far my own reasoning, without outside help, could extend itself from its own principles, and where it may have fallen short. For in the vast majority of what is written here, I saw no one whom I might follow as a guide. I confess that occasionally, as I was hurrying toward the end of the work, I happened upon certain passages from mystical authors which displayed some rays of light; however, like a flash of lightning, they disappeared suddenly, and were presented neither with their origin fixed and enduring, nor with sufficient clarity.

But now that the matter is finished, and having been granted the delay and opportunity to meditate more maturely on certain points, I will briefly advise here what the intelligent Reader might apply as a completion or emendation to the preceding pages. Nor shall I fear to profess that, among the chief occasions of truth being more clearly recognized afterward, I count the truly Heavenly Writings of the Divine Virgin *Antonia Bourignon* <note>Antonia Bourignon (1616–1680) was a famous Flemish mystic who claimed direct divine inspiration and attracted a significant following across Europe.</note>, in which Truths of such a kind are interspersed that I might compare them with those which *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius" — the Latinized name of René Descartes, the famous French philosopher.</note> said regarding natural things: that they are "capital" or principal truths, from which infinite other particular truths so flow that whatever he says he wrote about the natural world are merely the fruits or consequences of two or three such Truths; and that there still remained, to achieve his goal regarding the rest, the acquisition of two or three more such Truths, from which the rest would then sufficiently flow. Such Truths regarding Spiritual matters—and indeed, even natural ones—I have truly found in those Divine Writings,

...and fertilizing the Mind or intellect like a living seed, from which it might derive more vividly, clearly, and certainly into all other things: of which matter perhaps a specimen will be given to see in those things which I am soon to write about **Predestination**. Nor do I linger much here if some puffed-up Doctors, envious Ecclesiastics who rejoice in being called spiritual, little masters ignorant of the trifles of the Liberal arts, and Pedagogues—fascinated by the opinion of their own fullness, blinded by passions, and struck by the **Darkness** <note>original: *Scotomate* (scotoma), a medical term for a blind spot in the visual field; here used metaphorically for intellectual blindness</note> of their Scholastic trifles, and driven about by them as if in a dizzying whirl and circle—should enviously and out of their thick ignorance slander those lucid Writings, and some even to the point of madness; blaspheming things which they neither grasp, nor are they more fit to grasp solidly and with fruit (so long as they wish to be slaves of their own foolish wisdom, their affections, and worldly Parties) than a blind man is for colors, or **an ass for the lyre** <note>A classical proverb (*asinus ad lyram*) denoting total incompetence or lack of appreciation for art or wisdom.</note>; thereafter forging monsters out of these things, which nevertheless are seen nowhere except in their own dark little brains. Such indeed was, is, and shall be the Lot of Truth: that by those with bleary eyes, terrified by its splendor, it cannot be endured without curses, not even regarding those things which are natural.

Even **Descartes** <term>Carteſius</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher whose rationalist approach revolutionized science and metaphysics. The author here defends him against contemporary religious critics.</note> himself—whose genius, if we consider it naturally, I believe no one more excellent or equal has existed since the world was founded—was held and declared guilty by this troublesome sort of men of *Atheism, Blasphemy against the Veracity of God, Skepticism, and madness*, and this almost at the cost of his life: although he demonstrated the **Existence and Veracity of God** more evidently and certainly than has ever been done by any other, and began to restore truly right reasoning (from which some who call themselves his followers now depart too much) with a foundation of unshakable certainty. To be sure, those who have corrupted right reason in natural things do not want to allow it to be restored; and these same subverters of Christian Truths and Virtues cannot even tolerate the instruments by which God restores them: so that they may more securely continue to hawk their wares everywhere with the pretense and smoke of Truth.

But I, who approach the matter candidly, and wish to embrace naked truth without a dowry, or even endowed only with reproaches at my own expense, and to propose it to others, do not shrink from correction, emendation, and a more abundant illustration of the Truth, where there can truly be a place for them: indeed, as I said, I shall for that reason cast together here some things concerning certain points which I proposed in the preceding parts.

**II.** Regarding the material and corporeal things I have mentioned here and there—and indeed almost everything that **Physicists** <note>In this period, "Physicists" referred to natural philosophers who studied the laws of the physical world.</note> say—they rely on this hypothesis: *That the nature of things was established by God in the state we now see, and that we are inspecting the, as it were, inner and most essential parts of things.* In this matter, we are all deceived; nor is it possible to escape from error as long as we are not elevated beyond the present state of things, both spiritual and corporeal.

How could He have shut the **human Mind**—a Divine specimen of Goodness, Wisdom, and Power—into such a foul prison as this earth now is, and bound it with fetters and torturers in a dull body such as it is now?

Without any doubt, both God and man, and the nature of things, as they first met (if one may speak this way), regarded each other in the most excellent, glorious, and harmonious manner. Light passed, as it were, from God through man into the creatures, inasmuch as they were ruled by the judgment of man—who was a participant in <term>Divine Wisdom</term>—and at whose nod all things would have obeyed with even greater ease than the few movements of our own bodies now respond to the command of the **Mind**. And this would have persisted as long as man had properly looked toward his God, who had connected the good state and governance of man with the good state of the nature of things subject to him. 

But from the moment man turned himself away from God, and truly deprived himself of "the good" so that he might be filled with vanity, the creatures connected to him were also deprived of their good order and filled with confusion. <note>The author is making a technical theological point here: since "disorder" is a lack of something (a privation) rather than a physical "thing," God—who only creates real things—is not the cause. Instead, man is the "deficient cause" through his failure.</note> (Because these disorders are a privation, and thus a "non-being" and nothing real, they do not require an *efficient cause*, which would be God; but rather a *deficient cause*, which is man.) 

From this arose the disorders of motion and rest, the harshness and conflicts of the elements, lethargy, confused structures, thickening, strange compounds, and putrefactions. Thus, all of nature has been penetrated and covered over by a kind of <term>leprosy</term>, or a scab, or a rust (which is that "old garment" mentioned before, destined to be laid aside), the mere thickness of which strikes our dulled senses and often disturbs us against our will. 

These truths satisfy many doubts and, at the same time, are suited to pull us away from the vanity and pursuit of this world. I certainly confess that they have diminished in me, or clearly extinguished, the remains of the thirst with which I burned to penetrate the science of natural things. Indeed, I now feel a sense of nausea when I call "Physical Science" the **Science of the scab** <note>original: "Scientia scabiei"</note> with which the nature of things is incrusted, and which is soon to vanish forever. 

Nevertheless, just as in the **Mind**, even though it is corrupted by sin, many pieces of knowledge and outlines of the Divine image remain which it is right to cultivate (as I have attempted in this work), so too in **Nature**—or the faint corpse of the world—in the human body, and in its connection with the **Soul**, there remain very many proofs of the Divine image, Goodness, Wisdom, and Power. It is not improper to attend to these, as we have noted throughout this book. But let us not go too far, nor stay longer than necessary amidst this "leprosy," lest we forget the shallowness of our own knowledge which can grasp nothing perfectly! When we are restored with God, the rest of the things which now lie hidden—and which are nobler than those that appear—will be laid open at our pleasure.

For such a freedom is indeed granted to man: a freedom from which even now acts that are physically real (or good) proceed, although after the fall into sin, the will lost the power to produce moral realities, or truly spiritual ones, and thus stands in need of a **Restorer** <note>The "Restauratore" or Restorer refers to Christ, who restores the fallen human nature.</note>.

And so that it may be clear that nothing is attributed to the creature (as if one were suggesting that some reality could proceed from the creature itself, independently of God), and that nothing of reality is withdrawn from God, who causes all things; let us consider God’s willing, or God’s pleasure, as well as human liberty, as if in a state of duration. Imagine that at every single moment God were duplicating the act of willing that liberty; and as if the free will of the creature itself were every moment falling into nothingness by its own nature and needed to receive reality, or its very being, from elsewhere at every moment. In this way, we can see what reality proceeds from each side. From this it will be clear that **everything real is from God**, but from the human will comes nothing [real], or only evil.

I will illustrate this with a similar example. **Mathematicians** consider a circular figure as if it truly consisted of infinite straight lines meeting at infinite and infinitely large angles. Thus, it can be said at any point, "here is a straight line," and, "here is an infinitely large angle." Nevertheless, the whole figure is one uniform line, neither broken nor refracted, but continuous, where formally and precisely neither a straight line nor an angle exists. Yet the conclusions mathematicians draw from this consideration (or supposition) are entirely true; indeed, their truth or demonstration could not be understood in any other way. So also, in order that we may well grasp how reality...

<meta>This page continues the Appendix's investigation into the nature of human freedom and Divine providence. Having established that indifference can be viewed as "positive" when joined with God's creative will, the author now clarifies that this does not mean God recreates the soul at every single moment, but rather that He sustains a force He established once.</meta>

-> ### A P P E N D I X. <-

Everything that exists in the will and endures is brought about by God. We must conceive of this as if God instills it at every single moment; and as if the will, and the entire mind, having been extinguished every moment, as it were, are brought back to life. For all things are as much from God as if He were repeating the act of His powerful decree <note>original: "placiti"; refers to God's sovereign will or pleasure.</note> every moment; and they are just as little from the creature as if the creature actually relapsed into nothingness every moment and were placed there anew by Him. (I have already explained how all things, greatest and smallest, in bodies and minds, in all their determinations <note>The specific characteristics or "modes" that define a thing.</note>, are placed there by God alone, and not by man.) However, neither of these is precisely the case—that is, God does not literally repeat His acts every moment, nor does the creature fall back into nothingness only to receive new power through such a repetition.

For although everything that exists in the whole human being at every moment is made by God alone, God does not, strictly speaking, repeat His "positionings" <note>original: "positiones"; the acts of positing or establishing something in existence.</note> or His acts of placing anew. Likewise, a human being does not actually place themselves in a negative state every moment, as if they were actively bringing and adding negations at a first, second, and third moment, so to speak. But let this be a fixed point: namely, that nothing positive exists by human power in a way that depends on the human and is independent of God. Rather, God once bestowed a positive force upon the human when previously that human was nothing; and He willed once that it should endure, since without that will, the human would have relapsed into nothingness and remained there continually. Therefore, that force endures in the human and operates positively—not by human power, but by the power of God’s prior will. Yet it depends on the human alone, independently of all else, whether to resist or not to resist that divine force and decree. For God (we are speaking here of the state before sin) subjected that choice to the human's judgment alone to that extent, and willed that the positive force should remain and operate without hindrance as long as the human did not resist the Divine pleasure, but remained subject to it and dependent on Him from whom the human has both themselves and all their power. It is not, however, as if a human could claim to operate positively from themselves and independently; for this very thing is <term>disorder</term> <note>original: "ἀταξία" (ataxia); a lack of proper order or arrangement, often used to describe sin as a deviation from the natural order.</note>, or the absence of good, and therefore evil. In this sense, there is no proper and positive operation of a human being besides evil.

Now, after evil has been admitted, that active divine force given to the human certainly remains (by the power of the prior Divine establishment), but it is hindered, lulled to sleep, submerged in an evil state, and held back in injustice. Hence, it indeed produces physical acts; but if you look at their morality, they are weak and poorly composed. From this arises restlessness, terror, hell, and so on. In order to return to the former state and vigor, two things are required, from which a third follows—namely, the state of happiness itself.

### A P P E N D I X.

First, it is required that a person withdraw from their own false and fictitious sense of independence—the "right" by which they have tried to rule themselves as if they were independent of God in their positive actions. This is only achieved by fighting against bad habits. But by what means is this done? Through grace, God suggests new and real movements <note>In the philosophical language of the time, "movements" or "motions" refer to the internal stirrings of the heart or the will.</note> to which the human being joins that remaining active power they still possess. Or rather, God awakens and moves that power, impregnating it with new vigor. Thus, the person first conducts themselves purely passively, but then must also respond actively and cooperate with God, producing good works through that power received from God. Often, even when a person is not performing a positive action, they may still feel as if they are acting—specifically when they must endure the onslaught of bad habits so that they are not swept away by them, but instead let them pass by. This is like those who stand firm against the force of a wind or a river: they do not take a single step forward, yet because of their resistance, they feel as if they are doing a great deal.

Second, once the violence of these wicked impulses has been broken, the person must thereafter abstain from their own self-governance. Even though the "ego" has been cast down, it could easily return to its former state due to old habits and the lingering "folds" <note>original: "plicis"; a metaphor for deep-seated patterns or hidden recesses of the mind.</note> of the soul. In this stage, the human being is said to behave purely passively, and God Himself rules and acts through a singular and new grace, working more solid things in the innermost parts of the soul.

Finally, when the person is strengthened in these matters—so that they neither return to their old ways nor desire to escape from their dependence on the Divine—God heaps every blessing upon them. He restores and grants to the person a most powerful, effective, and fruitful force that lasts forever, through which the person may act, plan, and work securely and happily into eternity. I will not elaborate further on these points here.

It must be acknowledged that within the will—given by God with the power to act freely—there is something truly incomprehensible and infinite, exceeding the normal state of a creature. It can represent God Himself in a most singular and almost immediate way. In this sense, we are like "particles of the divine breath" <note>original: "particulae divinae aurae"; a classical reference to the soul's divine origin, often associated with the Stoics.</note> and bear His image in a most special manner. As Descartes <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), who argued in his *Meditations* that the human will is the faculty that most resembles God because of its unlimited nature.</note> excellently said, we are said to bear the Divine image most powerfully by reason of this freedom.

IX. What I said in Book III, chapter 21, concerning *God's Vindicative Justice* <note>original: "Justitia Dei Vindicativa"; this refers to the theological concept of justice that maintains the moral order, often through the "punishment" or "payment" for sin.</note> is clear enough in itself. However, it should be observed—especially regarding the occurrence of the greatest pains by which God's turning away from sin is witnessed—that we should not look so much at natural sensations as at the spiritual sorrow that exists in the mind of the Intercessor <note>Refers to Christ in his role as mediator between God and humanity.</note>. Nor should we look so much at the magnitude of this anguish in the physical senses, as at the ineffable greatness of the merit and dignity of the Person of the God-Man <note>original: "Θεανθρώπου" (Theanthropou); a Greek term for Christ, the "God-Man."</note>, and the love with which He grieved for the evil committed and ardently pressed on to obtain mercy, and that mercy...

<summary>This page explains the stages of human cooperation with divine grace: from resisting bad habits and remaining "passive" to receiving a renewed, permanent power to act in alignment with God. It concludes by linking human free will to the "image of God" as described by Descartes and begins a discussion on Christ's spiritual suffering as the basis for divine justice.</summary>
<keywords>free will, grace, cooperation with God, habits, Descartes, image of God, Vindicative Justice, Intercessor, God-Man, spiritual sorrow</keywords>

### A P P E N D I X.

...was moved to communicate [grace] through Him <note>original: "per ipsum"; referring to Christ, mentioned on the previous page</note>: For from these things it is certainly clear that sin is most hateful to God, since it had to be blotted out and forgiven through the intervention of such a great person <note>Christ</note>, who was so distressed on its account.

X. Regarding what I brought forward in the *conclusion* of this work about war, I would wish that no one think it comes from an affectation for some sect <note>The author likely refers to groups like the Quakers or Anabaptists, who were often criticized for their pacifism during this era of religious conflict.</note>, which considers itself commendable almost solely because of its contempt for war. But since I was exposed at that time to the devastations, lootings, robberies, and furies of armies in a small town, I could not help but be touched with horror by these mutual disasters of those who believe themselves to be true Christians and recognize each other as brothers in Christ, joined by a special bond of religion.

I cease to mention more, committing these and other matters to the judgment of any reader of sound mind, praying to God that He lead them to the true goal of both these things and all things, namely the one **Divine Love**, and not permit them to cling too much to means, especially those that are merely speculative <note>In this context, "speculative" refers to abstract theological or philosophical theorizing that lacks practical devotion or lived experience.</note>. It is better, like a child, to love much without much reasoning, than, like the Devil, to reason much without love. I say truly, Amen:

> *The things that were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Indeed, I count all things as loss because of the exceedingly excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them as dung, that I may gain Jesus Christ as my profit, and be found in Him.* (Phil. 3.) <note>A translation of Philippians 3:7-9 from the Latin Vulgate.</note>

### BOOK IV.
#### On Evil or Sin.

**CH. I.** §. 1—6. On those things which must be noted beforehand for the following sections. 253

**II.** §. 1. The most general notion of sin. 2–6. Those things which do not pertain to sin are more generally excluded from it: God, God's pleasure, God's work as it is from God; absolute nothingness, nothingness in existence, and nothingness mixed with reality, insofar as this is from God. 7. Not insofar as it is from man. 255

**III.** §. 1. 2. 3. 4. More specifically, what should be excluded from sin: (1) in the body. 5. (2) in the senses and passions. 6. 7. 8. (3) The material and formal aspects of the Mind—error, faculties, habits, acts, ignorance, knowledge, spontaneity—how do they relate to sin? It is not an explicit rejection of God. 9. A more specific designation of sin. 10. Reflection upon it is not required. 259

<column-break/>

**IV.** §. 1. Clearer notions concerning Liberty. 2. 3. 4. Concerning indifference <note>original: "indifferentia." In this context, it refers to the "liberty of indifference," or the will's power to choose between opposites without being determined by outside forces.</note>, and that it is granted. 5. It is multifaceted. 6–12. In a creature, it is not positive, but negative. This is demonstrated; proofs to the contrary are refuted. 13. Its two boundaries. 14. The most specific designation of sin. 265

**V.** §. 1. Notable difficulties from the seven preceding points. 2. 3. Should man perform anything positive of himself? 4. Does a negative state favor negligence? 5. 6. 7. Can the Mind remain in that state? How much perfection follows from it? 8. Does it provide the Mind an occasion for boasting? 8. 9. 10. Once sin is admitted, does indifference remain? What is the cause for the removal of sin? The three primary types of sin. 11. 12. Concerning God's foreknowledge and Governance <note>original: "Regimine." Refers to God's providential rule or management of the universe.</note> regarding sins. 13. Could God have removed indifference? And why did He not remove it? 272

**VI.** Properties of sin, or several of its designations, are explained. 1. That it is Unjust. 2. Negation of God. 3. Privation <note>The theological concept that evil is not a "thing" in itself, but the absence or lack of a good that ought to be present.</note>. 4. Adherence to oneself, appropriation, self-will, etc. 5. Pride. 6. How the sinner is to be regarded. 285

**VII.** §. 1. 2. 3. 4. A few points on the extension or repression of sin in actions and at its root. 5. 6. On the distinction between the sins of the righteous and the unrighteous. 7. On the certainty of one's own state. 8. Conclusion. 289
